title: Applied Regression Analysis
text: Preface

title: Applied Regression Analysis
text:
Description
This is a (bare-bones, first-draft) textbook on applied regression analysis. It’s a “Just the facts, ma’am”-style treatment of the material that focuses more on concepts and less on math.
The course as I teach it is built around this course description, which I did not write:

Topics include model interpretation, model building, and model assessment for linear regression with continuous outcomes, logistic regression with binary outcomes, and proportional hazards regression with survival time outcomes. Specific topics include regression diagnostics, confounding and effect modification, goodness of fit, data transformations, splines and additive models, ordinal, multinomial, and conditional logistic regression, generalized linear models, overdispersion, Poisson regression for rate outcomes, hazard functions, and missing data. The course will provide students with the skills necessary to perform regression analyses and to critically interpret statistical issues related to regression applications in the public health literature.

title: 1  Exponents
text:
1.1 Learning Objective
Manipulate exponents.

title: 1  Exponents
1  Exponents
text:
1.3 Problems

1.3.1 Problem 1
Simplify this expression: \(a^2 a^{-3} a^4 a^{-1} a\).






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
a^2 a^{-3} a^4 a^{-1} a &= a^{2 - 3 + 4 - 1 + 1} \\
&= a^3
\end{align*}
\]





1.3.2 Problem 2
Simplify this expression: \[
\frac{\exp\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1(x+1)\right)}{\exp\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1x\right)} \text{.}
\]






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
\frac{\exp\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1(x+1)\right)}{\exp\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1x\right)} &= \frac{\exp\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1x + \beta_1\right)}{\exp\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1x\right)} \\
&= \exp\left(\beta_0 - \beta_0 + \beta_1x - \beta_1 x + \beta_1\right) \\
&= \exp\left(\beta_1\right)
\end{align*}
\]

title: 2  Logarithms
text:
2.1 Learning Objective
Manipulate logarithms.

title: 2  Logarithms
2  Logarithms
text:
2.3 Problems

2.3.1 Problem 1
Solve for \(a\): \[
40 \log_{13} 13 = a \text{.}
\]






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
40 \log_{13} 13 &= a \\
\log_{13} 13^{40} &= a \\
13^{40} &= 13^a \\
40 &= a
\end{align*}
\]





2.3.2 Problem 2
Solve for \(a\): \[
a = \log_{42} 3.5 + 2 \log_{42} 2 + \log_{42} 3 \text{.}
\]






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
a &= \log_{42} 3.5 + 2 \log_{42} 2 + \log_{42} 3 \\
&= \log_{42} 3.5 + \log_{42} 2^2 + \log_{42} 3 \\
&= \log_{42} \left(3.5 \times 2^2 \times 3\right) \\
&= \log_{42} 42 \\
&= 1
\end{align*}
\]

title: 3  Intercept and Slope
text:
3.1 Learning Objective
Interpret the intercept and slope of a line.

title: 3  Intercept and Slope
text:
3.2 Lesson
We will talk about intercepts and slopes over and over again in this course. So, it’s important to start with a good foundation.
Consider the line \(y = 2x + 4\):









The intercept is 4. This means that when \(x = 0\), \(y = 4\):









The slope is 2. This means that for each one-unit increase in \(x\), \(y\) increases by two units.

title: 3  Intercept and Slope
text:
3.3 Problems

3.3.1 Problem 1
If \(x\) is the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit and \(y\) is the temperature in degrees Celsius, then \(y = \frac{5}{9}(x - 32)\).

3.3.1.1 Part (a)
When it’s 0 degrees Fahrenheit, what is the temperature in degrees Celsius?






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
y &= \frac{5}{9}(0 - 32) \\
&= -\frac{160}{9} \\
&\approx - 17.78
\end{align*}
\]





3.3.1.2 Part (b)
If the temperature increases ten degrees Fahrenheit, how much does it increase in degrees Celsius?






TipSolution





The slope of the line is \(\frac{5}{9}\), so with each one-degree Fahrenheit increase in temperature, there is a corresponding \(\frac{5}{9}\)-degree Celsius increase. This means that with a ten-degree Fahrenheit increase in temperature, there is a corresponding \(\frac{5}{9}\times 10 \approx 5.56\)-degree Celsius increase in temperature.






3.3.2 Problem 2
There are 2.54 centimeters in every inch. Write a function connecting \(y\), the length in inches, to \(x\), the length in centimeters.






TipSolution





The first time I answered this question, I wrote \(y = 2.54x\), but I knew that couldn’t be right because it would imply that we would always have more inches than centimeters. But one centimeter is less than one inch, so the same distance should require more centimeters than inches. So, it’s actually the case that \(2.54y = x\), or \[
\begin{align*}
2.54y &= x \\
y &= \frac{x}{2.54} \\
y &= 0.3937x \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]

title: 4  Integrals
text:
4.1 Learning Objective
Use and interpret the terms “integral” and “integrate”.

title: 4  Integrals
text:
4.2 Lesson
First, let me say that you do not need to know calculus in order to understand this material. All I want is for you to understand the concept. Essentially, the integral of a function is the area under it. In each of the following plots, the blue area represents the integral of the function from \(a\) to \(b\).

title: 4  Integrals
text:
4.3 Problems

4.3.1 Problem 1
For this problem, I do want you to compute an integral, but I promise that you can do it without any knowledge of calculus. Consider the function \(f(x) = x\), or \(y = x\), plotted below.









What is the integral of this function from 0 to 1?






TipSolution





The integral of the function is the area under the curve. This curve is a straight line. It intersects the \(y\)-axis at \(x = 0\). So, the integral from 0 to 1 will be the area of the triangle with base 1 and height 1. That’s \(1 \times 1 / 2 = \frac{1}{2}\).














4.3.2 Problem 2
Consider the function \(f(x) = 1\), or \(y = 1\), plotted below.









What is the integral of this function from 0 to 1?






TipSolution





This is a square. It has area 1.

title: 5  Derivatives
text:
5.1 Learning Objective
Use and interpret the terms “derivative” and “differentiate”.

title: 5  Derivatives
text:
5.2 Lesson
Again, you do not need to know calculus here; I just want you to understand the concept. The derivative of a function at a point is its slope at that point. To differentiate a function is to find its derivative.
The plot below shows the function \(f(x) = -x^2 + 4\). I’ve plotted the tangent lines, in red, at \(x = -2\), \(x = 0\), and \(x = 1\).









The derivative at \(x = -2\), represented by \(f'(-2)\), is 4. So, the tangent line is increasing. The derivative at \(x = 0\) is \(f'(0) = 0\), so the tangent line is flat, and the derivative at \(x = 1\) is \(f'(1) = -2\), so the tangent line is decreasing.
The plot below shows the function \(f(x) = \frac{x}{2} + \sin(x)\). I’ve plotted the tangent lines, in red, at \(x = 2\) and \(x = 4\).









The derivative at \(x = 2\), represented by \(f'(2)\), is around 0.08. So, the tangent line is increasing. The derivative at \(x = 4\) is \(f'(4) \approx -0.15\), so the tangent line is decreasing.

title: 5  Derivatives
text:
5.3 Problems

5.3.1 Problem 1
What is the derivative of the function \(f(x) = 2 - 3x\) at \(x = 0\)?






TipSolution





This is a line, so it has the same slope everywhere. That slope is \(-3\).





5.3.2 Problem 2
What is the sign (positive or negative) of the derivative of the function below at \(x = -2\)?















TipSolution





When \(x = -2\), the function is decreasing, so its slope is negative.

title: 6  Probability
text:
6.1 Learning Objective
Use the notation for probabilities and conditional probabilities.

title: 6  Probability
text:
6.2 Lesson

6.2.1 Probability
In this class, we will interpret probability as the long-run relative frequency of an event. For example, when we say that the probability of a coin landing heads is 0.5, we mean that if we were to flip the coin infinitely many times, half of the flips would land heads. Similarly, when we say that the probability of a die landing with the 1 face-up is one-sixth, we mean that if we were to roll the die infinitely many times, one-sixth of the rolls would land with the 1 face-up.
My guess is that this matches your intuition, so I won’t belabor the point. What’s more important is the notation. We use a capital \(P(\text{event})\) to indicate the probability of an event. So, \(P(\text{rain}) = 0.2\) means that there is a 20% chance of rain.


6.2.2 Conditional Probability
We are often concerned about the probability of an event given that some other event has occurred. For example, the overall probability of rain tomorrow might be 20%, but the probability of rain tomorrow might be higher if it rained today. We would represent the probability of rain tomorrow given that it rained today by \(P(\text{rain tomorrow}|\text{rain today})\). So, if \(P(\text{rain tomorrow}|\text{rain today}) = 0.4\) and \(P(\text{rain tomorrow}|\text{no rain today}) = 0.1\), then the probability of rain tomorrow given rain today is 40% and the probability of rain tomorrow given no rain today is 10%.

title: 6  Probability
text:
6.3 Problems

6.3.1 Problem 1
What is wrong with the expression \(P(3)\)?






TipSolution





\(P(3)\) is “the probability of 3”, which doesn’t make sense. 3 is a number, not an event.





6.3.2 Problem 2
The table below displays data for 100 people at bar. Most of the patrons are over 21, but a few people under 21 have managed to sneak in.




Alcoholic Beverage
Non-Alcoholic Beverage
Total




Over 21
45
45
90

9
1

6.3.2.1 Part (a)
What is \(P\left(\text{Over 21}\right)\)?






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
P\left(\text{Over 21}\right) &= \frac{90}{100} \\
&= 0.9
\end{align*}
\]





6.3.2.2 Part (b)
What is \(P\left(\text{Alcoholic Beverage}\middle|\text{Under 21}\right)\)?






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
P\left(\text{Alcoholic Beverage}\middle|\text{Under 21}\right) &= \frac{9}{10} \\
&= 0.9
\end{align*}
\]





6.3.2.3 Part (c)
What is \(P\left(\text{Under 21}\middle|\text{Alcoholic Beverage}\right)\)?






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
P\left(\text{Under 21}\middle|\text{Alcoholic Beverage}\right) &= \frac{9}{54} \\
&\approx 0.167
\end{align*}
\]

title: 7  Random Variable
text:
7.1 Learning Objective
Use and interpret the term “random variable”.

title: 7  Random Variable
text:
7.2 Lesson

7.2.1 Random vs. Fixed
If I write the number “1” on a golf ball, that’s an example of something that’s fixed. Five minutes later, I can be certain that the number on the golf ball will still be “1”. If I write the numbers “1” through “1,000” on 1,000 golf balls, put those golf balls in a large basket, shake up the basket so the golf balls mix, and then select a golf ball from the basket, that’s an example of something that’s random. Before pulling the golf ball, I can’t predict with perfect certainty which number I’ll see.
This might seem like a very obvious point, but in my experience teaching statistics, I’ve noticed two things:

It’s very easy to get confused about whether a quantity is random or fixed.
It’s very important to understand which quantities are random and which are fixed.

As we go, I’ll try to point out which quantities are random and which are fixed, especially when making a mistake would cause problems down the line.
Before moving on, let’s consider an example that is less contrived. Suppose you want to measure your resting heart rate in beats per minute. So, every morning for two weeks in a row, you measure your heart rate the moment you wake up in the morning. In this example, we might assume that your resting heart rate is some fixed value. In contrast, the number of beats per minute that you measure on any given day is random. On Monday, we can’t predict with perfect certainty what your heart rate will be the next morning; there will probably be some natural variation from day to day.


7.2.2 Random Variable
If I flip a coin, there are two possible outcomes: heads or tails. In practice, it’s often easier to work with numerical outcomes than words. So, we might assign the value 1 to heads and the value 0 to tails. Similarly, in survival analysis, we might assign a value of 1 to death and a value of 0 to survival.
We use the term “random variable” to refer to a real number that is the result of a random process. We usually denote random variables with capital letters. So, I might say that \[
Y = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{rain tomorrow} \\
0 & \text{no rain tomorrow.}
\end{cases}
\] Then, I could represent the probability of rain tomorrow as either \(P(\text{rain tomorrow})\) or \(P(Y = 1)\).

title: 7  Random Variable
text:
7.3 Problems

7.3.1 Problem 1
What is wrong with the statement \(X = \text{heads}\)?






TipSolution





Random variables must take on numeric values. Even if we’re flipping a coin, and the outcomes are “heads” and “tails”, we have to assign these outcomes numbers if we want to use random variables.





7.3.2 Problem 2
In the expression \(P(X = x)\), what is random and what is fixed?






TipSolution





\(X\) is random. Prior to collecting our data, we don’t know what value \(X\) will take. If we repeat the experiment, \(X\) may take on a different value.
In contrast, \(x\) is fixed. It’s some value, like 0 or 4.8. The expression represents the probability that the random variable \(X\) takes on the value \(x\).
For completeness, I guess you could say \(P\) is fixed. It’s a function, and non-random. Also, \(P(X = x)\) is fixed. It’s some value between 0 and 1, inclusive, and will not change if we collect new data.





7.3.3 Problem 3
True or false: The sample average, \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\), is a random variable.






TipSolution





True, assuming \(X_1,\dotsc,X_n\) are also proper random variables. The same average is a function of the data, and we don’t know what the data will be until we collect them. So, the data are random, and, as a result, the sample average is random.

title: 8  Distribution
text:
8.1 Learning Objective
Use and interpret the term “distribution”.

title: 8  Distribution
text:
8.2 Lesson

8.2.1 Two Meanings
In statistics, there are at least two meanings of the word “distribution”. The first refers to the data. If someone asks how the data are distributed, you might show them a histogram or boxplot. What they want to know is where the points fall on the number line. Here are a histogram and boxplot of the pH of 53 lakes in Florida:
















We can see that most of the lakes have a pH between 5 and 8, none has a pH below 3 or above 10, and the distribution is symmetric.
The second meaning of the word “distribution” has to do with where the data come from. I don’t mean who collected them or where they were collected; I mean the random process that generated the data. If we know the distribution in this sense, we know the exact probability of observing any number. It might help to consider some examples.


8.2.2 Examples

8.2.2.1 Bernoulli Distribution
The Bernoulli distribution is the simplest possible distribution. There are only two possible outcomes: 0 and 1. Suppose \(X\) is Bernoulli-distributed with \(P(X = 1) = 0.2\). Now we know the probability that \(X\) takes on any value. If \(P(X = 1) = 0.2\) and \(X\) can only be 0 or 1, then \(P(X = 0) = 1 - P(X = 1) = 1 - 0.2 = 0.8\). \[
\begin{align*}
P(X = 0) &= 1 - P(X = 1) \\
&= 1 - 0.2 \\
&= 0.8 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] If \(x \ne 0\) and \(x \ne 1\), then \(P(X = x) = 0\).
The Bernoulli distribution describes any random variable that can only take on two values. Suppose we follow 100 patients for one year and record whether each has a heart attack in that year. If a patient does have a heart attack, we record a value of 1; if they don’t, we record a value of 0. In this case, we have 100 random variables, and each follows the Bernoulli distribution.


8.2.2.2 Normal Distribution
The normal distribution is probably the one that gets talked about the most in introductory statistics courses. It has a classic bell shape:









The normal distribution always has this shape, although it may be moved to the left or right or squished together or spread apart. For example, here is the same normal distribution, but moved one unit to the right:









And here is the same normal distribution as in the first plot, but squished to the center:









The pH data from above kind of look like they might be normally distributed:









What I mean is that the empirical pH distribution (the first meaning of the word) appears to match an idealized normal distribution, so the data may have been generated from a normal distribution (the second meaning of the word).



8.2.3 Identically Distributed
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are identically distributed, it means they have the same distribution. This means that if \(P(X = 3) = 0.2\), then \(P(Y = 3) = 0.2\) as well. If \(P(X \le -4) = 0.8\), then \(P(Y \le -4) = 0.8\) as well. This comes up a lot in statistics, because we often assume that data are identically distributed.

title: 8  Distribution
text:
8.3 Problems

8.3.1 Problem 1
If I say, “The gene counts are not Poisson-distributed,” what does that mean?






TipSolution





This means that the gene counts differ from the Poisson distribution in some way. Perhaps the gene counts are more variable or spread out than the Poisson distribution. Perhaps there are more zeroes in the gene counts than you would expect from the Poisson distribution. It could mean a lot of things, but practically, it means we should probably not use the Poisson distribution to model the gene counts.





8.3.2 Problem 2
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are identically distributed and \(P(Y \le 10) = 0\), what is \(P(X > 10)\)?






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
P(X > 10) &= P(Y > 10) \\
&= 1 - P(Y \le 10) \\
&= 1 - 0 \\
&= 1
\end{align*}
\]

title: 9  Support
text:
9.1 Learning Objective
Define, use, and interpret the term “support”.

title: 9  Support
text:
9.2 Lesson
The support of a distribution is the possible values it can take.
For example, height cannot be negative. So, the support for the height of a randomly-selected person is positive real numbers. (We might want to restrict that even further and say the support is real numbers between 0 and 10 feet, since the tallest human ever was 8 feet 11.1 inches tall.)
Another example is the Apgar score. This is a score from 0 to 10 that is assigned to babies immediately after birth based on their breathing, heart rate, muscle tone, response to stimulation, and skin color. The support for this variable is the whole numbers from 0 to 10, no fractions or decimals allowed.

title: 9  Support
text:
9.3 Problems

9.3.1 Problem 1
If I say, “The gamma distribution and the normal distribution don’t have the same support,” what does that mean?






TipSolution





It means that these two distributions differ in the possible values they can take. Although you don’t need to know this now, a random variable following the gamma distribution cannot be negative, whereas a random variable following the normal distribution can be negative.





9.3.2 Problem 2
Do the normal distribution and the Bernoulli distribution have the same support?






TipSolution





No. The support of the normal distribution is the entire real line. The support of the Bernoulli distribution is just 0 and 1.

title: 10  Continuous and Discrete Random Variables
text:
10.1 Learning Objective
Define, use, and interpret the terms “continuous random variable” and “discrete random variable”.
crumbs: 10  Continuous and Discrete Random Variables

title: 10  Continuous and Discrete Random Variables
text:
10.2 Lesson
A continuous random variable is a random variable whose support is an interval. For example, the a normally distributed random variable is continuous because it can take on any value between \(-\infty\) and \(+\infty\). An exponential random variable is continuous because it can take on any value between 0 and \(+\infty\). A continuous uniform random variable is continuous because it can take on any value between two points, \(a\) and \(b\).
In contrast, a discrete random variable is a random variable whose support is separated values. For example, a Bernoulli random variable is discrete because it can only take on two values, 0 and 1. A binomial random variable is discrete because it can be any whole number between 0 and \(n\). A Poisson random variable is discrete because it can be any whole number between 0 and \(+\infty\).
Why does this matter? We often use a certain distribution to represent, or model, our outcome. It’s important to be able to evaluate the appropriateness of that distribution as a model for our outcome. If the distribution is continuous but the outcome can only take on discrete values, the distribution may not be appropriate.
crumbs: 10  Continuous and Discrete Random Variables

title: 10  Continuous and Discrete Random Variables
text:
10.3 Problems

10.3.1 Problem 1
When thought of as a random variable, is height continuous or discrete?






TipSolution





Height is continuous, because it can be any value between 0 and 10 feet or so. People are not required to be a whole number of inches tall.
Of course, you could argue that when measuring height, people only use the gradations that are marked on the measuring tool, leading to a finite number of possible heights. That’s a fair argument for why height could be thought of as discrete. However, tools for measuring height often have markings that are fine enough for height to be modeled by a continuous random variable.





10.3.2 Problem 2
When thought of as a random variable, is the number of new cases of measles in Massachusetts in 2025 continuous or discrete?






TipSolution





This has to be a whole number, so it’s discrete.
crumbs: 10  Continuous and Discrete Random Variables

title: 11  Probability Mass Function
text:
11.1 Learning Objective
Explain what a probability mass function (PMF) is.

title: 11  Probability Mass Function
text:
11.2 Lesson

11.2.1 Overview
Every discrete random variable has a probability mass function (PMF), which is a function telling you the probability it will take on each value in its support. Suppose \(X\) is a discrete random variable. I would generally write the probability mass function as \(P(X = x)\), where \(x\) is some value in the support of \(X\). If \(x\) is not in the support of \(X\), then \(P(X = x) = 0\).
We call this a probability mass function because we use “mass” to refer to a positive probability. The PMF tells you how much mass to place on each number. You can think of a dump truck depositing piles of dirt on different values along the number line.


11.2.2 Bernoulli Example
If \(X\) is Bernoulli distributed then \(P(X = 1) = p\) and \(P(X = 0) = 1 - p\). We can write this concisely as \(P(X = x) = p^x (1-p)^{1-x}\).


11.2.3 Poisson Example
The Poisson PMF is \[
P(X = x) = e^{-\mu} \frac{\mu^x}{x!} \text{,}
\] where \(\mu\) is the expected value (which must be positive) and \(x\) is any non-negative whole number (0, 1, 2, 3, etc.).
Here are plots of the Poisson PMF for various values of \(\mu\):

title: 11  Probability Mass Function
text:
11.3 Problems

11.3.1 Problem 1
True or false: Continuous random variables have probability mass functions.






TipSolution





False. Only discrete random variables have probability mass functions.

title: 12  Probability Density Function
text:
12.1 Learning Objective
Explain what a probability density function is.

title: 12  Probability Density Function
text:
12.2 Lesson

12.2.1 Overview
Continuous random variables do not have probability mass functions. In fact, for any continuous random variable \(X\) and any real number \(x\), \(P(X = x) = 0\). This is because, if \(X\) is a continuous random variable, it can take on any value in an interval. So, if \(P(X = x) > 0\) for the values in that interval, then the probability that \(X\) equals anything will exceed 1, which is impossible. I will return to this idea later, so if it doesn’t make sense now, hold tight.
If \(X\) is continuous, it has a probability density function (PDF). I will usually use \(f(x)\) to denote the PDF of a continuous random variable \(X\). In order to compute probabilities for continuous random variables, we integrate under the PDF. So, for example, \[
P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \text{.}
\]
This is why \(P(X = x) = 0\) for continuous random variables. If you integrate under a single point, you get zero: \[
P(X = x) = \int_x^x f(u)\,du = 0 \text{.}
\] An integral is the area under a curve. If the area is zero, the integral is zero.
“Density” here means mass per unit length (or mass per unit distance). So in order to get a probability mass (i.e., a positive probability), we have to integrate over a positive length.
This might seem too mathematical to be relevant, but it will come up again when we encounter hazard rates.


12.2.2 Normal Example
A normal distribution with expected value \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\) has PDF \[
f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{\left(x-\mu\right)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \text{,}
\] where \(\mu\) can be any real number, \(\sigma^2 > 0\), and \(x\) can be any real number.

title: 12  Probability Density Function
text:
12.3 Problems

12.3.1 Problem 1
Suppose \(Y\) is a continuous random variable with \(f(y) = \lambda \exp(-\lambda y)\), where \(\lambda > 0\) and \(y > 0\). What is $P(Y = 4)?






TipSolution





Zero. It’s a continuous random variable, so the probability it equals any single number is 0.

title: 13  Graphical Representations of Probability
text:
13.1 Learning Objective
Create, use, and interpret graphical representations of probability.

title: 13  Graphical Representations of Probability
text:
13.2 Lesson
In statistics, we often want to represent probability visually. This is especially common when talking about distributions. In previous statistics courses, you probably used graphical representations of probability when talking about p-values.
The shortest summary is that we tend to use surface area, especially area under the curve, to represent probability. (This is consistent with the principle of proportional ink.) Let’s consider the normal distribution to demonstrate this idea, since many people are familiar with the normal distribution.
Here is a plot of the standard normal distribution, which has mean 0 and variance 1.









The area under the entire curve is 1, since the probability of a standard normal random variable taking on any value is 1.









The area under the curve for \(x \le 0\) is 0.5, since the probability of a standard normal random variable being less than or equal to 0 is 0.5.









The area under the curve for \(x \ge 1.96\) or \(x \le -1.96\) is 0.05, since the probability of a standard normal random variable being greater than or equal to 1.96 or less than or equal to -1.96 is 0.05.









What this implies is that values near 0 are more likely than values far from 0, because integrating under \(f(x)\) near 0 produces a larger area than integrating under \(f(x)\) far from 0.
The normal distribution is a continuous distribution, but the principle is the same for discrete distributions. Let’s consider the Bernoulli distribution. In the plot below, I’ve drawn a Bernoulli distribution where \(P(X = 1) = 0.75\).









The area of the bar over \(x = 1\) is equal to 0.75, because \(P(X = 1) = 0.75\).









The area of the bar over \(x = 0\) is equal to 0.25, because \(P(X = 0) = 0.25\).









Why does any of this matter? We often use probability distributions to represent real-world quantities. It’s important to be able to evaluate whether a distribution is an accurate representation of a real-world quantity. For example, suppose I said that I wanted to use this distribution to represent \(T\), the time from birth to death for a randomly-selected American.









Does that make sense? No! It would mean that the chance of death is highest around age 18 and lowest around age 0 and after age 40. That’s not an accurate representation of the real world.
At this point, I should point out an exception to the rule stated above. Although we often use area under the curve to represent probability, there is one domain in which we commonly use the height of the curve to represent probability. That domain is survival analysis. When the outcome is time to an event (e.g., heart attack, death, progression), we often plot the probability of surviving past a certain time. It looks something like this:









Sometimes we use \(S(t)\) instead of \(P(T > t)\), but the meaning is the same. In this situation, the height of the curve is a probability, not the area under the curve. This is why it’s always very important to read the axis labels on a plot, and to include axis labels when creating a plot.

title: 13  Graphical Representations of Probability
text:
13.3 Problems

13.3.1 Problem 1
Would it make sense to use this distribution to represent time from birth until death? Why or why not?















TipSolution





It would not make sense to use this distribution to represent time from birth until death. Time from birth until death is positive, but this distribution places positive probability over negative numbers.





13.3.2 Problem 2
Would it make sense to use this distribution to represent death at 1 year post chemotherapy for breast cancer? Why or why not?















TipSolution





It would not make sense. Death at 1 year post chemotherapy for breast cancer can only take on two values, death or no death, whereas with this distribution, any number is possible.

title: 14  Expected Value
text:
14.1 Learning Objective
Define, use, and interpret the term “expected value” in the context of random variables.

title: 14  Expected Value
text:
14.2 Lesson

14.2.1 Notation
We use \(E(X)\) to represent the expected value of \(X\). You might see “expectation” instead of “expected value”.


14.2.2 Visual Representation
The expected value of a random variable is where you would have to place a fulcrum to get it to balance. Let’s look at a few examples.
This is a standard normal distribution. It’s expected value is 0.









This is a uniform distribution from 0 to 1. It’s expected value is 0.5.









This is an exponential distribution with expected value equal to 1.









This is a Bernoulli distribution with \(P(X = 1) = 0.75\). It’s expected value is 0.75.









This example shows that the expected value of a random variable doesn’t need to be in its support. \(E(X)\) can be a value that \(X\) can’t take.


14.2.3 Verbal Description
The expected value is a weighted average. Each possible value of \(X\) is weighted by its probability (or density–a technical term that you don’t have to memorize, but that I can’t, in good conscience, not use), and then these weighted values are summed.
Consider this image.









I’m going to take each value and weight it by it’s relative frequency.



Value
Relative Frequency
Product




-5
3/12
-15/12


-3
1/12
-3/12


-1
2/12
-2/12


2
5/12
10/12


3
1/12
3/12



The sum of the weighted values is

sum(c(-15 / 12,
      -3 / 12,
      -2 / 12,
      10 / 12,
      3 / 12))

[1] -0.5833333


This is the expected value of this distribution.


14.2.4 Math
For a continuous random variable, the expected value is \[
E(X) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x f(x)\,dx \text{.}
\] For a discrete random variable, the expected value is \[
E(X) = \sum_x x P(X = x) \text{.}
\]


14.2.5 Example
Let’s consider the simplest (non-degenerate) distribution possible, the Bernoulli distribution. Suppose \(P(X = 1) = p\) and \(P(X = 0) = 1 - p\), with \(0 < p < 1\). What is \(E(X)\)? \[
\begin{align*}
E(X) &= \sum_x x P(X = x) \\
&= 0 P(X = 0) + 1 P(X = 1) \\
&= P(X = 1) \\
&= p
\end{align*}
\] It may be counterintuitive that a probability could be an expected value, but it’s true. If \(X\) can only be 0 or 1, then \(E(X) = P(X = 1)\).

title: 14  Expected Value
text:
14.3 Problems

14.3.1 Problem 1
True or false: The expected value is the most commonly occurring value in a data set. That’s why it’s the “expected” value; it’s the one you most expect to see.






TipSolution





False. We reserve “expected value” for random variables, not for data sets. The most commonly occurring value in a data set is the mode of that data set. The expected value may not even be a value that the random variable can take.





14.3.2 Problem 2
True or false: \(P(X > E(X))\) is always 0.5.






TipSolution





False. This is only true when \(E(X)\) is the median of the distribution, which is not always the case.





14.3.3 Problem 3
Suppose \(Y\) is the (eventual) age at death for a (living) human being selected uniformly at random from the earth in 2021.

14.3.3.1 Part (a)
A colleague wants to estimate \(P(Y = y)\) for various values of \(y\). He finds this graph: Probability of dying, by age, World, 2021. Explain to your colleague why that graph is or is not an estimate of \(P(Y = y)\).






TipSolution





This graph is not an estimate of \(P(Y = y)\), for at least the following reasons:

The area under the curve of a distribution needs to integrate or sum to 1. This is the graphical analogue to the fact that \(P(Y = \text{anything}) = 1\). In this graph, the bars sum to a value greater than 1. If you just add up the top six bars, moving from the top of the page down, you get 1.02, which is greater than 1.
The subtitle of the graph is, “The annual probability of death among people in a given age group, expressed as a fraction.” So, each bar represents the probability of death for someone selected from a given age group; for \(Y\), we are sampling someone from the earth at large, so they could be from any age group.






14.3.3.2 Part (b)
Another colleague wants to estimate \(E(Y)\) She finds this graph: Life expectancy at birth, total (years). Explain to your colleague why that graph can or cannot provide an estimate of \(E(Y)\).






TipSolution





This graph cannot be used to estimate \(E(Y)\). The title of the graph is “Life expectancy at birth”, so the population is restricted to newborns. \(Y\) is the life expectancy for someone selected uniformly at random, so the population includes anyone of any age. \(E(Y)\) should be higher than the life expectancy for 2021 in this graph; someone who has already lived to age 10 is going to have a higher life expectancy than someone who hasn’t yet reached age 1.





14.3.3.3 Part (c)
What is the support of \(Y\)? Justify your answer.






TipSolution





I would say that the support of \(Y\) is the interval \((0,\infty)\). You could select someone of any age, no matter how close to birth, which is why my interval goes all the way down to zero. I didn’t include zero because no one can be alive and dead at the same time. My interval goes all the way up to infinity because, even though no one has lived past 122 (Guinness), we don’t know if someone born in 2021 will live longer.
By the way, here is an explanation of the notation I used above.

\((a,b)\) is the line segment containing all points between \(a\) and \(b\), but not \(a\) and \(b\) themselves.
\([a,b]\) is the line segment containing all points between \(a\) and \(b\), and also \(a\) and \(b\) themselves.
\(\{a,b\}\) is the set containing only the points \(a\) and \(b\).

It’s not important that you learn to use this notation for this class. You can use words instead of symbols to communicate the support of a random variable.

title: 15  Independence
text:
15.1 Learning Objective
Define, use, and interpret the term “independent”.

title: 15  Independence
text:
15.2 Lesson
Two events are independent if the occurrence of one has no effect on the probability of the occurrence of another. In symbols, \(A\) and \(B\) are independent if \(P(A|B) = P(A)\).
An example of independent events is me choosing to wear a red shirt to work and someone in Mozambique choosing to wear a red shirt to work. I don’t know anyone in Mozambique, and I don’t coordinate my outfit with anyone, so one event has no influence on the other. An example of non-independent events is me choosing to take the bus to work and it raining in Boston. I am far more likely to take the bus to work if it’s raining than if it’s clear. So, if you know the weather in Boston, you can do a better job predicting whether I will take the bus or walk.
Two random variables are independent if knowing the value of one doesn’t change the distribution of the other. For discrete random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), we might write independence as \(P(X = x|Y = y) = P(X = x)\). For continuous random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), we might write independence as \(f(x|y) = f(x)\).
An example of independent random variables is the speed of the northbound Vermonter Amtrak train between Northampton and Greenfield on September 5, 2027, and the speed of an ant crawling on a leaf in Topeka, Kansas, on the same day. These things have nothing to do with each other. Knowing one will not help you predict the other. An example of non-independent random variables is the outdoor temperature in Burlington, Vermont, and the rate at which a maple creemee will melt. (“Creemee” is the Vermont word for soft serve ice cream. Not frozen yogurt, just soft serve ice cream.) The hotter it is outside, the faster creemees melt.
Why do we care about this? It’s often (in fact, almost always) a requirement that we assume independence at some point in a statistical analysis. So, we have to know when our observational units are and are not independent.

title: 15  Independence
text:
15.3 Problems

15.3.1 Problem 1
Suppose \(X\) is my LDL cholesterol level and \(Y\) is my dad’s LDL cholesterol level. Are \(X\) and \(Y\) independent?






TipSolution





No, these two variables are related. The higher my dad’s LDL cholesterol, the higher mine is likely to be.





15.3.2 Problem 2
Suppose \(X\) is my LDL cholesterol level and \(Y\) is the LDL cholesterol level of a randomly-selected person in Ohio. Are \(X\) and \(Y\) independent?






TipSolution





Yes. These two values are not related to each other.

title: 16  Population and Sample
text: 16.1 Learning Objectives

title: 16  Population and Sample
text:
Compare and contrast “population” and “sample”.
Identify the population for an analysis.

title: 16  Population and Sample
text:
16.2 Lesson

16.2.1 Practical Definitions
Very generally, the goal of statistics is to use a sample to make inferences about a population. The population is broad group that you want to know something about. It’s generally impossible to investigate every member of a population, so instead we draw some members of the population and investigate them. This smaller group is called a sample.
Suppose I want to know the relationship between frequency of indoor cooking and lung capacity. Before collecting any data, I should decide what my population is. Am I concerned about the lung capacity of humans or pets? If I’m concerned about humans, are there any age restrictions? Am I only concerned about people who cook with gas, coal, or wood, but not electric stoves? Do I only want to know about this relationship in people with lung problems like asthma?
Once I’ve decided what my population is, I need to recruit participants from that population. How I do that recruitment affects what statistical analysis I can do; for now, we’ll assume that I can recruit participants in such a way that they are independent from each other and, together, they are representative of the population. This group of participants is now my sample.


16.2.2 Unobserved vs. Observed
We often think of the population as being a sort of “Platonic ideal”. It’s not something we observe directly. It’s almost a theoretical concept. The sample is something we can observe. We collect data and analyze them.

title: 16  Population and Sample
text:
16.3 Problems

16.3.1 Problem 1
Suppose I want to conduct a political opinion poll, so I go to Jamaica Pond at 6am on a Tuesday and ask people questions. I analyze the data, write up my results, and submit a manuscript titled “80% of Americans support Candidate X”. What’s wrong with my claim?






TipSolution





The claim is about “Americans”, but my sample is not representative of all Americans. People at Jamaica Pond at 6am on a weekday probably don’t work three jobs, they probably value green space and exercise, and they can afford to live near Jamaica Pond. The population in the claim doesn’t match the population from which the participants were sampled.





16.3.2 Problem 2
Is the expected value a function of the population or the sample?






TipSolution





The expected value is a function of the population. The expected value is fixed, i.e., non-random. The sample is random. If you drew a second sample, it would look different.

title: 17  Sample Average
text:
17.1 Learning Objective
Define and compute a sample average.

title: 17  Sample Average
text:
17.2 Lesson
The sample average is probably what you’ve been taught an average is. It’s what you get when you add up all your values and then divide by the number of values you have. We usually use \(\bar{X}\), read “X bar”, to denote the sample average. We can write the formula like so: \[
\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \text{.}
\]
The sample average is itself a random variable. Even if you’re sampling from the same population, every time you draw a new sample, you will probably get a different sample average. This is in contrast to the expected value, which is always the same for the same population.

title: 17  Sample Average
text:
17.3 Problems

17.3.1 Problem 1
What is the average of these numbers: 3, 2, 4, 6, and 5?






TipSolution





\[
\frac{3 + 2 + 4 + 6 + 5}{5} = \frac{20}{5} = 4
\]





17.3.2 Problem 2
Suppose \(n\) people use the restroom in the lobby of a hospital. Let \(X_i = 1\) if the \(i\)th person washed their hands afterward and let \(X_i = 0\) if they didn’t. Let \(\hat{p}\) denote the proportion of people who washed their hands. What’s the relationship between \(\hat{p}\) and \(\bar{X}\)?






TipSolution





They are the same. Note that \(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is a count of the number of people who washed their hands. When we divide that by the number of people who used the restroom in total, we get the proportion of people who washed their hands. We also get the sample average of the \(X_i\)’s.

title: 18  Parameter and Statistic
text: 18.1 Learning Objectives

title: 18  Parameter and Statistic
text:
Compare and contrast the terms “parameter” and “statistic”.
Determine whether a quantity is a parameter or statistic.

title: 18  Parameter and Statistic
text:
18.2 Lesson
A parameter is a function of a population. For example, the expected value is a parameter. A statistic is a function of a sample. For example, the sample average is a statistic.
Unfortunately, it is often the case that the same word could be a parameter or statistic depending on context. Consider the median. Every population distribution has a median. For a continuous random variable, the area under the curve to the right of the median is 0.5. (The definition of the median for a discrete random variable is more complicated, so I’m just going to avoid it for now.)
Every sample has a median, too. To get the sample median, you line up all the values in the sample from smallest to largest. If there are \(n\) observations, and \(n\) is odd, the median is the \(\frac{n+1}{2}\)th value in the list. For example, in the data set \(\{0,3,4,5,15\}\), the median is 4. If there are \(n\) observations, and \(n\) is even, the median is the average of the \(\frac{n}{2}\)th and \(\left(\frac{n}{2}+1\right)\)th values in the list. For example, in the data set \(\{0,3,4,5,15,24\}\), the median is \[
\frac{4 + 5}{2} = 4.5 \text{.}
\]

title: 18  Parameter and Statistic
text:
18.3 Problems

18.3.1 Problem 1
Is the maximum value in my sample a parameter or a statistic?






TipSolution





It’s a statistic, because it’s something you computed from your data.





18.3.2 Problem 2
In clinical trials, we often want to know the expected difference in some outcome (e.g., blood pressure, risk of death) between people who take a drug and people who don’t Is this a parameter or a statistic?






TipSolution





This is a parameter. If we randomly assign some people to receive a drug and some people to receive a placebo, and then compute the difference between the averages of the outcome across the groups, that would be a statistic.





18.3.3 Problem 3
Suppose \(X_1,\dotsc,X_n\) are iid random variables. Suppose also that \(Var(X_1) > 0\).

18.3.3.1 Part (a)
Is \(X_1 = X_2\)?






TipSolution





It’s impossible to know ahead of time. These are random variables, so they could have the same value, or they could have different values. We won’t know until we collect our data. Also, if \(X_1\) is a continuous random variable, then \(P(X_1 = X_2) = 0\).





18.3.3.2 Part (b)
Is \(E(X_1) = E(X_2)\)?






TipSolution





Yes. Because these random variables have the same distributions, they must have the same expected values. The expected value is a parameter of the distribution; it is fixed.





18.3.3.3 Part (c)
Is \(E(X_1) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\)?






TipSolution





It’s impossible to know beforehand. This could happen by chance, but if \(X_1\) is a continuous random variable, it has probability zero of occurring.





18.3.3.4 Part (d)
Is \(E(X_1)\) a parameter, a statistic, both, or neither?






TipSolution





Parameter.





18.3.3.5 Part (e)
Is \(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) a parameter, a statistic, both, or neither?






TipSolution





Statistic.






18.3.4 Problem 4
You are the statistical consultant for doctoral students in another department. One of these students interviewed 33 teenage girls for her dissertation. She had recruited them from Boston Latin School, near HSPH. Of these 33 teenage girls, 22 said they had been bullied. The doctoral student includes this line in her dissertation: “Sixty-seven percent of teenage girls have experienced bullying.” What feedback/advice would you give her about this line?






TipSolution





Sixty-seven percent of the girls in the sample have experienced bullying, but that doesn’t necessarily imply that sixty-seven percent of all teenage girls have experienced bullying. Sixty-seven percent is a statistic computed from the sample, not the parameter for the population. Also, the sample may not be representative of the whole population. Boston Latin School requires applicants to take an exam in order to qualify for admission, so its students are very high-achieving. Finally, 33 observations is a pretty small sample size. In order to make more reliable claims about the population of teenage girls, we should probably collect more data.

title: 19  Tilde
text:
19.1 Learning Objective
Use and interpret the “~” symbol in the context of random variables.

title: 19  Tilde
text:
19.2 Lesson
When we’re talking about random variables, the “~” symbol can be read as “is distributed as”. For example, \(X\sim N(0,1)\) means that \(X\) is a normal random variable with expected value (mean) 0 and variance 1. The mean and variance are the parameters of the normal distribution.
Similarly, \(X\sim\text{Poisson}(\mu)\) means that \(X\) is a Poisson random variable with mean \(\mu\). The mean is the only parameter of the Poisson distribution.

title: 19  Tilde
text:
19.3 Problems

19.3.1 Problem 1
How do you interpret \(X\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p)\)?






TipSolution





\(X\) is a Bernoulli random variable with parameter \(p\). You may not have learned this yet, but \(p = P(X = 1)\). The important thing is just to recognize what \(\sim\) means and to recognize that \(p\) is a parameter.

title: 20  Estimator and Estimand
text:
20.1 Learning Objective
Define, use, and interpret the terms “estimator” and “estimand”.

title: 20  Estimator and Estimand
text:
20.2 Lesson

20.2.1 Definitions
In statistics, there are usually things that we don’t know but want to find out. Things things are often quantities that we want to estimate, like the prevalence of cystic fibrosis in the US, or the mean duration of flu symptoms in winter 2026-2027. If we are trying to estimate something, it is an estimand.
Usually, we cannot observe the estimand directly. We cannot observe every single person who is infected with influenza in the winter of 2026-2027. So, we collect data (we take a sample), apply some function to the data, and get an estimate of our estimand. If we were to take a different sample and apply the same function, we would get a different estimate. Although the function doesn’t change, the sample is random, so the data change, and then the estimate changes as a result.
We use the term “estimator” to refer to the outcome of this function we’re using to estimate the estimand. The estimator is a random variable because it changes with each new sample.
There’s something very tricky about defining the estimator. Once we collect a sample and feed our data into our function, we get an estimate. That’s not random. The function itself is not random, because it’s the same no matter what data we have. So perhaps the way to think about the estimator is that it’s the output from the function before you’ve observed any data. You don’t know what value you’ll get, so it’s random.

title: 20  Estimator and Estimand
text:
20.3 Observed vs. Unobserved
The heart of statistics is making inferences about unobserved quantities based on observed data. Here’s an example: Suppose we are conducting a randomized clinical trial of a new treatment for cancer. We recruit 200 people with the cancer of interest and randomly assign half to the drug; the other half gets a placebo. For all participants, we measure the time until death. We want to measure the effect of the drug, i.e., how much longer, on average, people live on the drug versus on placebo. This difference is unobserved and fixed. What we observe are the individual survival times of the participants in the study.
In this class, it’s very common that we will make inferences about fixed, unobserved quantities based on random, observed quantities. If you take a course in longitudinal data analysis or Bayesian statistics, you will spend a lot of time working with random, unobserved quantities.

20.3.1 Notation
It’s very common in statistics to use Greek letters to represent parameters and estimands. For example, we usually use the Greek letter \(\mu\) (“mu”) to represent the expected value of a distribution, and \(\sigma^2\) (“sigma-squared”) to represent the variance.
It’s also very common to add a hat to an estimand to indicate the estimator. So, \(\hat{\mu}\) is an estimator of \(\mu\) and \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) is an estimator of \(\hat{\sigma}^2\).

title: 20  Estimator and Estimand
text:
20.4 Problems

20.4.1 Problem 1
Suppose \(\lambda\) is the number of late departures per day from Boston Logan International Airport. I select 10 days uniformly at random from 2027 and divide the number of late departures on those days by the total number of departures on those days. I call this \(\hat{\lambda}\). What’s the estimand and what’s the estimator?






TipSolution





\(\lambda\) is the estimand and \(\hat{\lambda}\) is the estimator.





20.4.2 Problem 2
Which is a function of the population, the estimand or the estimator?






TipSolution





The estimand is a function of the population. The estimator is a function of the sample.

title: 21  Variance
text: 21.1 Learning Objectives

title: 21  Variance
text:
Explain the underlying concept of variance and standard deviation.
State the units of variance and standard deviation.
Interpret the terms “variance”, “standard deviation”, and “standard error”.

title: 21  Variance
21  Variance
text:
21.3 Problems

21.3.1 Problem 1
Which of the following distributions has higher variance, the one with a dashed line or the one with a solid line?















TipSolution





The distribution with a dashed line has higher variance. You can tell because it’s more spread out.





21.3.2 Problem 2
If I say that \(X\) is more variable or dispersed than \(Y\), what does that imply about \(Var(X)\) and \(Var(Y)\)?






TipSolution





\(Var(X) > Var(Y)\)

title: 22  Bias
text:
22.1 Learning Objective
Define, use, and interpret the term “bias”.

title: 22  Bias
text:
22.2 Lesson
Suppose \(\theta\) is an estimand and \(\hat{\theta}\) is an estimator of \(\theta\). We define bias as \[
\text{bias}\left(\hat{\theta}\right) = E\left(\hat{\theta}\right) - \theta \text{.}
\] Bias is how far off your estimator is from the estimand, on average.
It is perfectly equivalent to say \[
\text{bias}\left(\hat{\theta}\right) = E\left(\hat{\theta}  - \theta\right) \text{.}
\] Writing it this way, you can say that bias is the average error.
If bias is positive, your estimator is, on average, too high. If bias is negative, your estimator is, on average, too low. If bias is zero, your estimator is, on average, just right.
In the real world, statistical bias appears when your estimator is consistently off by a certain amount. For example, imagine the scale at your doctor’s office always says people are one pound heavier than they are. That would be analogous to positive bias. (Strictly, this is not bias, and is more of a measurement error issue. I’m using it because I think it conveys the big idea of bias.)
You may have noticed that we define population variance as \[
Var(X) = E\left(\left(X - E(X)\right)^2\right)
\] and measure it with \[
\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(X_i - \bar{X}\right)^2 \text{.}
\] Bias is the reason for using \(n - 1\) in the denominator of \(\hat{\sigma}^2\) rather than \(n\). If we used \(n\), the estimator would be biased; it would be just a little too low, on average. When we use \(n - 1\), the estimator is unbiased, meaning its bias is zero.

title: 22  Bias
text:
22.3 Problems

22.3.1 Problem 1
Suppose I’m trying to estimate the prevalence of the BRCA1 gene in America. My estimator has a bias of two percentage points. What does that mean?






TipSolution





If the estimator has a bias of two percentage points, it overestimates the prevalence by two percentage points, on average.





22.3.2 Problem 2
Suppose I’m trying to estimate the change in respiratory mortality associated with a \(10 \mu g / m^3\) increase in PM10 (particulate matter that are ten micrometers or less across). My estimator is unbiased. What does that mean?






TipSolution





Your estimator, on average, accurately estimates the change.

title: 23  Accuracy and Precision
text:
23.1 Learning Objective
Explain accuracy and precision in statistics.

title: 23  Accuracy and Precision
text:
23.2 Lesson
When discussing accuracy and precision, I’m legally obligated to show you the following figures.






























Accuracy is a concept that is measured by bias; it’s about how far away from the target you are, on average. Precision is a concept that is measured by variance; it’s about how widely dispersed your shots are.
Ideally, we would like to be both accurate (low bias) and precise (low variance). Sometimes, however, we can only increase one by decreasing the other. This is called the bias-variance tradeoff.

title: 23  Accuracy and Precision
text:
23.3 Problems

23.3.1 Problem 1
If I say an estimator is biased, what does that imply about its variance?






TipSolution





Nothing. You can’t infer anything about an estimator’s variance from its bias.





23.3.2 Problem 2
Suppose I want to estimate the ratio of wingspan to height among HSPH graduate students. Propose an estimator that has zero variance (perfect precision).






TipSolution





You can pick a number, like 1. This won’t ever change, no matter how many samples you collect, so its variance will be zero. Of course, we don’t know what its bias will be.

title: 24  Hypothesis Test
text: 24.1 Learning Objectives

title: 24  Hypothesis Test
text:
State the steps of a hypothesis test.
Propose null and alternative hypotheses for a real research question.
Interpret a p-value.

title: 24  Hypothesis Test
text:
24.2 Lesson

24.2.1 Steps
Hypothesis testing is a method for making claims about an unobserved population based on an observed sample. It consists of the following steps:

State the null and alternative hypotheses.
Compute a test statistic.
Compute the p-value.
State the conclusion.



24.2.2 Null and Alternative Hypotheses
The null and alternative hypotheses are statements about the population. We often denote the null hypothesis with \(H_0\) and the alternative hypothesis with \(H_1\) or \(H_A\). So, for example, if we are comparing two groups, we might use \(H_0 : \mu_1 = \mu_2\) to indicate that the null hypothesis is that the mean of group 1 is equal to the mean of group 2. Then we might use \(H_1 : \mu_1 \ne \mu_2\) to indicate that the alternative hypothesis is that the mean of group 1 is not equal to the mean of group 2.
The null hypothesis is always the uninteresting thing, for example, there is no difference between two groups, there is no change in the outcome associated with a change in the predictor, there is no correlation between two variables, etc. The alternative hypothesis is usually the complement of the null hypothesis, e.g. there is a difference between two groups, there is a change in the outcome associated with a change in the predictor, there is a correlation between two variables, etc.
The null and alternative hypotheses are not statements about statistics. It’s not correct to write something like \(H_0 : \bar{X} = 0\). This is because our goal is to make claims about the population, not a specific sample.


24.2.3 Test Statistic
Since we cannot observe the population directly, we draw a sample and then compute a test statistic. The test statistic has a known distribution “under the null”. This means that if the null hypothesis is true, we know the distribution of the test statistic.


24.2.4 P-Value
The p-value is the probability of the test statistic being at least as extreme as was observed, if the null is true. Since we know the distribution of the test statistic under the null, we can compute the probability of different scenarios assuming the null hypothesis is true. So, we look at the observed value of the test statistic and ask, “What’s the probability of observing something at least as extreme as this, assuming the null hypothesis is true?” The answer to that question is the p-value.

title: 24  Hypothesis Test
text:
24.3 Problems

24.3.1 Problem 1
Suppose I am conducting a study to determine if a new drug decreases blood pressure. State the null and alternative hypotheses.






TipSolution





We can define \(\Delta\) as the change in blood pressure, with \(\Delta > 0\) indicating an increase and \(\Delta < 0\) indicating a decrease. The null hypothesis would then be \(H_0 : \Delta \ge 0\) and the alternative hypothesis would be \(H_1 : \Delta < 0\).
In practice, we almost always use two-sided tests, meaning we would use \(H_0 : \Delta = 0\) and \(H_1 : \Delta \ne 0\).





24.3.2 Problem 2
True or false: The p-value is the probability the null hypothesis is true.






TipSolution





False. The null hypothesis is either true or it isn’t. It’s not an event that may or may not happen.
In Bayesian statistics, the probability of the null hypothesis can be computed, but we are not covering Bayesian statistics here.

title: 25  Marginal and Conditional Distributions
text:
25.1 Learning Objective
Define, use, and interpret the terms “marginal distribution” and “conditional distribution”.

title: 25  Marginal and Conditional Distributions
text:
25.2 Lesson
According to the American Cancer Society’s Key Statistics for Breast Cancer, “Overall, the average risk that a woman in the US will develop breast cancer sometime in her life is about 13%.” This is a marginal probability, meaning that it’s an overall probability. It doesn’t take into account any risk factors. Since the only two outcomes are breast cancer or no breast cancer, this single marginal probability determines the entire marginal distribution. If “the average risk that a woman in the US will develop breast cancer sometime in her life is about 13%”, then the probability that a woman in the US won’t develop breast cancer sometime in her life is about 87%.
According to the American Cancer Society’s Breast Cancer Risk and Prevention site, “About 1 in 2 women with changes in these genes [BRCA1 and BRCA2] will develop breast cancer”. This is a conditional probability; it’s a probability based on knowing other information (in this case, gene status). Again, since there are only two outcomes, this single conditional probability determines the entire conditional distribution. About 1 in 2 women with changes in BRCA1 or BRCA2 won’t develop breast cancer.

25.2.1 Example

title: 25  Marginal and Conditional Distributions
text:
25.3 Problems

25.3.1 Problem 1
Take a look at Figure 4A in Effects of Temperature on the Thermal Biology and Locomotor Performance of Two Sympatric Extreme Desert Lizards. It shows the distribution of sprint speeds of lizards as a function of species and environmental temperature. Are these marginal or conditional distributions?






TipSolution





This is a bit of an unfair question because “marginal” and “conditional” are relative terms. In the breast cancer example above, the overall risks could be considered conditional because they’re conditional on female sex.
Having said that, I think it’s reasonable to consider the distributions in this problem as conditional, since they are conditional on two obvious factors, namely species and environmental temperature.





25.3.2 Problem 2
According to Regional variations and trends in hemophilia prevalence: A global analysis with future projection, the global prevalence of hemophilia is 3.75 per 100,000 people. The prevalence in the Americas is 6.03 per 100,000 people. Which of these is a marginal rate, and which is a conditional rate? Justify your response.






TipSolution





The global prevalence is marginal because it doesn’t take into account location. The prevalence in the Americas is conditional because it takes into account location.

title: 26  Conditional Expectation
text:
26.1 Learning Objective
Define, use, and interpret the term “conditional expectation”.

title: 26  Conditional Expectation
text:
26.2 Lesson
Conditional expectation is the expected value of one random variable, conditional on the value of some other random variable. We use \(E(Y|X)\) to denote “the expected value of \(Y\) conditional on \(X\)”, or “the expected value of \(Y\) given \(X\)”. We use \(E(Y|X = x)\) to denote “the expected value of \(Y\) conditional on \(X = x\)”, or “the expected value of \(Y\) given \(X = x\)”.
As an example, consider the World Population Review’s Average Height by Country 2026. The unconditional average height for a boy, age 19, in 2019, was 163.1 cm, or 5 ft 4 in. If \(Y\) is the height of a 19-year-old boy in 2019 (in cm), then \(E(Y) = 163.1\). The average height for a 19-year-old boy in the Netherlands in 2019, though, was 183.78 cm, or 6 ft. If we put the countries in alphabetical order, the Netherlands is the 123rd country in the list. If we let \(X\) equal the country number in that list, we could say \(E(Y|X = 123) = 183.78\). Timor-Leste is 175th in the list; there, boys have an average height of 160.13 cm. So, \(E(Y|X = 175) = 160.13\).
This example highlights that marginal and conditional are relative. I used \(E(Y)\) to denote a marginal expectation, but it was still the expectation of a random variable that had a lot of qualifiers (boy, age 19, in 2019). So, conditioning on country makes \(E(Y|X)\) conditional relative to \(E(Y)\).

title: 26  Conditional Expectation
text:
26.3 Problems

26.3.1 Problem 1
According to NerdWallet, the average retirement savings for people under age 35 is $49,130; the average retirement savings for people age 35-44 is $141,520; and the average retirement savings for people age 45-54 is $313,220. Are these marginal or conditional expectations?






TipSolution





These are conditional expectations. They are conditional on age.





26.3.2 Problem 2
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, what will be the relationship between \(E(Y)\) and \(E(Y|X)\)?






TipSolution





If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, having information about one doesn’t change the distribution of the other. So, \(E(Y)\) will be equal to \(E(Y|X)\).





26.3.3 Problem 3
True or false: \(E(Z|X,Y)\) is always equal to \(E(Z|Y)\).






TipSolution





False. This is probably easier to see with a real-world example. Suppose

\(Z\) is the weight of a dog in pounds.
\(X = 1\) if the dog is a chihuahua and \(X = 0\) if the dog is a Great Dane.
\(Y\) is the age of the dog in years.

\(E(Z|X,Y)\) would the be expected weight of a dog, conditional on its breed and age \(E(Z|Y)\) would be the expected weight a dog, conditional on just its age. It’s reasonable to assume there would be a difference between these, since chihuahuas and Great Danes are of vastly different sizes, even when age is held constant.

title: 27  Linearity Assumption
text:
27.1 Learning Objective
Explain the linearity assumption of simple linear regression.

title: 27  Linearity Assumption
text:
27.2 Lesson
I’m going to explain the first assumption of simple linear regression in three ways: first with words, then with a procedural form of math, and finally with an abstract form of math.

27.2.1 Words
The first assumption of simple linear regression is that the relationship between the predictor and the outcome is linear. (I’m using the term “predictor” now, but it’s also known as the explanatory variable, covariate, feature, or just \(X\). Also, I’m using the term “outcome”, but it’s also known as the response variable, target, or just \(Y\).)
What does this look like in a plot? Consider the following simulated points:









As \(X\) increases, we can see \(Y\) increasing linearly. We can draw a straight line through the cloud of points that describes the relationship well:









It’s probably helpful to look at some points where the relationship is not linear, to see the contrast. Consider these points:









I’ve tried drawing a straight line through them, but it clearly doesn’t describe them well. Here, the relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\) is U-shaped, not linear.


27.2.2 Procedural Math
Another way of looking at the first assumption of simple linear regression is as a procedure. We start with \(X_1\). We might know something about where it came from, or we might not. In the plots above, I drew \(X_1\) from a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation of 2. In symbols, \(X_1\sim N(0,4)\). (If the standard deviation is 2, the variance is \(2^2 = 4\).) Often, we don’t care so much about where \(X_1\) came from, because we’re more concerned about its relationship with \(Y_1\). In this particular simulation, \(X_1\) turned out to be -1.2529076.
Our next step is to plug \(X_1\) into a formula. In the first plot above, I used \(1 + \frac{1}{2}X_1\). Note that this is a linear formula. That brought me to the blue line in the second plot above. The height of the line at \(X_1\) is 0.3735462.









The next step is to add some random error. I’m going to use \(\epsilon_1\) to represent this random error. In the simulation above, \(\epsilon_1\sim N(0,1)\). The first assumption doesn’t require that the random error be normally distributed, just that it have mean 0. On average, we want the points to land on the line. (Obviously not every point will fall on the line; we just want that to be the case on average.) In the simulation above, \(\epsilon_1\) turned out to be 1.1349651. If we add that value to the line at \(X_1\), we get \(Y_1\).









In symbols, \(Y_1 = 1 + \frac{1}{2}X + \epsilon_1\). Of course, that was only for this example. In general, we write \(Y_1 = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \epsilon_1\).
That’s the procedure for one observation. We repeat it for \(X_2,X_3,\dotsc,X_n\), where \(n\) is the sample size. Here are the next few points visualized:























To summarize the entire process, I’d write that for \(i\) from \(1\) to \(n\), \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \epsilon_i\), where \(E(\epsilon_i|X_i) = 0\).


27.2.3 Abstract Math
The most abstract way to write this first assumption is \(E(Y_i|X_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i\). Given \(X_i\), we expect \(Y_i\) to fall on the line \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i\). Why use such an abstract representation? When we move on to logistic regression, Poisson regression, and really every other form of regression in this class, we won’t have any epsilons. They’re nice for visualizing what’s going on and understanding the procedure, but they cease to be relevant once we depart linear regression.


27.2.4 Note
Strictly, the linearity assumption is \[
E(Y_i|X_1,\dotsc,X_n) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i \text{,}
\] but that’s very cumbersome to write, and it will be more cumbersome once we get to multiple linear regression. So, I’m simplifying the notation a bit to \[
E(Y_i|X_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i \text{.}
\] This first assumption is much easier to write with linear algebra, but linear algebra is not a prerequisite for this course.

title: 27  Linearity Assumption
text:
27.3 Problems

27.3.1 Problem 1
Do these data satisfy the first assumption of simple linear regression?















TipSolution





No. The relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\) seems to be cyclical, not linear.





27.3.2 Problem 2
Does the first assumption of simple linear regression require a certain variance for \(\epsilon_i\)?






TipSolution





No. It only requires that the expected value of \(\epsilon_i\), conditional on \(X_i\), is zero.

title: 28  Consequences of the Linearity Assumption
text:
28.1 Learning Objective
Explain the consequences of violations of the linearity assumption of simple linear regression.
crumbs: 28  Consequences of the Linearity Assumption

title: 28  Consequences of the Linearity Assumption
text:
28.2 Lesson

28.2.1 Intuition
If the first assumption of simple linear regression is not met, the results are basically meaningless. Consider an example. The plot below shows mean monthly temperatures in Moscow for 2023 and 2024.









If I perform simple linear regression on these data, I get that each additional month of the year is associated with a 0.63-degree Celsius increase in temperature.









That’s clearly not true.
Simple linear regression is the most basic form of regression, and it’s only appropriate when you have a clear linear relationship between two variables.


28.2.2 Bias
In technical terms, we say that if the linearity assumption is not met, the estimators are biased. On average, they don’t equal the estimand they’re estimating. If the linearity assumption is met, the estimators are unbiased.
crumbs: 28  Consequences of the Linearity Assumption

title: 28  Consequences of the Linearity Assumption
text:
28.3 Problems

28.3.1 Problem 1
Should you use simple linear regression if a scatterplot of your data forms the shape of an M?






TipSolution





No.
crumbs: 28  Consequences of the Linearity Assumption

title: 29  Fitted Values and Residuals
text:
29.1 Learning Objective
Define, use, and interpret the terms “fitted value” and “residual”.

title: 29  Fitted Values and Residuals
text:
29.2 Lesson
Now that we know how catastrophic it would be for our first assumption to be violated, we need to know how to check it. Before we can do that, though, we need a couple vocab terms. The first is “fitted value”. In simple linear regression, we assume \(E(Y_i|X_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i\). We estimate \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) (the parameters) with \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\) (the statistics). The fitted value of \(Y_i\) is \[
\hat{Y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i \text{.}
\] In other words, the fitted value of the \(i\)th observation is the height of the regression line at \(X_i\).
The second vocab term is “residual”. I’ll use \(\hat{\epsilon}_i\) to represent the \(i\)th residual. Then \[
\hat{\epsilon}_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i \text{.}
\] I’d like to say that the residual is the vertical distance between the fitted value and the observed value of the outcome, but that’s incomplete. Distances are positive, but residuals can be positive or negative. If a point lies above the regression line, its residual is positive, and if a point lies below the regression line, its residual is negative. It’s possible to show that the sum of all the residuals is zero.

title: 29  Fitted Values and Residuals
text:
29.3 Problems

29.3.1 Problem 1
True or false: The residual is the same thing as the random error.






TipSolution





False. We never observe the random error, \(\epsilon\). We do observe residuals, and these are estimates of the random errors.





29.3.2 Problem 2
True or false: The fitted value is the same as the sample average.






TipSolution





False. There’s only one sample average for the entire data set, but there are \(n\) fitted values.
I should say that you could make this true by not including a slope term (\(\beta_1\)) in your regression model, but that’s such a specific case that I wouldn’t really refer to it as simple linear regression anymore.





29.3.3 Problem 3

29.3.3.1 Part (a)
Suppose we have a regression line \(\hat{E}(Y_i|X_i) = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i\). Suppose we want to estimate the mean outcome value when the explanatory variable is equal to \(z\), but no observation in the data set has its explanatory variable equal to \(z\). What should we do?






TipSolution





We can just plug \(z\) into the formula: \(\hat{E}(Y_i|X_i = z) = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 z\). Even if there’s no \(i\) such that \(X_i = z\), we can still use the regression line to estimate the expected value of the outcome if we were to observe the explanatory variable equal to \(z\).





29.3.3.2 Part (b)
Are there any restrictions to your proposed answer to Part (a)?






TipSolution





Yes. If \(z\) is very far away from all the observed values of the explanatory variable, we wouldn’t want to just plug it into our formula. This would be extrapolating beyond our data.

title: 30  Checking the Linearity Assumption
text:
30.1 Learning Objective
Evaluate the validity of the linearity assumption of simple linear regression in a data set.

title: 30  Checking the Linearity Assumption
text:
30.2 Lesson
It might seem straightforward to check the linearity assumption of simple linear regression. You can create a scatterplot of the data and eyeball whether the relationship between the two variables is linear. This is, in fact, a fantastic idea. You should always look at your data before trying to model it.
I will add one thing, though: It can be easier to evaluate this (and the remaining) assumptions if we look at the residuals, particularly when we move on to multiple linear regression. So, let’s start getting practice with that technique now.
Let’s take a look at these simulated data again:









Now I’m going to plot the residuals as a function of \(X\).









Why is this better than just plotting the data? Well, it’s not, at least not yet. Recall that we’re trying to check the assumption that \(E(\epsilon_i|X_i) = 0\). (This is from the “procedural math” way of looking at simple linear regression.) What this equation means in words is that, no matter the value of \(X_i\), the expected value of the random error should be zero. So, no matter the value of \(X_i\), the sample average of the residuals should be zero.
I’m going to add a horizontal line at 0 so we have something to compare to.









Again, no matter what value we choose on the horizontal axis, the average of the residuals at that point should be zero. Let’s look at the points around \(X = 2\), specifically, those points were \(1.9 \le X_i \le 2.1\).









The residuals in this band should average out to zero. Do they?

mean(mod_01$residuals[x >= 1.9 & x <= 2.1])

[1] 0.02226383


Just about! There will always be a little bit of random error, but this is pretty close to zero.
Let’s consider another band.









Do these residuals average out to zero?

mean(mod_01$residuals[x >= -3.1 & x <= -2.9])

[1] 0.1866407


This average is farther from zero because there are few points in the band, but it’s still close.
In practice, we don’t actually cut out vertical slices from the plot and compute averages. Instead, we look at the residual scatterplot and eyeball it. Why is this better than the original scatterplot? Sometimes zeroing out the slope makes it easier to assess the linearity assumption. Also, when we start learning about multiple linear regression, it will be too difficult to visualize a scatterplot of the outcome against all the covariates.

title: 30  Checking the Linearity Assumption
text:
30.3 Problems

30.3.1 Problem 1
Below is a plot of annual expenditures (in dollars) as a function of age (in years) for 1,000 individuals supported by the California Department of Developmental Services (DDS). (The data have been altered slightly to protect privacy.) Is the first assumption of simple linear regression met for these data?















TipSolution





No. There is clearly not a linear relationship between age and expenditures.





30.3.2 Problem 2
Below are simulated data. Is the first assumption of simple linear regression met for these data?






















TipSolution





Yes. This might be a case where it’s a little harder to tell with the standard scatterplot than the residual scatterplot.

title: 31  IID Assumption
text:
31.1 Learning Objective
Explain the iid assumption of simple linear regression.

title: 31  IID Assumption
text:
31.2 Lesson
“IID” stands for “independent and identically distributed.” In simple linear regression, we assume the points \((X_1,Y_1),\dotsc,(X_n,Y_n)\) are iid. Another way of saying this is that we assume the observations are sampled independently from the same population.

31.2.1 Independent
We assume the observations are independent of each other. This isn’t something we can visualize; it has to do with how the data were collected.
Again, let’s consider an example where this assumption is met and an example where it isn’t. The summer after my first year of college, I worked at a survey organization called ORC Macro. (I don’t think it exists anymore.) I sat at a computer that dialed ten-digit numbers at random. If the number belonged to someone and they picked up, I would ask them questions. Our biggest survey was commissioned by NOAA, and it was about fishing. I had to ask people how many fish they had caught in the last year. The participants in these surveys can probably be considered independent from each other. Knowing one person’s answers to the survey probably wouldn’t tell me anything about another person’s answers. The respondents had nothing to do with each other.
Now suppose that in addition to asking questions of each person who answered the phone, I asked questions of everyone in their household. Now, the respondents are no longer independent. People in the same household tend to be more similar to each other than to people in different households. For the fishing survey, two people in the same household are likely to catch similar numbers of fish. They might go fishing together, for example, as a family on vacation. So, knowing how many fish one person in the household caught would be be informative about how many fish another person in the household caught. This would be a violation of independence.


31.2.2 Identically Distributed
In simple linear regression, we assume the pairs of points are identically distributed.
