If we go back to the procedural view of simple linear regression, this means that we assume \(X_1,\dotsc,X_n\) are identically distributed; every point uses the same \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\); and then the \(\epsilon_1,\dotsc,\epsilon_n\) are identically distributed.
Another way of looking at this is that we assume we’re sampling from the same population. A violation of this assumption would occur if the population we’re sampling from changes over time, especially if the variability of the explanatory variable decreases over time.
Consider cell phone ownership. According to Pew Research, 62% of US adults owned a cell phone in 2002. By 2025, the proportion had increased to 98%. Suppose we started a study in 2002 examining the relationship between cell phone ownership and anxiety. We planned to use simple linear regression with anxiety as the outcome and cell phone ownership as the explanatory variable. It wouldn’t make sense to continue that study, with the same analysis, through 2025. Here are some reasons why:

The relationship between cell phone ownership and anxiety probably changed over those 23 years.
If you didn’t change your recruitment practices, you would probably stop enrolling people who don’t own a cell phone, since they’re so rare.
By 2025, people who did own a cell phone and people who didn’t probably differed in systematic ways that were related to anxiety.

At the very least, we’d want to incorporate other variables in the analysis, like year. This would make the analysis multiple linear regression, which we will talk about later.
I recognize that this is a contrived example. However, it’s important in any statistical analysis to make sure you’re very clear about what population you’re trying to generalize to. If that population changes over time, you need to make sure you account for that.


31.2.3 Sampling
Note the importance of sampling to this assumption. Ideally, we want to conduct a “simple random sample”, where each member of the population has an equal chance of being included in the sample. If we do that, there’s a low probability that any two members of our sample will belong to the same natural cluster, like household.
In some situations, clustered sampling is unavoidable. For example, consider dentistry. We generally don’t sample teeth independently from the population of all human teeth. Instead, we sample individual people, and then look at all the teeth in their mouths. Since teeth in the same mouth are more similar to each other than teeth in different mouths, sampling people rather than teeth induces correlation.
Sorry to use such an unsettling example! It comes up a lot, though. Consider an ophthalmologist studying eyes, or an oncologist studying breast, kidney, or lung cancer. In each of these examples, it probably makes the most sense to sample individuals and not individual organs.
Another place where sampling interacts with the iid assumption is when the population is finite and the sample is a large percentage of that finite population. If I deal you five cards and four of them are aces, you know there are no more aces in the deck.

title: 31  IID Assumption
text:
31.3 Problems

31.3.1 Problem 1
Suppose you want to investigate the relationship between number of hours worked per week and job satisfaction. You randomly select 1,000 US companies and survey five workers at each company. Have you satisfied the iid assumption of simple linear regression?






TipSolution





No. Workers at the same company are more similar to each other than to workers at other companies. So, the observation are not independent.





31.3.2 Problem 2
Suppose you want to investigate the relationship between number of hours worked per week and job satisfaction. You randomly select 5,000 US workers. Have you satisfied the iid assumption of simple linear regression?






TipSolution





Probably. You should still check to see how many workers in the sample have the same employer, but it might be low enough to be ignorable.





31.3.3 Problem 3
Suppose you are studying the relationship between age and approval of the new Spider-Man movie. So, you survey the members of your D&D (Dungeons and Dragons) group; then you ask them to recruit the members of their other D&D groups; then you ask them to recruit the members of their other D&D groups; and so forth, until you’ve surveyed 100 D&D players. Have you satisfied the iid assumption of simple linear regression?






TipSolution





No. People who play D&D together are more similar to each other than people who don’t play D&D together. If you know what one player thinks of the new Spider-Man movie, you’ll be better able to guess what other players in the same group think about the new Spider-Man movie. So, group membership should be included in the analysis. This would require some other analysis besides simple linear regression.
By the way, this form of recruitment is a version of respondent-driven sampling, which is a method for finding hard-to-reach or stigmatized populations.
It’s worth pointing out that, if there is a relationship between a player’s responses and their group membership, it would exist irrespective of the sampling mechanism. The sampling mechanism will influence how many players with shared group membership are in the sample; with respondent-driven sampling, you’re virtually guaranteeing that no participant in the sample will be the only member of their D&D group in the sample. With a simple random sample, you might get a few participants with shared group membership, but you might get a lot of singletons.
The number of players in the sample with shared group membership, along with the strength of the relationship between the individual responses and group membership, will affect the variance of our estimators. For example, suppose that within each group, the baseline approval of the movie is highly correlated, such that people of the same age in the same group have nearly identical approval ratings. If people in the same group also have similar ages, then recruiting lots of people from the same group will not be as informative as recruiting lots of people from different groups. Normally, increasing the sample size increases our precision, but with highly correlated data, it depends on how we increase the sample size.

title: 32  Consequences of the IID Assumption
text:
32.1 Learning Objective
Explain the consequences of violations of the iid assumption of simple linear regression.
crumbs: 32  Consequences of the IID Assumption

title: 32  Consequences of the IID Assumption
text:
32.2 Lesson
For our purposes, the main consequence of violations of the iid assumption of simple linear regression is that the standard errors will be wrong.
A standard error is the standard deviation of an estimator; it’s a measure of how variable the estimator is, or how much it will change from sample to sample. The higher the standard error, the less precise our estimator is; the lower the standard error, the more precise our estimator is. Getting a good measure of the variability of the estimator helps us know how wrong we might be.
In simple linear regression, we are generally most interested in \(\hat{\beta}_1\), the estimator of the slope. We often conduct a statistical test where the null hypothesis test is that \(\beta_1 = 0\), i.e., that there is no (linear) relationship between the explanatory and outcome variables. The statistical test is only correct if the standard error is correct.
Let’s consider an example. Below is a plot of commute time (in minutes) as a function of commute distance (in miles) for a sample of 500 individuals in Atlanta. I’ve made the points partially transparent because there’s so much overlap, so darker circles indicate more individuals with the same commute distance and time.









If I run a simple linear regression with time as the outcome and distance as the explanatory variable, this is the resulting residual plot.









The linearity assumption appears to be met, although in a real-world setting, it would behoove us to look into a few of the “weird” points, for lack of a better word. Who has a five mile commute that takes two hours?
Since we’re focusing on the effects of violating the iid assumption of simple linear regression, let’s take a look at the estimates and their standard errors.



Call:
lm(formula = Time ~ Distance, data = d)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-26.124  -6.693  -2.027   4.246 106.824 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  7.12034    0.90659   7.854  2.5e-14 ***
Distance     1.21115    0.03977  30.454  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 12.26 on 498 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6506,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6499 
F-statistic: 927.4 on 1 and 498 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The standard errors are in the Coefficients table in the Std. Error column. If these commuters weren’t sampled independently from the same population, we cannot trust these standard errors. For example, what if we sampled people who carpool together? We would have a bunch of people with similar (or even identical) commutes because they’re in the same vehicle (for at least a portion of the trip). In that case, the standard errors presented in this table would be wrong. Since the t value column is computed from the Std. Error column, the t value column would be wrong, and since the Pr(>|t|) column is computed from the t value column, the Pr(>|t|) column would be wrong.
I should say that violations of the iid assumption don’t mean you can’t do any regression at all. There are several subfields within statistics devoted to analyzing correlated data. For example, many statisticians focus on longitudinal data, where participants are observed more than once over time; in this case, observations within individuals are correlated with each other. Many educational researchers specialize in hierarchical models, since students are nested within classrooms, which are nested within schools, which are nested within districts, etc.
So, what I mean to say is that, when data are correlated, the standard errors computed from the most straightforward version of simple linear regression are incorrect.
crumbs: 32  Consequences of the IID Assumption

title: 32  Consequences of the IID Assumption
text:
32.3 Problems

32.3.1 Problem 1
True or false: If the commuters in the example above were not independent, the slope estimate is meaningless and uninterpretable.






TipSolution





False. This is something that I find counterintuitive, but a violation of the iid assumption of simple linear regression doesn’t imply that we have to throw out the coefficient estimates. So long as the linearity assumption is met, the coefficients are unbiased, meaning that their expectation is equal to the true value of the population parameter. This is a very powerful result in statistics.





32.3.2 Problem 2
True or false: If the iid assumption of simple linear regression is not met, we cannot trust the confidence intervals computed for the coefficients.






TipSolution





True. The confidence interval formula (which we haven’t seen) uses the standard error, so if the standard error is wrong, the confidence interval is wrong.
crumbs: 32  Consequences of the IID Assumption

title: 33  Checking the IID Assumption
text:
33.1 Learning Objective
Evaluate the validity of the iid assumption of simple linear regression in a data set.

title: 33  Checking the IID Assumption
text:
33.2 Lesson
Unlike the other assumptions of simple linear regression, we cannot check this one by making a plot or computing a statistic. Instead, we have to find out how the data were collected. Here are some questions to ask:

Are there any unmeasured variables that might make some observations more similar to each other than to others?
Are the observations grouped or clustered in some way?
Is there a hierarchical structure to the data?
Is the population changing over time?
Do the observations exist in a network, with some of them connected and some of them not connected?
Do we have multiple observations on the same person over time?

If the answer to any of these questions is yes, you might have a violation of the iid assumption.

title: 33  Checking the IID Assumption
text:
33.3 Problems

33.3.1 Problem 1
True or false: A plot of the residuals as a function of the explanatory variable can rule out violations of the iid assumption of simple linear regression.






TipSolution





False. In order to check this assumption, you need to examine the sampling process. How were observations drawn from the population of interest?





33.3.2 Problem 2
Suppose you want to investigate the relationship between physical activity and resting heart rate. This requires expensive equipment, so you can only observe ten people. You happen to be teaching a class, so you select ten students uniformly at random from the roster. Have you violated the iid assumption of simple linear regression? Why or why not?






TipSolution





You have not violated the iid assumption. You’ve sample uniformly at random from your population, so each student is equally likely to be selected. They are not grouped, clustered, or related in any meaningful way. (It is true that your population is really just “students taking your class”, which may not be a useful population, but you haven’t violated the iid assumption.)

title: 34  Homoscedasticity Assumption
text:
34.1 Learning Objective
Explain the homoscedasticity assumption of simple linear regression.

title: 34  Homoscedasticity Assumption
text:
34.2 Lesson
Similar to with the linearity assumption, I’m going to try to explain this assumption in three ways.

34.2.1 Words
The word “homoscedasticity” comes from the Greek words “homos”, meaning “same”, and “skedastikos”, meaning “able to disperse”. So the word means “same dispersion”. If this assumption is met, then there is equal dispersion, or equal variability, of the points around the regression line, no matter the value of the explanatory variable.
It will probably help to look at some pictures. Consider these simulated data:









If we look at the vertical spread of the points where \(X \approx 0\) and where \(X \approx 2\), it’s about the same. Even though \(X\) has changed, the variability around the regression line has not. So, these points are homoscedastic.
I have to acknowledge that you might disagree with me on this point. You might be thinking that the cloud of points looks more like a football, with lower variability at very high and very low values of \(X\). That’s fair. Having generated the data, I know that the assumption of homoscedasticity is met. So why the football shape? This is because, for any value of \(X\), points are more likely to be close to the line than far away. If there are a lot of points at a certain value of \(X\) (like around \(X = 0\)), there will be a few points far from the line, just by chance. If there are only a couple points at a certain value of \(X\) (like around \(X = -6\)), it’s unlikely to observe many points far from the line. So, it appears that the vertical spread of the points tapers off for high and low values of \(X\).
Now look at these points:









The variability of the points around the regression line when \(X \approx 0\) is way different than the variability of the points around the regression line when \(X \approx 2\). So, these points are heteroscedastic.


34.2.2 Procedural Math
Recall that we’re assuming that \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \epsilon_i\). This assumption can be written as \(Var(\epsilon_i|X_i) = \sigma^2\). Note that \(\sigma^2\) doesn’t depend on \(X_i\) or even \(i\); it’s the same no matter which observation you’re talking about.
When we’re walking through our procedure (draw \(X_i\) from its distribution; plug it into \(f(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\); add random error), we’re not changing the variability of the random error for each observation. It stays the same.




































CautionCaution: Math





Some of you might be saying, “Isn’t this assumption included in the second assumption, when we assume the observations are identically distributed.” Not exactly. If the data-generating procedure were \[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \epsilon_i X_i \text{,}
\] where \(E(\epsilon_i|X_i) = 0\) (assumption 1), \(X_1,\dotsc,X_n\) are iid (assumption 2), and \(\epsilon_1,\dotsc,\epsilon_n\) are iid (assumption 2), we would satisfy the first two assumptions but not the third. This is because \[
\begin{align*}
E\left(\epsilon_i X_i\right) &= E\left(E\left(\epsilon_i X_i\middle|X_i\right)\right) \\
&= E\left(X_i E\left(\epsilon_i \middle|X_i\right)\right) \\
&= E\left(X_i \left(0\right)\right) \\
&= E(0) \\
&= 0
\end{align*}
\] but \[
\begin{align*}
Var\left(\epsilon_i X_i\right) &= E\left(Var\left(\epsilon_i X_i\middle|X_i\right)\right) + Var\left(E\left(\epsilon_i X_i\middle|X_i\right)\right) \\
&= E\left(X_i^2 Var\left(\epsilon_i \middle|X_i\right)\right) + Var\left(0\right) \\
&= E\left(X_i^2 \sigma^2\right) \\
&= \sigma^2 E\left(X_i^2\right) \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]





34.2.3 Abstract Math
In its most abstract form, we can write this assumption as \(Var(Y_i|X_i) = \sigma^2\). Again, the \(\sigma^2\) doesn’t depend on \(X_i\) or even \(i\), so it’s the same across all \(X_i\). Why do we go to this level of abstraction? It will be useful when we talk about logistic regression and Poisson regression.

title: 34  Homoscedasticity Assumption
text:
34.3 Problems

34.3.1 Problem 1
Suppose \(Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \epsilon_i\) where \(Var(\epsilon_i|X_i) = \tau^2\). Would this satisfy the homoscedasticity assumption of simple linear regression? Why or why not?






TipSolution





Yes. It’s not important which Greek letter you use to represent the variance of the random error, just so long as that variance is a constant, and does not change with \(X_i\) or \(i\).





34.3.2 Problem 2
What is the opposite of homoscedasticity?






TipSolution





Heteroscedasticity, when the variability of the points around the regression line varies as a function of \(X_i\).

title: 35  Consequences of the Homoscedasticity Assumption
text:
35.1 Learning Objective
Explain the consequences of violations of the homoscedasticity assumption of simple linear regression.
crumbs: 35  Consequences of the Homoscedasticity Assumption

title: 35  Consequences of the Homoscedasticity Assumption
text:
35.2 Lesson
If the homoscedasticity assumption of simple linear regression is violated, the standard errors will be wrong.
Consider the following example. Each observation is a forest fire in Montesinho Park (Portugal) between January 2000 and December 2003 where at least 0.01 hectare (100 square meters) was burned. In the figure below, I’ve plotted \(\log_{10}(\text{area burned})\) as a function of the outside temperature.









If I regress \(\log_{10}(\text{area burned})\) on temperature, this is the resulting residual plot:









Note that the variance of the residuals is greater when the outside temperature is 20-25 degrees than when the outside temperature is 5-10 degrees.
This doesn’t appear to be due to the fact that there are more observations between 20 and 25 degrees than between 5 and 10 degrees. If we look at vertical slices with approximately equal numbers of observations, the variance is greater for higher temperatures. For example, there are 16 observations with temperature less than 7.5:

sum(mod_01$model$Temp < 7.5)

[1] 16


This is a histogram of the residuals for those points:









There are 19 observations with temperature between 25 and 27.5:

sum(mod_01$model$Temp < 27.5 & mod_01$model$Temp >= 25)

[1] 19


This is a histogram of the residuals for those points:









Now let’s take a look at the regression results.



Call:
lm(formula = Log10_Area_No_0 ~ Temp, data = d)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-1.82331 -0.47682 -0.00182  0.39920  2.25799 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  0.872689   0.132791   6.572 2.58e-10 ***
Temp        -0.003702   0.006550  -0.565    0.572    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.6639 on 268 degrees of freedom
  (247 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.00119,   Adjusted R-squared:  -0.002537 
F-statistic: 0.3194 on 1 and 268 DF,  p-value: 0.5724


Because of the heteroscedasticity, we can’t trust the values in the Std. Error column. The values in the t value column are based on the standard errors, so those will also be wrong; and the values in the last column, the p-values, are based on the \(t\) values, so those will be wrong.
crumbs: 35  Consequences of the Homoscedasticity Assumption

title: 35  Consequences of the Homoscedasticity Assumption
text:
35.3 Problems

35.3.1 Problem 1
True or false: In the presence of heteroscedasticity, the estimated coefficients are biased.






TipSolution





False. Heteroscedasticity does not cause bias. As long as the first assumption is met, the regression coefficients will be unbiased. Heteroscedasticity only affects the standard errors (and anything calculated from the standard errors, like the p-values).





35.3.2 Problem 2
True or false: If the homoscedasticity assumption is met, the standard errors are guaranteed to be correct.






TipSolution





False. Remember that the iid assumption is also necessary for the standard errors to be correct.
crumbs: 35  Consequences of the Homoscedasticity Assumption

title: 36  Checking the Homoscedasticity Assumption
text:
36.1 Learning Objective
Evaluate the validity of the homoscedasticity assumption of simple linear regression in a data set.

title: 36  Checking the Homoscedasticity Assumption
text:
36.2 Lesson
In order to evaluate the validity of the homoscedasticity assumption of simple linear regression, we plot the residuals as function of the explanatory variable. If the vertical spread of the residuals varies as a function of \(X\), we have heteroscedasticity. Let’s consider a couple examples.

36.2.1 Fire Ants
The red imported fire ant has invaded some of the habitats of fence lizards (e.g., southern Alabama), but not all (e.g., eastern Arkansas). The venom from the fire ant can kill a lizard, whether the ants are attacking the lizard or the lizard has eaten some ants. In 2009, Tracy Langkilde published a study in which she exposed lizards from invaded and uninvaded habitats to fire ants and counted the number of times the lizards twitched. Here are side-by-side boxplots of the data:









You might be thinking, “How can we do regression with these data? The outcome is quantitative, but the explanatory variable is categorical.” It turns out that you can do simple linear regression with a categorical explanatory variable that only has two levels. You just have to recode the levels as 0 and 1. I’ll change every “Uninvaded” to a 0, and every “Invaded” to a 1, then regress the number of twitches on the new habitat variable. Here’s a plot of the data and the fitted regression line:









Let’s look at boxplots of the residuals:









It seems like the variability of the residuals is greater for invaded than uninvaded lizards. So, I’m not convinced we’ve satisfied the homoscedasticity assumption of simple linear regression.


36.2.2 Weight and Red Blood Cell Density in Mice
Below are data on weight (in grams) and red blood cell density (I couldn’t find the units) for 72 mice.









Only 5 mice (6.94%) have weights under 5 grams.


[1] 5


[1] 6.944444


I’m going to remove those mice, because I think they are so different from the other mice as to represent a different population.
Here is the scatterplot again, without the five tiny mice.









If I regress red blood cell density on weight, this is the residual scatter plot.









The vertical spread of the residuals is fairly constant across all weights. So, the homoscedasticity assumption is met.

title: 36  Checking the Homoscedasticity Assumption
text:
36.3 Problems

36.3.1 Problem 1
In the residual plot below, is the homoscedasticity assumption met?















TipSolution





It is not met. Variance is highest when \(X\) is around 0 and lowest when \(|X|\) is around 1. This is not due to there just being fewer points with \(|X|\) around 1. The points are partially transparent, so the darker shading at the left and right of the plot means there are lots of points there.





36.3.2 Problem 2
In the residual plot below, is the homoscedasticity assumption met?















TipSolution





Yes, the homoscedasticity assumption is met. It might look like the variance is lower at the far left and far right, but that’s because there are fewer points there, and points closer to the regression line are more likely than points far away.

title: 37  Normality Assumption
text:
37.1 Learning Objective
Explain the normality assumption of simple linear regression.

title: 37  Normality Assumption
text:
37.2 Lesson
The final assumption of simple linear regression is that the random errors are normally distributed. In symbols, we assume \(\epsilon_i|X_i\) is normally distributed. Equivalently, we can say that we assume \(Y_i|X_i\) is normally distributed.
In this plot, all four assumptions are met.









In the next three plots, the first three assumptions are met, but not the fourth. I’ve used three non-normal distributions for the random errors.

title: 37  Normality Assumption
text:
37.3 Problems

37.3.1 Problem 1
If the errors are Laplace distributed, does that satisfy the normality assumption of simple linear regression?






TipSolution





No. The normality assumption is that the errors are normally distributed.

title: 38  Consequences of the Normality Assumption
text:
38.1 Learning Objective
Explain the consequences of violations of the normality assumption of simple linear regression.
crumbs: 38  Consequences of the Normality Assumption

title: 38  Consequences of the Normality Assumption
text:
38.2 Lesson

38.2.1 Consequence
If the normality assumption of simple linear regression is not satisfied, the test statistic for each coefficient will not be \(t\)-distributed, so the p-value in the output will be wrong.
Let’s return to the example where we regressed red blood cell density on weight in mice. As before, I’m going to remove the five anomalous mice with very low weights.









If I regress red blood cell density on weight, these are the results.



Call:
lm(formula = RBC ~ Weight, data = d2)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-0.85802 -0.18339  0.08133  0.21887  0.83900 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -0.57833    0.66632  -0.868    0.389    
Weight       0.35342    0.03194  11.066   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.3501 on 65 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6532,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6479 
F-statistic: 122.4 on 1 and 65 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The values in the Pr(>|t|) column are p-values. For them to be correct, all four assumptions must be true.
Let’s go a little deeper and look at how the p-values are computed.
Each value in the t value column is computed by taking the corresponding value in the Estimate column and dividing it by the corresponding value in the Std. Error column. So, \[
\begin{align*}
-\frac{0.57833}{0.66632} &= -0.868 \\
\frac{0.35342}{0.03194} &= 11.066 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
These are the test statistics. If all four assumptions are met, each should follow a \(t\) distribution with \(n - 2\) degrees of freedom. In this example, \(n = 67\), so \(n - 2 = 65\).
Each value in the Pr(>|t|) is computed by integrating under the probability density function of a \(t_{n-2}\) distribution from \(|\texttt{t value}|\) to \(+\infty\) and from \(-|\texttt{t value}|\) to \(-\infty\). I can show this visually for the (Intercept) row of the Coefficients: table.









I can also directly compute the p-value.

2 * pt(q = -0.868,
       df = 65)

[1] 0.3885878


If the random errors are not normally distributed, the test statistics will not be \(t\) distributed, so the p-values won’t be correct.


38.2.2 Qualification
If the first three assumptions are met (linearity, iid, homoscedasticity) and the sample size is large, the test statistics will be approximately normally distributed, with mean 0 and variance 1. As the sample size gets larger, this approximation gets better.
You may have noticed that the \(t_{65}\) distribution looks basically normal. I’ll plot a \(t_{65}\) distribution and a standard normal distribution over each other so you can compare.









Can you tell the difference? They’re nearly identical.
As \(n\) increases, \(t_{n-2}\) gets closer and closer to \(N(0,1)\). I’ll plot a bunch of \(t\) distributions with increasing degrees of freedom so you can see how they change.









As the degrees of freedom increases, the peak rises and the tails flatten. (Since the tails flatten, and p-values are tail areas, this means p-values decrease as degrees of freedom increases.)
To summarize: If the first three assumptions are met and the sample size is large, the test statistics will be approximately normal. If the sample size is large, the corresponding \(t\) distribution will be approximately normal. So, if the first three assumptions are met and the sample size is large, you can use the p-values in the output, regardless of whether the random errors are normal or not.


38.2.3 What’s “Large”?
You might be wondering what sample size is large enough for the test statistics to be approximately normal. This depends. Very asymmetric random errors will require a larger sample size for the test statistic to be approximately normal. I recommend you consult a statistician.
crumbs: 38  Consequences of the Normality Assumption

title: 38  Consequences of the Normality Assumption
text:
38.3 Problems

38.3.1 Problem 1
If the random errors are not normally distributed, can we trust the p-values?






TipSolution





It depends. The more symmetric the random errors are, and the larger the sample size, the more trustworthy the p-values become.





38.3.2 Problem 2
If the random errors are not normally distributed, can we trust the standard errors?






TipSolution





It depends on whether or not the first three assumptions are met. If yes, then yes.

title: 39  Checking the Normality Assumption
text:
39.1 Learning Objective
Evaluate the validity of the normality assumption of simple linear regression in a data set.

title: 39  Checking the Normality Assumption
text:
39.2 Lesson

39.2.1 Three Plots
I like to use three plots to evaluate the validity of the normality assumption. For each plot, you use the residuals as input.
The first plot is a histogram. Here is what a histogram looks like when the underlying data are normal.









The second plot is a boxplot. In actuality, I really only use this to check if the data are symmetric or not. Here is what a boxplot looks like when the underlying data are normal.









The third plot is a q-q plot. If the data are normal, the points on the q-q plot will follow the reference line. This is what a q-q plot looks like when the underlying data are normal.











39.2.2 Mice Example
Let’s return to the example where we regressed red blood cell density on weight in mice. As before, I’m going to remove the five anomalous mice with very low weights. We already know the relationship is linear and the variance is constant. I’m going to assume the mice are independent. All we have to check is normality. Here’s the histogram of the residuals.









This is left skewed, but other than that, it’s approximately normal.
Let’s check the boxplot.









The asymmetry seems less pronounced than in the histogram, but it’s still present. The median sits more than halfway up the box, and the bottom whisker is slightly longer than the top whisker.
Now let’s check the q-q plot.









Most of the points follow the reference line; it’s only when the theoretical quantiles get below about -0.75 that the points diverge from the line.
Ultimately, I would say these residuals are more left-skewed than you would expect from a normal distribution. So, I wouldn’t say the normality assumption is categorically met. But, since the sample size is relatively large, and the residuals are close to normal, I would trust the p-values.


39.2.3 Atlanta Commutes
Let’s return to the data about commuting in Atlanta.









If we regress time on distance, here is the residual scatter plot.









It’s hard for me to assess the variance. It’s possible that there’s heteroscedasticity. Let’s check the normality assumption anyway.
Here’s a histogram, boxplot, and q-q plot of the residuals.























These residuals are very right-skewed. I would say the linearity and iid assumptions are met, but the homoscedasticity and normality assumptions are not. So, the estimators of the coefficients are unbiased, but I wouldn’t trust the standard errors and p-values.
This is not directly relevant to assumption-checking, but I want to know why there seems to be a hard line below which we don’t see any points. I’ll plot the line \(y = x\) to show what I mean.









What’s going on here?

title: 39  Checking the Normality Assumption
text:
39.3 Problems

39.3.1 Problem 1
Do these residuals satisfy the normality assumption? Why or why not?















TipSolution





Absolutely not. Those points don’t follow the reference line at all.





39.3.2 Problem 2
Do these residuals satisfy the normal assumption? Why or why not?















TipSolution





I’d like to see a histogram and q-q plot before making a decision, but it seems like this distribution is too peaked and heavy-tailed to be normal. I say that it’s peaked because the box is so small and I say it’s heavy-tailed because there are so many dots beyond the whiskers.

title: 40  LINE
text: 40.1 Learning Objectives

title: 40  LINE
text:
State and recognize an acronym for the four assumptions.
Synthesize the four assumptions, their consequences, and how to check them.

title: 40  LINE
text:
40.2 Lesson
The four assumptions are commonly organized into the acronym “LINE”:

Linearity
Independence (other texts commonly leave out the assumption of identical distributions)
Normality
Equal variance

When I presented the four assumptions, I put them in descending order from most to least catastrophic when not met. Unfortunately, that spells “LIEN”, which is harder to remember.
In each of the following plots, the title contains a letter if it meets the corresponding assumption.

title: 40  LINE
text:
40.3 Problems
For each problem below, assume an assumption is met if its corresponding letter from the acronym is present. What are the consequences for the analysis?

40.3.1 Problem 1
IN






TipSolution





Since the linearity assumption is not met, you need to fix your underlying model before doing anything else





40.3.2 Problem 2
LE






TipSolution





If the independence assumption is not met, you need other tools besides simple linear regression.





40.3.3 Problem 3
LI






TipSolution





The coefficients are unbiased but the standard errors, test statistics, and p-values are untrustworthy.

title: 41  Interpretation
text:
41.1 Learning Objective
Interpret the coefficients in simple linear regression.

title: 41  Interpretation
text:
41.2 Lesson

41.2.1 Overview
Simple linear regression has two coefficients: the intercept (\(\beta_0\)) and slope (\(\beta_1\)). The intercept is the expected value of the outcome when the explanatory variable is zero. The slope is the expected change in the outcome associated with a one-unit increase in the explanatory variable. We can also interpret the slope as the expected difference in the outcome between two populations, one with the explanatory variable equal to \(x\) and the other with the explanatory variable equal to \(x + 1\).
Note that I used the word “expected” in interpreting both coefficients. We’re working with random variables, so we can’t guarantee that the outcome will take on a certain value when the explanatory variable takes on a certain value. We can only speak in means and averages.
Also, note that I used “associated with” in the interpretation of the slope. In many situations, we do not know if the explanatory variable causes a change in the outcome variable. We don’t want to make any causal claims unless we’re sure they’re warranted.


41.2.2 Atlanta Commutes
Consider the data on commuting in Atlanta. Although the assumptions of homoscedasticity and normality were not satisfied, the assumption of linearity was, meaning the coefficient estimates are unbiased. So, we can interpret them.



Call:
lm(formula = Time ~ Distance, data = d)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-26.124  -6.693  -2.027   4.246 106.824 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  7.12034    0.90659   7.854  2.5e-14 ***
Distance     1.21115    0.03977  30.454  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 12.26 on 498 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6506,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6499 
F-statistic: 927.4 on 1 and 498 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Recall that the units for distance were miles and the units for time were minutes. So, an intercept estimate of 7.1 means that we would expect a commute of 7.1 minutes for a distance of zero miles. Does that sound reasonable? I’m not sure. Were there any observed commutes of zero miles?

sum(d$Distance == 0)

[1] 11

sort(d$Time[d$Distance == 0])

 [1]  1  1  2  2  3  3  5  5  5 10 10


Apparently there were 11 commutes of zero miles, two of which took ten minutes. I’m curious how these data were collected . . .
Moving on to the slope, there is an expected increase of 1.2 minutes associated with each additional mile in the commute. (Alternatively, we could say that we would expect Atlantans with a commute of \(x + 1\) miles to have a commute that is 1.2 minutes longer than Atlantans with a commute of \(x\) miles.) Does that sound reasonable? Sure.


41.2.3 Fire Ants
Recall the fire ants example. There were two groups of lizards, those whose habitats had been invaded by fire ants and those whose habitats had not. The outcome was the number of twitches a lizard exhibited when exposed to fire ants.
In the output below, Habitat_01 is the recoded habitat variable. It equals 1 if the habitat is invaded and 0 if the habitat is uninvaded.



Call:
lm(formula = Twitches ~ Habitat_01, data = d2)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
 -2.75  -1.10  -0.75   1.25   4.90 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   1.1000     0.3075   3.577 0.000601 ***
Habitat_01    1.6500     0.4349   3.794 0.000291 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 1.945 on 78 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1558,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1449 
F-statistic: 14.39 on 1 and 78 DF,  p-value: 0.0002914


The intercept is the expected value of the outcome when the explanatory variable equals zero. When the explanatory variable is zero, that means the habitat is uninvaded (in this example). So, for lizards whose habitat has not been invaded by fire ants, we would expect 1.1 twitches when exposed to fire ants.
The slope is the expected change in the outcome variable associated with a one-unit increase in the explanatory variable. The only way for the explanatory variable to increase by one unit is to change from uninvaded to invaded. So, when the habitat changes from uninvaded to invaded, we would expect an increase of 1.65 twitches. In other words, we expect lizards from invaded habitats to exhibit 1.65 more twitches than lizards from uninvaded habitats.

text:
41.3 Problems

41.3.1 Problem 1
Below are the results of regressing red blood cell density on weight for 67 mice. I’m not sure what the units were for red blood cell density, but weight was measured in grams. Interpret the intercept and slope.



Call:
lm(formula = RBC ~ Weight, data = d3)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-0.85802 -0.18339  0.08133  0.21887  0.83900 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -0.57833    0.66632  -0.868    0.389    
Weight       0.35342    0.03194  11.066   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Multiple R-squared:  0.6532,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6479 
F-statistic: 122.4 on 1 and 65 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

We would expect a mouse weighing zero grams to have a red blood cell density of -0.58. Each additional gram of weight is associated with a 0.35-unit increase in red blood cell density. Alternatively, we would expect mice weighing \(x + 1\) grams to have a red blood cell density that is 0.35 units greater than mice weighting \(x\) grams.

title: 42  Hypothesis Testing
text:
42.1 Learning Objective
Interpret the results of a hypothesis test in the context of simple linear regression.

title: 42  Hypothesis Testing
text:
42.2 Lesson

42.2.1 Overview
When conducting simple linear regression in R, R will automatically compute p-values for each of the two coefficients. For each coefficient, the null hypothesis is that the coefficient is zero, and the alternative hypothesis is that the coefficient is not zero. In symbols, the two hypothesis tests are \[
\begin{align*}
H_0 &: \beta_0 = 0 \\
H_1 &: \beta_0 \ne 0
\end{align*}
\] and \[
\begin{align*}
H_0 &: \beta_1 = 0 \\
H_1 &: \beta_1 \ne 0 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]


42.2.2 Red Blood Cell Density and Weight in Mice
Below are the results of regressing red blood cell density on weight for 67 mice. Enough of our assumptions were satisfied for these data that I feel comfortable interpreting the p-values.



Call:
lm(formula = RBC ~ Weight, data = d3)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-0.85802 -0.18339  0.08133  0.21887  0.83900 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -0.57833    0.66632  -0.868    0.389    
Weight       0.35342    0.03194  11.066   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.3501 on 65 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6532,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6479 
F-statistic: 122.4 on 1 and 65 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The p-value for the (Intercept) line of the Coefficients table is 0.389. This is above any reasonable cutoff we would use in hypothesis testing. So, we fail to reject the null hypothesis that \(\beta_0 = 0\). This makes sense; we wouldn’t want the expected red blood cell density for a mice weighing zero grams to be anything other than zero.
The p-value for the Weight line of the Coefficients table is <2e-16, which means \(< 2\times 10^{-16}\). This is below any reasonable cutoff we would use in hypothesis testing, so we reject the null hypothesis that \(\beta_1 = 0\) and conclude \(\beta_1 \ne 0\). In real-world terms, this means that the expected change in red blood cell density associated with a one-gram increase in weight is greater than zero. We could also say that the increase in red blood cell density associated with a one-gram increase in weight is significantly different from zero.
You may have noticed that when I said “significantly different”, I dropped “expected”. This is because I’m describing the statistical significance of an observed change. If I’m talking about the population, either the change is zero or it isn’t, so it doesn’t make sense to talk about statistical significance. If I’m talking about the observed change in the sample, it will almost always be different from zero; the question, then, is whether that difference is statistically significant. This is getting deeper into semantics than is practically necessary (probably).

title: 42  Hypothesis Testing
text:
42.3 Problems

42.3.1 Problem 1
One hundred men had their neck circumference (in cm) and biceps circumference (extended, in cm) measured. Below, I’ve regressed neck circumference on biceps circumference. Assuming all necessary assumptions are met, interpret the results of the hypothesis tests relating to the coefficients. Use a cutoff of \(\alpha = 0.05\).



Call:
lm(formula = Neck ~ Biceps, data = d)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-6.0640 -1.1864  0.0041  1.2545  3.7277 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 20.88426    1.75550  11.896  < 2e-16 ***
Biceps       0.52675    0.05412   9.733 4.61e-16 ***
---

Residual standard error: 1.651 on 98 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.4915,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.4863 
F-statistic: 94.72 on 1 and 98 DF,  p-value: 4.608e-16








TipSolution





Both p-values are much lower than 0.05, so we reject the null hypotheses that \(\beta_0 = 0\) and \(\beta_1 = 0\). So, we conclude that the expected neck circumference for a man with a biceps circumference of 0 cm is different from 0, and that the expected increase in neck circumference associated with a one-cm increase in biceps circumference is greater than zero.





42.3.2 Problem 2
Below, I’ve regressed neck circumference (in cm) on age (in years) for the same 100 men as above. Assuming all necessary assumptions are met, interpret the results of the hypothesis tests relating to the coefficients. Use a cutoff of \(\alpha = 0.05\).



Call:
lm(formula = Neck ~ Age, data = d)

Residuals:

-5.0949 -1.5321  0.0167  1.4912  5.3051 

Coefficients:

(Intercept) 37.545477   0.942563  39.833   <2e-16 ***
Age          0.007766   0.020360   0.381    0.704    
---

Residual standard error: 2.313 on 98 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.001482,  Adjusted R-squared:  -0.008707 
F-statistic: 0.1455 on 1 and 98 DF,  p-value: 0.7037








TipSolution





The p-value for the intercept is far less than 0.05, so we reject the null hypothesis that \(\beta_0 = 0\) and conclude that the expected neck circumference for a man age 0 is different from zero.
The p-value for age is \(0.704 > 0.05\), so we fail to reject the null hypothesis that \(\beta_1 = 0\). We cannot conclude that neck circumference changes linearly with age.

title: 43  Ordinary Least Squares
text:
43.1 Learning Objective
Explain the term “ordinary least squares (OLS)”.

title: 43  Ordinary Least Squares
text:
43.2 Lesson
The kind of regression we’ve been using is called “ordinary least squares”, or “OLS” for short. This is because we find the line of best fit by minimizing (hence, “least”) the sum of squared errors (hence, “squares”) between the points and the line.
Let’s see what this looks like visually. Consider these 20 points.









Now let’s look at the points with the regression line.









Now let’s visualize the residuals.









Finally, let’s visualize the squared residuals. To find the line, we’re minimizing the sum of these squared residuals.









That’s a little cluttered, but we can focus on just one squared residual to get the idea.









This is where the name “ordinary least squares” comes from.
Why don’t we use some other method? Good question. Basically, this method is mathematically convenient, and there’s a lot of theory supporting it.
What are the consequences? Points farther from the line have larger residuals than points closer to the line, and much larger squared residuals than points closer to the line. Since we want to minimize the squared residuals, this gives points farther from the line more power. You may have learned in introductory statistics that the sample average is sensitive to outliers; this is the same idea. And, like the median is robust to outliers, there are nonparametric forms of regression that are robust to outliers. We won’t cover those.

title: 43  Ordinary Least Squares
text:
43.3 Problems

43.3.1 Problem 1
True or false: The name “ordinary least squares” indicates that we are choosing the line that has the least squared error.






TipSolution





True.





43.3.2 Problem 2
True or false: Typically in regression, we minimize the sum of the absolute values of the residuals.






TipSolution





False. We minimize the sum of the squares of the residuals.

title: 44  Log-Transformed Outcomes
text:
44.1 Learning Objective
Interpret the coefficients when the outcome has been logged.

title: 44  Log-Transformed Outcomes
text:
44.2 Lesson

44.2.1 Problem
When we log the outcome, the linearity assumption becomes \[
E\left(\log Y_i \middle| X_i\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i \text{.}
\] This poses problems for interpretation; we’d like to talk about the untransformed outcome, but \[
E\left(\log Y_i \middle| X_i\right) \ne \log E\left(Y_i \middle| X_i\right) \text{.}
\] So, for example, our interpretation of \(\beta_0\) is “the expected value of the log of the outcome when \(X_i = 0\).” That’s not very useful. Also, \[
\begin{align*}
\beta_1 &= \beta_0 + \beta_1(x+1) - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\right) \\
&= E\left(\log Y_i \middle| X_i = x + 1\right) - E\left(\log Y_i \middle| X_i = x\right) \text{,}
\end{align*}
\] which isn’t very useful, either.


44.2.2 More Assumptions
Suppose we change our model to \[
\log Y_i|X_i \sim N\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i,\sigma^2\right) \text{.}
\] Then the coefficients are more interpretable. Specifically, \[
\begin{align*}
E\left(Y_i\middle|X_i = 0\right) &= \exp\left(\beta_0 + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right) \\
\frac{E\left(Y_i\middle|X_i = x+1\right)}{E\left(Y_i\middle|X_i = x\right)} &= \exp\left(\beta_1\right) \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] In words, when the explanatory variable equals 0, we would expect the outcome variable to equal \[
\exp\left(\beta_0 + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right) \text{.}
\] An increase of one unit in the explanatory variable is associated with a \[
\left(\exp\left(\beta_1\right) - 1\right) \times 100\%
\] increase in the outcome variable. (If this is negative, it’s a decrease.) Another way of phrasing this is that a population with the explanatory variable equal to \(x + 1\) is expected to have an outcome \(\exp(\beta_1)\) times that of a population with the explanatory variable equal to \(x\).
Note that, in order to interpret the coefficients this way, all four assumptions need to be met in the data. Also, you need to have used the natural log (base \(e\)) in order to transform the outcome. If you use any other base, the interpretation above is not justified.


44.2.3 Math
I have a tendency to forget the math behind these interpretations, so I’m going to store it here. You don’t need to know it; it’s more for me.






CautionCaution: Math





Define \(Z_i = \log Y_i\). Then \[
Z_i|X_i \sim N\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i,\sigma^2\right)
\] and \[
f(z|x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{\left(z - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x\right)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \text{.}
\] Further, \[
Y_i = \exp\left(Z_i\right)
\] and \[
\begin{align*}
E\left(Y_i\middle|X_i = x\right) &= E\left(\exp\left(Z_i\right)\middle|X_i = x\right) \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^\infty \exp\left(z\right) f(z|x)\,dz \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^\infty \exp\left(z\right) \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{\left(z - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x\right)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \,dz \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(z-\frac{\left(z - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x\right)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \,dz \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(z-\frac{z^2 - 2z\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\right) + \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\right)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \,dz \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{z^2 - 2z\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\right) - 2z\sigma^2 + \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\right)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \,dz \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{z^2 - 2z\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x+\sigma^2\right)  + \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\right)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \,dz \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{z^2 - 2z\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x+\sigma^2\right) + \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \sigma^2\right)^2 - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \sigma^2\right)^2 + \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\right)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \,dz \\
&= \exp\left(\frac{\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \sigma^2\right)^2 - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\right)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{z^2 - 2z\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x+\sigma^2\right) + \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \sigma^2\right)^2 }{2\sigma^2}\right) \,dz \\
&= \exp\left(\frac{2\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\right)\sigma^2 + \sigma^4}{2\sigma^2}\right) \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{\left(z - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x - \sigma^2\right)^2 }{2\sigma^2}\right) \,dz \\
&= \exp\left(\frac{2\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\right)\sigma^2 + \sigma^4}{2\sigma^2}\right)  \\
&= \exp\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right) \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\]
Thus, \[
E\left(Y_i\middle|X_i = 0\right) = \exp\left(\beta_0 + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right)
\] and \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{E\left(Y_i\middle|X_i = x+1\right)}{E\left(Y_i\middle|X_i = x\right)} &= \frac{\exp\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 (x+1) + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right)}{\exp\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right)} \\
&= \exp\left(\beta_1\right) \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]





44.2.4 Forest Fire Example
Let’s return to the forest fire example. Each observation is a forest fire in Montesinho Park (Portugal) between January 2000 and December 2003. In the scatterplot below, I’ve plotted total burned area (in hectares) as a function of relative humidity (%).









It’s hard to detect a relationship between the two variables. This might be easier if we log the outcome. However, we can’t take the log of zero, and 47.8% of the observations have zero as the outcome.

sum(d$Area == 0)

[1] 247

sum(d$Area == 0) / nrow(d)

[1] 0.4777563


According to the description of the data, a zero indicates that less than 0.01 hectare (100 square meters) was burned. So, we can remove the zeros and take the natural log of the outcome.









This scatterplot is easier to interpret. If we regress the log-transformed total burned area on relative humidity, we get this residual scatterplot:









It appears that the linearity assumption is met, and I’m willing to assume that the data are iid (even though it’s possible that one forest fire changes the probability of another). It appears that there is lower variability in the residuals for higher relative humidities, but that may be because there are just fewer observations at the higher relative humidities. Let’s check the distribution of the residuals.























These look (mostly) normal to me. So, we can interpret the coefficients.
Here’s the output from the regression analysis:



Call:
lm(formula = Log_Area_No_0 ~ RH, data = d)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-4.2766 -1.0295 -0.0201  0.8831  5.0657 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  2.064810   0.285675   7.228 5.12e-12 ***
RH          -0.005030   0.006177  -0.814    0.416    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 1.528 on 268 degrees of freedom
  (247 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.002468,  Adjusted R-squared:  -0.001254 
F-statistic: 0.6632 on 1 and 268 DF,  p-value: 0.4162


Note that \[
\begin{align*}
\hat{\beta}_0 &= 2.064810 \\
\hat{\beta}_1 &= -0.005030 \\
\hat{\sigma} &= 1.528 \text{,}
\end{align*}
\] so
\[
\begin{align*}
\hat{E}\left(Y_i\middle|X_i = 0\right) &= \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right) \\
&= \exp\left(2.064810 + \frac{1.528^2}{2}\right) \\
&= 25.3 \\
\frac{\hat{E}\left(Y_i\middle|X_i = x+1\right)}{\hat{E}\left(Y_i\middle|X_i = x\right)} &= \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_1\right) \\
&= \exp\left(-0.005030 \right) \\
&= 0.995 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] This means that, when the relative humidity is 0%, we would expect 25.3 hectares to burn. For each additional percentage point of relative humidity, we would expect a decrease of 0.5% in total area burned.

title: 45  Shifting the Data to Make the Intercept Interpretable
text: 45.1 Learning Objectives
crumbs: 45  Shifting the Data to Make the Intercept Interpretable

title: 45  Shifting the Data to Make the Intercept Interpretable
text:
Shift the data to make the intercept interpretable.
Interpret the intercept for the shifted data.
crumbs: 45  Shifting the Data to Make the Intercept Interpretable

title: 45  Shifting the Data to Make the Intercept Interpretable
text:
45.2 Lesson
You may have noticed that in some of the examples I’ve used, the intercept has not made sense. For example, when I regressed red blood cell density on weight in mice, I said, “We would expect a mouse weighing zero grams to have a red blood cell density of -0.58.” That was based on these results:



Call:
lm(formula = RBC ~ Weight, data = d)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-0.85802 -0.18339  0.08133  0.21887  0.83900 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -0.57833    0.66632  -0.868    0.389    
Weight       0.35342    0.03194  11.066   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.3501 on 65 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6532,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6479 
F-statistic: 122.4 on 1 and 65 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Even though I don’t know the units for red blood cell density, I doubt they can be negative. Perhaps more important, among the 67 mice in the data set I used, none had weight lower than 17.725 grams.

range(d$Weight)

[1] 17.725 23.219


Estimating the red blood cell density for a mouse weighing less than that is extrapolating beyond the data, which is never a good idea. This may be why the intercept was so weird.
What should we do in this case? Typically, we subtract the same value (we can call it \(c\)) from the explanatory variable for every observation. Then, we refit the model with the new explanatory variable. The new intercept is the expected value of the outcome when the new explanatory variable is zero, which happens when the old explanatory variable is equal to \(c\).
Let’s look at the math, and then apply it to the mice example. Suppose \(X_i\) is the value of the explanatory variable for the \(i\)th observation and \(Y_i\) is the value of the explanatory variable for the \(i\)th observation. Define \(Z_i = X_i - c\). Then \[
\begin{align*}
E\left(Y_i \middle| Z_i = 0\right) &= E\left(Y_i \middle| X_i - c = 0\right) \\
&= E\left(Y_i \middle| X_i = c\right) \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
Since all the mice in my data set weigh between 17.725 and 23.219 grams, I’m going to choose \(c = 20\). This is a bit arbitrary, but it’s a round number in the range of my data.

d$Weight_20 <- d$Weight - 20

Now I’m going to re-do the regression, but with the new explanatory variable.

mod_02 <- lm(formula = RBC ~ Weight_20,
             data = d)
summary(mod_02)


Call:
lm(formula = RBC ~ Weight_20, data = d)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-0.85802 -0.18339  0.08133  0.21887  0.83900 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  6.49002    0.05015  129.42   <2e-16 ***
Weight_20    0.35342    0.03194   11.07   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.3501 on 65 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6532,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6479 
F-statistic: 122.4 on 1 and 65 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The new intercept is about 6.5. So, we would expect a red blood cell density of 6.5 for a mouse weighing 20 grams. This is far more trustworthy than the original intercept because we observed mice weighing around 20 grams, but no mice weighing about 0 grams.
Note that the slope didn’t change. If we shift the explanatory variable to the left or right, the slope of the line should not change. Only the intercept should change.
How do you decide what to subtract? It should be a value in the range of your data, or not too far from it. It should be meaningful to your scientific question. Some people recommend using the sample average of the explanatory variable, but I don’t like to do that because the sample average changes with every sample.

title: 46  Robust Standard Errors
text:
46.1 Learning Objective
Use robust standard errors in the presence of heteroscedasticity.

title: 46  Robust Standard Errors
text:
46.2 Lesson

46.2.1 Overview and Example
If the linearity and iid assumptions of simple linear regression are met, and if you have a large sample size, but your residuals are heteroscedastic, you can compute robust standard errors. “Robust” in statistics typically means “correct even when assumptions are violated”. You’ll need two packages, lmtest and sandwich. (“Sandwich” comes from the form for the standard errors when expressed in linear algebra.)
Let’s take a look at an example that met the linearity and iid assumptions, had a large sample size, and had heteroscedastic residuals. The forest fire example fits these requirements. Each observation is a forest fire in Montesinho Park (Portugal) between January 2000 and December 2003 where at least 0.01 hectare (100 square meters) was burned. In the figure below, I’ve plotted \(\log_{10}(\text{area burned})\) as a function of the outside temperature.









If I regress \(\log_{10}(\text{area burned})\) on temperature, this is the resulting residual plot:









Here’s the regression results without robust standard errors:

You can see that the Estimate column hasn’t changed, but the remaining columns have. This is because the standard errors have been re-computed, and the \(t\)-values and p-values depend on the standard errors. In this example, the conclusions drawn from the p-values have not changed. The intercept is still significantly different from zero and the slope is not.


46.2.2 Simulation Study
In the example above, the conclusions didn’t change after using robust standard errors. How heteroscedastic do the errors have to be for the robust standard errors to make a difference? Let’s conduct a simulation study to find out.

46.2.3 Math
If you’re curious about how the robust standard errors are computed, click on the button below.






CautionCaution: Math





I’m going to explain this as though we’re talking about multiple linear regression rather than simple linear regression, because it’s more general. In multiple linear regression, we have \(p\) explanatory variables. In simple linear regression, we have one explanatory variable.
Our estimator is \[
\mathbf{\hat{\beta}} = \left(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{Y} \text{,}
\] where

\(\mathbf{\hat{\beta}}\) is the \((p+1)\times 1\) column vector of coefficient estimates;
\(\mathbf{X}\) is the \(n\times(p+1)\) matrix of covariate values; and
\(\mathbf{Y}\) is the \(n\times 1\) column vector of outcome variable values.

We have \[
\begin{align*}
Cov\left(\mathbf{\hat{\beta}}\middle|\mathbf{X}\right) &= Cov\left(\left(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{Y}\middle|\mathbf{X}\right) \\
&= \left(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}^\top Cov\left(\mathbf{Y}\middle|\mathbf{X}\right) \mathbf{X} \left(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\] If the iid and homoscedasticity assumptions are true then \[
\begin{align*}
Cov\left(\mathbf{\hat{\beta}}\middle|\mathbf{X}\right) &= \left(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}^\top Cov\left(\mathbf{Y}\middle|\mathbf{X}\right) \mathbf{X} \left(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \\
&= \left(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}^\top \left(\sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_n\right) \mathbf{X} \left(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \\
&= \sigma^2 \left(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}^\top \ \mathbf{X} \left(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \\
&= \sigma^2 \left(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\] The standard errors you see in the output from lm are the square root of the diagonal of \[
\widehat{Cov}\left(\mathbf{\hat{\beta}}\middle|\mathbf{X}\right) = \hat{\sigma}^2 \left(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \text{.}
\]
If the iid and/or homoscedasticity assumptions are not met, then you have to use \[
\begin{align*}
\widehat{Cov}\left(\mathbf{\hat{\beta}}\middle|\mathbf{X}\right) &= \left(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}^\top \widehat{Cov}\left(\mathbf{Y}\middle|\mathbf{X}\right) \mathbf{X} \left(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\right)^{-1}  \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\] This is what’s used to get the robust/sandwich standard errors. The word “sandwich” is used because you have a symmetric expression with two similar things enclosing a different thing.

Let’s return to the lizard and ant study, in which lizards from invaded and uninvaded habitats were exposed to fire ants. The outcome variable is the number of times the lizards twitched. Both p-values are far below 0.05, so in each case we reject the null hypothesis. We can conclude that the expected number of twitches among lizards from uninvaded habitats is not equal to zero and that there is a statistically significant difference between the average number of twitches by lizards from uninvaded habitats and lizards from invaded habitats.
Another way of phrasing the conclusion about the slope is that the expected number of twitches among lizards from uninvaded habitats is different from the expected number of twitches among lizards from invaded habitats.
