title: 47  Linearity Assumption
text: 47.1 Learning Objective

title: 47  Linearity Assumption
text:
Explain the linearity assumption of multiple linear regression.
Explain the consequences of violations of the linearity assumption of multiple linear regression.
Evaluate the validity of the linearity assumption of multiple linear regression in a data set.

title: 47  Linearity Assumption
text:
47.2 Lesson

47.2.1 Assumption
I’m going to express the linearity assumption of multiple linear regression in two ways. The first is with \(\epsilon_i\) denoting the random error. In multiple linear regression, we assume \[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 X_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} + \epsilon_i
\] and \[
E\left(\epsilon_i\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right) = 0 \text{.}
\] In simple linear regression, we had one explanatory variable. In multiple linear regression, we have \(p\) explanatory variables, where \(p \ge 2\). We use \(X_{ij}\) to denote the value of the \(j\)th explanatory variable for the \(i\)th observation. We still just have one random error for the \(i\)th observation, denoted \(\epsilon_i\). We assume this random error has mean zero, conditional on the explanatory variables.
The second way to denote the linearity assumption of multiple linear regression is \[
E\left(Y_i\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 X_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \text{.}
\] I find this representation to be less intuitive, but it will be useful later, when we encounter logistic regression and Poisson regression.


47.2.2 Note
Strictly, the linearity assumption is \[
E(Y_i|X_{11},\dotsc,X_{1p},\dotsc,X_{n1},\dotsc,X_{np}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 X_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \text{,}
\] but that’s very cumbersome to write. It’s far simpler using linear algebra: \[
E\left(\mathbf{Y}\middle|\mathbf{X}\right) = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{\beta} \text{.}
\] Since linear algebra is not required for this course, I’ll stick to the simpler notation used in the previous section.


47.2.3 Consequences
If the linearity assumption is met, then the coefficient estimates (i.e., \(\hat{\beta}_0\), \(\hat{\beta}_1\), \(\hat{\beta}_2\), etc.) are unbiased. This means we can interpret them.


47.2.4 Evaluation
The best and most comprehensive way to check the linearity assumption of multiple linear regression is to make scatterplots. In each one, the residuals will be on the vertical axis and a different explanatory variable will be on the horizontal axis. We can also make a scatterplot with the residuals on the vertical axis and the fitted values on the horizontal axis.
Let’s look at some examples.

47.2.4.1 Example 1: Not met in either variable
In this example, the outcome doesn’t have a linear relationship with either explanatory variable. The underlying regression equation is \[
E\left(Y_i\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right) = 1 + X_{i1}^2 + X_{i2}^2 \text{.}
\] Note that \(\beta_0 = \beta_1 = \beta_2 = 1\). Let’s look at the resulting plots.























In each plot, there is a non-linear relationship between the mean of the residuals and the variable on the horizontal axis.


47.2.4.2 Example 2: Met in one variable
In this example, the outcome doesn’t have a linear relationship with one explanatory variable, but it does with the other. The underlying regression equation is \[
E\left(Y_i\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right) = 1 + X_{i1} + X_{i2}^2 \text{.}
\] Note that \(\beta_0 = \beta_1 = \beta_2 = 1\). Let’s look at the resulting plots.























For two of the plots (the one with \(X_1\) on the horizontal axis and the one with \(\hat{Y}\) on the horizontal axis), it appears that the residuals have mean 0 regardless of the value of the variable on the horizontal axis. For one of the plots (the one with \(X_2\) on the horizontal axis), there is a clear non-linear relationship between the mean of the residuals and the variable on the horizontal axis.
There are a couple important things to note here. The first is that in practice, many people only look at a plot of the residuals as a function of the fitted values. This saves time, especially if you have many explanatory variables. However, as shown in this example, if you do this you may not catch a non-linearity.
Second, it may appear as though the mean of the residuals is not 0 for all values of \(X_1\) (or for all fitted values) since so many of the points lie below the horizontal line at 0. Recall that the mean of the residuals needs to be 0 throughout the plot, not the median. If we look at a histogram of the residuals, we see that they are right-skewed.









I put a vertical blue line at the mean (which is equal to zero) and a vertical purple line at the median. If you can’t distinguish blue from purple, just know that the mean is the right-most vertical line. Since the residuals are right-skewed, and the mean is sensitive to outliers, the mean is greater than the median.
So, in the scatterplots above, the median may lie below the red horizontal line, but the mean is approximately at the red horizontal line, no matter the value of \(X_1\) or \(\hat{Y}\).


47.2.4.3 Example 3: Met in both variables
In this example, the outcome has a linear relationship with both explanatory variables. The underlying regression equation is \[
E\left(Y_i\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right) = 1 + X_{i1} + X_{i2} \text{.}
\] Note that \(\beta_0 = \beta_1 = \beta_2 = 1\). Let’s look at the resulting plots.























In all three plots, the mean of the residuals is approximately zero, no matter the value of the variable on the horizontal axis.


47.2.4.4 Note
Note that it’s not necessarily a problem if the underlying regression equation is \[
E\left(Y_i\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right) = 1 + X_{i1}^2 + X_{i2}^2 \text{.}
\] We can just treat \(X_{i1}^2\) and \(X_{i2}^2\) as the explanatory variables instead of \(X_{i1}\) and \(X_{i2}\). For the plots below, I’ve fit this model.























Note that, no matter the value of the variable on the horizontal axis, the mean of the residuals is approximately zero.
If you’re curious about why the residuals are bunched up to the left, it’s because \(X_1,X_2\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}N(0,4)\). Most of the values of \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are thus close to zero. When they get squared, we double up on the values that are close to zero but positive. Recall that \((-x)^2 = x^2 \ge 0\).

title: 47  Linearity Assumption
text:
47.3 Problems

47.3.1 Problem 1
According to the following scatterplots, is the linearity assumption of multiple linear regression met for these data?





























TipSolution





The linearity assumption is not met for these data. Although the residuals have approximate mean zero for any value of \(X_1\) and \(\hat{Y}\), their mean has a non-linear relationship with \(X_2\). The mean of the residuals is above zero when \(|X_2| \ge 3\), and the man of the residuals is below zero when \(0 \le X_2 \le 2\).





47.3.2 Problem 2
Given your answer to Problem 1, should you interpret the estimated coefficients in that model?






TipSolution





No. Since the linearity assumption was not met, we should not interpret the coefficient estimates.
Some might argue that even when the linearity assumption is not met for some of the explanatory variables, you can interpret the coefficient estimates for the other explanatory variables. My suggestion is that you leave this judgment up to a statistician, at least at this stage in your training.

title: 48  IID Assumption
text: 48.1 Learning Objective

title: 48  IID Assumption
text:
Explain the iid assumption of multiple linear regression.
Explain the consequences of violations of the iid assumption of multiple linear regression.
Evaluate the validity of the iid assumption of multiple linear regression in a data set.

title: 48  IID Assumption
text:
48.2 Lesson

48.2.1 Assumption
This assumption is identical to the iid assumption of simple linear regression. We assume that the observations were drawn independently from the same population.


48.2.2 Note
We assume that the observations are independent; it’s okay if the explanatory variables are correlated. For example, suppose an instructor wants to know how performance on the final exam is associated with performance on the two midterms. Scores on the two midterms are probably positively correlated with each other; students who performed well on the first midterm are more likely to do well on the second midterm than students who performed poorly on the first midterm. The iid assumption doesn’t mean we can’t include both midterms as explanatory variables. In this example, the iid assumption seems to be met; our observations are drawn independently from the population of students of this one instructor for this one class. (In fact, if the instructor uses every student from this class in their analysis, they have a census.)


48.2.3 Consequences
For our purposes, the consequence of this assumption not being met is that the standard errors of the coefficient estimates will not be accurate. This means that our test statistics and p-values will not be accurate, either, since both are computed from the standard errors.


48.2.4 Evaluation
As with simple linear regression, we can’t check this assumption by looking at a plot. We have to examine how the data were collected. Ideally, the observations should be sampled uniformly at random from some population. Common data types that violate this assumption, and thus require different methods, are:

Longitudinal data, where the same unit (i.e., person, country, mouse) is observed more than once over time.
Hierarchical data, where units are organized into groups. This often includes educational data, where students are grouped within classrooms, which are grouped within schools, which are grouped within districts, and so forth.
Respondent-driven sampling, where participants refer their contacts into the study.

title: 48  IID Assumption
text:
48.3 Problems

48.3.1 Problem 1
Suppose a researcher wants to examine factors that influence visual acuity after laser eye surgery. The researcher recruits patients from several surgeons across Montreal and measures visual acuity in each eye, both before and after surgery. Would these data satisfy the iid assumption?






TipSolution





Probably not. For these data, the unit of observation is eye, which is clustered within individual, which is clustered within surgeon. We would need special techniques to analyze these data.





48.3.2 Problem 2
Suppose a researcher wants to examine factors that influence voice quality after vocal node removal. The researcher recruits patients seeing a single surgeon in New York City. Vocal quality (as measured by the harmonics-to-noise ratio) is measured before and after the surgery, and the before measurement is used as an explanatory variable. Would these data satisfy the iid assumption?






TipSolution





It sounds like it, yes. Each participant only has one voice and there’s only one surgeon. Although multiple measurements are taken over time, the pre-surgery measurement is used an explanatory variable, not as an outcome variable. So, it seems like the observations are iid.

title: 49  Homoscedasticity Assumption
text: 49.1 Learning Objective

title: 49  Homoscedasticity Assumption
text:
Explain the homoscedasticity assumption of multiple linear regression.
Explain the consequences of violations of the homoscedasticity assumption of multiple linear regression.
Evaluate the validity of the homoscedasticity assumption of multiple linear regression in a data set.

title: 49  Homoscedasticity Assumption
text:
49.2 Lesson

49.2.1 Assumption
The homoscedasticity assumption of multiple linear regression can be written in at least two ways. First, we assume \[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 X_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} + \epsilon_i
\] and \[
Var\left(\epsilon_i\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right) = \sigma^2 \text{.}
\] Note that \(\sigma^2\) doesn’t depend on \(i\) or any of the \(X_{ij}\)’s; it’s a constant. As in simple linear regression, “homoscedasticity” means “constant (or same) variance”.
The other way of writing this assumption is \[
Var\left(Y_i\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right) = \sigma^2 \text{.}
\]


49.2.2 Consequences
We need this assumption for our standard errors to be correct. If this assumption is not met (but the linearity and iid assumptions are and either the normality assumption is met or the sample size is large), we can use robust standard errors to get valid p-values. The code is the same as for simple linear regression.


49.2.3 Evaluation
Typically, to evaluate this assumption, we look at a scatterplot with the residuals on the vertical axis and the fitted values on the horizontal axis. What we want to see is constant vertical spread throughout the plot. This is similar to the evaluation of this assumption for simple linear regression, except for simple linear regression, we put the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis. With multiple linear regression, we have multiple explanatory variables, so to efficiently check the assumption we put the fitted value on the horizontal axis.
I don’t know of anyone who, in practice, checks for heteroscedasticity by plotting the residuals against each covariate. It’s good to plot the residuals against each covariate to check for non-linearity; if you did this and noticed that some of the plots had non-constant variance and some didn’t, it would be worth investigating.
One situation that would lead to this happening is if one variable had no relationship with the outcome. To make the plots below, I generated \(X\) and \(Y\) independently from each other, then generated \(Z\) from the model \[
Z_i = X_i + X_i \epsilon_i \text{.}
\] In other symbols, \[
E(Z_i|X_i) = X_i
\] but \[
Var(Z_i|X_i) = X_i^2 \sigma^2 \text{.}
\] \(Y\) is totally independent of \(Z\).









If we make three residual scatterplots, each of which has something different on the horizontal axis, we see heteroscedasticity in some of them but not all.

title: 49  Homoscedasticity Assumption
text:
49.3 Problems

49.3.1 Problem 1
As stated in the manual for the Lock5Data package, “The California Department of Developmental Services (DDS) allocates funds to support developmentally disabled California residents (such as those with autism, cerebral palsy, or intellectual disabilities) and their families. We refer to those supported by DDS as DDS consumers. The dataset DDS includes data on annual expenditure (in $), ethnicity, age, and gender for 1000 DDS consumers. [. . .] The dataset has been altered slightly for privacy reasons, but is based on actual DDS consumers.”

Is the homoscedasticity assumption met for this model? Justify your answer.






TipSolution





The homoscedasticity assumption is not met for this model. In the plot of the residuals as a function of the fitted values, we see far lower variability for lower fitted values than for higher fitted values.
This example is interesting because it’s a real-world example where there’s heteroscedasticity for some variables but not others. When ethnicity and age cohort are on the horizontal axis, we see non-constant variance; when gender is on the horizontal axis, we see equal variance in males and females. I’m not sure why this is, but practically, because there’s such obvious heteroscedasticity in the fitted value plot, we would need to use the robust (sandwich) standard errors.
If we look at the results from the model, we see that the p-value for Gender is very small, indicating that there is a statistically significant difference in expenditures between males and females, holding all else constant. So, this example doesn’t appear to be the same as the simulated data above.

title: 50  Normality Assumption
text: 50.1 Learning Objective

title: 50  Normality Assumption
text:
Explain the normality assumption of multiple linear regression.
Explain the consequences of violations of the normality assumption of multiple linear regression.
Evaluate the validity of the homoscedasticity assumption of multiple linear regression in a data set.

title: 50  Normality Assumption
text:
50.2 Lesson

50.2.1 Assumption
We can write this assumption in a couple ways. The first is \[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 X_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} + \epsilon_i
\] and \(\epsilon_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\) is normally distributed. In words, we’re assuming that the random error that gets added to our linear function is normally distributed. The second is that \(Y_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\) is normally distributed.


50.2.2 Consequences
If this assumption is not met, and you have a small sample size, the p-values that R outputs are not trustworthy. If this assumption is not met, but you have a large sample size and the linearity, iid, and homoscedasticity assumptions are met, you can still trust the default p-values in R output.
How large of a sample is large enough? This depends on how many covariates are in your model (how large \(p\) is) and how asymmetric your residuals are. It’s hard to give a single rule, so when in doubt, consult a statistician.


50.2.3 Evaluation
The way we check this assumption is exactly the same as for simple linear regression: we check if the residuals are normal. I like to use a boxplot, histogram, and q-q plot to check this.

title: 50  Normality Assumption
text:
50.3 Problems

50.3.1 Problem 1
The following plots are of residuals from a regression of heart rate (in beats per minute) on age (in years), sex (male or female), admission type (elective or emergency), and consciousness (conscious, deep stupor, or coma). The participants were 200 patients admitted to an adult intensive care unit (ICU).























Does this model satisfy the normality assumption?






TipSolution





Yes. From the boxplot, we see the residuals are symmetric; the histogram shows the residuals have a bell shape (with maybe a slight right skew); and in the q-q plot the points mostly follow the reference line. So, the residuals are normal, which is evidence that the random errors are normal.

title: 51  Categorical Explanatory Variables
text:
51.1 Learning Objective
Explain how R handles categorical explanatory variables.

title: 51  Categorical Explanatory Variables
text:
51.2 Lesson
The math underlying regression requires that all the variables be numeric, but it’s often desirable to use non-numeric data, especially as an explanatory variable. For example, you might want to investigate the relationship between stove type (e.g., gas, electric, coal, wood) and lung function. The different types of stove don’t fall along the number line; they can’t even really be ordered. So, if you pass a categorical variable (also called a polytomous variable) as an explanatory variable, what does R do?
Suppose your categorical variable is stove_type, and it has four levels: gas, electric, coal, and wood. R will choose one of the levels as a reference level (or reference group). If stove_type is a character vector, R will choose the first level in alphabetical order (in this case, coal). If stove_type is a factor vector, R will choose the first level. You can set the order of the levels using the factor function and you can change the reference level of a factor vector using the relevel function.
For every level that isn’t the reference, R will create a binary variable, meaning it only contains 0’s and 1’s. These new variables are called dummy variables. (R doesn’t actually add them to your data frame, it just creates them for the purposes of the regression.) In the example above, the new dummy variables would be stove_typegas, stove_typeelectric, and stove_typewood. The following table shows how the old levels would be coded for the new dummy variables.









Original Level
stove_typegas
stove_typeelectric
stove_typewood

electric
0
1

coal
0

wood

Which level should you choose to be the reference level? If all you care about is statistics, you should make the most common level the reference level. This will result in smaller standard errors for the coefficient estimates. If you care about interpretation, you should choose the level that you most want to compare to the other levels. As you’ll see in the section on interpretation, the coefficients for the dummy variables are interpreted as comparisons to the reference level.

title: 52  Interpretation
text:
52.1 Learning Objective
Interpret the coefficients in multiple linear regression.

title: 52  Interpretation
text:
52.2 Lesson

52.2.1 General Interpretation
The interpretation of coefficients in multiple linear regression is very similar to the interpretation of coefficients in simple linear regression, with one added detail. The intercept (\(\beta_0\)) is still the expected value of the outcome when all the explanatory variables equal 0. The coefficient corresponding to the \(j\)th explanatory variable, denoted \(\beta_j\), is the expected change in the outcome associated with a one-unit increase in the \(j\)th explanatory variable, holding all else constant. If \(\beta_j > 0\), the expected change is an increase; if \(\beta_j < 0\), the expected change is a decrease. The “else” in “holding all else constant” refers to the other explanatory variables. Another way of interpreting \(\beta_j\) is as the expected difference in the outcome between two populations that differ by one unit on the \(j\)th explanatory variable and have identical values for the other explanatory variables.


52.2.2 Math
\[
\begin{align*}
& E\left(Y_i\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ij} = x + 1,\dotsc,X_{ip}\right) - E\left(Y_i\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ij} = x ,\dotsc,X_{ip}\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_j (x+1) + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_j x + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_j x + \beta_j + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_{i1} - \cdots - \beta_j x - \cdots - \beta_p X_{ip} \\
&= \beta_j
\end{align*}
\]


52.2.3 Example
The following output comes from a regression of heart rate (in beats per minute) on age (in years), sex (male or female), admission type (elective or emergency), and consciousness (conscious, deep stupor, or coma). The participants were 200 patients admitted to an adult intensive care unit (ICU).

lm(formula = HeartRate ~ Age + sex + type + consciousness, data = d)

Residuals:

Age                       0.11394    0.09674   1.178  0.24032    
sexMale                  -0.70045    3.91747  -0.179  0.85828    
typeEmergency            12.40458    4.41874   2.807  0.00551 **

Multiple R-squared:  0.04968,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.02519

Let’s interpret each estimate.

52.2.3.1 Intercept
The estimated mean heart rate among female patients aged zero, who elected to come to the ICU, and who are in a coma, is about 72 beats per minute. Note that this intercept doesn’t make sense. How could a newborn in a coma elect to come to the adult ICU? Even if a newborn in a coma went to the ICU for a non-urgent reason, her heart rate wouldn’t be 72 beats per minute. That’s way too low.


52.2.3.2 Continuous Explanatory Variable
The estimated mean increase in heart rate associated with a one-year increase in age, holding all else constant, is 0.1 beats per minute.


52.2.3.3 Binary Explanatory Variable
The estimated mean difference in heart rate between males and females, holding all else constant, is 0.7 beats per minute, with men having the lower estimated mean heart rate. How did I know that men had the lower estimated mean heart rate? This coefficient is the expected increase in heart rate associated with a one-unit increase in the explanatory variable, holding all else constant. This particular explanatory variable only has two possible values: 0 (for females) and 1 (for males). So, a one-unit increase corresponds to a change from female to male. Since the coefficient estimate is negative, males have a lower estimated mean heart rate, holding all else constant.
Patients coming to the ICU for an emergency are expected to have a heart rate 12 beats per minute faster than patients electing to come to the ICU, holding all else constant.


52.2.3.4 Categorical Explanatory Variable
Conscious patients are expected to have a heart rate that is 1 beat per minute higher than comatose patients, holding all else equal. Why did I compare conscious patients to comatose patients? The dummy variable consciousnessConscious has two possible values, 0 and 1. A 1 can only mean one thing: that patient was conscious. A 0 can mean one of two things: either that patient was comatose or that patient was in a deep stupor. So why is it that the estimated coefficient associated with consciousnessConscious doesn’t compare comatose and deep stupor patients to conscious patients?
Recall that when interpreting a coefficient in multiple linear regression, we increase the corresponding covariate value by one unit and hold all other covariate values constant. So, when interpreting the coefficient estimate for consciousnessConscious, we have to increase consciousnessConscious by one unit and hold consciousnessDeep Stupor constant. As the following table shows, the only way to increase consciousnessConscious by one unit and hold consciousnessDeep Stupor constant is to increase consciousnessConscious by one unit and hold consciousnessDeep Stupor at 0. This means we compare comatose patients to conscious patients.

Holding all else constant, White not Hispanic recipients are expected to receive $3,116.09 more than American Indian recipients.






52.3.2 Problem 2
Suppose you run the following multiple linear regression with “country” as the unit of observation (i.e., each line in the data set is a country).

Outcome variable

Life expectancy (in years)

Explanatory variables

Pharmaceutical spending as a percentage of total health spending (in percentage points)
Total pharmaceutical spending (in millions of USD)
Pharmaceutical spending per capita (in USD)


“Pharmaceutical spending” refers to spending by consumers on both prescription and over-the-counter medication.
For the following questions, assume all relevant assumptions have been met.

52.3.2.1 Part (a)
How would you interpret the intercept for this analysis? Is it meaningful? Why or why not?






TipSolution





The intercept is the expected life expectancy for a country where consumers spend no money whatsoever on pharmaceuticals. This would make pharmaceutical spending zero as a percentage of total health spending; per capita; and in total. This is not meaningful, because such a country doesn’t exist. Even in very poor countries, people spend money on drugs.





52.3.2.2 Part (b)
How would you interpret the coefficient on “Pharmaceutical spending as a percentage of total health spending”? What are the implications of “holding all else equal” for the interpretation of this coefficient?






TipSolution





This is the expected increase in life expectancy associated with a one percentage point increase in pharmaceutical spending as a percentage of total health spending, holding all else equal.
If we increase pharmaceutical spending as a percentage of total health spending while fixing total pharmaceutical spending, we must be decreasing total health spending. If we increase pharmaceutical spending as a percentage of total health spending while fixing total pharmaceutical spending and pharmaceutical spending per capita, we must be decreasing total health spending and fixing the population of the country. So, this coefficient is a measure of the effect of decreasing total health spending (to the extent that we can interpret this causally).
Another way to interpret this coefficient is the expected difference between two countries that differ in their pharmaceutical spending as a percentage of total health spending by one percentage point, but that have identical total pharmaceutical spending, identical pharmaceutical spending per capita, and (as a result of the first two) identical populations. Even in this interpretation, one country must spend more on total health spending than the other in order to achieve the percentage difference, and the coefficient is a measure of the effect of decreasing total health spending (to the extent that we can interpret this causally).





52.3.2.3 Part (c)
How would you interpret the coefficient on “Total pharmaceutical spending”? What are the implications of “holding all else equal” for the interpretation of this coefficient?






TipSolution





This is the expected increase in life expectancy associated with a one million USD increase in total pharmaceutical spending, holding all else equal.
If we increase total pharmaceutical spending while fixing pharmaceutical spending per capita, we must be increasing the population as well. If we increase total pharmaceutical spending while fixing pharmaceutical spending as a percentage of total health spending, we must be increasing total health spending as well. So, this coefficient is measuring the expected change in life expectancy associated with an increase in total pharmaceutical spending, population, and total health spending. That’s a lot all at once!





52.3.2.4 Part (d)
How would you interpret the coefficient on “Pharmaceutical spending per capita”? What are the implications of “holding all else equal” for the interpretation of this coefficient?






TipSolution





This is the expected increase in life expectancy associated with a one USD increase in pharmaceutical spending per capita, holding all else equal.
If we increase pharmaceutical spending per capita while fixing total pharmaceutical spending, we must be decreasing the population. If we’re fixing total pharmaceutical spending and pharmaceutical spending as a percentage of total health spending, then we must be fixing total health spending. So, this coefficient is a measure of the effect of decreasing the population while holding total pharmaceutical spending and total health spending constant.






52.3.3 Problem 3
Consider the paper Association between Traffic Air Pollution and Reduced Forced Vital Capacity: A Study Using Personal Monitors for Outdoor Workers. Suppose we run two analyses, both with forced vital capacity (FVC; in liters) as the outcome. The first analysis is a simple linear regression with “time in job” (in years) as the explanatory variable, and the second is a multiple linear regression with “time in job” (in years) and age (in years) as the explanatory variables. Feel free to try this in R!

52.3.3.1 Part (a)
Interpret the intercept for the simple linear regression.






TipSolution





This is the expected FVC for an outdoor worker who just started their job.





52.3.3.2 Part (b)
Interpret the intercept for the multiple linear regression.






TipSolution





This is the expected FVC for an outdoor worker who just started their job and is zero years old.





52.3.3.3 Part (c)
Interpret the coefficient on “time in job” for the simple linear regression.






TipSolution





This is the expected increase in FVC associated with a one-year increase in time in job. Alternatively, it’s the expected difference in FVC between two workers who differ by one year in their time in the job.





52.3.3.4 Part (d)
Interpret the coefficient on “time in job” for the multiple linear regression.






TipSolution





This is the expected increase in FVC associated with a one-year increase in time in job, holding age constant. Alternatively, this is the expected difference in FVC between two workers who have the same age but differ by one year in their time in the job.





52.3.3.5 Part (e)
Interpret the coefficient on age for the multiple linear regression.






TipSolution





This is the expected increase in FVC associated with a one-year increase in age, holding time in job constant. Alternatively, this is the expected difference in FVC between two workers who have the same years of experience but who differ by one year in their age.






52.3.4 Problem 4
Suppose we run two analyses, both with prostate-specific antigen level (PSA; in ng/mL) as the outcome. The first analysis is a simple linear regression with smallpox vaccination (yes = 1, no = 0) as the explanatory variable, and the second is a multiple linear regression with smallpox vaccination and age (in years) as the explanatory variables.

52.3.4.1 Part (a)
Interpret the intercept for the simple linear regression.






TipSolution





This is the expected PSA for someone who was not vaccinated against smallpox.





52.3.4.2 Part (b)
Interpret the intercept for the multiple linear regression.






TipSolution





This is the expected PSA for someone who was not vaccinated against smallpox and is zero years old.





52.3.4.3 Part (c)
Interpret the coefficient on smallpox vaccination for the simple linear regression.






TipSolution





This is the expected difference in PSA between someone who has not been vaccinated against smallpox and someone who has.





52.3.4.4 Part (d)
Interpret the coefficient on smallpox vaccination for the multiple linear regression.






TipSolution





This is the expected difference in PSA between two people of the same age, one of whom has not been vaccinated against smallpox and one of whom has.





52.3.4.5 Part (e)
Interpret the coefficient on age in the multiple linear regression.






TipSolution





This is the expected increase in PSA associated with a one-year increase in age, holding vaccination status constant. Alternatively, this is the expected difference in PSA between people age \(x\) and people age \(x + 1\), where both groups have the same vaccination status.





52.3.4.6 Part (f)
According to the Mayo Clinic, “PSA levels normally increase with age”. According to the CDC, “Routine smallpox vaccination among the American public stopped in 1972 after the disease was eradicated in the United States.” What sign (positive, negative, or zero) do you think the slope in the simple linear regression would have? Justify your answer.






TipSolution





People who have been vaccinated against smallpox must be older, and probably have higher PSA levels. So, the slope in the simple linear regression should be positive.






52.3.5 Problem 5
Suppose you wanted to predict weight with height. Could you include height in feet and height in meters as explanatory variables in the same model? Why or why not?






TipSolution





No. Continuing with the theme of these problems, we can think about what the interpretation of the coefficients would be. The coefficient on height in feet would be the expected increase in weight associated with a one-foot increase in height, holding height in meters constant. You can’t increase height in feet while holding height in meters constant. Alternatively, the coefficient on height in feet would be the expected difference in weight between two groups of people that differ in height by one foot but have the same height in meters. That’s impossible.
That’s not really a reason, though; as you’ll see in the next question, it’s possible to run a regression even if the coefficients are not interpretable. The real reason this isn’t possible is mathematical. To summarize, one explanatory variable cannot be a linear combination of the others. Problems can even arise if one explanatory variable is close to being a linear combination of the others. If you get an error or warning about this while running multiple linear regression, you may need to remove one or more explanatory variables. Consult a statistician.





52.3.6 Problem 6
Suppose you regress salary (in USD) on age (in years) and age\(^2\) (in years\(^2\)).

52.3.6.1 Part (a)
How would you interpret the intercept?






TipSolution





This is the expected salary for someone who is zero years old.





52.3.6.2 Part (b)
How would you interpret the coefficient on age?






TipSolution





You can’t interpret this on its own because it’s impossible to increase age by one unit and not change age\(^2\). Interpreting the coefficients in a polynomial model is tricky; consult a statistician. Running this regression is possible because even though age\(^2\) is a function of age, it’s not a linear function of age. So, R will not complain.

title: 53  Hypothesis Testing
text:
53.1 Learning Objective
Interpret the results of a hypothesis test in the context of multiple linear regression.

title: 53  Hypothesis Testing
text:
53.2 Lesson

53.2.1 Overview
When conducting simple linear regression in R, R will automatically compute p-values for each of the coefficients. For each coefficient, the null hypothesis is that the coefficient is zero, and the alternative hypothesis is that the coefficient is not zero. In symbols, each hypothesis test is \[
\begin{align*}
H_0 &: \beta_j = 0 \\
H_1 &: \beta_j \ne 0
\end{align*}
\] where \(0 \le j \le p\).


53.2.2 Example
Let’s return to the ICU admissions data. The outcome is heart rate (in beats per minute) and the explanatory variables are age minus 20 (in years), sex (male or female), admission type (elective or emergency), and consciousness (conscious, deep stupor, or coma). The participants were 200 patients admitted to an adult intensive care unit (ICU). I subtracted 20 from age because the range of ages in the data set is 16 to 92, with first, second, and third quartiles at 46.75, 63, and 57.55.



Call:
lm(formula = HeartRate ~ age_20 + sex + type + consciousness, 
    data = d)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-62.112 -19.023  -3.831  16.990  87.614 

Coefficients:
                         Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)              74.00217   13.59321   5.444 1.56e-07 ***
age_20                    0.11394    0.09674   1.178  0.24032    
sexMale                  -0.70045    3.91747  -0.179  0.85828    
typeEmergency            12.40458    4.41874   2.807  0.00551 ** 
consciousnessConscious    1.17048   14.54758   0.080  0.93596    
consciousnessDeep Stupor 12.86837   12.01987   1.071  0.28568    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 26.49 on 194 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.04968,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.02519 
F-statistic: 2.029 on 5 and 194 DF,  p-value: 0.07631


How do we interpret the hypothesis test results? Let’s use \(\alpha = 0.05\) as our threshold for significance.

The p-value for the intercept is less than 0.05, so we conclude that the expected heart rate for a twenty-year-old female who came to the the ICU in a non-urgent coma is not equal to zero.
The p-value for age_20 is greater than 0.05, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis that this coefficient is equal to zero. There is no linear relationship between age and heart rate, holding all else constant.
The p-value for sexMale is greater than 0.05, so there is no difference between the expected heart rate for males and females, holding all else constant.
The p-value for typeEmergency is less than 0.05, so the expected heart rate for emergent patients is different from the expected heart rate for elective patients, holding all else equal.
The p-value for consciousnessConscious is greater than 0.05, so conscious patients do not have a different expected heart rate than comatose patients, holding all else equal.
The p-value for consciousnessDeep Stupor is greater than 0.05, so patients in a deep stupor do not have a different expected heart rate than comatose patients, holding all else equal.

title: 53  Hypothesis Testing
text:
53.3 Problems
For the regression below, each data point corresponds to a man who had his percent body fat estimated by underwater weighing. The explanatory variables are age (in years), weight (in pounds), height (in inches), neck circumference (in centimeters), chest circumference (in centimeters), abdomen circumference (in centimeters), ankle circumference (in centimeters), extended biceps circumference (in centimeters), and wrist circumference (in centimeters).



Call:
lm(formula = Bodyfat ~ Age + Weight + Height + Neck + Chest + 
    Abdomen + Ankle + Biceps + Wrist, data = d2)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-10.9819  -2.7798  -0.1037   2.7939   9.3505 

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -23.664200  29.459443  -0.803  0.42393    
Age           0.083779   0.050655   1.654  0.10163    
Weight       -0.083322   0.084706  -0.984  0.32792    
Height        0.035932   0.265770   0.135  0.89276    
Neck          0.001123   0.380079   0.003  0.99765    
Chest        -0.138742   0.160900  -0.862  0.39082    
Abdomen       1.032741   0.145857   7.080 3.06e-10 ***
Ankle         0.225943   0.541725   0.417  0.67761    
Biceps        0.148276   0.229519   0.646  0.51990    
Wrist        -2.203399   0.812923  -2.710  0.00805 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 4.136 on 90 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.7575,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.7332 
F-statistic: 31.23 on 9 and 90 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16



53.3.1 Problem 1
Interpret the hypothesis test corresponding to each coefficient. Use \(\alpha = 0.05\).






TipSolution






The p-value for the intercept is greater than 0.05, so we cannot conclude that the expected body fat percentage for a newborn weighing zero pounds and having zero for all length measurements is different from zero. This makes sense. Someone who effectively doesn’t exist should have zero percent body fat.
The p-value for Age is greater than 0.05, so there is not a linear relationship between age and the expected body fat percentage.
The p-value for Weight is greater than 0.05, so there is not a linear relationship between weight and the expected body fat percentage.
The p-value for Height is greater than 0.05, so there is not a linear relationship between height and the expected body fat percentage.
The p-value for Neck is greater than 0.05, so there is not a linear relationship between neck circumference and the expected body fat percentage.
The p-value for Chest is greater than 0.05, so there is not a linear relationship between chest circumference and the expected body fat percentage.
The p-value for Abdomen is less than 0.05, so there is a linear relationship beteen abdomen circumference and the expected body fat percentage.
The p-value for Ankle is greater than 0.05, so there is not a linear relationship between ankle circumference and the expected body fat percentage.
The p-value for Biceps is greater than 0.05, so there is not a linear relationship between biceps circumference and the expected body fat percentage.
The p-value for Wrist is less than 0.05, so there is a linear relationship beteen wrist circumference and the expected body fat percentage.

By the way, all of these conclusions only apply to men, since all the participants in the study were men.





53.3.2 Problem 2
Why do you think height was measured in inches but the circumferences were measured in centimeters? I don’t have any special knowledge for why this was done, but it’s worth brainstorming ideas.






TipSolution





It’s possible that this was done because of convention. Maybe body circumference measurements have traditionally been made by one profession that uses the metric system, whereas height is something everyone measures, and these participants came from a country that uses the imperial system.
There is a computational reason why you might use different units for different lengths. Computing the coefficient estimates can get messed up when the variables are on wildly different units. (If you’re curious why, look up condition number.) So, if you’re running a regression where one of the explanatory variables has very small values and another has very large values (like the weight of an elephant and the weight of the medicine it has been administered), you should consider changing the units of one or both so that the values are on similar scales (like measuring the elephant’s weight in kilograms and the medicine’s weight in milligrams). (Apparently, “the effective dose of ibuprofen is six milligrams per kilogram of weight for Asian elephants and seven milligrams per kilogram for African elephants, given every 12 hours.” Who knew?)

title: 54  Interaction Between Two Binary Variables
text: 54.1 Learning Objective
crumbs: 54  Interaction Between Two Binary Variables

title: 54  Interaction Between Two Binary Variables
text:
Interpret the coefficients of a multiple linear regression model with an interaction between two binary explanatory variables.
Define, use, and interpret the terms “moderation” and “moderator”.
Interpret the results of a hypothesis test in the context of multiple linear regression with an interaction term.
crumbs: 54  Interaction Between Two Binary Variables

title: 54  Interaction Between Two Binary Variables
text:
54.2 Lesson

54.2.1 Math
Suppose our linear model is \[
E(Y_i|X_{i1},X_{i2}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \beta_2 X_{i2} + \beta_3 X_{i1} X_{i2} \text{,}
\] where both \(X_{i1}\) and \(X_{i2}\) can only be 0 or 1. The product of the two explanatory variables, \(X_{i1} X_{i2}\), is called an interaction. How do we interpret the coefficients when there’s an interaction?
\(\beta_0\) is still the expected value of the outcome when all the explanatory variables are equal to zero: \[
\begin{align*}
E(Y_i|X_{i1} = 0,X_{i2} = 0) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 (0) + \beta_3 (0) (0) \\
&= \beta_0 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
\(\beta_1\) is the expected difference in the outcome between observations with \(X_{1} = 0\) and \(X_{1} = 1\), holding \(X_2\) constant at zero: \[
\begin{align*}
E(Y_i|X_{i1} = 1,X_{i2} = 0) - E(Y_i|X_{i1} = 0,X_{i2} = 0) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (1) + \beta_2 (0) + \beta_3 (1) (0) - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 (0) + \beta_3 (0) (0)\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1  - \left(\beta_0 \right) \\
&= \beta_1 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] Note that with the interaction term, we are not just holding the other variable constant in general, we are holding it constant at a specific value.
\(\beta_2\) is the expected difference in the outcome between observations with \(X_{2} = 0\) and \(X_{2} = 1\), holding \(X_1\) constant at zero: \[
\begin{align*}
E(Y_i|X_{i1} = 0,X_{i2} = 1) - E(Y_i|X_{i1} = 0,X_{i2} = 0) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 (1) + \beta_3 (0) (1) - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 (0) + \beta_3 (0) (0)\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_2 (1)  - \left(\beta_0 \right) \\
&= \beta_2 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
\(\beta_1 + \beta_3\) is the expected difference in the outcome between observations with \(X_{1} = 0\) and \(X_{1} = 1\), holding \(X_2\) constant at 1: \[
\begin{align*}
E(Y_i|X_{i1} = 1,X_{i2} = 1) - E(Y_i|X_{i1} = 0,X_{i2} = 1) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (1) + \beta_2 (1) + \beta_3 (1) (1) - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 (1) + \beta_3 (0) (1)\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1 + \beta_2 + \beta_3 - \left(\beta_0  + \beta_2 \right) \\
&= \beta_1 + \beta_3 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
\(\beta_2 + \beta_3\) is the expected difference in the outcome between observations with \(X_{2} = 0\) and \(X_{2} = 1\), holding \(X_1\) constant at 1: \[
\begin{align*}
E(Y_i|X_{i1} = 1,X_{i2} = 1) - E(Y_i|X_{i1} = 1,X_{i2} = 0) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (1) + \beta_2 (1) + \beta_3 (1) (1) - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 (1) + \beta_2 (0) + \beta_3 (1) (0)\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1 + \beta_2 + \beta_3 - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1  \right) \\
&= \beta_2 + \beta_3 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]


54.2.2 Example
Let’s return to the ICU admissions data. The outcome is heart rate (in beats per minute). In the following regression analysis, I interacted sex (male or female) and admission type (elective or emergency). The participants were 200 patients admitted to an adult intensive care unit (ICU).



Call:
lm(formula = HeartRate ~ sex * type, data = d)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
-62.07 -17.22  -3.07  18.18  90.93 

Coefficients:
                      Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)            90.4667     6.8696  13.169   <2e-16 ***
sexMale                 0.9018     8.1129   0.111    0.912    
typeEmergency          12.2219     7.6679   1.594    0.113    
sexMale:typeEmergency  -2.5205     9.2550  -0.272    0.786    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 26.61 on 196 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.03143,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.01661 
F-statistic:  2.12 on 3 and 196 DF,  p-value: 0.09894


How do we interpret the coefficient estimates? To make this a little more clear, I’m going to write the regression equation with words: \[
\hat{E}\left(\texttt{HeartRate}\middle|\texttt{sexMale},\texttt{typeEmergency}\right) = 90.4667 + 0.9018 \texttt{sexMale} + 12.2219 \texttt{typeEmergency} - 2.5205 \texttt{sexMale}\times \texttt{typeEmergency} \text{.}
\]
The estimated mean heart rate among females who elected to come to the ICU is 90.4667 beats per minute: \[
\begin{align*}
\hat{E}\left(\texttt{HeartRate} \middle|\texttt{sexMale}= 0,\texttt{typeEmergency}= 0\right) &= 90.4667 + 0.9018 (0) + 12.2219 (0) - 2.5205 (0)\times (0) \\
&= 90.4667 \\
\end{align*}
\]
The estimated mean heart rate among males who elected to come to the ICU is \(90.4667 + 0.9018 = 91.3685\) beats per minute: \[
\begin{align*}
\hat{E}\left(\texttt{HeartRate} \middle|\texttt{sexMale}= 1,\texttt{typeEmergency}= 0\right) &= 90.4667 + 0.9018 (1) + 12.2219 (0) - 2.5205 (1)\times (0) \\
&= 90.4667 + 0.9018 \\
&= 91.3685 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
As a result of the previous two interpretations, the estimated mean difference in heart rate between males and females who elected to come to the ICU is 0.9018 beats per minute. This is the coefficient on \(\texttt{sexMale}\).
The estimated mean heart rate among females who came to the ICU for an emergency is \(90.4667 + 12.2219 = 102.6886\) beats per minute: \[
\begin{align*}
\hat{E}\left(\texttt{HeartRate} \middle|\texttt{sexMale}= 0,\texttt{typeEmergency}= 1\right) &= 90.4667 + 0.9018 (0) + 12.2219 (1) - 2.5205 (0)\times (1) \\
&= 90.4667 + 12.2219 \\
&= 102.6886 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
The estimated mean heart rate among males who came to the ICU for an emergency is \(90.4667 + 0.9018 + 12.2219 - 2.5205 = 101.0699\): \[
\begin{align*}
\hat{E}\left(\texttt{HeartRate} \middle|\texttt{sexMale}= 1,\texttt{typeEmergency}= 1\right) &= 90.4667 + 0.9018 (1) + 12.2219 (1) - 2.5205 (1)\times (1) \\
&= 90.4667 + 0.9018 + 12.2219 - 2.5205 \\
&= 101.0699 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
As a result of the previous two interpretations, the estimated mean difference in heart rate between males and females who came to the ICU for an emergency is \(102.6886 - 101.0699 = 2.5205 - 0.9018 = 1.6187\) beats per minute.


54.2.3 Moderation
An interaction is the statistical way to model moderation. With moderation, the association of one explanatory variable with the outcome is moderated by another explanatory variable. This second explanatory variable, the one that does the moderating, is called a moderator. (Some people say “effect modification” instead of “moderation”, but I’m avoiding the word “effect” because I want to use these terms even for non-causal data.)
In the example above, the association between visit type and heart rate is modified by gender. For men, coming to the ICU for an emergency is associated with a \(101.0699 - 91.3685 = 9.7014\) bpm increase in mean heart rate. For women, though, coming to the ICU for an emergency is associated with a \(102.6886 - 90.4667 = 12.2219\) bmp increase in mean heart rate.
It would be equivalent to say that the association between gender and heart rate is modified by visit type. For elective visits, the estimated mean difference between male and female heart rates is \(91.3685 - 90.4667 = 0.9018\) bpm. For emergency visits, though, the estimated mean difference between male and female heart rates is \(101.0699 - 102.6886 = -1.6187\) bpm. (I used a negative here to indicate that the direction is opposite that for elective visits. For elective visits, males have the higher estimated mean heart rate, but for emergency visits, females have the higher estimated mean heat rate.)


54.2.4 Hypothesis Testing
Now, I’ve said that gender is a moderator and I’ve said that visit type is a moderator, but I really shouldn’t be making that claim without a hypothesis test. Although the association between gender and heart rate is different for the two different visit types, we should check if that difference is statistically significant. The difference is quantified by the coefficient on the interaction term itself, so we should check the p-value for that coefficient. In the output above, we want the p-value associated with sexMale:typeEmergency. This p-value is 0.786, which is way higher than any reasonable threshold we would use. So, we fail to reject the hypothesis that the interaction coefficient is zero. We can conclude that there is no evidence for moderation of the association between gender and heart rate by visit type (or between visit type and heart rate by gender). For parsimony, we should re-fit the model without the interaction term, which is what I’ve done below.



Call:
lm(formula = HeartRate ~ sex + type, data = d)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
-62.31 -17.47  -2.82  17.94  90.69 

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)     91.855      4.593  20.001   <2e-16 ***
sexMale         -1.035      3.895  -0.266   0.7907    
typeEmergency   10.492      4.284   2.449   0.0152 *  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 26.54 on 197 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.03107,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.02123 
F-statistic: 3.158 on 2 and 197 DF,  p-value: 0.04466

title: 54  Interaction Between Two Binary Variables
text:
54.3 Problems

54.3.1 Problem 1
Suppose a researcher finds that suicidal ideation is a risk factor for attempted suicide. For someone who does not own a gun, exhibiting suicidal ideation is not associated with a large increase in risk of suicide, but for someone who does own a gun, exhibiting suicidal ideation is associated with a large increase in risk of suicide. What is the moderator in this example?






TipSolution





Gun ownership. For those with a gun, there is a strong association between suicidal ideation and suicide risk, but for those without a gun, the association is weaker.





54.3.2 Problem 2
Suppose you are conducting a clinical trial in which patients are randomized to drug or placebo. You measure the outcome before administration of the drug/placebo and again after. Define the following:

\(Y_{ij}\) is the outcome for the \(i\)th patient at the \(j\)th time-point. So, \(i\in\{1,2,3,\dotsc,n\}\) and \(j\in\{1,2\}\). (If you haven’t seen this notation before, \(\in\) means “in” or “is in” or “is an element of”.)
\(D_i = 1\) if patient \(i\) received the drug and \(D_i = 0\) if patient \(i\) received the placebo.
\(A_2 = 1\) and \(A_1 = 0\). You can think of \(A\) as meaning “after”.

Suppose our model is \[
Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \beta_2 A_j + \beta_3 D_i A_j + \epsilon_{ij} \text{.}
\] This is an example of non-independent data because we have two observations per individual. We can still interpret our coefficients if our first assumption is met, so let’s assume it is.

54.3.2.1 Part (a)
What is the expected change in the outcome from before to after administration of the drug?






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
    &E(Y_{ij}|D_i = 1,A_i = 1) - E(Y_{ij}|D_i = 1,A_i = 0) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (1) + \beta_2 (1) + \beta_3 (1) (1) - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 (1) + \beta_2 (0) + \beta_3 (1) (0)) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1  + \beta_2  + \beta_3  - (\beta_0 + \beta_1  ) \\
    &= \beta_2 + \beta_3
\end{align*}
\]





54.3.2.2 Part (b)
What is the expected change in the outcome from before to after administration of the placebo?






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
    &E(Y_{ij}|D_i = 0,A_i = 1) - E(Y_{ij}|D_i = 0,A_i = 0) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 (1) + \beta_3 (0) (1) - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 (0) + \beta_3 (0) (0)) \\
    &= \beta_0  + \beta_2  - (\beta_0 ) \\
    &= \beta_2 \\
\end{align*}
\]





54.3.2.3 Part (c)
What is the expected difference between the change in the outcome from before to after administration of the drug and the change in the outcome from before to after administration of the placebo?






TipSolution





\(\beta_3\)

title: 55  Interaction Between One Binary Variable and One Categorical Variable
text:
55.2 Lesson
Jeremy Groves, an anesthetist in the UK, timed his commute when using two different bikes. Below are the results of a regression of commute time in minutes on bike type (steel or carbon) and month of the year (January through July), with an interaction between the two explanatory variables. The distance traveled was approximately 27 miles for each commute.



Call:
lm(formula = Minutes ~ Bike * Month, data = d2)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-5.8433 -2.2657 -0.2564  1.5394  7.3280 

Coefficients:
                     Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)           114.755      2.538  45.224  < 2e-16 ***
BikeSteel               0.655      3.589   0.183 0.856050    
Month2Feb               3.588      3.276   1.095 0.279596    
Month3Mar              -3.662      2.877  -1.273 0.210094    
Month4Apr             -11.698      3.276  -3.571 0.000908 ***
Month5May             -10.215      3.589  -2.847 0.006809 ** 
Month6June            -14.375      3.589  -4.006 0.000247 ***
Month7July             -9.655      2.877  -3.356 0.001689 ** 
BikeSteel:Month2Feb    -5.972      4.633  -1.289 0.204457    
BikeSteel:Month3Mar    -3.465      4.107  -0.844 0.403642    
BikeSteel:Month4Apr     5.622      4.444   1.265 0.212757    
BikeSteel:Month5May    -2.473      4.747  -0.521 0.605221    
BikeSteel:Month6June    3.567      4.679   0.762 0.450109    
BikeSteel:Month7July    0.947      4.159   0.228 0.820964    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 3.589 on 42 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6751,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.5745 
F-statistic: 6.713 on 13 and 42 DF,  p-value: 1.033e-06


How do we interpret these coefficients? We can represent the model as follows (please forgive the abbreviations): \[
\begin{align*}
& \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste},\texttt{Feb},\texttt{Mar},\texttt{Apr},\texttt{May},\texttt{Jun},\texttt{Jul}\right) \\
&= 114.755 + 0.655 \texttt{Ste} + 3.588 \texttt{Feb} - 3.662\texttt{Mar} - 11.698\texttt{Apr} - 10.215 \texttt{May} - 14.375 \texttt{Jun} -9.655 \texttt{Jul} \\
&\qquad - 5.972 \texttt{Ste}\times\texttt{Feb} - 3.465 \texttt{Ste}\times\texttt{Mar} + 5.622 \texttt{Ste}\times\texttt{Apr} - 2.473 \texttt{Ste}\times\texttt{May} + 3.567 \texttt{Ste}\times\texttt{Jun} + 0.947 \texttt{Ste}\times\texttt{Jul} \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]

55.2.1 Intercept
The estimated mean commute time in January on a carbon bike is 114.755 minutes. \[
\begin{align*}
& \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste}=0,\texttt{Feb}=0,\texttt{Mar}=0,\texttt{Apr}=0,\texttt{May}=0,\texttt{Jun}=0,\texttt{Jul=0}\right) \\
&= 114.755 + 0.655 (0) + 3.588 (0) - 3.662(0) - 11.698(0) - 10.215 (0) - 14.375 (0) -9.655 (0) \\
&\qquad - 5.972 (0)\times(0) - 3.465 (0)\times(0) + 5.622 (0)\times(0) - 2.473 (0)\times(0) + 3.567 (0)\times(0) + 0.947 (0)\times(0) \\
&= 114.755 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]


55.2.2 Comparing Months on a Carbon Bike
The estimated mean difference in commute times between January and February on a carbon bike is 3.588 minutes, with February taking longer. \[
\begin{align*}
& \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste}=0,\texttt{Feb}=1,\texttt{Mar}=0,\texttt{Apr}=0,\texttt{May}=0,\texttt{Jun}=0,\texttt{Jul}=0\right) \\
&\qquad - \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste}=0,\texttt{Feb}=0,\texttt{Mar}=0,\texttt{Apr}=0,\texttt{May}=0,\texttt{Jun}=0,\texttt{Jul}=0\right) \\
&= 114.755 + 0.655 (0) + 3.588 (1) - 3.662(0) - 11.698(0) - 10.215 (0) - 14.375 (0) -9.655 (0) \\
&\qquad - 5.972 (0)\times(1) - 3.465 (0)\times(0) + 5.622 (0)\times(0) - 2.473 (0)\times(0) + 3.567 (0)\times(0) + 0.947 (0)\times(0) \\
&\qquad - 114.755 \\
&= 3.588 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
The estimated mean difference in commute times between January and March on a carbon bike is 3.662 minutes, with January taking longer. \[
\begin{align*}
& \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste}=0,\texttt{Feb}=0,\texttt{Mar}=1,\texttt{Apr}=0,\texttt{May}=0,\texttt{Jun}=0,\texttt{Jul}=0\right) \\
&\qquad - \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste}=0,\texttt{Feb}=0,\texttt{Mar}=0,\texttt{Apr}=0,\texttt{May}=0,\texttt{Jun}=0,\texttt{Jul}=0\right) \\
&= 114.755 + 0.655 (0) + 3.588 (0) - 3.662(1) - 11.698(0) - 10.215 (0) - 14.375 (0) -9.655 (0) \\
&\qquad - 5.972 (0)\times(0) - 3.465 (0)\times(1) + 5.622 (0)\times(0) - 2.473 (0)\times(0) + 3.567 (0)\times(0) + 0.947 (0)\times(0) \\
&\qquad - 114.755 \\
&= -3.662 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
I hope this demonstrates a pattern: The coefficients on each month variable represent a comparison between that month and January, on a carbon bike.

The estimated mean difference in commute times between January and April on a carbon bike is 11.698 minutes, with January taking longer.
The estimated mean difference in commute times between January and May on a carbon bike is 10.215 minutes, with January taking longer.
The estimated mean difference in commute times between January and June on a carbon bike is 14.375 minutes, with January taking longer.
The estimated mean difference in commute times between January and July on a carbon bike is 9.655 minutes, with January taking longer.



55.2.3 Comparing Months on a Steel Bike
The estimated mean difference in commute times between January and February on a steel bike is \(|3.588-5.972| = |-2.384| = 2.384\) minutes, with January taking longer: \[
\begin{align*}
& \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste}=1,\texttt{Feb}=1,\texttt{Mar}=0,\texttt{Apr}=0,\texttt{May}=0,\texttt{Jun}=0,\texttt{Jul}=0\right) \\
&\qquad - \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste}=1,\texttt{Feb}=0,\texttt{Mar}=0,\texttt{Apr}=0,\texttt{May}=0,\texttt{Jun}=0,\texttt{Jul}=0\right) \\
&= 114.755 + 0.655 (1) + 3.588 (1) - 3.662(0) - 11.698(0) - 10.215 (0) - 14.375 (0) -9.655 (0) \\
&\qquad - 5.972 (1)\times(1) - 3.465 (1)\times(0) + 5.622 (1)\times(0) - 2.473 (1)\times(0) + 3.567 (1)\times(0) + 0.947 (1)\times(0) \\
&\qquad - (114.755 + 0.655 (1) + 3.588 (0) - 3.662(0) - 11.698(0) - 10.215 (0) - 14.375 (0) -9.655 (0) \\
&\qquad - 5.972 (1)\times(0) - 3.465 (1)\times(0) + 5.622 (1)\times(0) - 2.473 (1)\times(0) + 3.567 (1)\times(0) + 0.947 (1)\times(0)) \\
&= 114.755 + 0.655 + 3.588 - 5.972 - (114.755 + 0.655) \\
&= 3.588 -5.972 \\
&= -2.384 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
The estimated mean difference in commute times between January and March on a steel bike is \(|-3.662-3.465| = |-7.127| = 7.127\) minutes, with January taking longer: \[
\begin{align*}
& \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste}=1,\texttt{Feb}=0,\texttt{Mar}=1,\texttt{Apr}=0,\texttt{May}=0,\texttt{Jun}=0,\texttt{Jul}=0\right) \\
&\qquad - \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste}=1,\texttt{Feb}=0,\texttt{Mar}=0,\texttt{Apr}=0,\texttt{May}=0,\texttt{Jun}=0,\texttt{Jul}=0\right) \\
&= 114.755 + 0.655 (1) + 3.588 (0) - 3.662(1) - 11.698(0) - 10.215 (0) - 14.375 (0) -9.655 (0) \\
&\qquad - 5.972 (1)\times(0) - 3.465 (1)\times(1) + 5.622 (1)\times(0) - 2.473 (1)\times(0) + 3.567 (1)\times(0) + 0.947 (1)\times(0) \\
&\qquad - (114.755 + 0.655) \\
&= 114.755 + 0.655 - 3.662 - 3.465 - (114.755 + 0.655) \\
&= -3.662 - 3.465 \\
&= -7.127 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
If we want to compare a month to January on a steel bike, we must combine the coefficient on that month with the coefficient on the interaction term between that month and steel.

The estimated mean difference in commute times between January and April on a steel bike is \(|-11.698 + 5.622| = |-6.076| = 6.076\) minutes, with January taking longer.
The estimated mean difference in commute times between January and May on a steel bike is \(|-10.215-2.473| = |-12.688| = 112.688\) minutes, with January taking longer.
The estimated mean difference in commute times between January and June on a steel bike is \(|-14.375+3.567| = |-10.808| = 10.808\) minutes, with January taking longer.
The estimated mean difference in commute times between January and July on a steel bike is \(|-9.655+0.947| = |-8.708| = 8.708\) minutes, with January taking longer.



55.2.4 Comparing Carbon to Steel by Month
The estimated mean difference in commute times between carbon and steel bikes during the month of January is 0.655 minute, with the steel taking longer: \[
\begin{align*}
& \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste}=1,\texttt{Feb}=0,\texttt{Mar}=0,\texttt{Apr}=0,\texttt{May}=0,\texttt{Jun}=0,\texttt{Jul}=0\right) \\
&\qquad - \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste}=0,\texttt{Feb}=0,\texttt{Mar}=0,\texttt{Apr}=0,\texttt{May}=0,\texttt{Jun}=0,\texttt{Jul}=0\right) \\
&= 114.755 + 0.655 (1) + 3.588 (0) - 3.662(0) - 11.698(0) - 10.215 (0) - 14.375 (0) -9.655 (0) \\
&\qquad - 5.972 (1)\times(0) - 3.465 (1)\times(0) + 5.622 (1)\times(0) - 2.473 (1)\times(0) + 3.567 (1)\times(0) + 0.947 (1)\times(0) \\
&\qquad - 114.755 \\
&= 0.655 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
The estimated mean difference in commute times between carbon and steel bikes during the month of February is \(|0.655-5.972| = |-5.317| = 5.317\) minutes, with the carbon taking longer: \[
\begin{align*}
& \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste}=1,\texttt{Feb}=1,\texttt{Mar}=0,\texttt{Apr}=0,\texttt{May}=0,\texttt{Jun}=0,\texttt{Jul}=0\right) \\
&\qquad - \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste}=0,\texttt{Feb}=1,\texttt{Mar}=0,\texttt{Apr}=0,\texttt{May}=0,\texttt{Jun}=0,\texttt{Jul}=0\right) \\
&= 114.755 + 0.655 (1) + 3.588 (1) - 3.662(0) - 11.698(0) - 10.215 (0) - 14.375 (0) -9.655 (0) \\
&\qquad - 5.972 (1)\times(1) - 3.465 (1)\times(0) + 5.622 (1)\times(0) - 2.473 (1)\times(0) + 3.567 (1)\times(0) + 0.947 (1)\times(0) \\
&\qquad - (114.755 + 0.655 (0) + 3.588 (1) - 3.662(0) - 11.698(0) - 10.215 (0) - 14.375 (0) -9.655 (0) \\
&\qquad - 5.972 (0)\times(1) - 3.465 (0)\times(0) + 5.622 (0)\times(0) - 2.473 (0)\times(0) + 3.567 (0)\times(0) + 0.947 (0)\times(0)) \\
&= 114.755 + 0.655 + 3.588 - 5.972 - (114.755 + 3.588) \\
&= 0.655 - 5.972 \\
&= -5.317 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
The estimated mean difference in commute times between carbon and steel bikes during the month of March is \(|0.655-3.465| = |-2.81| = 2.81\) minutes, with the carbon taking longer: \[
\begin{align*}
& \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste}=1,\texttt{Feb}=0,\texttt{Mar}=1,\texttt{Apr}=0,\texttt{May}=0,\texttt{Jun}=0,\texttt{Jul}=0\right) \\
&\qquad - \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Min}\middle|\texttt{Ste}=0,\texttt{Feb}=0,\texttt{Mar}=1,\texttt{Apr}=0,\texttt{May}=0,\texttt{Jun}=0,\texttt{Jul}=0\right) \\
&= 114.755 + 0.655 (1) + 3.588 (0) - 3.662(1) - 11.698(0) - 10.215 (0) - 14.375 (0) -9.655 (0) \\
&\qquad - 5.972 (1)\times(0) - 3.465 (1)\times(1) + 5.622 (1)\times(0) - 2.473 (1)\times(0) + 3.567 (1)\times(0) + 0.947 (1)\times(0) \\
&\qquad - (114.755 + 0.655 (0) + 3.588 (0) - 3.662(1) - 11.698(0) - 10.215 (0) - 14.375 (0) -9.655 (0) \\
&\qquad - 5.972 (0)\times(0) - 3.465 (0)\times(1) + 5.622 (0)\times(0) - 2.473 (0)\times(0) + 3.567 (0)\times(0) + 0.947 (0)\times(0)) \\
&= 114.755 + 0.655 - 3.662 - 3.465 - (114.755 - 3.662) \\
&= 0.655 - 3.465 \\
&= -2.81 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
I hope this demonstrates a pattern: If we want to compare carbon to steel in January, we just need the coefficient on steel. If we want to compare carbon to steel in another month, we have to combine the coefficient on steel with the coefficient on the interaction term between that month and steel.

The estimated mean difference in commute times between carbon and steel bikes during the month of April is \(|0.655+ 5.622| = |6.277| = 6.277\) minutes, with the steel taking longer.
The estimated mean difference in commute times between carbon and steel bikes during the month of May is \(|0.655-2.473| = |-1.818| = 1.818\) minutes, with the carbon taking longer.
The estimated mean difference in commute times between carbon and steel bikes during the month of June is \(|0.655+3.567| = |4.222| = 4.222\) minutes, with the steel taking longer.
The estimated mean difference in commute times between carbon and steel bikes during the month of July is \(|0.655+0.947| = |1.602| = 1.602\) minutes, with the steel taking longer.

55.3 Problems

55.3.1 Problem 1
Is there evidence of moderation between month, bike type, and commute time? Justify your answer.






TipSolution





Since none of the interaction term coefficients have p-values below 0.05, any moderation we’re seeing is not more than would be expected by chance alone. So, no, there isn’t evidence of moderation. I would refit the model without the interaction terms.

56.1 Learning Objective
Interpret the coefficients of a multiple linear regression model with an interaction between one binary variable and one continuous variable.
crumbs: 56  Interaction Between One Binary Variable and One Continuous Variable

title: 56  Interaction Between One Binary Variable and One Continuous Variable
text:
56.2 Lesson
Researchers in Brazil randomly assigned 264 high school students to activities that involved either synchronized or non-synchronized movements. The researchers measured pain tolerance with a blood pressure cuff before and after the activity. In the model below, I’ve regressed pain tolerance after the activity on pain tolerance before, synchronicity (1 for synchronized, 0 for not synchronized), and the interaction between the two.



Call:
lm(formula = PainTolerance ~ PainToleranceBefore * Synchronized, 
    data = d)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-146.714  -36.714    7.394   28.731  144.166 

Coefficients:
                                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)                      50.06363   13.79080   3.630 0.000341 ***
PainToleranceBefore               0.75550    0.06099  12.386  < 2e-16 ***
Synchronized                     38.94123   19.21848   2.026 0.043761 *  
PainToleranceBefore:Synchronized -0.08173    0.08762  -0.933 0.351766    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 51.66 on 260 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.5118,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.5062 
F-statistic: 90.85 on 3 and 260 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


How do we interpret these coefficients? We can write the linear model as follows (please forgive the abbreviations): \[
\hat{E}\left(\texttt{Tol}\middle|\texttt{TolBef},\texttt{Syn}\right) = 50.06363 + 0.75550 \texttt{TolBef} + 38.94123 \text{Syn} - 0.08173 \texttt{TolBef}\times\texttt{Syn} \text{.}
\]
50.06363 mmHg is the estimated mean pain tolerance among people who were assigned to the non-synchronized activity and who had zero pain tolerance before the activity. \[
\begin{align*}
\hat{E}\left(\texttt{Tol}\middle|\texttt{TolBef}=0,\texttt{Syn}=0\right) &= 50.06363 + 0.75550 (0) + 38.94123 (0) - 0.08173 (0)\times(0) \\
&= 50.06363 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
0.75550 mmHg is the estimated mean increase in pain tolerance associated with a one mmHg increase in prior pain tolerance, among people assigned to the non-synchronized activity. In other words, it is the estimated mean difference in pain tolerance between people with prior pain tolerance \(x\) and people with prior pain tolerance \(x + 1\), assuming all these people were assigned to the non-synchronized activity. People with higher prior pain tolerance are expected to have the higher pain tolerance after doing the activity. \[
\begin{align*}
&\hat{E}\left(\texttt{Tol}\middle|\texttt{TolBef}=x+1,\texttt{Syn}=0\right) - \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Tol}\middle|\texttt{TolBef}=x,\texttt{Syn}=0\right) \\
&= 50.06363 + 0.75550 (x+1) + 38.94123 (0) - 0.08173 (x+1)\times(0) \\
&\qquad - (50.06363 + 0.75550 x + 38.94123 (0) - 0.08173 x\times(0)) \\
&= 50.06363 + 0.75550x + 0.75550 - (50.06363 + 0.75550x) \\
&= 0.75550 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
38.94123 mmHg is the estimated mean difference in pain tolerance between people who were assigned to the synchronized activity and people who were assigned to the non-synchronized activity, assuming all these people had prior pain tolerance of zero. We would expect the people assigned to the synchronized activity to have higher pain tolerance. \[
\begin{align*}
&\hat{E}\left(\texttt{Tol}\middle|\texttt{TolBef}=0,\texttt{Syn}=1\right) - \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Tol}\middle|\texttt{TolBef}=0,\texttt{Syn}=0\right) \\
&= 50.06363 + 0.75550 (0) + 38.94123 (1) - 0.08173 (0)\times(1) \\
&\qquad - 50.06363  \\
&= 38.94123 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
\(0.75550 - 0.08173 = 0.67377\) mmHg is the estimated mean increase in pain tolerance associated with a one mmHg increase in prior pain tolerance, among people assigned to the synchronized activity. In other words, it is the estimated mean difference in pain tolerance between people with prior pain tolerance \(x\) and people with prior pain tolerance \(x + 1\), assuming all these people were assigned to the synchronized activity. People with higher prior pain tolerance are expected to have the higher pain tolerance after doing the activity. \[
\begin{align*}
&\hat{E}\left(\texttt{Tol}\middle|\texttt{TolBef}=x+1,\texttt{Syn}=1\right) - \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Tol}\middle|\texttt{TolBef}=x,\texttt{Syn}=1\right) \\
&= 50.06363 + 0.75550 (x+1) + 38.94123 (1) - 0.08173 (x+1)\times(1) \\
&\qquad - (50.06363 + 0.75550 x + 38.94123 (1) - 0.08173 x\times(1)) \\
&= 50.06363 + 0.75550 x + 0.75550 + 38.94123  - 0.08173x - 0.08173 \\
&\qquad - (50.06363 + 0.75550 x + 38.94123  - 0.08173 x) \\
&= 0.75550 - 0.08173 \\
&= 0.67377 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
\(38.94123 - 0.08173x\) mmHg is the estimated mean difference in pain tolerance between people who were assigned to the synchronized activity and people who were assigned to the non-synchronized activity, assuming all these people had prior pain tolerance of \(x\). Since \(x\) was only observed between 30 and 300, \(14.42223 \le 38.94123 - 0.08173x \le 36.48933\), and we would expect the people assigned to the synchronized activity to have higher pain tolerance. \[
\begin{align*}
&\hat{E}\left(\texttt{Tol}\middle|\texttt{TolBef}=x,\texttt{Syn}=1\right) - \hat{E}\left(\texttt{Tol}\middle|\texttt{TolBef}=x,\texttt{Syn}=0\right) \\
&= 50.06363 + 0.75550 x + 38.94123 (1) - 0.08173 x\times(1) \\
&\qquad - (50.06363 + 0.75550 x + 38.94123 (0) - 0.08173 x\times(0))  \\
&= 38.94123 - 0.08173x \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
We can observe this in a plot.









If the moderation were stronger, these lines would have different slopes.
