title: 56  Interaction Between One Binary Variable and One Continuous Variable
text:
56.3 Problems

56.3.1 Problem 1
Check out Figure 2 in “Factors in Hand Surgery Access for Rheumatoid Arthritis Before vs After the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act” (Dwivedi et al., 2024). This is an example of piecewise linear regression. For each procedure, the researchers fit a simple linear regression before the ACA and another one after. This can be achieved through interaction terms.
In my opinion, linear regression was not the appropriate analysis for these data. As the authors write in the section “Outcomes of Interest”, “Surgical incidence was defined as the number of hand surgeries performed each year divided by the population of each cohort.” I think Poisson regression would be more appropriate for this outcome. We will learn about Poisson regression later in this course.
For this problem, let’s use an outcome that is better-suited for linear regression. Suppose our sample consists of \(n\) patients who underwent hand surgery for rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Define the following:

\(P_i\) is the pain level of patient \(i\), measured on a scale from 1 to 100.
\(Y_i\) is the number of years since 2014. Assume each patient was only measured once, so we only have one time value per person.
\(S_i = 1\) if patient \(i\) had a synovectomy and \(S_i = 0\) otherwise.
\(A_i = 1\) if \(Y_i > 0\) and \(A_i = 0\) if \(Y_i \le 0\). You can think of \(A_i\) being an indicator that the observation was after 2014.

Suppose our model is \[
P_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Y_i + \beta_2 S_i + \beta_3 A_i + \beta_4 Y_i S_i + \beta_5 Y_i A_i + \beta_6 S_i A_i + \beta_7 Y_i S_i A_i + \epsilon_i \text{.}
\]

56.3.1.1 Part (a)
What is the expected pain level for a patient who had arthrodesis \(y\) years since 2014, where \(y \le 0\)?






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
    &E(P_i|Y_i = y,S_i = 0,A_i = 0) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 y + \beta_2 (0) + \beta_3 (0) + \beta_4 y (0) + \beta_5 y (0) + \beta_6 (0) (0) + \beta_7 y (0) (0) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 y
\end{align*}
\]





56.3.1.2 Part (b)
What is the expected pain level for a patient who had denervation \(y\) years since 2014, where \(y > 0\)?






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
    &E(P_i|Y_i = y,S_i = 0,A_i = 1) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 y + \beta_2 (0) + \beta_3 (1) + \beta_4 y (0) + \beta_5 y (1) + \beta_6 (0) (1) + \beta_7 y (0) (1) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 y  + \beta_3   + \beta_5 y   \\
    &= (\beta_0 + \beta_3) + (\beta_1 + \beta_5) y
\end{align*}
\]





56.3.1.3 Part (c)
What is the expected pain level for a patient who had a synovectomy \(y\) years since 2014, where \(y \le 0\)?






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
    &E(P_i|Y_i = y,S_i = 1,A_i = 0) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 y + \beta_2 (1) + \beta_3 (0) + \beta_4 y (1) + \beta_5 y (0) + \beta_6 (1) (0) + \beta_7 y (1) (0) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 y + \beta_2   + \beta_4 y  \\
    &= (\beta_0 + \beta_2) + (\beta_1 + \beta_4) y
\end{align*}
\]





56.3.1.4 Part (d)
What is the expected pain level for a patient who had a synovectomy \(y\) years since 2014, where \(y > 0\)?






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
    &E(P_i|Y_i = y,S_i = 1,A_i = 1) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 y + \beta_2 (1) + \beta_3 (1) + \beta_4 y (1) + \beta_5 y (1) + \beta_6 (1) (1) + \beta_7 y (1) (1) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 y + \beta_2  + \beta_3  + \beta_4 y  + \beta_5 y  + \beta_6  + \beta_7 y  \\
    &= (\beta_0 + \beta_2 + \beta_3 + \beta_6) + (\beta_1 + \beta_4 + \beta_5 + \beta_7) y
\end{align*}
\]





56.3.1.5 Part (e)
What is the expected difference in pain levels between a patient who had a synovectomy in 2017 and a patient who had sagittal band reconstruction, also in 2017?






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
    &E(P_i|Y_i = 3,S_i = 1,A_i = 1) - E(P_i|Y_i = 3,S_i = 0,A_i = 1) \\
    &= (\beta_0 + \beta_2 + \beta_3 + \beta_6) + (\beta_1 + \beta_4 + \beta_5 + \beta_7) (3) - ((\beta_0 + \beta_3) + (\beta_1 + \beta_5) (3)) \\
    &= (\beta_2  + \beta_6) + ( \beta_4  + \beta_7) (3)  
\end{align*}
\]






56.3.2 Problem 2
This problem is about the study “Association between Traffic Air Pollution and Reduced Forced Vital Capacity: A Study Using Personal Monitors for Outdoor Workers” (Santos et al., 2016). Define the following:

\(F_i\) is the forced vital capacity (FVC) for the \(i\)th individual, measured in liters.
\(D_i = 1\) if the \(i\)th individual was a taxi driver and \(D_i = 0\) otherwise.
\(C_i = 1\) if the \(i\)th individual was a traffic controller and \(C_i = 0\) otherwise.
\(Y_i\) is the number of years that the \(i\)th individual has worked in their job.

Suppose our model is \[
F_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \beta_2 C_i + \beta_3 Y_i + \beta_4 D_i Y_i + \beta_5 C_i Y_i + \epsilon_i \text{.}
\]

56.3.2.1 Part (a)
Why don’t we need terms for \(D_i C_i\) and \(D_i C_i Y_i\)?






TipSolution





\(D_i\) and \(C_i\) cannot both be 1, so any term with their product must be 0. Each individual has only one occupation (in this data set).





56.3.2.2 Part (b)
Interpret \(\beta_2    + \beta_5  y\) in real-world terms.






TipSolution





This is the expected difference in FVC between a traffic controller and a forest ranger, both of whom have worked in their job for \(y\) years.
\[
\begin{align*}
    &E(F_i|D_i = 0,C_i = 1,Y_i = y) - E(F_i|D_i = 0,C_i = 0,Y_i = y) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 (1) + \beta_3 y + \beta_4 (0) y + \beta_5 (1) y \\
    &\qquad - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 (0) + \beta_3 y + \beta_4 (0) y + \beta_5 (0) y) \\
    &= \beta_0  + \beta_2  + \beta_3 y  + \beta_5  y  - (\beta_0  + \beta_3 y ) \\
    &=  \beta_2    + \beta_5  y   \\
\end{align*}
\]

title: 57  Correlated Covariates
text: 57.1 Learning Objectives

title: 57  Correlated Covariates
text:
Explain the effects of correlated explanatory variables.
Define, use, and interpret variance inflation factors (VIFs).

title: 57  Correlated Covariates
text:
57.2 Lesson
It is not uncommon for the explanatory variables in a regression model to be correlated with each other. Usually, you’ve chosen the explanatory variables because you think they are related to the outcome, and if they’re all related to the outcome, they’re probably related to each other. Unfortunately, problems can arise when explanatory variables are highly correlated with each other, which we will examine here.
First, let’s consider the case where two explanatory variables are perfectly correlated, i.e., one is a linear function of the other. Suppose our outcome is body fat percentage and the explanatory variables are weight in pounds and weight in ounces. Weight in ounces is just weight in pounds times 16.



Call:
lm(formula = Bodyfat ~ Weight_pounds + Weight_ounces, data = d)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-17.0346  -3.9516  -0.3173   4.1811  19.1868 

Coefficients: (1 not defined because of singularities)
               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   -10.09418    3.95883  -2.550   0.0123 *  
Weight_pounds   0.16171    0.02201   7.347  6.1e-11 ***
Weight_ounces        NA         NA      NA       NA    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 6.462 on 98 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3552,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3486 
F-statistic: 53.98 on 1 and 98 DF,  p-value: 6.1e-11


As you can see, R did not even estimate anything for weight in ounces. If you try to include an explanatory variable that is a linear combination of any of the other explanatory variables, R will refuse. This is because it’s impossible to do the math required to get estimates, standard errors, etc.
What if you have two explanatory variables that are not perfectly correlated, but are still highly correlated? Let’s regress body fat percentage on weight in pounds and abdomen circumference in centimeters. These two explanatory variables have a correlation of 0.888.

cor(d$Weight_pounds,
    d$Abdomen)

[1] 0.8883167

mod_02 <- lm(formula = Bodyfat ~ Weight_pounds + Abdomen,
             data = d)
summary(mod_02)


Call:
lm(formula = Bodyfat ~ Weight_pounds + Abdomen, data = d)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-9.5953 -2.9776 -0.0177  2.8974  9.1920 

Coefficients:
               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   -48.77854    4.18098 -11.667  < 2e-16 ***
Weight_pounds  -0.16082    0.03101  -5.185 1.18e-06 ***
Abdomen         1.04408    0.08918  11.707  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 4.181 on 97 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.7328,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.7273 
F-statistic:   133 on 2 and 97 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


That worked. Does that mean there’s no problem? Maybe. Watch what we get if we just use weight in pounds.



Call:
lm(formula = Bodyfat ~ Weight_pounds, data = d)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-17.0346  -3.9516  -0.3173   4.1811  19.1868 

Coefficients:
               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   -10.09418    3.95883  -2.550   0.0123 *  
Weight_pounds   0.16171    0.02201   7.347  6.1e-11 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 6.462 on 98 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3552,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3486 
F-statistic: 53.98 on 1 and 98 DF,  p-value: 6.1e-11


What changed? The estimated coefficient on Weight_pounds flipped signs. When both variables are included in the model, the coefficient on Weight_pounds is -0.16082, meaning we would expect body fat percentage to decrease by 0.16 percentage points with every additional pound of body weight, holding abdomen circumference constant. If someone’s abdomen circumference is staying the same but they are getting heavier, they are probably getting taller or more muscular. Either way, their body fat is decreasing.
When only Weight_pounds is included in the model, its coefficient is 0.16171, meaning we would expect body fat percentage to increase by 0.16 percentage points with every additional pound of body weight. This flipping of signs–going from an increase to a decrease or vice versa–is not uncommon when you fit a model with highly correlated covariates and then fit a model with only one of them.
This behavior is related to another effect of using correlated variables. In order to demonstrate it, I need to recreate mod_02 but somehow de-correlate the variables. The way to do that is to regress Abdomen on Weight_pounds and obtain the residuals. Note that these residuals are uncorrelated with Weight_pounds.

mod_04 <- lm(formula = Abdomen ~ Weight_pounds,
             data = d)
cor(d$Weight_pounds,
    mod_04$residuals)

[1] 5.824739e-17


Now I’m going to regress Bodyfat on Weight_pounds and the residuals from the regression of Abdomen on Weight_pounds.

mod_05 <- lm(d$Bodyfat ~ d$Weight_pounds + mod_04$residuals)
summary(mod_05)


Call:
lm(formula = d$Bodyfat ~ d$Weight_pounds + mod_04$residuals)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-9.5953 -2.9776 -0.0177  2.8974  9.1920 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)      -10.09418    2.56164  -3.941 0.000153 ***
d$Weight_pounds    0.16171    0.01424  11.354  < 2e-16 ***
mod_04$residuals   1.04408    0.08918  11.707  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 4.181 on 97 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.7328,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.7273 
F-statistic:   133 on 2 and 97 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Note the following:

The \(R^2\) for mod_05 is the same as for mod_02. The two models are explaining exactly the same amount of variance in the outcome.
The coefficient estimate for Weight_pounds is the same in mod_05 and in mod_03. Since Weight_pounds is uncorrelated with mod_04$residuals, controlling for mod_04$residuals doesn’t change the relationship between Weight_pounds and Bodyfat.
The variance of the coefficient estimate for Weight_pounds in mod_02 is much greater than the variance of the coefficient estimate for Weight_pounds in mod_05.


summary(mod_02)$coefficients[2,2]^2 / summary(mod_05)$coefficients[2,2]^2

[1] 4.741732


When explanatory variables in a model are correlated, the variances of their associated coefficients are inflated. In fact, the “variance inflation factor (VIF)” is the ratio of the variance of the coefficient estimate in a model to the variance of the same coefficient estimate in a model where the explanatory variables are uncorrelated. We can use the function vif from the package car to get the variance inflation factors:

vif(mod_02)

Weight_pounds       Abdomen 
     4.741732      4.741732 


Different sources use different cutoffs for when a VIF is “too high”, but you shouldn’t blindly follow them. Sometimes you want correlated variables in a model. For example, interaction terms tend to be highly correlated with their component variables, but that doesn’t mean we should exclude them. You have to use your judgment, and consider the goals of your analysis.
It’s important to note that problems don’t just arise when two variables are correlated with each other. It could be the case that no two variables in a data set are highly correlated, but one of the variables is close to being a linear combination of the others, and that will also inflate the variances. I’ll simulate some data to illustrate this.
In this model, I regressed Y on eleven explanatory variables.



Call:
lm(formula = Y ~ ., data = d_sim)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-4.4335 -1.2774  0.1293  1.3408  5.3777 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -0.05779    0.21314  -0.271 0.786929    
X1           0.97092    0.28652   3.389 0.001053 ** 
X2           1.37120    0.30121   4.552 1.69e-05 ***
X3           0.90271    0.28355   3.184 0.002012 ** 
X4           1.11546    0.30159   3.699 0.000377 ***
X5           1.08438    0.31412   3.452 0.000857 ***
X6           0.78362    0.30926   2.534 0.013052 *  
X7           0.96302    0.30126   3.197 0.001932 ** 
X8           1.63675    0.33668   4.861 5.05e-06 ***
X9           1.27966    0.30932   4.137 8.03e-05 ***
X10          0.69662    0.29496   2.362 0.020394 *  
X11          0.87490    0.22705   3.853 0.000221 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 2.038 on 88 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9069,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.8953 
F-statistic: 77.97 on 11 and 88 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The variable X11 is not super highly correlated with any single other variable.

cor(x = d_sim$X11,
    y = d_sim[-c(1,12)])

            X1        X2        X3        X4        X5        X6        X7
[1,] 0.3426916 0.3689755 0.2095533 0.2297657 0.2070774 0.2678992 0.3196746
            X8        X9       X10
[1,] 0.2808005 0.3690209 0.3762185


Yet, the VIF for X11 is very high.

vif(mod_06)

       X1        X2        X3        X4        X5        X6        X7        X8 
 1.636445  2.082965  1.796581  2.190896  2.697928  2.490307  2.074596  2.422044 
       X9       X10       X11 
 2.399622  2.173226 11.507711 


This is because X11 is nearly equal to the sum of the other ten variables. Because there are so many variables, X11 is not that correlated with any individual variable. Yet, in the model, the variance of the coefficient associated with X11 is far higher than it would be if the explanatory variables were uncorrelated.

title: 57  Correlated Covariates
text:
57.3 Problems

57.3.1 Problem 1
If the explanatory variables in a model are utterly uncorrelated, what should the VIFs be? (By the way, this might seem impossible, but you can perform principal components analysis on your explanatory variables to get uncorrelated variables that have the same information.)






TipSolution





If the explanatory variables are uncorrelated, their VIFs should be 1.





57.3.2 Problem 2
What will happen if I try to regress \(Y\) on \(X\) and \(X^2\), where \(X\) can only be 0 or 1?






TipSolution





R won’t provide a result for the \(X^2\) term. Note that if \(X = 0\) then \(X^2 = 0^2 = 0 = X\) and if \(X = 1\) then \(X^2 = 1^2 = 1 = X\), so \(X^2 = X\).





57.3.3 Problem 3
I simulated more data. X1 through X10 are completely independent of each other. X11 is equal to the sum of X1 through X4, plus some random error. Y is equal to the sum of X1 through X11, plus some random error. Below are the results of regressing Y on X1 through X11.



Call:
lm(formula = Y ~ ., data = d_sim)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
-4.195 -1.296 -0.165  1.165  5.112 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  -0.2328     0.2164  -1.076 0.284980    
X1            1.5004     0.3015   4.977 3.19e-06 ***
X2            1.1596     0.2869   4.041 0.000114 ***
X3            1.6663     0.3294   5.059 2.28e-06 ***
X4            1.7418     0.3087   5.643 2.01e-07 ***
X5            0.9002     0.2359   3.816 0.000252 ***
X6            1.1084     0.2323   4.771 7.23e-06 ***
X7            0.6805     0.2572   2.646 0.009656 ** 
X8            1.0065     0.2101   4.789 6.72e-06 ***
X9            1.2468     0.2134   5.843 8.49e-08 ***
X10           1.1508     0.2275   5.059 2.28e-06 ***
X11           0.5533     0.2113   2.618 0.010404 *  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 2.066 on 88 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.863, Adjusted R-squared:  0.8459 
F-statistic: 50.39 on 11 and 88 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


What do you predict will be the values of the pairwise correlations between X11 and X1 through X10? What do you predict will be the values for the VIFs?






TipSolution






cor(x = d_sim$X11,
    y = d_sim[-c(1,12)])

            X1       X2        X3        X4        X5         X6         X7
[1,] 0.3892744 0.466206 0.3983619 0.5310772 0.0881533 -0.1109829 0.04464207
              X8         X9        X10
[1,] -0.02793946 0.08313153 0.03036517


We see above that X11 is not correlated with X5 through X10, but has fairly high correlations with X1 through X4.

vif(mod_07)

      X1       X2       X3       X4       X5       X6       X7       X8 
2.466173 2.027240 2.421622 2.168287 1.299125 1.136459 1.130052 1.121878 
      X9      X10      X11 
1.065875 1.085257 5.450090 


We see above that X5 through X10 have low VIFs, X1 through X4 have slightly elevated VIFs, and X11 has a high VIF (though not as high as when it was nearly equal to the sum of all the other covariates).

title: 58  Splines
text:
58.1 Learning Objective
Explain each of the following words in the context of splines:

title: 58  Splines
text:
Natural.
Cubic.
Spline.
Knot.

title: 58  Splines
text:
58.2 Lesson
Suppose we have the following data:









Obviously, simple linear regression will not be a good fit for these data.









We may not do much better by incorporating polynomial terms. The blue line in this next plot is fit according to the model \[
E(Y|X) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \beta_1 X^2 + \beta_3 X^3 + \beta_4 X^4 \text{.}
\]









A different approach that works pretty well is called natural cubic splines. The blue line in this next plot was fit using natural cubic splines.









How did R get the blue curve above? First, it split the horizontal axis into five sections. Five is not the default; R used five sections because I set the parameter df in the function ns equal to 5. Here’s the code I used:
mod_03 <- lm(formula = y ~ ns(x = x,
                              df = 5),
             data = d_sim)
How did R choose the five sections? It used the quintiles, i.e., the values that split the data into five approximately equal bins. We can examine them using the function quantile:

quintiles <- quantile(x = x,
                      probs = seq(from = 0,
                                  to = 1,
                                  by = 1 / 5))
quintiles

          0%          20%          40%          60%          80%         100% 
 0.007356125  2.518445671  5.180908108  7.739377263 10.270148330 12.983930482 



0.0073561 is the minimum value of x.
20% of the values of x fall below 2.5184457 and 80% of the values of x fall above 2.5184457.
40% of the values of x fall below 5.1809081 and 60% of the values of x fall above 5.1809081.
60% of the values of x fall below 7.7393773 and 40% of the values of x fall above 7.7393773.
80% of the values of x fall below 10.2701483 and 20% of the values of x fall above 10.2701483.
12.9839305 is the maximum value of x.

These quintiles have a special name in the vocabulary of splines. They’re called “knots”. You can also think of them as breakpoints. We can visualize them on the plot.









We can see what values were used for knots using this code:

attr(x = terms(mod_03),
     which = "predvars")

list(y, ns(x = x, knots = c(2.5184456711635, 5.18090810789727, 
7.73937726281584, 10.270148329949), Boundary.knots = c(0.00735612493008375, 
12.9839304822963), intercept = FALSE))


After splitting up the data, R fit a separate model between each consecutive pair of knots, i.e., within each bin. Because this is a cubic spline, the model within each bin was a cubic polynomial, i.e., \(E(Y|X) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \beta_2 X^2 + \beta_3 X^3\). “Cubic” means the maximum exponent of the polynomial was 3.
Part of the meaning of “spline” is that the function is piecewise, meaning there’s a different model within each bin. The second part of the meaning of “spline” is that the function is smooth. This means that the pieces of the function are smoothly connected at the knots. As you can see in the plot, there aren’t gaps in the blue curve, nor are there hard angles. This is true for all splines.
What makes this a “natural” cubic spline? Below the lowest knot and above the highest knot, the function is linear.









There you have it. Here’s a summary of the new words:

A spline is a smooth, piecewise function.
The knots of a spline are the points that split the function into pieces.
A cubic spline uses cubic polynomials to model the data between knots.
A natural spline uses a linear function to model data beyond the minimum and maximum values observed.

A few more things:

What value should you choose for df? A higher value will give better fit, but can also lead to overfitting. Here’s a spline fit with df = 10.










Here’s a spline fit with df = 3.









I think people often choose a relatively small value (5 or 6) for df and go on their way. An arguably better, but more involved approach, is to use cross-validation.

Instead of telling the function how many sections or bins you want, you can tell it where you want the knots. In this plot, I’ve put the knots at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 9. (These are what you might call the “internal” knots, although that’s not a technical term. Unless I change the argument Boundary.knots, there will still be knots at the minimum and maximum x values.)


knots <- c(1:5,9)
mod_06 <- lm(formula = y ~ ns(x = x,
                              knots = knots),
             data = d_sim)
plot(x = x,
     y = y)
lines(x = x,
      y = mod_06$fitted.values,
      col = "blue",
      lwd = 3)
abline(v = c(min(x),
             knots,
             max(x)),
       lty = 2,
       col = "lightgray")









It’s generally not super useful to interpret the coefficient estimates or p-values of the splines.




Call:
lm(formula = y ~ ns(x = x, df = 5), data = d_sim)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-3.3851 -0.8387 -0.0330  0.7642  3.8303 

Coefficients:
                   Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)          2.2131     0.1736  12.749  < 2e-16 ***
ns(x = x, df = 5)1  -4.3235     0.2133 -20.270  < 2e-16 ***
ns(x = x, df = 5)2   7.4688     0.2731  27.346  < 2e-16 ***
ns(x = x, df = 5)3   1.1556     0.2111   5.475 5.54e-08 ***

title: 58  Splines
text:
58.3 Problems

58.3.1 Problem 1
True or false: Increasing df will decrease the size of the bins.






TipSolution





True. With more bins but the same number of observations, you’ll have fewer observations in each bin. So long as there aren’t a bunch of observations with identical values for \(X\), this will also decrease the width of the bins on the \(X\)-axis.





58.3.2 Problem 2
Is this blue curve a spline? Justify your answer.















TipSolution





No. Splines are smooth, and this blue curve is jagged.





58.3.3 Problem 3
The subparts of this problem refer to this figure:









You will be asked to draw some graphs, so please grab a writing implement and some scratch paper.

58.3.3.1 Part (a)
In the plot above, the relationship between \(x\) and \(y\) is not linear. However, we could model the relationship with a piecewise linear function. To create a piecewise linear function, you split the horizontal axis into pieces and fit a different linear function (i.e., a different straight line) for each piece. On your scratch paper, draw a piecewise linear function to represent the relationship between \(x\) and \(y\). Please connect each of your straight lines; there shouldn’t be any gaps.






TipSolution














Your figure need not look exactly like mine. You could’ve used more, fewer, or different line segments.





58.3.3.2 Part (b)
Draw a plot (it can be an approximate sketch) of the slopes of your piecewise linear function. The horizontal axis should be \(x\) and the vertical axis should be the slope.






TipSolution



















58.3.3.3 Part (c)
One issue with a piecewise linear function is that it’s not smooth; it has corners where the function abruptly changes direction. Draw a smooth function to represent the relationship between \(x\) and \(y\).






TipSolution














Your figure need not look exactly like mine.





58.3.3.4 Part (d)
Draw a plot (it can be an approximate sketch) of the slope (derivative) of your smooth function. The horizontal axis should be \(x\) and the vertical axis should be the slope (derivative).






TipSolution














What was the point of all this?

It is not uncommon for an explanatory variable to have a non-linear relationship with the outcome, and/or for the relationship between the variable and the outcome to be different for different values of the variable. One approach to this problem is to use a piecewise linear function.
Unfortunately, piecewise linear functions are not smooth. The function in Part (a) has hard corners where it abruptly changes direction. These corners correspond to abrupt changes in slope. In other words, a non-smooth function has a non-continuous derivative. (A continuous function is one that you can draw without lifting your pencil up from the paper.) A smooth function, like the one in Part (c), has a continuous derivative, like the one in Part (d).
Splines combine piecewise functions and smoothness. The most common type is cubic splines. When you use cubic splines, you split the horizontal axis into pieces; fit a different cubic polynomial (i.e., \(y = ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d\)) to each piece; make sure the polynomials connect across the pieces; and make sure that the first and second derivatives of the function as a whole is continuous.
In practice, you need to decide on the number of pieces, but not where they start or end. In the ns function from the splines package, you increase the number of pieces by increasing the df argument. You can change the breakpoints between the pieces if you want, by using the knots parameter.

title: 59  Linear Hypotheses
text:
59.2 Lesson
In the regression below, each observation corresponds to a person receiving funds from the California Department of Developmental Services (DDS). I used annual expenditure (in dollars) as the outcome and age cohort (0-5, 6-12, 13-17, 18-21, 22-50, 51 and above) and gender (male, female) as explanatory variables.

We can see from the results that there is not a statistically significant difference in expenditures between people age 6 to 12 and people age 0 to 5, holding gender constant, but there is a statistically significant difference in expenditures between people age 13 to 17 and people age 0 to 5, holding gender constant. Is there a statistically significant difference in expenditures between people age 6 to 12 and people age 13 to 17? We’ve seen that we can answer this question by changing the reference group for the regression, but there’s another, easier way. We can use the function linearHypothesis in the package car.

linearHypothesis(model = mod_01,
                 hypothesis.matrix = "AgeCohort6-12 = AgeCohort13-17")


Linear hypothesis test:
AgeCohort6-12 = AgeCohort13-17

Model 1: restricted model
Model 2: Expenditures ~ AgeCohort + Gender

  Res.Df        RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
1    994 1.5188e+10                                  
2    993 1.4899e+10  1 288712003 19.242 1.275e-05 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The null hypothesis in the code above is that the coefficient for AgeCohort6-12 is equal to the coefficient for AgeCohort13-17. Because the p-value is tiny, we can safely reject that null hypothesis and conclude that there is a statistically significant difference in expenditures between these two age cohorts, holding gender constant.
Our linear hypothesis can get more complex, but they can be tricky to interpret. For example, we could test if the sum of the coefficients for AgeCohort6-12, AgeCohort13-17, AgeCohort18-21, and AgeCohort22-50 is equivalent to the coefficient for AgeCohort51+.

linearHypothesis(model = mod_01,
                 hypothesis.matrix = "AgeCohort6-12 + AgeCohort13-17 + AgeCohort18-21 + AgeCohort22-50 = AgeCohort51+")


Linear hypothesis test:
AgeCohort6-12 + AgeCohort13-17 + AgeCohort18-21 + AgeCohort22-50 = AgeCohort51+

Model 1: restricted model
Model 2: Expenditures ~ AgeCohort + Gender

  Res.Df        RSS Df Sum of Sq      F Pr(>F)
1    994 1.4915e+10                           
2    993 1.4899e+10  1  15412455 1.0272 0.3111


The p-value is large. This does not mean that expenditures for people age 51+ are not significantly different from the sum of the expenditures for people in the four age cohorts on the left-hand side of the equation. This is because the coefficients represent deviations from the reference group. If you wanted to get the total expenditures in each cohort, you’d have to add back the expenditures for the reference group four times on the left hand side, but only once on the right-hand side. This is why you should be careful with linear hypotheses.

title: 60  Overfitting
text:
60.1 Learning Objective
Define, use, and interpret the term “overfitting”.

title: 60  Overfitting
text:
60.2 Lesson

60.2.1 Definition
As we’ve discussed, we usually want to make claims about a population but can only observe a sample. It’s important that the conclusions we draw from our sample are generalizable to the population. Even if our goal isn’t to generalize to some larger population, but is instead to make predictions, we want to make sure that we can accurately predict new data, not just the data in our sample. “Overfitting” is what happens when you create a model that describes your sample really well but does a poor job of generalizing to or predicting new data from the same population.


60.2.2 Conceptual Example
Suppose your roommate is from Portugal. You know he speaks Portuguese, he needs the shower at 7am, he likes to cook dinner, and on Saturdays he plays Frisbee with friends. So, you conclude that all Portuguese people speak Portuguese, shower at 7am, like to cook dinner, and play Frisbee with their friends on Saturdays. That’s an example of overfitting. You’ve done a great job of describing (and predicting) your roommate’s behavior, but there’s no reason to believe that the same descriptions and predictions will work for other people from the same country. (At least, not all of them; it is reasonable to predict that other people from Portugal speak Portuguese.)


60.2.3 Visual Depiction
Overfitting is usually depicted in the following way. Suppose you have these data:









You try fitting a simple linear regression:









You decide that’s not quite good enough. Although the regression line captures the general trend of the data, it doesn’t go through enough of the points. So you add a quadratic term. Now your linear model is \[
E(Y|X) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \beta_2 X^2 \text{.}
\]









That’s still not quite good enough, so you add a few more polynomial terms. Now your linear model is \[
E(Y|X) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \beta_2 X^2 + \beta_3 X^3 + \beta_4 X^4 + \beta_5 X^5 + \beta_6 X^6 + \beta_7 X^7 + \beta_8 X^8 + \beta_9 X^9 + \beta_{10} X^{10} + \beta_{11} X^{11}\text{.}
\]









This regression line goes through a lot of the points! But watch what happens when we collect more data:









The eleventh-degree polynomial function, which fit the original data set of twenty observations really well, does a terrible job of describing the new data set with 2,000 observations.


60.2.4 Note
There are lots of things that limit our ability to generalize from a sample to the population, including a small sample size or a biased sampling scheme. “Overfitting” is generally not used to refer to the size of the sample or how it was collected. Instead, it refers to the relationship between the model and the sample. When talking about overfitting, we’re kind of taking the sample for granted. We can’t change the sample now that we have it, but we can change the model, and we want to make sure the model isn’t overfit to the data.

title: 60  Overfitting
text:
60.3 Problems

60.3.1 Problem 1
Propose a method for determining whether a model is overfit to a sample.






TipSolution





We could hold out some data from the sample (call this the “test set”) and fit our model to the rest (call this the “training set”). If the model is overfit to the training set, it will do a poor job of predicting the outcome in the test set.





60.3.2 Problem 2
True or false: A Type II error is the same thing as overfitting.






TipSolution





False. You can make a Type II error even when the model is perfect. By chance alone, there is always a non-zero chance of making a Type II error.

title: 61  R-Squared
text: 61.1 Learning Objective

title: 61  R-Squared
text:
Define, use, and interpret \(R^2\).
Explain the purpose of the adjusted \(R^2\).
Use and interpret the adjusted \(R^2\).

title: 61  R-Squared
text:
61.2 Lesson

61.2.1 Definition 1
The coefficient of determination, denoted by \(R^2\), is defined as follows: \[
R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\right)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \bar{Y}\right)^2} \text{.}
\] As a reminder, \(n\) is the sample size, \(\hat{Y}_i\) is the fitted value for the \(i\)th observation, and \(\bar{Y}\) is the sample average.
How do we interpret this? Imagine that you’re pitting two different prediction methods against each other. In the first, you’re just using the sample average to predict every observation in the data set. In other words, you’re ignoring all the explanatory variables. The denominator of the fraction, \[
\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \bar{Y}\right)^2 \text{,}
\] is a measure of how wrong you are using this method.
In the second prediction method, you’re using the regression model. So, for each observation, you’re using the explanatory variables to get a prediction of the outcome. This prediction is the fitted value. The numerator of the fraction, \[
\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\right)^2 \text{,}
\] is a measure of how wrong you are using this method.
If the regression model performs better, i.e., if it’s less wrong, then \[
\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\right)^2 < \sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \bar{Y}\right)^2 \text{.}
\] This implies \[
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\right)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \bar{Y}\right)^2} < 1
\] and \[
R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\right)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \bar{Y}\right)^2} > 0 \text{.}
\]
If the regression model performs a lot better then \[
\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\right)^2 \ll \sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \bar{Y}\right)^2 \text{,}
\] \[
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\right)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \bar{Y}\right)^2} \ll 1 \text{,}
\] and \[
R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\right)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \bar{Y}\right)^2} \gg 0 \text{.}
\] (The symbol \(\ll\) means “much less than” and the symbol \(\gg\) means “much greater than”.)
All this together implies that the larger \(R^2\) is, the better job it does of predicting the outcome within the sample.


61.2.2 Definition 2
We can also define \(R^2\) like this: \[
R^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \left(\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y}\right)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \bar{Y}\right)^2} \text{.}
\] This definition is mathematically equivalent to the one above, but it allows for a different interpretation of \(R^2\).
In terms of the performance of the regression model, the worst case scenario is that \(\hat{Y}_i = \bar{Y}\), i.e., incorporating information about the explanatory variables does no good for predicting the outcome in the data set. In this case, the numerator of \(R^2\) is zero, so \(R^2 = 0\).
The best case scenario is that \(\hat{Y}_i = Y_i\), i.e., the regression model does a perfect job predicting the outcome in the data set. In this case, the numerator of \(R^2\) is equal to the denominator, and \(R^2 = 1\).
This shows us that \(R^2\) ranges from 0 to 1. If we think of the denominator as a measure of the total variability in the data set, we can interpret \(R^2\) as the proportion of variance explained by the model.


61.2.3 Overfitting
Note that \(R^2\) is only measuring the performance of the regression model in the sample, i.e., the same sample that was used to fit the regression model. If we try to optimize (i.e., maximize) \(R^2\), we may overfit the data.
Mathematically, adding a new explanatory variable to a linear regression model cannot decrease the \(R^2\). So, if we’re trying to increase the \(R^2\), we could just keep adding explanatory variables until we see improvement. This will probably cause overfitting because some of these explanatory variables will be related to the outcome in the sample just by chance. In the population, there may be no relationship, so the model will perform poorly with new data.


61.2.4 Adjusted R-Squared
The purpose of the adjusted \(R^2\) is to prevent overfitting. It is defined as follows: \[
R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - (1-R^2) \frac{n - 1}{n - p - 1} \text{,}
\] where \(p\) is the number of explanatory variables.
If we hold \(R^2\) and \(n\) constant while increasing \(p\), \[
\begin{align*}
p\uparrow &\implies -p \downarrow \\
&\implies n - p - 1 \downarrow \\
&\implies \frac{n - 1}{n - p - 1} \uparrow \\
&\implies (1-R^2) \frac{n - 1}{n - p - 1} \uparrow \\
&\implies -(1-R^2) \frac{n - 1}{n - p - 1} \downarrow \\
&\implies 1 -(1-R^2) \frac{n - 1}{n - p - 1} \downarrow \\
&\implies R^2_{\text{adj}} \downarrow \text{,}
\end{align*}
\] i.e., the adjusted \(R^2\) decreases. So, the adjusted \(R^2\) penalizes adding new explanatory variables to the model to offset the better fit you get.


61.2.5 Note
Although I keep saying that the fitted values come from a regression model, the \(R^2\) is agnostic to where the fitted values are coming from. You could compute the \(R^2\) using fitted values from a different prediction method. For these other methods, the two definitions above might not be exactly equal, but it would still be the case that a higher \(R^2\) would be better than a lower \(R^2\).

Eighteen of the variables were generated completely independently of the outcome and should be removed. There is overfitting happening, so there should be a gap between the adjusted and unadjusted \(R^2\).
The adjusted \(R^2\) for the large model is approximately equal to the adjusted \(R^2\) for the small model. This means that, adjusted for their size, they’re performing approximately equally. Since we often value parsimony in statistical models (smaller models are easier to interpret and have higher power to detect effects), we should probably go with the smaller model. This is good, since the smaller model is the correct one.

True or false: The linearity assumption of multiple linear regression must be true in order to interpret the \(R^2\).

False. The \(R^2\) is (essentially) just a measure of how close the fitted values are to the observed values of the outcome. Even if none of the assumptions are met, you can still compute and interpret the \(R^2\).

title: 62  Test Set Error
text:
62.1 Learning Objective
Define, use, and interpret the following terms:

title: 62  Test Set Error
text:
Training set
Test set
Cross-validation

title: 62  Test Set Error
text:
62.2 Lesson

62.2.1 Training Set and Test Set
The gold standard method for checking if your model is overfit to your data is to measure the performance of the model on new data. If you see a degradation in performance between the original sample and the new data, that’s evidence for overfitting. But what if you can’t obtain new data? You can solve this problem by holding out a subset of the data set for eventual use in testing performance. This subset is called a “test set”. The remaining data, which you use to fit your model, is called the “training set”.
Let’s examine this in a real data set. The package Lock5Data has a data set with 362 observations from “an in-class survey given to introductory statistics students over several years.” Let’s try to predict GPA. Unfortunately, 17 students are missing GPA, so we’ll have to remove them.









The first thing I’m going to do is split the data into two subsets, the training set and the test set. I’m going to use the package caret to do this, because it automatically performs a stratified random split of the data. This ensures the training set and test set are not too dissimilar in terms of the outcome. For example, you wouldn’t want (even by chance) to have the lowest GPAs in the training set and the highest GPAs in the test set.

set.seed(3)
in_train <- createDataPartition(y = d$GPA,
                                p = 0.8,
                                list = FALSE)
d_train <- d[in_train, ]
d_test <- d[-in_train, ]

I put 80% of the observations in the training set. There is not a hard-and-fast rule about what percentage of the observations to put in the training set. As the size of your original data set grows, you can put a smaller percentage in the test set, thus allowing more data for training.
Now that we’ve split our data, I’m going to train two models. The first is going to contain every possible variable. I’m not going to think, I’m just going to throw everything in.

mod_01 <- lm(formula = GPA ~ Year + Sex + Smoke + Award + Exercise + TV +
               Height + Weight + Siblings + BirthOrder + VerbalSAT + MathSAT +
               Pulse + Piercings,
             data = d_train)

For the second model, I’m only going to include a couple variables that I think could reasonably be related to GPA.

mod_02 <- lm(formula = GPA ~ Year + VerbalSAT + MathSAT,
             data = d_train)

I’m not going to check any assumptions because I’m just pretending that I only care about prediction. I don’t want to interpret any coefficients or p-values; I just want to measure how well the two models predict new data.
As a measure of performance, I’m going to use root mean squared error (RMSE): \[
\sqrt{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^m \left(Y_j - \hat{Y}_j\right)^2} \text{.}
\] Here \(m\) is the number of observations in the test set and \(\hat{Y}_j\) is the predicted outcome for the \(j\)th observation. I like the RMSE for continuous outcomes because it’s in the same units as the outcome.

y_hat_01 <- predict(object = mod_01,
                    newdata = d_test)
y_hat_02 <- predict(object = mod_02,
                    newdata = d_test)
RMSE_01 <- sqrt(mean(x = (d_test$GPA - y_hat_01)^2,
                     na.rm = TRUE))
RMSE_02 <- sqrt(mean((d_test$GPA - y_hat_02)^2))
RMSE_01

[1] 0.3311208

RMSE_02

[1] 0.3184888


The smaller model, Model 2, has slightly lower error than the larger model, meaning it does a slightly better job predicting new data. (Note that I had to remove missing values from the fitted values from Model 1. It must’ve been the case that some observations in the test set didn’t have values for all the covariates used in Model 1, so it was impossible to obtain fitted values for them.)
How did both models perform in the training set?

sqrt(mean(x = (d_train$GPA - predict(object = mod_01,
                                     newdata = d_train))^2,
          na.rm = TRUE))

[1] 0.3561529

sqrt(mean((d_train$GPA - mod_02$fitted.values)^2))

[1] 0.3774138


The larger model, Model 1, has slightly lower error in the training set than the smaller model. This is evidence of overfitting; the big model did better in the training set but worse in the test set. It failed to generalize to new data.


62.2.2 Validation Set
Sometimes, people will split the data into three subsets: a training set, a validation set, and a test set. Models are fit on the training set and their performance is measured in the validation set. Then, changes are made to the models and they are re-fit in the training set and re-evaluated in the validation set. This process proceeds iteratively until a final set of models is obtained. The performance of these final models is then measured in the test set.


62.2.3 Cross-Validation
Cross-validation is another method for testing the performance of a model in “new” data. In \(k\)-fold cross-validation, the original data set is split into \(k\) subsets. Then, the model is fit \(k\) times. In the first iteration, the model is fit on folds 2 through \(k\) and tested on fold 1. In the second iteration, the model is fit on fold 1 and folds 3 through \(k\) and tested on fold 2. After \(k\) iterations, the test error is summed (or averaged). Sometimes, people will split the original data set into a training set and a test set and then do cross-validation on the training set. This is common for regularized regression (LASSO and ridge), where you have to choose a penalty parameter, and ensemble methods, where you have to choose model weights.

title: 62  Test Set Error
text:
62.3 Problems

62.3.1 Problem 1
When you split your data into a training set and a test set, which plays the role of “new” data?






TipSolution





The test set. You don’t use it to fit the model(s), only to test the performance of the model(s).





62.3.2 Problem 2
In \(k\)-fold cross validation, how many times does each observation get used for testing?






TipSolution





Once.





62.3.3 Problem 2
In \(k\)-fold cross validation, how many times does each observation get used for training?






TipSolution





\(k - 1\) times.

title: 63  Likelihood
text: 63.1 Learning Objective

title: 63  Likelihood
text:
Define “likelihood”.
Explain why you would want to maximize the likelihood.
Explain when it would be inappropriate to use likelihoods to compare models.

title: 63  Likelihood
text:
63.2 Lesson

63.2.1 Normal Example
Suppose you draw a single observation from a normal distribution with expected value \(\mu\) and variance equal to 1. The value you get is \(-1\). In symbols, \(X\sim N(\mu,1)\) and you observe \(X = -1\).
The probability density function of \(X\) is \[
f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left(- \frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2}\right) \text{.}
\] We usually think of this as a function of \(x\), but it’s also a function of \(\mu\). We could write \[
f(x;\mu) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left(- \frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2}\right)
\] to make it explicit that this function depends on \(\mu\).
To make this more concrete, I’m going to plot \(f(x;\mu)\) for a variety of values of \(\mu\). In each one, I’m going to include dotted line segments to show the value of \(f(-1;\mu)\).





































When \(\mu = -3\), \(f(-1,-3)\) is pretty low; \(f(-1,-2)\) is higher, and \(f(-1,-1)\) is highest. As \(\mu\) continues to increase, the output of the function decreases again; \(f(-1,0)\) is lower and \(f(-1,1)\) is lower still.
The probability density function (PDF) is a measure of how likely it is to see certain values. The higher the PDF, the more likely that value. If we don’t know the value of \(\mu\), but we know what we observed, we might want to choose the value of \(\mu\) that maximizes the likelihood of observing what we observed. This is a way of estimating \(\mu\).
In this example, setting \(\mu = -1\) maximizes the PDF at \(x = -1\). So, we could argue that \(-1\) is a good estimate of \(\mu\).


63.2.2 Definition
“Likelihood” is commonly used in American English, but it has a special meaning in statistics. In statistics, the likelihood is the probability density function (PDF) or probability mass function (PMF), thought of as a function of the parameter(s) rather than the data.
By fixing the input to the PDF or PMF at the data we observed, and changing the value(s) of the parameter(s) until we maximize the likelihood, we find the value(s) of the parameter(s) that maximize(s) the likelihood of observing what we actually observed. This is a method for estimating the parameter(s).


63.2.3 Binomial Example
Suppose a magician has a special coin that lands heads with probability \(p\), where \(p \ne 0.5\). She flips the coin ten times and it lands heads seven times.
In this case, the number of heads follows a binomial distribution; we can write \(X\sim\text{binomial}(10,p)\). Below, I’ve plotted the probability mass function (PMF) of \(X\) for different values of \(p\). I’ve included a horizontal dashed line to indicate \(P(X = 7;p)\).





































I can also display \(P(X = 7;p)\) in a table.



\(p\)
\(P(X = 7;p)\)




0.5
0.117


0.6
0.215


0.7
0.267


0.8
0.201


0.9
0.057



We can see that \(P(X = 7;p)\) is highest for \(p = 0.7\). Although I didn’t test all possible values of \(p\), I can tell you that if you use calculus, you will find that \(P(X = 7;p)\) is maximized at \(p = 0.7\).


63.2.4 Different Sample Sizes
In the coin-flipping example above, we were effectively using the likelihood to compare models. Each candidate value of \(p\) was its own model, and we choose the one with the highest likelihood.
Suppose now that the magician flipped the coin twenty times and it landed heads sixteen times. The value of \(p\) that maximizes the likelihood for these twenty flips is \(16 / 20 = 0.8\). Yet, the value of the likelihood at \(p = 0.8\) is 0.218. This is lower than the maximized likelihood when the number of flips was ten and \(p\) was set to 0.7. Does that mean we should use \(p = 0.7\) instead?
The answer is no. We can’t use the likelihood to compare models that use different samples. One reason for this is that likelihoods tend to decrease as you add observations. If we flipped the coin a hundred times and observed eighty heads, the value of \(p\) that would maximize the likelihood is \(0.8\), even though the value of the likelihood for \(p = 0.8\) is only 0.099. With 100 coin flips, we should have more confidence in our estimate, not less.
By the way, if you want intuition for why the likelihood tends to decrease with more observations, it’s because you keep multiplying by something less than 1. Suppose you flip a fair coin one time. The probability it lands heads is \(\frac{1}{2}\). If you flip the coin again, the probability of two heads is \(\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{4}\). If you flip the coin a third time, the probability of three heads is \(\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{8}\). This isn’t just because three heads in a row is unlikely; the probability of any length-three sequence of heads and tails is \(\frac{1}{8}\). It doesn’t matter if it’s heads-heads-heads, heads-tails-heads, tails-heads-tails, or anything else.


63.2.5 Model Accuracy
If you’re computing a likelihood for a data set, you should believe the likelihood is accurate. What I mean is, it wouldn’t make sense to use the binomial PMF for normally distributed data, or the normal PDF for binomially distributed data. So, the likelihood should really be reserved for when you’re willing to make the argument that you know the underlying distribution of the data. (Some statisticians might disagree with me on this point.)


63.2.6 Maximum-Likelihood Estimator (MLE)
The value of the parameter that maximizes the likelihood for a given data set is called the maximum-likelihood estimator (MLE). There is a ton of statistical theory around MLEs. They have a lot of convenient and desirable properties.

title: 63  Likelihood
text:
63.3 Problems

63.3.1 Problem 1
If all four assumptions of simple linear regression are met, then we can write the likelihood as \[
f(y_1,\dotsc,y_n;\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\left(\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}\right)^n} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\right)^2\right) \text{.}
\] (I’m treating the observed values of the explanatory variable as constants rather than random variables, which is why I didn’t put them as input into the likelihood function.)
Ignoring \(\sigma^2\) for the moment, how should the maximum-likelihood estimates of \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) compare to the ordinary least squares (OLS) estimates?






TipSolution





They should be the same. Watch what happens as we decrease the sum of the squared errors: \[
\begin{align*}
\sum_{i=1}^n \left(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\right)^2 \downarrow &\implies - \sum_{i=1}^n \left(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\right)^2 \uparrow \\
&\implies -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\right)^2 \uparrow \\
&\implies \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\right)^2\right) \uparrow \\
&\implies \frac{1}{\left(\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}\right)^n} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\right)^2\right) \uparrow \\
&\implies f(y_1,\dotsc,y_n;\beta_0,\beta_1,\sigma^2) \uparrow \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] By minimizing the sum of squared errors, we maximize the likelihood. The same is true of multiple linear regression.





63.3.2 Problem 2
Suppose you regress depression, as measured by the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), on total sleep over the last seven days. Call this Model 1. You then decide that you want to add another explanatory variable, namely, number of interactions with friends or family over the last seven days that lasted an hour or more. Unfortunately, not everyone in your data set has this second explanatory variable recorded. You proceed anyone, regression depression on sleep and social interactions for those participants who have data for all variables. Call this Model 2.
Should you compare the likelihoods of Model 1 and Model 2? Justify your answer.






TipSolution





No. The models were fit on different samples. Model 1 was fit on the complete data set, and Model 2 was only fit on those participants who had all values for all variables. So, these likelihoods cannot be compared.

title: 64  AIC
text:
64.1 Learning Objective
Use the AIC to evaluate models.

title: 64  AIC
text:
64.2 Lesson

64.2.1 Formula
The Akaike information criterion (AIC) is a statistic that is used to compare the performance of different models. It is computed as follows: \[
\text{AIC} = 2k - 2 \log \hat{\mathcal{L}} \text{.}
\] In this formula, \(k\) is the number of parameters being estimated. For multiple linear regression, \(k = p + 2\); this counts the beta coefficients (\(p + 1\), for the number of covariates and the intercept) and \(\sigma^2\).
\(\hat{\mathcal{L}}\) is the maximized likelihood of the data, i.e., the value of the likelihood when you set the paramter(s) equal to the MLE(s).


64.2.2 Interpretation
A higher likelihood is better, so we want \(\hat{\mathcal{L}}\) to be big. Since \(f(x) = \log x\) is an increasing function (see below), a big \(\hat{\mathcal{L}}\) corresponds to a big \(\log \hat{\mathcal{L}}\), so we want \(\log \hat{\mathcal{L}}\) to be big. This means we want \(- 2 \log \hat{\mathcal{L}}\) to be very small. This means we want the AIC to be small.









Why do we add \(2k\) to the AIC? This is how we penalize adding covariates to the model, similar to with the adjusted \(R^2\). We add \(2k\) to prevent overfitting.


64.2.3 Example
Let’s return to the data set collected from introductory statistics students.

d <- Lock5Data::StudentSurvey
d <- d[!is.na(d$GPA), ]

I’d like to fit a large model and a small model, but there’s a problem. I know some observations in this data set are missing values for some variables.

colSums(is.na(d))

      Year        Sex      Smoke      Award  HigherSAT   Exercise         TV 
         0          0          0          0          0          1          1 
    Height     Weight   Siblings BirthOrder  VerbalSAT    MathSAT        SAT 
         7          5          0          3          0          0          0 
       GPA      Pulse  Piercings 
         0          0          1 


If I fit a model with Year, VerbalSAT, and MathSAT, I can use all 345 observations. If I fit a model with Height, the maximum number of observations I can use is \(345 - 7 = 338\). The two models will be based on two different samples, meaning I can’t compare their likelihoods, meaning I can’t compare their AICs. So, if I want to use the AIC to compare two models, I have to make sure they are fit on exactly the same samples first. In order to achieve this for this example, I’m going to first create a new data set with complete cases, i.e., observations with no missing values.

d_complete <- d[complete.cases(d), ]

Now I can fit my two models.

mod_01 <- lm(formula = GPA ~ Year + Sex + Smoke + Award + Exercise + TV +
               Height + Weight + Siblings + BirthOrder + VerbalSAT + MathSAT +
               Pulse + Piercings,
             data = d_complete)
mod_02 <- lm(formula = GPA ~ Year + VerbalSAT + MathSAT,
             data = d_complete)

Before looking at their AICs, I’m going to look at their log-likelihooods. The log-likelihood is just the log of the likelihood; in this case, it’s the log of the maximized likelihood. Statisticians often prefer the log-likelihood over the likelihood for reasons that I won’t go into here.


'log Lik.' -120.3773 (df=19)


'log Lik.' -138.9329 (df=7)


Note that the larger model, Model 1, has the higher log likelihood.
Now let’s look at the AICs.


[1] 278.7546


[1] 291.8658


Model 1 has the lower AIC! This is a surprise to me. It means that, according to the AIC, the improvement in fit for the larger model is “worth” all those extra variables. This contrasts with the conclusion from the test set error.


64.2.4 Warnings
The help file for the R function AIC, accessible with the command ?AIC, has some helpful warnings:

“The theory of AIC requires that the log-likelihood has been maximized: whereas AIC can be computed for models not fitted by maximum likelihood, their AIC values should not be compared.”
“Examples of models not ‘fitted to the same data’ are where the response is transformed (accelerated-life models are fitted to log-times) and where contingency tables have been used to summarize data.”

I’m not sure whether the first point will come up in this class, but it’s worth keeping in mind when you reach more advanced analyses. The second point is very important for this class; when using the AIC to compare models, make sure those models have the same outcome. If you transform your outcome, for example, by logging it, you shouldn’t use the AIC to compare the model with the transformed outcome to the model with the untransformed outcome.
I have another warning that isn’t in the AIC help file. You can’t use the AIC to compare two models when one is based on a discrete distribution and the other is based on a continuous distribution. This will become more relevant later, when we cover forms of regression that are designed for discrete outcomes, like counts. For example, you can’t use the AIC to compare a Poisson regression model to a linear regression model. The reason behind this is a little complicated, so you don’t need to know it. It took me forever to work out, though, so I’m going to include it in the callout below.






CautionCaution: Math





Suppose \(P\) and \(Q\) are probability measures on \(\left(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}\right)\) and \(P\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(Q\). (This means that \(\forall A\in\mathcal{B}\), \(Q(A) = 0 \implies P(A) = 0\). We denote this \(P \ll Q\) and say \(P\) is dominated by \(Q\).) The Kullback-Leibler divergence of \(P\) from \(Q\), also called the relative entropy from \(Q\) to \(P\), is \[
D_{KL}\left(P\parallel Q\right) = \int_{x\in\mathbb{R}} \log \frac{dP(x)}{dQ(x)} dP(x) \text{.}
\] Note that \[
\begin{align*}
    D_{KL}\left(P\parallel Q\right) &= \int_{x\in\mathbb{R}} \log \frac{dP(x)}{dQ(x)} dP(x) \\
    &= \int_{x\in\mathbb{R}} \log dP(x) dP(x) - \int_{x\in\mathbb{R}} \log dQ(x) dP(x) \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] If \(P\) is the true data-generating distribution, \(\int_{x\in\mathbb{R}} \log dP(x) dP(x)\) will be the same regardless of our hypothesized model \(Q\). The AIC is based on the second term.
Suppose \(Q_2\left(\left\{x\in\mathbb{R} : Q_2(x) = 0\right\}\right) = 0\).

This implies \(Q_2\left(\left\{x\in\mathbb{R} : Q_2(x) > 0\right\}\right) = 1\).
Define \(D_n = \left\{x\in\mathbb{R} : Q_2(x) \ge \frac{1}{n}\right\}\). Let \(|D_n| = M\). Then \(Q_2\left(\left\{x\in\mathbb{R} : Q_2(x) \ge \frac{1}{n}\right\}\right) \ge \frac{M}{n}\). Since \(Q_2\left(\left\{x\in\mathbb{R} : Q_2(x) \ge \frac{1}{n}\right\}\right) \le 1\), \[
\begin{align*}
  1 &\ge \frac{M}{n} \\
  n &\ge M \text{,}
\end{align*}
\] and \(|D_n| = M < +\infty\).
Since \(D_n\) has finitely many elements, \(\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty D_n\) has at most countably many elements. But \[
\begin{align*}
  \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty D_n &= \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \left\{x\in\mathbb{R} : Q_2(x) \ge \frac{1}{n}\right\} \\
  &= \left\{x\in\mathbb{R} : Q_2(x) > 0\right\} \text{,}
\end{align*}
\] so \(\left\{x\in\mathbb{R} : Q_2(x) > 0\right\}\) has at most countably many elements.

Suppose that

\(Q_2\left(\left\{x\in\mathbb{R} : Q_2(x) = 0\right\}\right) = 0\).
\(Q_1\ll\lambda\), where \(\lambda\) is Lebesgue measure.

If

\(P \ll Q_1\).

\(Q_1(A) = 0 \implies P(A) = 0\). Since \(Q_1\ll\lambda\), \(\lambda(A) = 0 \implies Q_1(A) = 0\). So, \(\lambda(A) = 0 \implies Q_1(A) = 0 \implies P(A) = 0\), and \(P \ll \lambda\).
\[
\begin{align*}
P\left(\left\{x\in\mathbb{R} : Q_2(x) = 0\right\}\right) &= 1 - P\left(\left\{x\in\mathbb{R} : Q_2(x) > 0\right\}\right) \\
&= 1 - \sum_{\left\{x\in\mathbb{R} : Q_2(x) > 0\right\}} P(x) \\
&= 1 - 0 \\
&= 1
\end{align*}
\]
So, \(P\) is not dominated by \(Q_2\).

\(P \ll Q_2\).

\(P\left(\left\{x\in\mathbb{R} : Q_2(x) = 0\right\}\right) = 0\).
\(P\left(\left\{x\in\mathbb{R} : Q_2(x) > 0\right\}\right) = 1\).
\(\exists x_0\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(P(x_0) > 0\). \(\lambda(x_0) = 0 \implies Q_1(x_0) = 0\).
\(Q_1\) does not dominate \(P\).

title: 64  AIC
text:
64.3 Problems

64.3.1 Problem 1
In the example above, I didn’t check any assumptions for the two models. Should I have? Why or why not?






TipSolution





Yes, I should’ve. The AIC is based on the likelihood, which is based on all of our assumptions being met. So, I should’ve checked the assumptions for both models.


























































Based on the plots, it seems like the linearity, homoscedasticity, and normality assumptions are met for both models. I don’t know much about how the data were collected, but I’m willing to go along with the assumption that the observations are independent.





64.3.2 Problem 2
If Model A has an AIC of 400 and Model B has an AIC of 405, which is better? Assume all relevant assumptions have been met.






TipSolution





Model A is better because it has the lower AIC.





64.3.3 Problem 3
If \(k\) is the number of parameters estimated and \(\hat{\mathcal{L}}\) is the maximized log-likelihood then the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) is \(k \log n - 2 \log \hat{\mathcal{L}}\). What are the consequences for using the BIC instead of the AIC?






TipSolution





If \(\log n > 2\), i.e., if \(n > e^2 \approx 7.4\), then the BIC will apply a bigger penalty to the size of the model than the AIC. Thus, for large sample size, the BIC will favor smaller models than the AIC.

title: 65  Likelihood Ratio Test
text: 65.1 Learning Objective

title: 65  Likelihood Ratio Test
text:
Interpret the results of a likelihood ratio test.
Explain when it would be inappropriate to use a likelihood ratio test.

title: 65  Likelihood Ratio Test
text:
65.2 Lesson
A likelihood ratio test (LRT) is a hypothesis test that can only be used with nested models. Nesting can get somewhat technical, but this statement will get you pretty far: If Model A estimates a subset of the parameters estimated by Model B, then Model A is nested within Model B.
For example, mod_02 below is nested within mod_01. This is because all the covariates in mod_02 are also in mod_01.

mod_01 <- lm(formula = GPA ~ Sex + Smoke + Award + Exercise + TV +
               Height + Weight + Siblings + BirthOrder + VerbalSAT + MathSAT +
               Pulse + Piercings,
             data = d_complete)
mod_02 <- lm(formula = GPA ~ VerbalSAT + MathSAT,
             data = d_complete)

mod_03 below is not nested within mod_01. MathSATHigher is a variable I created that equals 1 if the Math SAT score is higher than the Verbal SAT score and 0 otherwise.

mod_03 <- lm(formula = GPA ~ MathSATHigher,
             data = d_complete)

If you want to know what I mean by “Nesting can get somewhat technical,” click on the callout below.






CautionCaution: Math





mod_04, below, is nested within mod_01 and mod_02, even though it contains a covariate (SAT) that isn’t in mod_01 or mod_02.

mod_04 <- lm(formula = GPA ~ SAT,
             data = d_complete)

This is because SAT = VerbalSAT + MathSAT, and both mod_01 and mod_02 contain VerbalSAT and MathSAT.
In order to explain this further, I’m going to use mod_02 instead of mod_01 because mod_02 is simpler. mod_02 is this: \[
E\left(\texttt{GPA}\middle|\texttt{VerbalSAT},\texttt{MathSAT}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \texttt{VerbalSAT} + \beta_2 \texttt{MathSAT} \text{.}
\]
mod_04 is this: \[
\begin{align*}
E\left(\texttt{GPA}\middle|\texttt{SAT}\right) &= \beta_0 + \beta_3 \texttt{SAT} \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_3 \left(\texttt{VerbalSAT} + \texttt{MathSAT}\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_3 \texttt{VerbalSAT} + \beta_3 \texttt{MathSAT} \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\]
So, mod_04 is mod_02 but with the additional constraint that \(\beta_1 = \beta_2\). This counts as nesting.
What about mod_03? mod_03 is \[
\begin{align*}
E\left(\texttt{GPA}\middle|\texttt{MathSATHigher}\right) &= \beta_0 + \beta_4  \texttt{MathSATHigher.} \\
\end{align*}
\]
There’s no way to write mod_03 as a version of mod_2, but with some additional constraint. mod_03 is a discontinuous function of VerbalSAT and MathSAT, but mod_02 is a continuous function of these two variables.



The null hypothesis of the LRT is that the smaller model is the correct one. The alternative hypothesis is that the larger model is the correct one.
Let’s use the LRT to compare mod_01 to mod_02.

anova(mod_01,
      mod_02,
      test = "LRT")

Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: GPA ~ Sex + Smoke + Award + Exercise + TV + Height + Weight + 
    Siblings + BirthOrder + VerbalSAT + MathSAT + Pulse + Piercings
Model 2: GPA ~ VerbalSAT + MathSAT
  Res.Df    RSS  Df Sum of Sq  Pr(>Chi)    
1    316 40.567                            
2    328 45.414 -12   -4.8469 0.0001683 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The p-value is very small, so we can conclude that the larger model is better.
What happens if we try to get R to conduct a hypothesis test with two non-nested models?

anova(mod_01,
      mod_03,
      test = "LRT")

title: 65  Likelihood Ratio Test
text:
65.3 Problems

65.3.1 Problem 1
If you fail to reject the null hypothesis in an LRT, what should you do?






TipSolution





Generally you would conclude that the larger model is no better than the smaller one, and use the smaller one. We often prefer smaller models because they are easier to interpret and have greater power.





65.3.2 Problem 2
If I hadn’t removed observations with missing data, and instead had fit mod_02 on the data set with 345 observations instead of 331, could I still have used the LRT to compare the models?






TipSolution





No. The likelihood ratio test, like its name implies, uses the likelihood. So, you can only use it to compare models that have been fit on the same data.

66.3 Problems

66.3.1 Problem 1
If \(X\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p)\), is it possible for \(X\) to equal its own expected value?






TipSolution





Only in the trivial case where \(p = 0\), meaning it’s impossible to observe a 1, or \(p = 1\), meaning it’s impossible to observe a 0. So long as \(0 < p < 1\), \(X \ne E(X)\).

title: 67  Violated Assumptions of Linear Regression
text:
67.1 Learning Objective
Identify which of the four assumptions of linear regression are automatically violated when the outcome is Bernoulli.
crumbs: 67  Violated Assumptions of Linear Regression

title: 67  Violated Assumptions of Linear Regression
text:
67.2 Lesson
If our outcome variable is Bernoulli, some (but not all) of the assumptions of linear regression are automatically violated.

67.2.1 Linearity
The linearity assumption of linear regression is not automatically violated when we have a binary outcome. Consider this example: I can simulate \(X_1,\dotsc,X_{100}\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\text{uniform}(0,1)\) and then simulate Bernoulli random variables \(Y_1,\dotsc,Y_{100}\) such that \(E(Y_i|X_i = x) = x\). In this case, the mean of the outcome is a linear function of the explanatory variable, which is exactly the linearity assumption.

set.seed(2)
n <- 1e2
x <- runif(n)
y <- rbinom(n = n,
            size = 1,
            prob = x)
mod_01 <- lm(y ~ x)
plot(x = x,
     y = y)
abline(mod_01,
       col = "blue")







summary(mod_01)


Call:
lm(formula = y ~ x)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-0.88098 -0.30617  0.04265  0.34726  0.77258 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  0.11604    0.08351   1.389    0.168    
x            0.86241    0.14539   5.932 4.52e-08 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.4319 on 98 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.2642,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2567 
F-statistic: 35.18 on 1 and 98 DF,  p-value: 4.518e-08


I admit the residual scatterplot looks weird, but I know from having simulated the data that the linearity assumption is met.











67.2.2 IID
There’s nothing about a binary outcome that makes iid data impossible. In fact, the type of outcome has nothing to do with whether the data are iid or not.


67.2.3 Homoscedasticity
Recall that if \(Y\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p)\) then \(E(Y) = p\) and \(Var(Y) = p(1-p)\). So, if \(Y\in\{0,1\}\) and \(E(Y|X)\) is a function of \(X\), then \(Var(Y|X) = E(Y|X)\left(1 - E(Y|X)\right)\) will be a function of \(X\). This is a violation of homoscedasticity or equal variance. If the variance depends on the explanatory variable(s), then the variance is not constant. The only way the homoscedasticity assumption would not be violated is if \(X\) was not actually random and could only take on one value, or if \(Y\) and \(X\) had no relationship.


67.2.4 Normality
If \(Y\) is Bernoulli, it can only take on the values of 0 or 1. If \(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{p} + \epsilon\), \(\epsilon\) can only take on two values. Either \[
\epsilon = 1 - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{p}\right)
\] or \[
\epsilon = 0 - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{p}\right) \text{.}
\] So, obviously \(\epsilon\) cannot be normal.
crumbs: 67  Violated Assumptions of Linear Regression

title: 67  Violated Assumptions of Linear Regression
text:
67.3 Problems

67.3.1 Problem 1
If you perform linear regression with a binary outcome, are the coefficient estimates unbiased?






TipSolution





This depends. The linearity assumption would have to be met. As seen in the residual scatterplot above, this is kind of difficult to check with a residual scatterplot. You could try checking this with a calibration plot, which we’ll talk about in a later section.





67.3.2 Problem 2
If you perform linear regression with a binary outcome, are the standard errors correct?






TipSolution





No the default standard errors, because the homoscedasticity assumption is violated. You could use robust/sandwich standard errors instead.





67.3.3 Problem 3
If you perform linear regression with a binary outcome, are the p-values correct?






TipSolution





Not the default p-values, because they’re computed assuming homoscedasticity, which is violated. If you used robust/sandwich standard errors and had a large sample size (and if the linearity and iid assumptions were met), you could trust the p-values.
