title: 68  Assumptions of Logistic Regression
text:
68.1 Learning Objective
Explain the assumptions of logistic regression.

title: 68  Assumptions of Logistic Regression
text:
68.2 Lesson

68.2.1 Assumptions
Logistic regression has the following assumptions:

\(Y_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p_i)\).
\(\log\frac{p_i}{1-p_i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\).
The observations are iid.

We’ve already talked about the Bernoulli distribution and what it means for observations to be iid, but the weird function merits some unpacking.


68.2.2 Logit Function
The function \[
f(p) = \log\frac{p}{1-p}
\] is called the logit or log-odds function. A graph is below.









It’s probably more illuminating if we look at the inverse function, known as the “expit” function.


68.2.3 Expit Function
The expit function is the inverse of the logit function: \[
g(q) = \frac{\exp(q)}{1 + \exp(q)} \text{.}
\] Here’s the work if you’re curious: \[
\begin{align*}
q &= \log \frac{p}{1-p} \\
\exp(q) &= \frac{p}{1-p} \\
\exp(q) (1-p) &= p \\
\exp(q) - p \exp(q) &= p \\
\exp(q) &= p\exp(q) + p \\
\exp(q) &= p\left(\exp(q) + 1\right) \\
\frac{\exp(q)}{1 + \exp(q)} &= p \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
You might also see the expit function written in a different but equivalent manner: \[
\begin{align*}
g(q) &= \frac{\exp(q)}{1 + \exp(q)} \\
&= \frac{\exp(q)}{1 + \exp(q)} \frac{\exp(-q)}{\exp(-q)} \\
&= \frac{1}{\exp(-q) + 1} \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
Again, we can look at a graph:









So, the assumption \[
\log\frac{p_i}{1-p_i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}
\] can also be written as \[
p_i = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\right)\right)} \text{.}
\]
Why do we do this? There are a few reasons. First, note that the expit function can take in any value between \(-\infty\) and \(+\infty\) (exclusive). This means that \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\) can be any number, positive or negative. Second, the output of the expit function is between 0 and 1.
If we were to use linear regression and assume \(E(Y_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\), we might find that \(\hat{Y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \hat{\beta}_p X_{ip}\) is below zero or above one, which doesn’t make sense, since \(\hat{Y}_i = \hat{E}(Y_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip})\) should be a probability.
There are other reasons to use this weird function, which we will get to later.

title: 68  Assumptions of Logistic Regression
text:
68.3 Problems

68.3.1 Problem 1
In the logit function, what is the base of the logarithm?






TipSolution





The special number \(e\). The logarithm with base \(e\) is sometimes called the natural logarithm.





68.3.2 Problem 2
What are the possible values the logit function can produce? You might remember this as the “range” of the function.






TipSolution





Any real number, i.e., any positive or negative number, even those that can’t be represented by fractions.

title: 69  Odds
text: 69.1 Learning Objectives

title: 69  Odds
text:
Define odds.
Compare and contrast odds and probability.
Explain why odds ratios might be useful in case-control studies.

title: 69  Odds
text:
69.2 Lesson

69.2.1 Definition
If \(p\) is a probability (also called a risk or chance), then \[
\frac{p}{1-p}
\] is an odds.
Odds are often used in betting. For example, someone might say, “Odds are 3-to-1 that this horse will win the race on Sunday.” If a horse has 3-to-1 odds of winning, then \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{p}{1-p} &= \frac{3}{1} \\
p &= 3(1-p) \\
p &= 3 - 3p \\
4p &= 3 \\
p &= \frac{3}{4} \text{,}
\end{align*}
\] and the horse’s probability of winning is \(0.75\).
As you can see, the odds is not equal to the probability; 3 is not the same as 3/4. There is, however, a case where the two are approximately the same. This happens when the probability is very small. If \(p\) is near zero, then \[
\frac{p}{1-p} \approx \frac{p}{1} = p \text{.}
\] So, for rare events, the odds is a not-bad approximation of the risk.


69.2.2 Case-Control Studies
In public health, we often want to estimate the probability of a disease given some risk factor. Let’s call this probability \(P(D = 1|F)\). For simplicity, let’s assume both \(D\) and \(F\) are binary; either you have the disease or you don’t, and either you have the risk factor or you don’t.
It’s often desirable to estimate a risk ratio, i.e., \[
\frac{P(D = 1|F = 1)}{P(D = 1|F = 0)} \text{.}
\] This allows us to compare the probability of disease for people who have the risk factor to the probability of disease for people who don’t have the risk factor. If the risk ratio above is 1.5, then people who have the risk factor are 50% more likely to get the disease than people who don’t have the risk factor.
In a case-control study, we can’t estimate the risk ratio. This is because, in a case-control study, people are recruited conditional on their disease status. Then we estimate the probability of the risk factor, conditional on disease status. In other words, we estimate \(P(F = 1|D = 1)\), which is not equal to \(P(D = 1|F = 1)\).
This is where odds come in. Suppose the disease is very rare, so \[
\begin{align*}
P(D = 1|F = 1) &\approx 0 \\
P(D = 1|F = 0) &\approx 0 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] Then the probabilities are approximately equal to the corresponding odds, i.e., \[
\begin{align*}
P(D = 1|F = 1) &\approx \frac{P(D = 1|F = 1)}{1 - P(D = 1|F = 1)} \\
&= \frac{P(D = 1|F = 1)}{P(D = 0|F = 1)} \\
P(D = 1|F = 0) &\approx \frac{P(D = 1|F = 0)}{1 - P(D = 1|F = 0)} \\
&= \frac{P(D = 1|F = 0)}{P(D = 0|F = 0)} \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] Then the risk ratio is \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{P(D = 1|F = 1)}{P(D = 1|F = 0)} &\approx \frac{\frac{P(D = 1|F = 1)}{P(D = 0|F = 1)}}{\frac{P(D = 1|F = 0)}{P(D = 0|F = 0)}} \\
&= \frac{\frac{P(D = 1,F = 1)/P(F = 1)}{P(D = 0,F = 1)/P(F = 1)}}{\frac{P(D = 1,F = 0)/P(F = 0)}{P(D = 0,F = 0)/P(F = 0)}} \\
&= \frac{\frac{P(D = 1,F = 1)}{P(D = 0,F = 1)}}{\frac{P(D = 1,F = 0)}{P(D = 0,F = 0)}} \\
&= \frac{P(D = 1,F = 1)}{P(D = 0,F = 1)} \frac{P(D = 0,F = 0)}{P(D = 1,F = 0)} \\
&= \frac{P(D = 1,F = 1)}{P(D = 1,F = 0)} \frac{P(D = 0,F = 0)}{P(D = 0,F = 1)} \\
&= \frac{\frac{P(D = 1,F = 1)}{P(D = 1,F = 0)}}{\frac{P(D = 0,F = 1)}{P(D = 0,F = 0)}}  \\
&= \frac{\frac{P(D = 1,F = 1)/P(D = 1)}{P(D = 1,F = 0)/P(D = 1)}}{\frac{P(D = 0,F = 1)/P(D = 0)}{P(D = 0,F = 0)/P(D = 0)}}  \\
&= \frac{\frac{P(F=1|D=1)}{P(F=0|D=1)}}{\frac{P(F =1|D=0)}{P(F=0|D=0)}} \text{.}  \\
\end{align*}
\]
All that is to say that we can approximate the relative risk, which we can’t estimate directly, with an odds ratio, which we can estimate directly.

title: 69  Odds
text:
69.3 Problems

69.3.1 Problem 1
Can we use odds to approximate this risk difference: \[
P(D = 1|F = 1) - P(D = 1|F = 0) \text{?}
\]






TipSolution





No. Even if the disease is rare, this is as far as we can get: \[
\begin{align*}
P(D = 1|F = 1) - P(D = 1|F = 0) &\approx \frac{P(D = 1|F = 1)}{P(D = 0|F = 1)} - \frac{P(D = 1|F = 0)}{P(D = 0|F = 0)} \\
&= \frac{P(D = 1,F = 1)}{P(D = 0,F = 1)} - \frac{P(D = 1,F = 0)}{P(D = 0,F = 0)} \\
&= \frac{P(D = 1,F = 1)P(D = 0,F = 0) - P(D = 1,F = 0)P(D = 0,F = 1)}{P(D = 0,F = 1) P(D = 0,F = 0)} \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]





69.3.2 Problem 2
If \(p = 0.5\), what is the odds?






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
\frac{0.5}{1 - 0.5} &= \frac{0.5}{0.5} \\
&= 1
\end{align*}
\]

title: 70  Interpretation
text:
70.1 Learning Objective
Interpret the coefficients in logistic regression.

title: 70  Interpretation
text:
70.2 Lesson

70.2.1 Intercept
Recall that, in logistic regression, we assume \[
\log\frac{p_i}{1-p_i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \text{.}
\]
What happens when all the covariates equal zero? \[
\begin{align*}
\log\frac{p_i}{1-p_i} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \\
\log\frac{p_i}{1-p_i} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \cdots + \beta_p (0) \\
\log\frac{p_i}{1-p_i} &= \beta_0 \\
\frac{p_i}{1-p_i} &= \exp(\beta_0) \\
\end{align*}
\]
So, \(\exp(\beta_0)\) is the odds of the outcome being 1 when all the covariates equal zero.


70.2.2 Non-Intercept Coefficients
How do we interpret the non-intercept coefficients? Suppose observation \(i\) has \(X_{i1} = x\) and observation \(j\) has \(X_{j1} = x + 1\). For each \(k \ne 1\), \(X_{ik} = X_{jk}\). In words, the two observations are identical except for the first covariate, where the \(j\)th observation exceeds the \(i\)th observation by one unit. Then \[
\begin{align*}
\log \frac{\frac{p_j}{1-p_j}}{\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}} &= \log \frac{p_j}{1-p_j} - \log \frac{p_i}{1-p_i} \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{j1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{jp} - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (x+1) + \cdots + \beta_p X_{jp} - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_1 + \cdots + \beta_p X_{jp} - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\right) \\
&= \beta_1 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] By exponentiating both sides of this equation, we see \[
\begin{align*}
\log \frac{\frac{p_j}{1-p_j}}{\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}} &= \beta_1 \\
\frac{\frac{p_j}{1-p_j}}{\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}} &= \exp(\beta_1) \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\]
In words, \(\exp(\beta_1)\) is the odds ratio comparing two populations that are identical except that one exceeds the other by one unit on the first covariate. If \(\exp(\beta_1) > 1\), the odds that the outcome equals 1 is greater in the population with the higher value of the first covariate; if \(\exp(\beta_1) < 1\), the odds that the outcome equals 1 is lesser in the population with the higher value of the first covariate; if \(\exp(\beta_1) = 1\), the odds that the outcome equals 1 is the same in both populations.


70.2.3 Example
In this data set, “Study subjects were patients who had an elective surgical procedure during a three-year period to biopsy or remove a lesion of the lung, colon, breast, skin, ovary or uterus that was found to be non-cancerous.” (Lock5Data Package) Let’s regress smoking on years since age 40, vitamin use (no, occasional, or regular), and sex (male or female). I’m using “years since age 40” instead of age directly so we can get a more meaningful intercept

mod_01 <- glm(formula = SmokeYes ~ YearsSince40 + VitaminUse + Sex,
              family = binomial,
              data = d)
summary(mod_01)

title: 71  Calibration
text: 71.1 Learning Objective

title: 71  Calibration
text:
Explain calibration.
Interpret a calibration plot.

title: 71  Calibration
text:
71.2 Lesson

71.2.1 Assumption-Checking
How do we check the assumptions of logistic regression? As a reminder, here they are:

\(Y_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p_i)\).
\(\log\frac{p_i}{1-p_i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\).
The observations are iid.

The first one is easy to check: We just have to look at the outcome and make sure it’s binary. The third one we’ve checked before: We can look at how the data were collected to determine if there is any dependency between observations. But what about that weird logistic function?
One way to check the second assumption above is to see if the model is well-calibrated. In a well-calibrated model, the fitted values are close to the observed values. But how do we know if this is the case? The fitted values will be probabilities, but the observed values are 0s and 1s. I think the best way to understand the procedure is to walk through the creation of a calibration plot.


71.2.2 Calibration Plot
Let’s return to the nutrition study, where we regressed smoking on years since age 40, vitamin use (no, occasional, or regular), and sex (male or female).

mod_01 <- glm(formula = SmokeYes ~ YearsSince40 + VitaminUse + Sex,
              family = binomial,
              data = d)
summary(mod_01)


Call:
glm(formula = SmokeYes ~ YearsSince40 + VitaminUse + Sex, family = binomial, 
    data = d)

Coefficients:
                     Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)          -1.20773    0.27658  -4.367 1.26e-05 ***
YearsSince40         -0.04098    0.01398  -2.932  0.00337 ** 
VitaminUseOccasional -0.45047    0.41244  -1.092  0.27475    
VitaminUseRegular    -0.95796    0.41851  -2.289  0.02208 *  
SexMale               0.66759    0.50100   1.333  0.18269    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 251.10  on 314  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 235.49  on 310  degrees of freedom
AIC: 245.49

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5


This is a calibration plot for this model. It was created using the function cal_plot_breaks from the package probably.

library(probably)


Attaching package: 'probably'


The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    as.factor, as.ordered

cal_plot_breaks(.data = data.frame(truth = as.factor(mod_01$model$SmokeYes),
                                   estimate = mod_01$fitted.values),
                truth = truth,
                estimate = estimate,
                event_level = "second")








How was this plot made? These are the steps:

R split the interval from 0 to 1 into ten segments of equal length: 0 to 0.1, 0.1 to 0.2, 0.2 to 0.3, and so forth. Ten is the default number of segments, but you can change it by passing a different number to the num_breaks parameter in the function.
R put observations with similar fitted values into bins. Any observations with fitted values between 0 and 0.1 were put in the same bin; any observations with fitted values between 0.1 and 0.2 were put in the same bin; any observations with fitted values between 0.2 and 0.3 were put in the same bin; and so forth.
R computed the proportion of observations in each bin that had an observed outcome of 1.
R plotted the bin midpoints (0.05, 0.15, 0.25, etc.) on the horizontal axis and the observed proportions of 1s in the bins on the vertical axis. This function uses the term “Event Rate” to mean the observed proportion of 1s.
R added confidence bands around the points on the plot.
R added tick marks to the bottom of the plot to indicate 0s and tick marks at the top of the plot to indicate 1s. The locations of the tick marks along the horizontal axis correspond to the fitted values of the corresponding observations.

You might be wondering where R got the fitted values. This is the formula \[
\hat{Y}_i = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \hat{\beta}_p X_{ip}\right)\right)} \text{.}
\] If you want to see the fitted values, you don’t have to do that computation by hand. You can do either of the following:

y_hat_option_1 <- mod_01$fitted.values
y_hat_option_2 <- predict(object = mod_01,
                          newdata = d,
                          type = "response")
all.equal(target = y_hat_option_1,
          current = y_hat_option_2)

[1] TRUE


You’re probably also wondering how to interpret the plot. If the fitted values accurately reflect the true underlying probabilities, then the observed proportion of 1s in each bin should be approximately equal to the bin midpoint. In that case, the points on the plot would fall along the dashed reference line. In the plot above, we see a deviation from the reference line for the bin midpoint of 0.35. However, the confidence band around that point contains the reference line. In fact, the confidence band contains the reference line throughout the graph. So, this model is well-calibrated.
Why is the confidence band larger for the bin midpoint of 0.35 than for other bin midpoints? I can think of two reasons. First, there are probably fewer observations with fitted values between 0.3 and 0.4 than in other bins. We can check that.

sum(y_hat_option_1 < 0.1)

[1] 124

sum(y_hat_option_1 >= 0.1 & y_hat_option_1 < 0.2)

[1] 124

sum(y_hat_option_1 >= 0.2 & y_hat_option_1 < 0.3)

[1] 58

sum(y_hat_option_1 >= 0.3 & y_hat_option_1 < 0.4)

[1] 9


We see that there are only 9 observations with fitted values between 0.3 and 0.4, but 124 observations with fitted values between 0 and 0.1. With fewer observations, the confidence band gets wider.
Second, recall that Bernoulli random variables have their maximum variance when \(p = 0.5\). So, as the observed proportion gets closer to 0.5, the variability of the underlying data is higher, and we have to make the confidence band wider to account for that.


71.2.3 Simulation
I’m going to simulate data to see a calibration plot for a model where the assumptions are known to be met, and another plot for a model where the assumptions are known to not be met.
I’m going to generate the outcome according to the model \[
P(Y_i = 1|X_i) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \beta_2 X_i^2\right)\right)} \text{.}
\]
Next, I’m going to run logistic regression according to the true model and make a calibration plot.

mod_02 <- glm(formula = y ~ x + I(x^2),
              family = binomial)
summary(mod_02)


Call:
glm(formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), family = binomial)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)   0.9223     0.1010   9.133  < 2e-16 ***
x             1.8597     0.1974   9.419  < 2e-16 ***
I(x^2)        0.9788     0.1370   7.147  8.9e-13 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 1144.02  on 999  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance:  938.07  on 997  degrees of freedom
AIC: 944.07

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 7

cal_plot_breaks(.data = data.frame(truth = as.factor(mod_02$y),
                                   estimate = mod_02$fitted.values),
                truth = truth,
                estimate = estimate,
                event_level = "second")








This model is well-calibrated. The confidence band contains the reference line for all points.
What if our assumption is bad? Let’s run a regression without the squared term.

mod_03 <- glm(formula = y ~ x,
              family = binomial)
summary(mod_03)


Call:
glm(formula = y ~ x, family = binomial)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)  1.22421    0.08256  14.828   <2e-16 ***
x            0.83655    0.08735   9.577   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 1144.0  on 999  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 1032.7  on 998  degrees of freedom
AIC: 1036.7

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4

cal_plot_breaks(.data = data.frame(truth = as.factor(mod_03$y),
                                   estimate = mod_03$fitted.values),
                truth = truth,
                estimate = estimate,
                event_level = "second")








This very clearly does not follow the reference line. What it’s saying is that 100% of observations with fitted values between 0 and 0.3 have an outcome of 1. So, our fitted values are very inaccurate! Our predictions are only accurate for fitted values between about 0.8 and 1.0.

title: 71  Calibration
text:
71.3 Problems

71.3.1 Problem 1
Let’s return to the NHANES data set. The outcome is a 1 if the respondent bought any food labeled organic in the past 30 days, and 0 otherwise. I’ve regressed this on self-rated health (excellent, very good, good, fair, and poor) and monthly income (in thousands of dollars).



Call:
glm(formula = OrganicYes ~ Health + Income1000, family = binomial, 
    data = d2)

Coefficients:
                Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)     -0.75350    0.11490  -6.558 5.47e-11 ***
HealthFair      -0.73735    0.13271  -5.556 2.76e-08 ***
HealthGood      -0.31940    0.11368  -2.810  0.00496 ** 
HealthPoor      -0.58209    0.21071  -2.762  0.00574 ** 
HealthVery good -0.05688    0.11723  -0.485  0.62753    
Income1000       0.13783    0.01327  10.383  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 5493.5  on 4183  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 5288.4  on 4178  degrees of freedom
  (532 observations deleted due to missingness)
AIC: 5300.4

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4











Is this model well-calibrated? Justify your answer.






TipSolution





This looks great, except for the observations with the lowest fitted values. What’s going on?
If we look at the fitted values less than 0.2, we see that the smallest fitted value is actually 0.1880, which is greater than the bin midpoint of 0.15.


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.1880  0.1880  0.1965  0.1937  0.1965  0.1965 


Below, I’ve written a function that will do most of what cal_plot_breaks does, but use the average of the fitted values in each bin rather than the bin midpoint.

#' Make a calibration plot.
#'   
#' @param mod The logistic regression model, obtained using the glm function.
#' @param n_bins The number of bins to use.
#' @returns Doesn't return anything; draws a plot.
draw_cal_plot <- function(mod,n_bins){
  cal_data <- data.frame(truth = mod$y,
                         estimate = mod$fitted.values)
  cal_bins <- list()
  for(i in 1:(n_bins - 1)){
    cal_bins[[i]] <- cal_data[cal_data$estimate >= (i - 1) / n_bins & cal_data$estimate < i / n_bins, ]
  }
  cal_bins[[n_bins]] <- cal_data[cal_data$estimate >= (n_bins - 1) / n_bins, ]
  cal_plot_data <- matrix(data = as.numeric(NA),
                          nrow = n_bins,
                          ncol = 4)
  for(i in 1:n_bins){
    p_hat <- mean(cal_bins[[i]]$truth)
    n <- nrow(cal_bins[[i]])
    cal_plot_data[i,1] <- mean(cal_bins[[i]]$estimate)
    cal_plot_data[i,2] <- p_hat
    cal_plot_data[i,3] <- p_hat - qnorm(0.95) * sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)
    cal_plot_data[i,4] <- p_hat + qnorm(0.95) * sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)
  }
  plot(x = cal_plot_data[ ,1],
       y = cal_plot_data[ ,2],
       type = "b",
       main = "Calibration Plot",
       xlab = "Average Fitted Value in Bin",
       ylab = "Proportion of 1s in Bin",
       pch = 19,
       ylim = c(min(cal_plot_data,
                    na.rm = TRUE),
                max(cal_plot_data,
                    na.rm = TRUE)))
  grid()
  lines(x = cal_plot_data[ ,1],
        y = cal_plot_data[ ,3],
        lty = 3)
  lines(x = cal_plot_data[ ,1],
        y = cal_plot_data[ ,4],
        lty = 3)
  abline(a = 0,
         b = 1,
         lty = 2)
}

Now we can apply my function to this model.

draw_cal_plot(mod = mod_04,
              n_bins = 10)








My plot is not very pretty, but even for the smallest fitted values, the reference line is contained within the confidence band (between the dotted lines). So, this model is well-calibrated.





71.3.2 Problem 2
Let’s return to our ICU admissions data set. Our outcome will be 1 if the patient died and 0 otherwise. We’ll use two covariates: years since age 20 and whether or not the patient got CPR prior to admission (1 = yes, 0 = no).



Call:
glm(formula = Died ~ YearsSince20 + CPR, family = binomial, data = d3)

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)  -2.75981    0.53355  -5.173 2.31e-07 ***
YearsSince20  0.02961    0.01115   2.656  0.00792 ** 
CPR           1.78409    0.60730   2.938  0.00331 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 200.16  on 199  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 183.95  on 197  degrees of freedom
AIC: 189.95

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5











Is this model well-calibrated? Justify your answer.






TipSolution





This model is well-calibrated. The confidence band contains the reference line.





71.3.3 Problem 3
Some courts use algorithms to estimate a criminal defendant’s probability of re-offending. The scores generated from these algorithms–sometimes on a scale of 1 to 10–are used at various points, including to determine bond amounts and sentences. Much has been written about these algorithms (see, for example, Machine Bias and Can Racist Algorithms Be Fixed?). For this problem, I want you to answer this question: What would calibration mean in this context?






TipSolution





In this context, calibration would mean that defendants assigned a score of 1 would have a lower probability of re-offending than defendants assigned a score of 2, defendants assigned a score of 2 would have a lower probability of re-offending than defendants assigned a score of 3, and so on. Furthermore, we would hope that the difference between a score of 1 and 2 would be the same, approximately, as the difference between a score of 2 and 3.





71.3.4 Problem 4
What would calibration mean in the context of credit scores?






TipSolution





Credit scores are intended to measure the risk of non-payment for loans, rent, etc. Suppose we took a sample of people getting a loan to buy a car. At the end of the loan period, we checked to see who had defaulted and who had not. If we took everyone with a credit score between 651 and 700 and computed the proportion who defaulted, it should be higher than the proportion of defaults among borrowers with a credit score between 701 and 750. That would be a well-calibrated credit score.
If the proportion of defaults among borrowers with a credit score between 651 and 700 was lower than that among borrowers with a credit score between 701 and 750, we would not be doing a very good job of estimating risk. This would have serious consequences. We would be denying loans to people with low credit scores, even though they have a high probability of paying us back on time.

title: 72  Consequences of Violations of the Assumptions of Logistic Regression
text:
State how the coefficients in logistic regression are estimated.
Explain the consequences of violations of the assumptions of logistic regression.
crumbs: 72  Consequences of Violations of the Assumptions of Logistic Regression

title: 72  Consequences of Violations of the Assumptions of Logistic Regression
text:
72.2 Lesson
The coefficients in logistic regression are estimated by maximizing the likelihood, which I’ve written below. (This is not something you need to memorize.)
\[
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{L}(\beta_0,\beta_1,\dotsc,\beta_p) &= \prod_{i=1}^n p_i^{y_i} (1-p_i)^{1-y_i} \\
&= \prod_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \dotsc + \beta_p x_{ip} \right)\right)}\right)^{y_i} \left(1 - \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \dotsc + \beta_p x_{ip} \right)\right)}\right)^{1-y_i} \\
&= \prod_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \dotsc + \beta_p x_{ip} \right)\right)}\right)^{y_i} \left(\frac{\exp\left(-\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \dotsc + \beta_p x_{ip} \right)\right)}{1 + \exp\left(-\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \dotsc + \beta_p x_{ip} \right)\right)}\right)^{1-y_i} \\
&= \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{\exp\left(-(1-y_i)\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip}\right)\right)}{1 + \exp\left(-\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip}\right)\right)} \\
\end{align*}
\]
This likelihood above is based on all three assumptions, all at the same time. So, if any of them are wrong, the likelihood is wrong. Does that mean that if any of the assumptions are violated, we can’t interpret our estimates, trust the standard errors, or use the p-values? Not exactly.
If the first two assumptions are met, but the observations are not independent, the coefficient estimators will still be close to the true values if the sample size is large enough. This result comes to us from the theory of generalized estimating equations, more commonly known by the acronym GEE, which is usually taught in courses on longitudinal data analysis. I’m eliding a lot of details, so if you want to learn more, I recommend looking into GEE. For now, just know that if you have a binary outcome, a well-calibrated model, and a large sample size, you can go ahead and interpret the coefficients, even if the observations are not independent. If you want to do hypothesis testing, you should probably not use the default standard errors and p-values from logistic regression.
What if the second assumption isn’t met, as evidenced by a calibration plot where the confidence bands don’t contain the reference line? It depends. If your model is well-calibrated for some fitted values but not others, you could interpret your coefficients and conduct your hypothesis tests with the caveat that the results only apply to a certain subset of observations. If your model is poorly calibrated everywhere, you should probably consider changing your model.

title: 72  Consequences of Violations of the Assumptions of Logistic Regression
text:
72.3 Problems

72.3.1 Problem 1
Compare and contrast the relationship between sample size and the consequences of violating the assumptions for linear regression and logistic regression.






TipSolution





For linear regression, as long as the linearity, iid, and homoscedasticity assumptions are met, a large sample size allows us to interpret the p-values, even if the errors are not normally distributed.
For logistic regression, as long as the outcome is binary and the linear model is correct, a large sample size allows us to interpret the coefficient estimates, even if the observations are not independent.





72.3.2 Problem 2
Can you use the AIC to compare different logistic regression models?






TipSolution





Yes. Since logistic regression is fit with maximum likelihood estimation, you can use the AIC, the LRT, the BIC, and any other likelihood-based measure of performance to compare models.

title: 73  Hypothesis Testing
text:
73.1 Learning Objective
Interpret the results of a hypothesis test in the context of logistic regression.

title: 73  Hypothesis Testing
text:
73.2 Lesson

73.2.1 Interpretation in General
As in linear regression, R will conduct a hypothesis test for each coefficient estimated in logistic regression. The null hypothesis for each coefficient is that that coefficient is zero, and the alternative hypothesis is that the coefficient is not zero. It’s always a two-sided test.
What does it mean if the coefficient is zero? The answer to this is different if we’re talking about the intercept versus a non-intercept coefficient. Let’s start with the intercept. Recall that \(\exp(\beta_0)\) is the odds that the outcome equals 1 when all the covariates are equal to zero. If \(\beta_0 = 0\), then \(\exp(\beta_0) = 1\). What does an odds of 1 mean? \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{p}{1-p} &= 1 \\
p &= 1 - p \\
2p &= 1 \\
p &= \frac{1}{2}
\end{align*}
\] So, if \(\beta_0 = 0\), then the probability that the outcome equals 1 when all the explanatory variables equal 0 is \(1/2\). It’s a coin flip. If the p-value is small, we would reject this hypothesis, and conclude that the probability that the outcome equals 1 when all the explanatory variables equal 0 is not \(1/2\). Whether or not this is meaningful depends on your goals.
What about for the non-intercept coefficients? For \(j \ne 0\), \(\exp(\beta_j)\) is the odds ratio comparing two populations that are identical except one has \(X_{ij} = x + 1\) and the other has \(X_{kj} = x\). Again, if \(\beta_j = 0\), then \(\exp(\beta_j) = 1\). If an odds ratio is 1, then the two odds it’s comparing are equal to each other. So, the null hypothesis corresponds to equal odds for these two populations. If the p-value is small, we reject the null and conclude that these two populations have different odds that the outcome equals 1.
Note that if two odds are equal, the corresponding probabilities must also be equal. So, if an odds ratio is 1, the odds are equivalent, and the corresponding probabilities are equivalent.


73.2.2 Example
Let’s return to the nutrition study. We regressed smoking on years since age 40, vitamin use (no, occasional, or regular), and sex (male or female).

mod_01 <- glm(formula = SmokeYes ~ YearsSince40 + VitaminUse + Sex,
              family = binomial,
              data = d)
summary(mod_01)


Call:
glm(formula = SmokeYes ~ YearsSince40 + VitaminUse + Sex, family = binomial, 
    data = d)

Coefficients:
                     Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)          -1.20773    0.27658  -4.367 1.26e-05 ***
YearsSince40         -0.04098    0.01398  -2.932  0.00337 ** 
VitaminUseOccasional -0.45047    0.41244  -1.092  0.27475    
VitaminUseRegular    -0.95796    0.41851  -2.289  0.02208 *  
SexMale               0.66759    0.50100   1.333  0.18269    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 251.10  on 314  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 235.49  on 310  degrees of freedom
AIC: 245.49

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5


For our hypothesis tests, let’s use \(\alpha = 0.05\).

The p-value for the intercept is much less than \(\alpha\), so we can conclude that the odds of smoking among 40-year-old females who don’t use vitamins is different from 1. In other words, the probability of smoking among 40-year-old females who don’t use vitamins is different from 0.5.
Since the p-value for YearsSince40 is less than 0.05, the odds of smoking among people age \(x + 1\) is different than the odds of smoking among people age \(x\), holding vitamin use and sex constant.
Since the p-value for VitaminUseOccasional is greater than 0.05, we cannot conclude that there is a difference between the odds of smoking among people who occasionally use vitamins the odds of smoking among people who don’t use vitamins, holding age and sex constant.
Since the p-value on VitaminUseRegular is less than 0.05, we can conclude that the odds of smoking among people who regularly use vitamins is different than the odds of smoking among people who don’t use vitamins, holding age and sex constant.
Since the p-value on SexMale is greater than 0.05, we cannot conclude that the odds of smoking among males is different than the odds of smoking among females, holding age and vitamin use constant.

You may have noticed that I didn’t use the phrase “statistically significant”. I’m not trying to make a statement by doing that. For the p-values less than 0.05, we could conclude that the observed differences between the odds are statistically significant. For the p-values greater than 0.05, we could say that although we observed differences in the odds, those differences are not statistically significant.

title: 73  Hypothesis Testing
text:
73.3 Problems

73.3.1 Problem 1
Let’s return to the NHANES data. The outcome is a 1 if the respondent bought any food labeled organic in the past 30 days, and 0 otherwise. I’ve regressed this on self-rated health (excellent, very good, good, fair, and poor) and monthly income (in thousands of dollars).



Call:
glm(formula = OrganicYes ~ Health + Income1000, family = binomial, 
    data = d2)

Coefficients:
                Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)     -0.75350    0.11490  -6.558 5.47e-11 ***
HealthFair      -0.73735    0.13271  -5.556 2.76e-08 ***
HealthGood      -0.31940    0.11368  -2.810  0.00496 ** 
HealthPoor      -0.58209    0.21071  -2.762  0.00574 ** 
HealthVery good -0.05688    0.11723  -0.485  0.62753    
Income1000       0.13783    0.01327  10.383  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 5493.5  on 4183  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 5288.4  on 4178  degrees of freedom
  (532 observations deleted due to missingness)
AIC: 5300.4

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4


Interpret the hypothesis tests associated with the coefficients. Use \(\alpha = 0.05\).






TipSolution






Since the p-value on the intercept is less than 0.05, the odds of having bought organic in the past 30 days among people who make $0/month and rate their own health as excellent is different from 1 (and the probability is different from 0.5).
Since the p-value associated with HealthFair is less than 0.05, the odds of having bought organic in the past 30 days among people who rate their health as fair is different than the odds of having bought organic in the past 30 days among people who rate their health as excellent, holding income constant.
Since the p-value associated with HealthGood is less than 0.05, the odds of having bought organic in the past 30 days among people who rate their health as good is different than the odds of having bought organic in the past 30 days among people who rate their health as excellent, holding income constant.
Since the p-value associated with HealthPoor is less than 0.05, the odds of having bought organic in the past 30 days among people who rate their health as poor is different than the odds of having bought organic in the past 30 days among people who rate their health as excellent, holding income constant.
Since the p-value associated with HealthVery good is greater than 0.05, we cannot conclude that the odds of having bought organic in the past 30 days among people who rate their health as very good is different than the odds of having bought organic in the past 30 days among people who rate their health as excellent, holding income constant.
Since the p-value associated with Income1000 is less than 0.05, the odds of having bought organic in the past 30 days among people who make \(x + 1000\) dollars per month is different than the odds of having bought organic in the past 30 days among people who make \(x\) dollars per month, holding self-rated health constant.






73.3.2 Problem 2
Let’s return to our ICU admissions data set. Our outcome will be 1 if the patient died and 0 otherwise. We’ll use two covariates: years since age 20 and whether or not the patient got CPR prior to admission (1 = yes, 0 = no).



Call:
glm(formula = Died ~ YearsSince20 + CPR, family = binomial, data = d3)

Coefficients:

(Intercept)  -2.75981    0.53355  -5.173 2.31e-07 ***
YearsSince20  0.02961    0.01115   2.656  0.00792 ** 
CPR           1.78409    0.60730   2.938  0.00331 ** 
---

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

Residual deviance: 183.95  on 197  degrees of freedom
AIC: 189.95

Interpret the hypothesis tests associated with the coefficients. Use \(\alpha = 0.05\).






TipSolution






Since the p-value associated with the intercept is less than 0.05, the odds of death for a 20-year-old who did not receive CPR prior to admission to the ICU is different than 1 (and the probability is different than 0.5).
Since the p-value associated with YearsSince20 is less than 0.05, the odds of death for someone age \(x + 1\) is different than the odds of death for someone age \(x\), holding CPR status constant.
Since the p-value associated with CPR is less than 0.05, the odds of death among people who received CPR prior to admission is different than the odds of death of people who did not receive CPR prior to admission, holding age constant.

Define, compute, and interpret sensitivity and specificity.

title: 74  Performance
text:
74.2 Lesson

74.2.1 Discrimination
One measure of the performance of a logistic regression model is how well it discriminates between observed 0s and observed 1s. Each observation gets a fitted value; you can choose some cutoff such that any observation with a fitted value below the cutoff gets a predicted outcome of 0 and any observation with a fitted value above the cutoff gets a predicted outcome of 1. Then you can compare the predicted outcome to the observed outcome. There are a couple ways to make this comparison. In order to talk about them, it might be useful to use the terminology in the following table. Here, “positive” means a 1 and “negative” means a 0.




Predicted Positive
Predicted Negative
Total




Observed Positive
True Positive (TP)
False Negative (FN)
P


Observed Negative
False Positive (FP)
True Negative (TN)
N





74.2.2 Sensitivity
Sensitivity is the probability that an observed 1 will have a fitted value above the cutoff, and thus receive a predicted outcome of 1. Using the table above, we can compute the sensitivity as \[
\frac{TP}{P} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \text{.}
\] Sensitivity is also known as the true positive rate or the recall.
Sensitivity is often used in medical testing. In that context, it’s the probability that someone who actually has a disease will test positive for it.


74.2.3 Specificity
Specificity is the probability that an observed 0 will have a fitted value below the cutoff, and thus receive a predicted outcome of 0. Using the table above, we can compute the specificity as \[
\frac{TN}{N} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP} \text{.}
\] Specificity is also known as the true negative rate.
Specificity is often used in medical testing. In that context, it’s the probability that someone who does not have a disease will test negative for it.


74.2.4 ROC Curve
In order to compute the sensitivity and specificity, we need a cutoff to separate the predicted 1s from the predicted 0s. Different cutoffs yield different sensitivities and specificities. If we make a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, we can look at all these sensitivities and specificities at once.
Let’s walk through the creation of an ROC curve for a specific example. In the future, you will just use an R package to create the ROC curve, but making one (or at least going through a few of the steps) helps with understanding how to interpret it.
Let’s return to the nutrition study. We regressed smoking on years since age 40, vitamin use (no, occasional, or regular), and sex (male or female).

mod_01 <- glm(formula = SmokeYes ~ YearsSince40 + VitaminUse + Sex,
              family = binomial,
              data = d)
summary(mod_01)


Call:
glm(formula = SmokeYes ~ YearsSince40 + VitaminUse + Sex, family = binomial, 
    data = d)

Coefficients:
                     Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)          -1.20773    0.27658  -4.367 1.26e-05 ***
YearsSince40         -0.04098    0.01398  -2.932  0.00337 ** 
VitaminUseOccasional -0.45047    0.41244  -1.092  0.27475    
VitaminUseRegular    -0.95796    0.41851  -2.289  0.02208 *  
SexMale               0.66759    0.50100   1.333  0.18269    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 251.10  on 314  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 235.49  on 310  degrees of freedom
AIC: 245.49

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5


Let’s start with an empty plot. On the horizontal axis, we’ll put one minus the specificity (\(1 - \text{specificity}\)). I don’t know why we use one minus the specificity instead of the specificity itself, but that’s the way it is. On the vertical axis, we’ll put the sensitivity.









Next, I’m going to choose the lowest possible cutoff: 0. Because all the fitted values are above 0, every observation will get a predicted value of 1. What are the sensitivity and specificity for this cutoff?

sensitivity <- sum(mod_01$fitted.values > 0 & mod_01$model$SmokeYes == 1) / sum(mod_01$model$SmokeYes == 1)
sensitivity

[1] 1

specificity <- sum(mod_01$fitted.values <= 0 & mod_01$model$SmokeYes == 0) / sum(mod_01$model$SmokeYes == 0)
specificity

[1] 0


The sensitivity is 1 because all the observed 1s received predicted a predicted value of 1, because every observation received a predicted value of 1. This would be like opening and searching every single bag at the airport; you wouldn’t miss any dangerous objects, but you’d have to search every bag. The specificity, on the other hand, is 0. Since every observation received a predicted value of 1, no observed 0s were correctly categorized as 0s. In the airport example, you didn’t correctly identify any safe bags as safe.
Anyway, we can add this point to our plot.









Okay, let’s do a different cutoff. I’m going to choose the lowest fitted value.

# Get cutoff
sorted_unique_fitted <- sort(unique(mod_01$fitted.values))
cutoff <- sorted_unique_fitted[1]

# Sensitivity
numerator <- sum(mod_01$fitted.values > cutoff & mod_01$model$SmokeYes == 1)
denominator <- sum(mod_01$model$SmokeYes == 1)
sensitivity <- c(sensitivity,
                 numerator / denominator)
sensitivity[2]

[1] 1

# Specificity
numerator <- sum(mod_01$fitted.values <= cutoff & mod_01$model$SmokeYes == 0)
denominator <- sum(mod_01$model$SmokeYes == 0)
specificity <- c(specificity,
                 numerator / denominator)
specificity[2]

[1] 0.003676471


By increasing the cutoff, we slightly increased the specificity. It must be the case that the observation with the lowest fitted value had an observed outcome of 0. Let’s check:

mod_01$model$SmokeYes[mod_01$fitted.values == cutoff]

[1] 0


Yep! So by increasing the cutoff slightly, we correctly categorized one observed 0 as a predicted 0, increasing our specificity. Because all observed 1s remained categorized as predicted 1s, we didn’t decrease our sensitivity.
We can add this new point to our plot.









You can’t really tell there’s even a new point on the plot, because it’s so close to the first one.
Let’s skip ahead and just have R draw the entire ROC curve for us. There are many packages with functions that do this. I tend to use the package pROC.

mod_01_roc <- roc(response = mod_01$model$SmokeYes,
                  predictor = mod_01$fitted.values)

Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1


Setting direction: controls < cases

plot(mod_01_roc)








Now that it’s plotted, how do we interpret it? Well, we want specificity and sensitivity to both be high. So, ideally, we’d like the dark black line to go all the way to the upper left-hand corner of the plot. The closer we get to this ideal, the better the model performs at discriminating 0s and 1s.
What’s the worst we could do? You might think the worst possible ROC curve would be one that goes all the way to the lower right-hand corner of the plot. However, if it did, that would mean that the model does a perfectly bad job of discriminating 0s and 1s. In other words, it categorizes all observed 0s as predicted 1s and all observed 1s as predicted 0s. In that case, you could just flip the predicted labels and do a perfectly good job.
You may have noticed the following message that the function sent:
Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
Setting direction: controls < cases
The controls < cases message means that fitted values below each cutoff were categorized as predicted 0s. If the function detected that it could perform better by categorizing fitted values above each cutoff as predicted 0s, it would do that. It would tell the user controls > cases as well. In order to prevent this gaming of the system, you can use the direction parameter of the roc function.
So, what’s the worst you can do? The worst ROC curve is one that follows the reference line. it’s exactly between perfectly bad and perfectly good.
For the model above, the AUC is:


Area under the curve: 0.6757


This is better than chance. It’s hard to say how good or bad this is without knowing how well other models perform.


74.2.5 Area Under the Curve
The area under the curve (AUC) is a single value that summarizes the ROC curve. It’s literally the area under the ROC curve. The highest it can be is 1, and the lowest (assuming you haven’t changed the direction parameter) is 0.5. So, a higher AUC is better.
Surprisingly, the AUC has a more intuitive interpretation than just high = good and low = bad. The AUC is the probability that a randomly-selected observed 1 will have a higher fitted value than a randomly-selected observed 0. This is sometimes called the “probability of superiority” or the “common language effect size”. This interpretation might make it easier to understand why 0.5 is the worst you can do. An AUC of 0.5 means that a randomly-selected observed 1 is equally likely to have a fitted value above or below the fitted value of a randomly-selected observed 0.

title: 74  Performance
text:
74.3 Problems

74.3.1 Problem 1
Below are three ROC curves. Each was created from a different simulated data set. I’ll call the data sets A, B, and C, and I’ll describe how they differ. Your job is to match the data set to the correct plot.
Each data set was simulated according to the model \[
p_i = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-2 X_i\right)} \text{.}
\] The three data sets differ only in the distribution of the explanatory variable.

In data set A, the explanatory variable is normally distributed with mean -2.5 and variance 1. This means there are 28 observations where the outcome is 1 and 972 observations where the outcome is 0.
In data set B, the explanatory variable is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance 1. This means there are 502 observations where the outcome is 1 and 498 observations where the outcome is 0.
In data set A, the explanatory variable is normally distributed with mean 2.5 and variance 1. This means there are 972 observations where the outcome is 1 and 28 observations where the outcome is 0.

Simple linear regression was used to estimate the coefficients and obtain fitted values.
Which plot corresponds to which data set?


Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1


Setting direction: controls < cases









Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
Setting direction: controls < cases









Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
Setting direction: controls < cases















TipSolution






Plot 1 used data set C.
Plot 2 used data set A.
Plot 3 used data set B.

Recall that when we made our ROC curve, we started with a cutoff of 0, which led to perfect sensitivity and perfectly bad specificity. When we raised the cutoff slightly, one observed 0 got correctly categorized as a predicted 0. This increased the specificity but did not decrease the sensitivity. If we had a bunch of 0s with low fitted values, we would continue to see increases in specificity with no corresponding drops in sensitivity. Data set A has lots of 0s, and it’s probably the case that a lot of those 0s had low fitted values, since there was nothing wrong about how we fit the logistic regression. (For example, we didn’t include any unnecessary explanatory variables or leave out an necessary explanatory variables.) So, it’s reasonable to assume that data set A corresponds to Plot 2, which has a long, flat line at the top, indicating increases in specificity without drops in sensitivity. And this is correct.
If a data set has lots of observed 1s with high fitted values, then once you reach a certain cutoff, additional increases in the cutoff will categorize additional observed 1s as predicted 0s, decreasing the sensitivity without decreasing the specificity. This describes data set C and plot 1.
By process of elimination, the remaining data set matches the remaining plot.





74.3.2 Problem 2
This problem uses Figure 1 in Prediction of High Nodal Burden in Patients With Sentinel Node–Positive Luminal ERBB2-Negative Breast Cancer.

74.3.2.1 Part (a)
Interpret the AUC in panel A.






TipSolution





If you randomly selected one person with high nodal burden and one person without, both from the training set, there’s a 77% chance the person with high nodal burden would have a higher fitted value than the person without.





74.3.2.2 Part (b)
If someone has a fitted value of 0.25, what is their actual probability of high nodal burden?






TipSolution





We need the calibration plot, which is in panel C, to answer this. The fitted values are along the horizontal axis. A fitted value of 0.25 corresponds to an actual probability of about 0.35.

75.1 Learning Objective
Interpret the coefficients of a logistic regression model with an interaction term.

title: 75  Interactions
text:
75.2 Lesson

75.2.1 Example
Let’s return to the nutrition data set. We’ll regress smoking on years since age 40, vitamin use (no, occasional, or regular), and sex (male or female), but include an interaction between years since age 40 and vitamin use.

mod_01 <- glm(formula = SmokeYes ~ YearsSince40 * VitaminUse + Sex,
              family = binomial,
              data = d)
summary(mod_01)


Call:
glm(formula = SmokeYes ~ YearsSince40 * VitaminUse + Sex, family = binomial, 
    data = d)

Coefficients:

YearsSince40                      -0.01893    0.01949  -0.971   0.3314    
VitaminUseOccasional              -0.30396    0.44088  -0.689   0.4905    
VitaminUseRegular                 -0.70835    0.46433  -1.526   0.1271    
SexMale                            0.46789    0.51977   0.900   0.3680    
YearsSince40:VitaminUseOccasional -0.01266    0.03261  -0.388   0.6979    
YearsSince40:VitaminUseRegular    -0.07570    0.03792  -1.996   0.0459 *  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 251.10  on 314  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 230.75  on 308  degrees of freedom
AIC: 244.75

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 6


How do we interpret these coefficients? In order to save some space, I’m going to use the following notation. Suppose \(i\in\{1,\dotsc,315\}\). Define:

\(S_i = 1\) if the \(i\)th participant smokes and \(S_i = 0\) otherwise.
\(Y_i\) is years since age 40 for the \(i\)th participant.
\(O_i = 1\) if the \(i\)th participant used vitamins occasionally and \(O_i = 0\) otherwise.
\(R_i = 1\) if the \(i\)th participant used vitamins regularly and \(R_i = 0\) otherwise.
\(M_i = 1\) if the \(i\)th participant was male and \(M_i = 0\) otherwise.

Recall that the \(i\)th participant’s estimated odds of smoking can be computed like so: \[
\widehat{\text{odds}}_i = \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_i + \hat{\beta}_2 O_i + \hat{\beta}_3 R_i + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_i O_i + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_i R_i\right) \text{.}
\]
Intercept
\(\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0\right)\) is the estimated odds of smoking for a 40-year-old female who doesn’t use vitamins.

exp(mod_01$coefficients[1])

(Intercept) 
  0.2570249 


Main Effects

\(\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_1\right)\) is the estimated odds ratio comparing participants who differ in age by one year, are the same sex, and don’t use vitamins. \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{\widehat{\text{odds}}_i}{\widehat{\text{odds}}_j} &= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_i + \hat{\beta}_2 O_i + \hat{\beta}_3 R_i + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_i O_i + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_i R_i\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_j + \hat{\beta}_2 O_j + \hat{\beta}_3 R_j + \hat{\beta}_4 M_j + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_j O_j + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_j R_j\right)} \\
&= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 (y+1) + \hat{\beta}_2 (0) + \hat{\beta}_3 (0) + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 (y+1) (0) + \hat{\beta}_6 (y+1) (0)\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 y + \hat{\beta}_2 (0) + \hat{\beta}_3 (0) + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 y (0) + \hat{\beta}_6 y (0)\right)} \\
&= \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_1  \right) \\
\end{align*}
\]


exp(mod_01$coefficients[2])

YearsSince40 
   0.9812507 



\(\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_2\right)\) is the estimated odds ratio comparing participants who use vitamins occasionally to participants who don’t use vitamins, where both groups of participants are the same sex and are 40 years old. \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{\widehat{\text{odds}}_i}{\widehat{\text{odds}}_j} &= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_i + \hat{\beta}_2 O_i + \hat{\beta}_3 R_i + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_i O_i + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_i R_i\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_j + \hat{\beta}_2 O_j + \hat{\beta}_3 R_j + \hat{\beta}_4 M_j + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_j O_j + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_j R_j\right)} \\
&= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 (0) + \hat{\beta}_2 (1) + \hat{\beta}_3 (0) + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 (0) (1) + \hat{\beta}_6 (0) (0)\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 (0) + \hat{\beta}_2 (0) + \hat{\beta}_3 (0) + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 (0) (0) + \hat{\beta}_6 (0) (0)\right)} \\
&= \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_2\right)
\end{align*}
\]


exp(mod_01$coefficients[3])

VitaminUseOccasional 
           0.7378929 



\(\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_3\right)\) is the estimated odds ratio comparing participants who use vitamins regularly to participants who don’t use vitamins, where both groups of participants are the same sex and are 40 years old. \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{\widehat{\text{odds}}_i}{\widehat{\text{odds}}_j} &= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_i + \hat{\beta}_2 O_i + \hat{\beta}_3 R_i + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_i O_i + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_i R_i\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_j + \hat{\beta}_2 O_j + \hat{\beta}_3 R_j + \hat{\beta}_4 M_j + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_j O_j + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_j R_j\right)} \\
&= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 (0) + \hat{\beta}_2 (0) + \hat{\beta}_3 (1) + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 (0) (0) + \hat{\beta}_6 (0) (1)\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 (0) + \hat{\beta}_2 (0) + \hat{\beta}_3 (0) + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 (0) (0) + \hat{\beta}_6 (0) (0)\right)} \\
&= \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_3\right)
\end{align*}
\]


exp(mod_01$coefficients[4])

VitaminUseRegular 
        0.4924537 



\(\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_4\right)\) is the estimated odds ratio comparing male to non-male participants who are the same age and have the same vitamin use. \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{\widehat{\text{odds}}_i}{\widehat{\text{odds}}_j} &= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_i + \hat{\beta}_2 O_i + \hat{\beta}_3 R_i + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_i O_i + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_i R_i\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_j + \hat{\beta}_2 O_j + \hat{\beta}_3 R_j + \hat{\beta}_4 M_j + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_j O_j + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_j R_j\right)} \\
&= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_i + \hat{\beta}_2 O_i + \hat{\beta}_3 R_i + \hat{\beta}_4 (1) + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_i O_i + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_i R_i\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_i + \hat{\beta}_2 O_i + \hat{\beta}_3 R_i + \hat{\beta}_4 (0) + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_i O_i + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_i R_i\right)} \\
&= \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_4\right)
\end{align*}
\]


exp(mod_01$coefficients[5])

 SexMale 
1.596615 


Moderation of Age by Vitamin Use

\(\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_5\right)\) is the estimated odds ratio comparing participants who differ in age by one year, are the same sex, and use vitamins occasionally. \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{\widehat{\text{odds}}_i}{\widehat{\text{odds}}_j} &= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_i + \hat{\beta}_2 O_i + \hat{\beta}_3 R_i + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_i O_i + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_i R_i\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_j + \hat{\beta}_2 O_j + \hat{\beta}_3 R_j + \hat{\beta}_4 M_j + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_j O_j + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_j R_j\right)} \\
&= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 (y+1) + \hat{\beta}_2 (1) + \hat{\beta}_3 (0) + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 (y+1) (1) + \hat{\beta}_6 (y+1) (0)\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 y + \hat{\beta}_2 (1) + \hat{\beta}_3 (0) + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 y (1) + \hat{\beta}_6 y (0)\right)} \\
&= \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_5\right) \\
&= \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_1\right) \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_5\right) \\
\end{align*}
\]


exp(mod_01$coefficients[2] + mod_01$coefficients[6])

YearsSince40 
   0.9689091 

exp(mod_01$coefficients[2]) * exp(mod_01$coefficients[6])

YearsSince40 
   0.9689091 



\(\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_6\right)\) is the estimated odds ratio comparing participants who differ in age by one year, are the same sex, and use vitamins regularly. \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{\widehat{\text{odds}}_i}{\widehat{\text{odds}}_j} &= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_i + \hat{\beta}_2 O_i + \hat{\beta}_3 R_i + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_i O_i + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_i R_i\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_j + \hat{\beta}_2 O_j + \hat{\beta}_3 R_j + \hat{\beta}_4 M_j + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_j O_j + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_j R_j\right)} \\
&= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 (y+1) + \hat{\beta}_2 (0) + \hat{\beta}_3 (1) + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 (y+1) (0) + \hat{\beta}_6 (y+1) (1)\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 y + \hat{\beta}_2 (0) + \hat{\beta}_3 (1) + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 y (0) + \hat{\beta}_6 y (1)\right)} \\
&= \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_6\right) \\
&= \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_1\right) \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_6\right) \\
\end{align*}
\]


exp(mod_01$coefficients[2] + mod_01$coefficients[7])

YearsSince40 
   0.9097091 

exp(mod_01$coefficients[2]) * exp(mod_01$coefficients[7])

YearsSince40 
   0.9097091 


Moderation of Vitamin Use by Age

\(\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_2 + \hat{\beta}_5y\right)\) is the estimated odds ratio comparing participants who use vitamins occasionally to participants who don’t use vitamins, where both groups are the same sex and were 40 years old \(y\) years ago. \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{\widehat{\text{odds}}_i}{\widehat{\text{odds}}_j} &= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_i + \hat{\beta}_2 O_i + \hat{\beta}_3 R_i + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_i O_i + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_i R_i\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_j + \hat{\beta}_2 O_j + \hat{\beta}_3 R_j + \hat{\beta}_4 M_j + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_j O_j + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_j R_j\right)} \\
&= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 y + \hat{\beta}_2 (1) + \hat{\beta}_3 (0) + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 y (1) + \hat{\beta}_6 y (0)\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 y + \hat{\beta}_2 (0) + \hat{\beta}_3 (0) + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 y (0) + \hat{\beta}_6 y (0)\right)} \\
&= \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_2 + \hat{\beta}_5 y\right) \\
&= \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_2\right) \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_5 y\right) \\
\end{align*}
\]











\(\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_3 + \hat{\beta}_6y\right)\) is the estimated odds ratio comparing participants who use vitamins regularly to participants who don’t use vitamins, where both groups are the same sex and were 40 years old \(y\) years ago. \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{\widehat{\text{odds}}_i}{\widehat{\text{odds}}_j} &= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_i + \hat{\beta}_2 O_i + \hat{\beta}_3 R_i + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_i O_i + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_i R_i\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 Y_j + \hat{\beta}_2 O_j + \hat{\beta}_3 R_j + \hat{\beta}_4 M_j + \hat{\beta}_5 Y_j O_j + \hat{\beta}_6 Y_j R_j\right)} \\
&= \frac{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 y + \hat{\beta}_2 (0) + \hat{\beta}_3 (1) + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 y (0) + \hat{\beta}_6 y (1)\right)}{\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 y + \hat{\beta}_2 (0) + \hat{\beta}_3 (0) + \hat{\beta}_4 M_i + \hat{\beta}_5 y (0) + \hat{\beta}_6 y (0)\right)} \\
&= \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_3 + \hat{\beta}_6 y\right) \\
&= \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_3\right) \exp\left(\hat{\beta}_6 y\right) \\
\end{align*}
\]












75.2.2 Heuristic
When interpreting terms in a model that has an interaction terms, these might be some useful questions to ask:

Is this an intercept or a non-intercept term?

If you’re interpreting an intercept, the interaction term doesn’t really change anything. Interpreting the intercept always requires setting all the covariates to zero.
If you’re interpreting a non-intercept term, you may need to take into account the interaction term.

Is this coefficient attached to a single explanatory variable or a product?

It’s often really challenging to interpret a coefficient that’s attached to an interaction term. Usually it’s easier to interpret coefficients attached to single explanatory variables, or sums of coefficients, where one of the coefficients in the sum is attached to a single explanatory variable and the other coefficient in the sum is attached to an interaction term.

What is this thing?

For linear regression, the intercept is an expected value and each non-intercept term attached to a single explanatory variable is an expected difference. For logistic regression, the exponentiated intercept is an odds and each exponentiated non-intercept coefficient attached to a single explanatory variable is an odds ratio.

Does the explanatory variable attached to this coefficient also appear in an interaction term?

If no, you can interpret the coefficient as though there isn’t an interaction term in the model.
If yes, you have to decide if you want to interpret the coefficient by itself or combined with the coefficient attached to the interaction term.

If you interpret the coefficient by itself, it applies only to a population where the other explanatory variable in the interaction term equals zero.
If you interpret the coefficient combined with the coefficient attached to the interaction term, it applies only to a population where the other explanatory variable in the interaction term equals one. If the other explanatory variable is continuous, you can replace it with a lower-case letter to represent an algebraic variable (rather than a random variable).

title: 75  Interactions
text:
75.3 Problems

75.3.1 Problem 1
Let’s return to the NHANES data set. The outcome is a 1 if the respondent bought any food labeled organic in the past 30 days, and 0 otherwise. I’ve regressed this on self-rated health (excellent, very good, good, fair, and poor) and monthly income (in thousands of dollars), with an interaction term between the two explanatory variables.



Call:
glm(formula = OrganicYes ~ Health * Income1000, family = binomial, 
    data = d2)

Coefficients:

Interpret the exponentiated coefficients.

exp(mod_02$coefficients)

                 0.3915946                  0.7482764

                 0.9274793                  0.9581934 








TipSolution





Intercept

The odds of having bought organic food for someone who has no income and rates their own health as excellent is 0.39.

Main Effects

The odds of someone who rates their own health as fair having bought organic food are 25% lower than the same odds for someone who rates their own health as excellent, provided both these people have no income.
The odds of someone who rates their own health as good having bought organic food are 17% lower than the same odds for someone who rates their own health as excellent, provided both these people have no income.
The odds of someone who rates their own health as poor having bought organic food are 28% lower than the same odds for someone who rates their own health as excellent, provided both these people have no income.
The odds of someone who rates their own health as very good having bought organic food are 13% higher than the same odds for someone who rates their own health as excellent, provided both these people have no income.
The odds of of having bought organic food for someone who makes \(x + 1000\) dollars per month is 20% greater than the odds of having bought organic food for someone who makes \(x\) dollars per month, provided both these people rate their health as excellent.

Moderation of Self-Rated Health by Income

The odds of someone who rates their own health as fair having bought organic food are \(0.7482764\times 0.8714446^x\) times the same odds for someone who rates their own health as excellent, provided both these people make \(x\) dollars per month. The second term gets raised to the \(x\)th power because \[
\begin{align*}
\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_6 x\right) &=
\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_1 \right) \exp\left( \hat{\beta}_6 x\right) \\
&=
\exp\left(\hat{\beta}_1 \right) \exp\left( \hat{\beta}_6\right)^x \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
The odds of someone who rates their own health as good having bought organic food are \(0.8317762\times 0.9699155^x\) times the same odds for someone who rates their own health as excellent, provided both these people make \(x\) dollars per month.
The odds of someone who rates their own health as poor having bought organic food are \(0.7233798\times 0.9274793^x\) times the same odds for someone who rates their own health as excellent, provided both these people make \(x\) dollars per month.
The odds of someone who rates their own health as very good having bought organic food are \(1.1274843\times 0.9581934^x\) times the same odds for someone who rates their own health as excellent, provided both these people make \(x\) dollars per month.

Moderation of Income by Self-Rated Health

The odds of of having bought organic food for someone who makes \(x + 1000\) dollars per month is \(1.1999314\times 0.8714446\) times the odds of having bought organic food for someone who makes \(x\) dollars per month, provided both these people rate their health as fair.
The odds of of having bought organic food for someone who makes \(x + 1000\) dollars per month is \(1.1999314\times 0.9699155\) times the odds of having bought organic food for someone who makes \(x\) dollars per month, provided both these people rate their health as good.
The odds of of having bought organic food for someone who makes \(x + 1000\) dollars per month is \(1.1999314\times 0.7233798\) times the odds of having bought organic food for someone who makes \(x\) dollars per month, provided both these people rate their health as poor.
The odds of of having bought organic food for someone who makes \(x + 1000\) dollars per month is \(1.1999314\times 1.1274843\) times the odds of having bought organic food for someone who makes \(x\) dollars per month, provided both these people rate their health as very good.

Let’s return to our ICU admissions data set. Our outcome will be 1 if the patient died and 0 otherwise. We’ll use two covariates: years since age 20 and whether or not the patient got CPR prior to admission (1 = yes, 0 = no). I’ve also added an interaction term between the two covariates.
