75.3.3 Problem 3
This problem is about Table 2 in Ethnicity/Race, Paranoia, and Hospitalization for Mental Health Problems Among Men.

75.3.3.1 Part (a)
Interpret the odds ratio for “Ethnicity”.






TipSolution





Part of the difficulty of this problem is just figuring out what the heck the author means by “Ethnicity”. If you read the Results section, the author reveals that this is actually race. He writes “1 = White, 2 = Black”, but that doesn’t tell us what the reference group is. Later in the Results section, he writes, “Black men were more than 49 times more likely than White men to have had a mental health hospitalization.” This is incorrect in a couple ways, but at least we can combine it with Table 2 to determine that “White” is the reference group.
So, Black men without mild paranoia have 4869% greater odds of hospitalization for mental health problems than white men without mild paranoia, holding all else equal.
How was the author’s interpretation incorrect? First, he didn’t take into account the interaction term. If we’re just interpreting the odds ratio for “Ethnicity”, we need the value of the interaction term to be zero. So, we need the “Mild paranoia” variable to be zero. So, we are only talking about men who do not have mild paranoia.
Second, the author said that Black were “more than 49 times more”. If the odds ratio is 49.69, it should be “more than 49 times as” or “more than 48 times more”.
Finally, the author uses the word “likely”, which I think most people would interpret as a probability or chance, when in fact we’re talking about odds.





75.3.3.2 Part (b)
Interpret the odds ratio for “Mild paranoia (distrust)”.






TipSolution





The odds of hospitalization for mental health problems among white men with mild paranoia are 2.63 times the odds of hospitalization for mental health problems among white men without mild paranoia, holding all else equal.
We want to interpret the odds ratio for “Mild paranoia (distrust)” on its own, so we need the interaction term to be zero, so we need “Ethnicity” to be zero, so we need to restrict our focus to white men.





75.3.3.3 Part (c)
Suppose a white man with mild paranoia has 0.0789 odds of hospitalization for mental health problems. What is the odds of hospitalization for mental health problems for another man who differs only in that he is Black?






TipSolution





Because both of these men have mild paranoia, we have to take into account the interaction term. The odds ratio for this comparison is \(49.69 \times 0.03 = 1.4907\). Since the starting odds is 0.0789, the new odds is \(0.0789 \times 1.4907 = 0.11761623\).
Here’s an explanation that uses the coefficients explicitly: Suppose the white man in the statement of the problem is participant \(i\). We know he’s white and that he has mild paranoia. So, we can write \[
\begin{align*}
    \text{odds}_i &= \exp\left(-5.35 + 3.91 \text{Black}_i + 0.97 \text{paranoia}_i - 3.64 \text{Black}_i \times \text{paranoia}_i + \cdots \right) \\
    &= \exp\left(-5.35 + 3.91 (0) + 0.97 (1) - 3.64 (0) \times (1) + \cdots \right) \\
    &= \exp\left(-5.35  + 0.97  + \cdots \right) \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\] Now suppose the Black man in the statement of the problem is participant \(j\). We can write \[
\begin{align*}
    \text{odds}_j &= \exp\left(-5.35 + 3.91 \text{Black}_i + 0.97 \text{paranoia}_i - 3.64 \text{Black}_i \times \text{paranoia}_i + \cdots \right) \\
    &= \exp\left(-5.35 + 3.91 (1) + 0.97 (1) - 3.64 (1) \times (1) + \cdots \right) \\
    &= \exp\left(-5.35 + 3.91  + 0.97  - 3.64  + \cdots \right) \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\] To get odds\(_j\), we can do this: \[
\begin{align*}
    \frac{\text{odds}_j}{\text{odds}_i} &= \frac{\exp\left(-5.35 + 3.91  + 0.97  - 3.64  + \cdots \right)}{\exp\left(-5.35  + 0.97  + \cdots \right)} \\
    \frac{\text{odds}_j}{\text{odds}_i} &= \exp\left( 3.91    - 3.64   \right) \\
    \text{odds}_j &= \exp\left( 3.91    - 3.64   \right) \text{odds}_i \\
    \text{odds}_j &= \exp\left( 3.91 \right) \exp\left(   - 3.64   \right) \text{odds}_i \\
    \text{odds}_j &= \left( 49.69 \right) \left(   0.03   \right) (0.0789) \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\]





75.3.3.4 Part (d)
Suppose a Black man without mild paranoia has 1.4907 odds of hospitalization for mental health problems. What is the odds of hospitalization for mental health problems for another man who differs only in that he is has mild paranoia?






TipSolution





Because both of these men are Black, we have to take into account the interaction term. The odds ratio for this comparison is \(2.63 \times 0.03 = 0.0789\). Since the starting odds is 1.4907, the new odds is \(1.4907 \times 0.0789 = 0.11761623\).
Note that the answer is the same as for the previous question.
Here’s an explanation that uses the coefficients explicitly: Suppose the man without mild paranoia in the statement of the problem is participant \(i\). We know he’s Black and that he does not have mild paranoia. So, we can write \[
\begin{align*}
    \text{odds}_i &= \exp\left(-5.35 + 3.91 \text{Black}_i + 0.97 \text{paranoia}_i - 3.64 \text{Black}_i \times \text{paranoia}_i + \cdots \right) \\
    &= \exp\left(-5.35 + 3.91 (1) + 0.97 (0) - 3.64 (1) \times (0) + \cdots \right) \\
    &= \exp\left(-5.35 + 3.91  + \cdots \right) \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\] Now suppose the man with mild paranoia in the statement of the problem is participant \(j\). We can write \[
\begin{align*}
    \text{odds}_j &= \exp\left(-5.35 + 3.91 \text{Black}_i + 0.97 \text{paranoia}_i - 3.64 \text{Black}_i \times \text{paranoia}_i + \cdots \right) \\
    &= \exp\left(-5.35 + 3.91 (1) + 0.97 (1) - 3.64 (1) \times (1) + \cdots \right) \\
    &= \exp\left(-5.35 + 3.91  + 0.97  - 3.64  + \cdots \right) \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\] To get odds\(_j\), we can do this: \[
\begin{align*}
    \frac{\text{odds}_j}{\text{odds}_i} &= \frac{\exp\left(-5.35 + 3.91  + 0.97  - 3.64  + \cdots \right)}{\exp\left(-5.35 + 3.91  + \cdots \right) } \\
    \frac{\text{odds}_j}{\text{odds}_i} &= \exp\left(  0.97  - 3.64   \right) \\
    \text{odds}_j &= \exp\left(  0.97  - 3.64   \right) \text{odds}_i \\
    \text{odds}_j &= \exp\left(  0.97\right) \exp\left(  - 3.64   \right) \text{odds}_i \\
    \text{odds}_j &= \left(  2.63\right) \left(  0.03  \right) (1.4907) \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\]





75.3.3.5 Part (e)
Interpret the “odds ratio” for “Constant”.






TipSolution





This is not an odds ratio, it’s an odds. The intercept for the model was \(-5.35\) and \(\exp(-5.35) = 0.004748151\). The author then rounded up to 0.01 to get the odds. This would be the odds of hospitalization for mental health problems for a man with zeroes for all the explanatory variables, i.e., a man who is white, does not have mild paranoia, is zero years old, has never been married, has less than a high school education, makes under $7,000/year, has a zero occupational prestige score, has no diagnosis of a mental disorder, has no moderate or severe paranoia, and has a zero social desirability score.

title: 76  Poisson Distribution
text: 76.1 Learning Objective

title: 76  Poisson Distribution
text:
State the following, regarding the Poisson distribution:

What the distribution is intended to represent.
The support.
What the parameter represents.
The variance.
How to represent the mean in terms of rate and time.

title: 76  Poisson Distribution
text:
76.2 Lesson

76.2.1 What’s Important to Know
The Poisson distribution is a discrete distribution that forms the basis of Poisson regression. If \(Y\sim\text{Poisson}(\mu)\), this is what is important to know:

\(Y\) is a count. More specifically, \(Y\) is a count of the number of events happening in a defined time and place, where the rate of events is constant.
Since \(Y\) is a count, \(Y\) can be any non-negative whole number, i.e., 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, etc. There is no upper limit.
The single parameter, \(\mu\), represents the expected value. So, \(\mu = E(Y)\).
The variance of the Poisson distribution is exactly equal to its mean. So, \(Var(Y) = \mu\).
The expected value, \(\mu\), can also be represented as the product of the rate, \(\lambda\), and the time period over which the counting is occurring. The duration of this time period is \(t\). So, we can write \(\mu = \lambda t\).



76.2.2 Examples

76.2.2.1 Measles
Suppose \(Y_i\) is the number of new cases of measles in the state of Massachusetts in year \(i\). \(Y_i\) is a count, so we won’t see a negative or fractional number. It might be reasonable to assume that the expected (or mean) number of measles is the same each year, i.e., that measles cases in Massachusetts occur at the same, low rate. We can call the yearly rate \(\lambda\), where the units of \(\lambda\) are cases per year. The yearly mean is \(\mu = \lambda \times 1 = \lambda\). If we wanted \(Y_i\) to be the number of new cases in month \(i\), then \(\mu\) would be \(\lambda / 12\).


76.2.2.2 Words
Suppose \(Y_i\) is the number of times the word “the” appears on the \(i\)th page of a book. Again, \(Y_i\) is a count. It might be reasonable to assume that the expected number of times the word “the” appears on a page is the same for each page. We can call this count per page \(\lambda\), so that \(E(Y_i) = \lambda = \mu\). If we wanted \(Y_i\) to be the number of times the word “the” appears in the \(i\)th chapter of the book, we would need to know \(t_i\), the number of pages in the \(i\)th chapter. Then \(\mu_i = \lambda t_i\). In this example, \(t_i\) varies with \(i\), and it’s not a time, it’s a count of pages. This is common with the Poisson distribution; \(t\) may not be a literal duration in time, but may represent some other quantity.


76.2.2.3 Trees
Tongass National Forest, at nearly 17 million acres, is the largest national forest in the US. Suppose we wanted to estimate the number of spruce trees in the forest. We could sample several small sections of the forest and count the number of spruce trees in each section. Suppose each section is one acre, and we sample 100 acres. We could let \(Y_i\) be the number of (live) spruce trees in the \(i\)th section. Again, this would be a non-negative whole number. \(E(Y_i) = \mu\) would be the expected number of spruce trees in a single acre.
If we wanted to vary the size of our sections, we could let \(t_i\) denote the number of acres in the \(i\)th section, and \(\lambda\) denote the expected number of spruce trees per acre. Then \(E(Y_i) = \mu_i = \lambda t_i\). In this example, \(t_i\) is not a measure of time, but of area.

title: 77  Assumptions of Poisson Regression
text: 77.1 Learning Objectives

title: 77  Assumptions of Poisson Regression
text:
Explain the assumptions of Poisson regression.
Define, use, and interpret the term “offset”.

title: 77  Assumptions of Poisson Regression
text:
77.2 Lesson
Poisson regression has the following assumptions:

\(Y_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\sim\text{Poisson}(\lambda_i t_i)\).
\(\log\lambda_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\).
The observations are iid.

This is the first time we’re not modeling a mean. Here, we’re modeling \(\lambda_i\), which is a rate. We can model the mean if we include something called an “offset”: \[
\begin{align*}
\log\lambda_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \\
\log\lambda_i + \log t_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} + \log t_i \\
\log \left(\lambda_i t_i\right) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} + \log t_i \\
\log \mu_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} + \underbrace{\log t_i}_{\text{offset}} \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\]
The offset is the additional term, \(\log t_i\), that is added to the linear model so that we can model the mean instead of the rate.

title: 77  Assumptions of Poisson Regression
text:
77.3 Problems

77.3.1 Problem 1
If \(t_i = 1\), what is \(\log \mu_i\)?






TipSolution





If \(t_i = 1\) then \(\log t_i = \log 1 = 0\), so \[
\log \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \text{.}
\] Another way of saying this is that if \(t_i = 1\) then \(\mu_i = \lambda_i\).





77.3.2 Problem 2
Which of the four assumptions of linear regression are automatically violated when the outcome is a count?






TipSolution





The assumption that the random errors are normally distributed, conditional on the explanatory variables, is automatically violated. Suppose \(E(Y_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip})\) is 3.5. The only possible random errors are \(\{-3.5,-2.5,-1.5,-0.5,0.5,1.5,2.5,3.5,\dotsc\}\) because the outcome needs to be in \(\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,\dotsc\}\). A normally distributed random variable can be any real number. So, the errors can’t be normally distributed.
The assumption of constant variance is not automatically violated, but it is often violated. Suppose the outcome is Poisson-distributed. Recall that the mean of the Poisson distribution is equal to its variance. So, the variance will change as the mean changes.

title: 78  Residuals in Poisson Regression
text:
78.1 Learning Objective
State that there are different types of residuals for Poisson regression.

title: 78  Residuals in Poisson Regression
text:
78.2 Lesson
Residuals played a big role in linear regression, but I barely mentioned them for logistic regression. One of the reasons for that is that we can write the assumptions of linear regression in terms of random error, i.e., \(\epsilon_i\), but we can’t do the same for logistic regression. We can’t write the assumptions of Poisson regression in terms of random error, either. Still, it’s worth taking a look at the residuals to get a more visceral sense of why they can be less helpful for regression that isn’t linear regression.
I’m going to start by simulating data according to the assumptions of Poisson regression. To simplify things, I’m just going to assume that \(t_i = 1\) for every \(i\).

# Set random seed to make this reproducible
set.seed(3)

# Parameters
n <- 1e3
beta_0 <- 0
beta_1 <- 0.1

# Generate explanatory variable
x <- rnorm(n)

# Generate outcome variable
mu <- exp(beta_0 + beta_1 * x)
y <- rpois(n = n,
           lambda = mu)

Now I’m going to perform Poisson regression. I know all the assumptions are met because I simulated the data that way.

# Poisson regression
mod_01 <- glm(formula = y ~ x,
              family = poisson)
summary(mod_01)


Call:
glm(formula = y ~ x, family = poisson)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)   
(Intercept)  0.03257    0.03117   1.045  0.29600   
x            0.08066    0.03107   2.596  0.00943 **
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for poisson family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 1093.2  on 999  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 1086.5  on 998  degrees of freedom
AIC: 2616.7

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5


Now let’s talk about residuals. With Poisson regression, logistic regression, and any form of regression that uses the glm function, there are many types of residuals. This is a partial list:

Response

The \(i\)th residual is \(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\).
These are what we know from linear regression.
They don’t work as well for logistic and Poisson regression because logistic and Poisson regression have restrictions on what values the outcome can take. These restrictions on the outcome create restrictions on the residuals. The other types of residuals are attempts at addressing these restrictions and making residuals more useful when the outcome is not simply continuous.

Working

The \(i\)th residual is \(\displaystyle \left(\frac{d}{d\mu_i} \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} +\cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\right)\right) \left(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\right)\).
These are what you get from mod_01$residuals if mod_01 is the result of a glm call.

Deviance

The \(i\)th residual is \(\text{sign}(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i) \sqrt{2 \left(\ell(Y_i,Y_i) - \ell(Y_i,\hat{Y}_i)\right)}\). The \(\ell\)’s are used to denote log-likelihoods for different models.
These are what you get from residuals(mod_01) if mod_01 is the result of a glm call.

Pearson

The \(i\)th residual is \(\displaystyle \frac{Y_i - \hat{Y}_i}{\sqrt{\widehat{Var}(Y_i)}}\).
This is a residual that we have standardized to have variance 1.


Let’s look at plots of these different types of residuals for our Poisson regression model. Remember: we know the assumptions of Poisson regression are met for these data.

res_res <- residuals(object = mod_01,
                     type = "response")
res_wor <- residuals(object = mod_01,
                     type = "working")
res_dev <- residuals(object = mod_01,
                     type = "deviance")
res_pea <- residuals(object = mod_01,
                     type = "pearson")

# Scatterplot
plot(x = x,
     y = res_res,
     ylab = "Residual",
     main = "Response")
abline(h = 0,
       col = "red")







plot(x = x,
     y = res_wor,
     ylab = "Residual",
     main = "Working")
abline(h = 0,
       col = "red")







plot(x = x,
     y = res_dev,
     ylab = "Residual",
     main = "Deviance")
abline(h = 0,
       col = "red")







plot(x = x,
     y = res_pea,
     ylab = "Residual",
     main = "Pearson")
abline(h = 0,
       col = "red")







# Boxplot
boxplot(x = res_res,
        main = "Response")







boxplot(x = res_wor,
        main = "Working")







boxplot(x = res_dev,
        main = "Deviance")







boxplot(x = res_pea,
        main = "Pearson")







# Histogram
hist(x = res_res,
     xlab = "Residual",
     main = "Response")







hist(x = res_wor,
     xlab = "Residual",
     main = "Working")







hist(x = res_dev,
     xlab = "Residual",
     main = "Deviance")







hist(x = res_pea,
     xlab = "Residual",
     main = "Pearson")







# Q-Q Plot
qqnorm(y = res_res,
       main = "Response")
qqline(y = res_res)







qqnorm(y = res_wor,
       main = "Working")
qqline(y = res_wor)







qqnorm(y = res_dev,
       main = "Deviance")
qqline(y = res_dev)







qqnorm(y = res_pea,
       main = "Pearson")
qqline(y = res_pea)








It’s hard to know what we should be checking for here. None of the types of residuals look normal here, that’s for sure.
The whole purpose of this exercise is to demonstrate that there are multiple types of residuals when it comes to Poisson regression, but they aren’t necessarily useful for checking our assumptions.

title: 79  Interpretation
text:
79.1 Learning Objective
Interpret the coefficients in Poisson regression.

title: 79  Interpretation
text:
79.2 Lesson

79.2.1 Intercept
Recall that, in Poisson regression, we assume \[
\log\lambda_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \text{.}
\]
What happens when all the covariates equal zero? \[
\begin{align*}
\log\lambda_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \\
\log\lambda_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \cdots + \beta_p (0) \\
\log\lambda_i &= \beta_0 \\
\lambda_i &= \exp(\beta_0) \\
\end{align*}
\]
So, \(\exp(\beta_0)\) is the rate when all the covariates equal zero.


79.2.2 Non-Intercept Coefficients
How do we interpret the non-intercept coefficients? Suppose observation \(i\) has \(X_{i1} = x\) and observation \(j\) has \(X_{j1} = x + 1\). For each \(k \ne 1\), \(X_{ik} = X_{jk}\). In words, the two observations are identical except for the first covariate, where the \(j\)th observation exceeds the \(i\)th observation by one unit. Then \[
\begin{align*}
\log \frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_i} &= \log \frac{p_j}{1-p_j} - \log \frac{p_i}{1-p_i} \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{j1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{jp} - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (x+1) + \cdots + \beta_p X_{jp} - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_1 + \cdots + \beta_p X_{jp} - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\right) \\
&= \beta_1 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] By exponentiating both sides of this equation, we see \[
\begin{align*}
\log \frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_i} &= \beta_1 \\
\frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_i} &= \exp(\beta_1) \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\]
In words, \(\exp(\beta_1)\) is the rate ratio comparing two populations that are identical except that one exceeds the other by one unit on the first covariate. If \(\exp(\beta_1) > 1\), the rate is greater in the population with the higher value of the first covariate; if \(\exp(\beta_1) < 1\), the rate is lesser in the population with the higher value of the first covariate; if \(\exp(\beta_1) = 1\), the rate is the same in both populations.


79.2.3 Example
This data set comes from A Canadian Study of Smoking and Health–Second Report. These are the variables:

age_group: Age group, with the following levels:

40-44
45-49
50-54
55-59
60-64
65-69
70-74
75-79
80+

smoke_group: Smoking status, which has the following levels:

Never smoked
Cigar and pipe only
Cigarette and other
Cigarette only

population: The number of people in that age group who had that smoking status, at the start of the six-year follow-up period.
deaths: The number of people in that age group who had that smoking status and who died by the end of the six-year follow-up period.

Each row corresponds to a unique combination of age_group and smoke_group.
These are the modeling decisions I’ve made for this data set:

Our outcome will be deaths. Note that this is a count, which is appropriate for the Poisson distribution.
The offset will be log(population / 1000). This means we will be modeling the expected number of deaths per thousand people.
If I don’t make any changes, the reference age group will be <30 because it’s first alphabetically. This is not a great idea because it’s the smallest age group.


tapply(X = d$population,
       INDEX = d$age_group,
       FUN = sum)

  <30 30-34 35-39 40-44 45-49 50-54 55-59 60-64 65-69 70-74 75-79   80+ 
  526  8682 12592  8742  5732  4465  8956 11756  8147  4720  2335  1269 


I’m going to make 35-39 the reference group because it’s the largest age group.

d$age_group <- relevel(x = as.factor(d$age_group),
                       ref = "35-39")


If I don’t make any changes, the reference smoke group will be cigar_and_pipe_only because it’s first alphabetically. This is not a great idea because it’s the smallest smoke group.


tapply(X = d$population,
       INDEX = d$smoke_group,
       FUN = sum)

cigar_and_pipe_only cigarette_and_other      cigarette_only        never_smoked 
               4897               39198               26764                7063 


I’m going to make never_smoked the reference group because it’s a larger smoke group and because it’s logical to want to compare different forms of smoking to never having smoked

d$smoke_group <- relevel(x = as.factor(d$smoke_group),
                         ref = "never_smoked")


I’m going to regress the outcome on age_group and smoke_group without an interaction term. I am primarily concerned with the association between smoke group and deaths, controlling for age. I’m willing to assume (at least for now) that the association between smoke group and deaths is the same, regardless of age group.


mod_01 <- glm(formula = deaths ~ age_group + smoke_group + offset(log(population / 1000)),
              family = poisson,
              data = d)
summary(mod_01)

title: 80  Hypothesis Testing
text:
80.1 Learning Objective
Interpret the results of a hypothesis test in the context of Poisson regression.

title: 80  Hypothesis Testing
text:
80.2 Lesson

80.2.1 Interpretation in General
As in linear and logistic regression, R will conduct a hypothesis test for each coefficient estimated in Poisson regression. The null hypothesis for each coefficient is that that coefficient is zero, and the alternative hypothesis is that the coefficient is not zero. It’s always a two-sided test.
What does it mean if the coefficient is zero? The answer to this is different if we’re talking about the intercept versus a non-intercept coefficient. Let’s start with the intercept. Recall that \(\exp(\beta_0)\) is the expected rate when all the covariates are equal to zero. If \(\beta_0 = 0\), then \(\exp(\beta_0) = 1\). So, the null hypothesis for the intercept is that the expected rate is 1. Whether or not this is meaningful depends on your goals.
What about for the non-intercept coefficients? For \(j \ne 0\), \(\exp(\beta_j)\) is the rate ratio comparing two populations that are identical except one has \(X_{ij} = x + 1\) and the other has \(X_{kj} = x\). Again, if \(\beta_j = 0\), then \(\exp(\beta_j) = 1\). If a rate ratio is 1, then the two rates it’s comparing are equal to each other. So, the null hypothesis corresponds to equal rates for these two populations. If the p-value is small, we reject the null and conclude that these two populations have different rates.

Residual deviance:   31.291  on 33  degrees of freedom

How do we interpret the hypothesis tests? Since we have quite a few coefficients being estimated, and thus quite a few hypothesis tests being conducted, I’m going to use a more conservative threshold for the p-values. Since we’re estimating 15 coefficients, I’m going to use a threshold of \(0.05 / 15 = 0.00333\). (This is called a Bonferroni correction.)

Since the p-value for the intercept is less than 0.00333, we can conclude that the expected number of deaths per 1,000 35-39 year-olds who have never smoked is different from 1.
Since the p-value for age_group<30 is greater than 0.00333, we cannot conclude that the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people under 30 is different than the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 35-39, holding smoking group constant.
Since the p-value for age_group30-34 is greater than 0.00333, we cannot conclude that the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 30-34 is different than the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 35-39, holding smoking group constant.
Since the p-value for age_group40-44 is less than 0.00333, we can conclude that the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 40-44 is different than the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 35-39, holding smoking group constant.
Since the p-value for age_group45-49 is less than 0.00333, we can conclude that the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 45-49 is different than the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 35-39, holding smoking group constant.
Since the p-value for age_group50-54 is less than 0.00333, we can conclude that the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 50-54 is different than the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 35-39, holding smoking group constant.
Since the p-value for age_group55-59 is less than 0.00333, we can conclude that the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 55-59 is different than the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 35-39, holding smoking group constant.
Since the p-value for age_group60-64 is less than 0.00333, we can conclude that the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 60-64 is different than the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 35-39, holding smoking group constant.
Since the p-value for age_group65-69 is less than 0.00333, we can conclude that the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 65-69 is different than the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 35-39, holding smoking group constant.
Since the p-value for age_group70-74 is less than 0.00333, we can conclude that the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 70-74 is different than the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 35-39, holding smoking group constant.
Since the p-value for age_group75-79 is less than 0.00333, we can conclude that the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 75-79 is different than the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 35-39, holding smoking group constant.
Since the p-value for age_group80+ is less than 0.00333, we can conclude that the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 80 and above is different than the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people age 35-39, holding smoking group constant.
Since the p-value for smoke_groupcigar_and_pipe_only is greater than 0.00333, we cannot conclude that the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people who have only smoked cigars or pipes is different than the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people who have never smoked, holding age group constant.
Since the p-value for smoke_groupcigarette_and_other is less than 0.00333, we can conclude that the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people who have smoked cigarettes and other things is different than the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people who have never smoked, holding age group constant.
Since the p-value for smoke_groupcigarette_only is less than 0.00333, we can conclude that the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people who have only smoked cigarettes is different than the expected number of deaths per 1,000 people who have never smoked, holding age group constant.

title: 81  Quasi-Poisson Regression
text: 81.1 Learning Objectives

title: 81  Quasi-Poisson Regression
text:
Define, use, and interpret the term “overdispersion”.
Interpret a dispersion parameter.
Explain how and why the output for quasi-Poisson regression differs from the output for Poisson regression.

title: 81  Quasi-Poisson Regression
text:
81.2 Lesson

81.2.1 Definitions
Recall that if \(Y\sim\text{Poisson}(\mu)\), then \(\mu = E(Y) = Var(Y)\). It’s a very strong assumption to assume that the expectation is equal to the variance, and it’s often violated in practice. With real count data, the variance is often greater than the mean. This is known as overdispersion. (The opposite phenomenon, underdispersion, where the variance is less than the mean, is much less common.)
Quasi-Poisson regression is a form of Poisson regression that relaxes the assumption that \(Var(Y) = E(Y)\). In quasi-Poisson regression, we assume \(Var(Y) = \phi E(Y)\), where \(0 < \phi < \infty\). The parameter \(\phi\) is known as a dispersion parameter. If \(\phi > 1\), there is overdispersion.


81.2.2 Example
Let’s return to the data from A Canadian Study of Smoking and Health–Second Report. These are the variables:

age_group: Age group, with the following levels:

40-44
45-49
50-54
55-59
60-64
65-69
70-74
75-79
80+

smoke_group: Smoking status, which has the following levels:

Never smoked
Cigar and pipe only
Cigarette and other
Cigarette only

population: The number of people in that age group who had that smoking status, at the start of the six-year follow-up period.
deaths: The number of people in that age group who had that smoking status and who died by the end of the six-year follow-up period.

These are the results:



Call:
glm(formula = deaths ~ age_group + smoke_group + offset(log(population/1000)), 
    family = poisson, data = d)

Now let’s try quasi-Poisson regression and see what changes.

    family = quasipoisson, data = d)

age_group55-59                  2.00652    0.06750  29.728  < 2e-16 ***
age_group60-64                  2.28120    0.06527  34.952  < 2e-16 ***
age_group65-69                  2.62518    0.06544  40.115  < 2e-16 ***

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for quasipoisson family taken to be 0.8579232)

    Null deviance: 7941.034  on 47  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance:   31.291  on 33  degrees of freedom
AIC: NA

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4


What did and did not change when we used quasi-Poisson regression?

The coefficient estimates did not change at all. This is true in general; using quasi-Poisson will not change the estimates of the beta coefficients from what they are in Poisson regression.
The standard errors, \(t\) values, and p-values changed. For each coefficient, the standard error in quasi-Poisson regression is smaller than in Poisson regression. Since the coefficient estimates did not change, smaller standard errors mean larger \(t\) values and smaller p-values. This will not necessarily be true each time you run Poisson and quasi-Poisson regression. Sometimes the standard errors will increase, and sometimes they will decrease.
With quasi-Poisson regression, the dispersion parameter is estimated to be \(0.8579232\). This is one of those rare scenarios when there appears to be underdispersion.
With quasi-Poisson regression, there is no AIC. This is because quasi-Poisson regression is not fit with maximum likelihood estimation. In fact, you can’t write down a likelihood for the data in quasi-Poisson regression. There isn’t a real distribution that corresponds to quasi-Poisson regression. This means that we can’t use any likelihood-based methods to evaluate models fit with quasi-Poisson regression.



81.2.3 Threshold
Students always ask me how much overdispersion is too much, i.e., at what point should you use quasi-Poisson regression instead of Poisson regression. Unfortunately, I don’t think there’s a single answer to that question. It probably depends on your goals and your data set.
I know that’s often an unsatisfactory answer, so I’ll use An empirical approach to determine a threshold for assessing overdispersion in Poisson and negative binomial models for count data to offer 1.2 as a threshold. If \(\hat{\phi} \ge 1.2\), consider using quasi-Poisson regression instead of traditional Poisson regression.

title: 82  Interactions
text:
82.1 Learning Objective
Interpret the coefficients of a Poisson regression model with an interaction term.

title: 82  Interactions
text:
82.2 Lesson
Let’s return to the data set examining text messages sent by high school seniors in Pennsylvania in 2023 and 2024. These are the variables:

TextsSent: Number of text messages sent on the previous day.
Gender: Male or female.
HangHours: Hours spent hanging out with friends in the previous week.

The results below are for a quasi-Poisson regression with an interaction between gender and hours spent hanging out.



Call:
glm(formula = TextsSent ~ Gender * HangHours, family = quasipoisson, 
    data = d)

Coefficients:
                      Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)           3.966289   0.125460  31.614   <2e-16 ***
GenderMale           -0.225848   0.203775  -1.108   0.2683    
HangHours             0.012592   0.005701   2.209   0.0276 *  
GenderMale:HangHours -0.009417   0.010792  -0.873   0.3833    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for quasipoisson family taken to be 137.1013)

    Null deviance: 38517  on 499  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 37091  on 496  degrees of freedom
AIC: NA

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 6


How do we interpret the coefficients? In service of answering that question, let’s look at the model: \[
\begin{align*}
&\log \hat{E}\left(\texttt{TextsSent}\middle|\texttt{GenderMale},\texttt{HangHours}\right) \\
&= 3.966289 -0.225848\ \texttt{GenderMale} + 0.012592\ \texttt{HangHours} - 0.009417\ \texttt{GenderMale} \times \texttt{HangHours} \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] This implies that \[
\begin{align*}
&\hat{E}\left(\texttt{TextsSent}\middle|\texttt{GenderMale},\texttt{HangHours}\right) \\
&= \exp\left(3.966289 -0.225848\ \texttt{GenderMale} + 0.012592\ \texttt{HangHours} - 0.009417\ \texttt{GenderMale} \times \texttt{HangHours}\right) \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] So, we actually need to exponentiate the coefficients before interpreting them.

exp(mod_01$coefficients)

         (Intercept)           GenderMale            HangHours 
          52.7882917            0.7978395            1.0126721 
GenderMale:HangHours 
           0.9906268 


Now we can interpret the coefficients.

52.7882917 is the expected number of text messages sent in one day by a female senior who spent zero hours hanging out with friends the previous week. \[
\begin{align*}
&\hat{E}\left(\texttt{TextsSent}\middle|\texttt{GenderMale} = 0,\texttt{HangHours} = 0\right) \\
&= \exp\left(3.966289 -0.225848 (0) + 0.012592 (0) - 0.009417 (0) \times (0)\right) \\
&= \exp\left(3.966289 \right) \\
&= 52.7882917 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] In case you were wondering, zero is a reasonable number of hours to have spent hanging out with friends. Seven of the girls in the data set said they spent zero hours hanging out with friends in the previous week.



[1] 7



Among seniors who spent zero hours hanging out with friends in the previous week, boys sent about 20% fewer text messages per day than girls. \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{\hat{E}\left(\texttt{TextsSent}\middle|\texttt{GenderMale} = 1,\texttt{HangHours} = 0\right)}{\hat{E}\left(\texttt{TextsSent}\middle|\texttt{GenderMale} = 0,\texttt{HangHours} = 0\right)} &= \frac{\exp\left(3.966289 -0.225848 (1) + 0.012592 (0) - 0.009417 (1) \times (0)\right)}{\exp\left(3.966289 -0.225848 (0) + 0.012592 (0) - 0.009417 (0) \times  (0) \right)} \\
&= \exp\left(-0.225848\right) \\
&= 0.7978395 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
Among girls, each additional hour spent hanging out with friends is associated with a 1.26721% increase in the number of text messages sent per day. \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{\hat{E}\left(\texttt{TextsSent}\middle|\texttt{GenderMale} = 0,\texttt{HangHours} = x+1\right)}{\hat{E}\left(\texttt{TextsSent}\middle|\texttt{GenderMale} = 0,\texttt{HangHours} = x\right)} &= \frac{\exp\left(3.966289 -0.225848 (0) + 0.012592 (x+1) - 0.009417 (0) \times (x+1)\right)}{\exp\left(3.966289 -0.225848 (0) + 0.012592 x - 0.009417 (0) \times  x \right)} \\
&= \exp(0.012592) \\
&= 1.0126721 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
Among seniors who spent \(x\) hours hanging out with friends in the previous week, boys sent \(\exp(-0.225848-0.009417x)\) as many text messages per day as girls. \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{\hat{E}\left(\texttt{TextsSent}\middle|\texttt{GenderMale} = 1,\texttt{HangHours} = x\right)}{\hat{E}\left(\texttt{TextsSent}\middle|\texttt{GenderMale} = 0,\texttt{HangHours} = x\right)} &= \frac{\exp\left(3.966289 -0.225848 (1) + 0.012592 x - 0.009417 (1) \times x\right)}{\exp\left(3.966289 -0.225848 (0) + 0.012592 x - 0.009417 (0) \times  x \right)} \\
&= \exp(-0.225848-0.009417x) \\
\end{align*}
\]
Among boys, each additional hour spent hanging out with friends is associated with a 0.318% increase in the number of text messages sent per day. \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{\hat{E}\left(\texttt{TextsSent}\middle|\texttt{GenderMale} = 1,\texttt{HangHours} = x+1\right)}{\hat{E}\left(\texttt{TextsSent}\middle|\texttt{GenderMale} = 1,\texttt{HangHours} = x\right)} &= \frac{\exp\left(3.966289 -0.225848 (1) + 0.012592 (x+1) - 0.009417 (1) \times (x+1)\right)}{\exp\left(3.966289 -0.225848 (1) + 0.012592 x - 0.009417 (1) \times  x \right)} \\
&= \exp\left(0.012592-0.009417\right) \\
&= 1.00318 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]

title: 83  Generalized Linear Models
text: 83.1 Learning Objectives

title: 83  Generalized Linear Models
text:
Explain the key components of generalized linear models (GLMs).
For a given GLM, do the following:

Interpret the coefficients.
Interpret the results of a hypothesis test.

title: 83  Generalized Linear Models
text:
83.2 Lesson
So far, we’ve covered three forms of regression:

Linear
Logistic
Poisson

They all fall under a broader umbrella of models called “generalized linear models” (GLMs). A GLM has two main components:

A distribution for the outcome, conditional on the covariates.
A link function connecting the expected value of the distribution to the covariates through a linear model.

Let’s examine how each of the three forms of regression we’ve covered contains these two components.

Linear regression

The distribution is the normal distribution. We assume \(Y_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\sim\text{normal}(\mu_i,\sigma^2)\).
The link function is the identity function. We assume \(\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\).

Logistic regression

The distribution is the Bernoulli distribution. We assume \(Y_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\sim\text{Bernoulli}(\mu_i)\).
The link function is the logit function. We assume \(\log\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\).

Poisson regression

The distribution is the Poisson distribution. We assume \(Y_i|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\sim\text{Poisson}(\mu_i)\).
The link function is the log function. We assume \(\log\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} + \log t_i\).


These are not the only distributions that fit into the GLM framework. The other two most commonly-used distributions are the gamma distribution and the negative binomial distribution. Both are right-skewed distributions. The gamma is continuous and the negative binomial is discrete.
Here are some graphs the negative binomial distribution:


















































































































Here are some graphs of the gamma distribution:


















































































































The default link function for the negative binomial distribution is the log function, meaning that with negative binomial regression, we assume \(\log \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\). The default link function for the gamma distribution is the inverse function, meaning that with negative binomial regression, we assume \(\frac{1}{\mu_i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\). You don’t need to memorize this; if you type ?family into the R console and press enter, a help page will pop up showing all the distributions and their default link functions. (The one exception to this is the negative binomial distribution. For some reason, negative binomial regression is not included in base R. You have to install the package MASS to perform negative binomial regression. The function is glm.nb. To find its default link function, use ?negative.binomial.)
It’s important to know that you can change the link function you use. Although each distribution has a default, it’s not set in stone. So, you can use the family = binomial(link = "identity"), and your coefficients will be interpreted like in linear regression, as risk differences. It’s also important to know that the distribution determines the relationship between the mean and the variance. With linear regression, there is no relationship; the variance can be anything, irrespective of the mean. With logistic regression, the variance is equal to \(\mu (1 - \mu)\), and with Poisson regression, the variance is equal to the mean.

title: 83  Generalized Linear Models
text:
83.3 Problems

83.3.1 Problem 1
Suppose I own a shop, and every morning I measure the time between opening my shop and the first customer arriving. Let \(T_i\) represent this time in minutes on the \(i\)th day of my study. Let \(E_i = 1\) if the \(i\)th day is on the weekend and \(E_i = 0\) if the \(i\)th day is during the work week. I use gamma regression with the default link function to regress \(T_i\) on \(E_i\). My estimated intercept is 0.1 and the estimated coefficient on \(E_i\) is also 0.1. Interpret these coefficients.






TipSolution





Our model is \[
\frac{1}{E(T_i|E_i)} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 E_i \text{,}
\] so \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{\hat{E}(T_i|E_i)} &= \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 E_i \\
\frac{1}{\hat{E}(T_i|E_i)} &= 0.1 + 0.1 E_i \\
\frac{1}{0.1 + 0.1 E_i} &= \hat{E}(T_i|E_i) \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\] This means \[
\begin{align*}
\hat{E}(T_i|E_i = 0) &= \frac{1}{0.1} \\
&= 10 \\
\hat{E}(T_i|E_i = 1) &= \frac{1}{0.1 + 0.1} \\
&= \frac{1}{0.2} \\
&= 20 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] So, during the work week we would expect to wait 10 minutes for the first customer to arrive and on the weekend we would expect to wait 20 minutes for the first customer to arrive.





83.3.2 Problem 2
Could I use a logit link with Poisson regression? Justify your answer.






TipSolution





This sounds like a bad idea. For simplicity, assume there’s no offset. Then we’re assuming \[
\log\frac{\mu_i}{1 - \mu_i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \text{.}
\] If \(\mu_i = 1\), the term \(\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}\) is not defined. If \(\mu_i > 1\), then \(\frac{\mu_i}{1 - \mu_i} < 0\) and the term \(\log\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}\) is not defined, because you can’t take the log of a negative number. This is really something you should only consider if your outcome is binary.

title: 84  Censoring
text:
84.1 Learning Objective
Define, use, and interpret the following terms:

title: 84  Censoring
text:
Left censoring
Right censoring
Interval censoring
Independent censoring

title: 84  Censoring
text:
84.2 Lesson
It is very common in medical research for the outcome to be the time from some origin to some event. Here are some examples:

Time from diagnosis to death.
Time from treatment onset to recovery.
Time from treatment completion to disease progression.

When time-to-event is the outcome, it’s very common to have partial information about the outcome. There are a few ways this information can be missing, as described in the following subsections.

84.2.1 Right Censoring
The most common version of partial information for time-to-event data is “right censoring”. Right censoring occurs when you know the event happened after some amount of time, but you don’t know exactly when. If \(T\) is the time to event, you know \(T > t\), but not the exact value of \(T\). Right censoring is depicted in this figure:









Here are a couple examples of right censoring:

You recruit people into a study and follow them for five years. If a participant doesn’t have the event before the five years are up, you know their event occurred after the study ended, but you don’t know exactly when.
If someone in your study moves away and ceases participating, you know their event occurred after this rupture, but not exactly when.



84.2.2 Left Censoring
As you might be able to guess, left censoring occurs when you know the event occurred before some time, but not exactly when. If \(T\) is the time to the event, you know \(T < t\), but not the exact value of \(T\). Left censoring is depicted in the following figure:









An example of left censoring is when a patient enters your clinic with a rash, but they don’t remember exactly when it started. You know the rash appeared before their clinic visit, but not exactly when.


84.2.3 Interval Censoring
Interval censoring occurs when you know the event happened between two time-points, but not exactly when. If \(T\) is the time to the event, interval censoring occurs when you know \(t_1 < T < t_2\), but not the exact value of \(T\). Interval censoring is depicted in the following figure:









Interval censoring might happen if you check in with participant in a study at regular intervals. If someone has not had the event by check-in #3, but they have had the event by check-in #4, you know the event occurred between those two time-points.


84.2.4 No Censoring
Just for completeness, the following figure depicts no censoring:











84.2.5 Independent Censoring
The following definition of independent censoring is taken from page 38 of Survival Analysis: A Self-Learning Text (3rd ed.), by Kleinbaum and Klein (author’s emphasis):

Independent censoring essentially means that within any subgroup of interest, the subjects who are censored at time t should be representative of all the subjects in that subgroup who remained at risk at time t with respect to their survival experience.

Kleinbaum and Klein provide the following example: Suppose you start a study at time 0 with 100 participants. At the three year mark, twenty participants have experienced the event. This leaves 80 participants who have not experienced the event.
Suppose that 40 of the remaining participants are censored at the three year mark, and 40 continue with the study. Independent censoring means that the distribution in times to event should be the same among the 40 who were censored and the 40 who were not censored. So, if we check in again at the five year mark, we would expect approximately the same number of events among the 40 who were censored and the 40 who were not censored.
I hope you can see why independent censoring would be important for analyzing time-to-event data. We can only draw conclusions based on the values we observe. If the people who remain in our study are fundamentally different from the people who drop out, we will draw conclusions that will only be true for the subset of people who remained in the study. If the people who remain in our study are essentially the same as the people who drop out, any conclusions based on the people who remain will also apply to the people who dropped out.

title: 84  Censoring
text:
84.3 Problems

84.3.1 Problem 1
Suppose my dad and I leave the house at the same time to go for a run. We run exactly the same distance, but on different routes. When I return to the house, my dad has already returned home. What kind of censoring has occurred for my dad’s run time?






TipSolution





Left censoring. I know he took less time than I did, but I don’t know exactly what time he finished his run.





84.3.2 Problem 2
In the 1963 film It’s a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World, a group of motorists stop to help a car crash victim who, with his dying breath, tells them he has buried $350,000 (about $3.9 million in 2026) in Santa Rosita State Park under a big W. The motorists then race to the park so they can claim the money. Unbeknownst to them, a police officer named Captain Culpeper has the motorists shadowed; the money was stolen, and the captain wants to close the case before retiring.
Suppose (contrary to what actually happens in the film), that the canniest motorists not only manage to shake the police officers following them, but also arrive earliest at the big W. Thus, the police do not know their arrival times. Is this an example of independent censoring?






TipSolution





No, because the censored times are shorter than the observed observed times.





84.3.3 Problem 3
Categorize each of the following as left, right, or interval censoring.

84.3.3.1 Part (a)
Every year you send a holiday card to a former coworker. You haven’t worked together in years, and you don’t talk on the phone or see each other anymore, but you still send a holiday card every December. One year, the card comes back marked “No longer at this address.” You ask yourself, “When did they move?”






TipSolution





This is interval censoring. You know your former coworker lived at that address last year and you know they don’t live there now, but you don’t know when exactly between those two dates they moved.





84.3.3.2 Part (b)
You know your parents got married before you were born, but you don’t remember the exact year.






TipSolution





This is left censoring. You know the event occurred before a certain time, but you don’t know more than that.





84.3.3.3 Part (c)
Your bathroom scale has a maximum weight of 400 pounds. You get your pet elephant, Rufus, to step on the scale. It breaks. You know Rufus weighs at least 400 pounds, but you don’t know what his exact weight is.






TipSolution





This is right censoring.





84.3.3.4 Part (d)
You are a geologist. You find a cool new fossil between two layers of sedimentary rock. You don’t know how old the fossil is, but you know the layer of rock above it is 1 million years old and the layer of rock beneath it is 2 million years old.






TipSolution





This is interval censoring.

Create a Kaplan-Meier curve.
Interpret a Kaplan-Meier curve.
Define, use, and interpret median survival.

title: 85  Kaplan-Meier Curve
text:
85.2 Lesson
Suppose we run a study where we recruit 100 people with a serious disease and measure time from diagnosis until death. We only have the money to run the study for ten years, so any participant who is still alive after ten years is automatically censored at that time. Some participants drop out or are lost to follow-up for other reasons, leading to censoring. These are the first ten rows of data:


          time death
1   2.17925490     0
2   2.91964018     1
3   0.06812466     0
4  10.00000000     0
5   0.64579488     1
6   1.93972095     0
7   7.74991871     1
8  10.00000000     0
9   2.17138564     0
10  0.63484797     0


The variable time is time from diagnosis to either death or censoring, in years. The variable death equals 1 for any participant whose time to death was observed, and 0 for any participant who was censored. In this section we will learn how to display these data graphically, in what’s called a Kaplan-Meier curve.
The horizontal axis of the Kaplan-Meier curve is time from some origin. It’s very important that this axis label include (a) what that time origin is and (b) what the units of time are. The vertical axis is probability of survival, i.e., \(P(T > t)\), where \(T\) is the time from the origin to the event. The Kaplan-Meier curve always starts at the point \((0,1)\), because at time zero, no one has had the event.









Where do we go from here? Moving from left to right, the curve will remain constant until there is at least one event. When there is at least one event, the curve will drop. The trick is figuring out how much the curve should drop.
In order to explain the next steps, I need to use some new notation. To be consistent with the example, I’m going to use “death” and “event” interchangeably. Also, I’m going to assume the deaths all happened at different times. Define the following:

\(k\) is the index for the deaths. So, \(k = 1\) indicates the first death, \(k = 2\) indicates the second death, and so forth.
\(t_k\) is the time of the \(k\)th death.
\(N_k\) is the number of people at risk at time \(t_k\). In other words, \(N_k\) is the number of people who have neither died nor been censored before \(t_k\).
\(D_k\) is the number of deaths at \(t_k\). Since we’re assuming that all the deaths happened at unique times, \(D_k\) will just be 1 for each \(k\).

In order to make our Kaplan-Meier curve, we are going to fill in the following table:












\(k\)
\(t_k\)
\(N_k\)
\(D_k\)
\(\hat{P}(T = t_k|T \ge t_k)\)
\(\hat{P}(T > t_k | T \ge t_k)\)
\(\hat{P}(T > t_k)\)




0
0




1



How do we get those last three columns?

\(\hat{P}(T = t_k|T \ge t_k)\) is an estimate of the probability that the death happens exactly at \(t_k\), given that it hasn’t happened before \(t_k\). This is fairly straightforward to compute: We will divide the number of deaths at \(t_k\) by the number of people at risk at \(t_k\). In symbols, \[
\hat{P}(T = t_k|T \ge t_k) = \frac{D_k}{N_k} \text{.}
\]
\(\hat{P}(T > t_k | T \ge t_k)\) is an estimate of the probability that the death happens after \(t_k\), i.e., that someone survives past \(t_k\), given that the death didn’t happen before \(t_k\). This is \[
\begin{align*}
\hat{P}(T > t_k | T \ge t_k) &= 1 - \hat{P}(T = t_k | T \ge t_k) \\
&= 1 - \frac{D_k}{N_k} \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\]
\(\hat{P}(T > t_k)\) is what we actually want to plot; unfortunately, it’s the least straightforward quantity to compute. We use the following logic: \[
\begin{align}
\hat{P}(T > t_k) &= \hat{P}(T > t_k, T \ge t_{k}) \\
&= \hat{P}(T > t_k | T \ge t_{k}) \hat{P}(T \ge t_{k}) \\
&= \hat{P}(T > t_k | T \ge t_{k}) \hat{P}(T > t_{k-1}) \text{.}
\end{align}
\]

Let’s start filling in the table. In order to do so, we must first sort our data set from smallest to largest time.


         time death

Note that \(t_1 = 0.02841937\). At the time of the first death, no one has been censored, so there are 100 people at risk. There’s exactly one death at \(t_1\), so \[
\begin{align*}
\hat{P}(T = t_1|T \ge t_1) &= \frac{D_1}{N_1} \\
&= \frac{1}{100} \\
\hat{P}(T > t_1 | T \ge t_1) &= 1 - \hat{P}(T = t_1|T \ge t_1) \\
&= 1 - \frac{1}{100} \\
&= \frac{99}{100} \\
\hat{P}(T > t_1) &= \hat{P}(T > t_1 | T \ge t_{1}) \hat{P}(T > t_{0}) \\
&= \frac{99}{100} \times 1 \\
&= \frac{99}{100} \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]

Moving on, we have \(t_2 = 0.11406225\). At the time of the second death, three people have been censored and one has already died, so there are 96 people at risk. There’s exactly one death at \(t_2\), so \[
\begin{align*}
\hat{P}(T = t_2|T \ge t_2) &= \frac{D_2}{N_2} \\

\hat{P}(T > t_2 | T \ge t_2) &= 1 - \hat{P}(T = t_2|T \ge t_2) \\
&= 1 - \frac{1}{96} \\
&= \frac{95}{96} \\
\hat{P}(T > t_2) &= \hat{P}(T > t_2 | T \ge t_{2}) \hat{P}(T > t_{1}) \\
&= \frac{95}{96} \times \frac{99}{100} \times 1 \\
&\approx 0.9796875 \text{.}
\end{align*}

Instead of doing this 48 more times, let’s have R plot the Kaplan-Meier curve for us. We can use base R or the package ggsurvfit to make the plot. Either way, we need the package survival.

# Have survival package work its magic

                       event = death) ~ 1,
                  data = d_survival)

     xlab = "Years Since Diagnosis",
     ylab = "Probability of Survival")

                        event = death) ~ 1,
                   data = d_survival)) +
  labs(x = "Years Since Diagnosis",
       y = "Probability of Survival")








Ta-da! Now we have an estimate of \(P(T > t)\) for each value of \(t\) from 0 to 10.
There’s one more term we have to learn, which is “median survival”. Median survival is the time \(t_{0.5}\) such that \(P(T > t_{0.5}) = 0.5\), i.e., the time that we would expect approximately half the people to survive past. It’s very easy to get median survival from the survfit object:


Call: survfit(formula = Surv(time = time, event = death) ~ 1, data = d_survival)

       n events median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL
[1,] 100     51   5.98    4.58     7.6


As we can see, the median survival is 5.98. So, people have a 50% chance of surviving past 5.98 years after their diagnosis.
On the Kaplan-Meier curve, the median survival is the point on the horizontal axis where the height of the curve is 0.5.

title: 85  Kaplan-Meier Curve
text:
85.3 Problems

85.3.1 Problem 1
In the example above, what is the probability of surviving past 2.5 years?






TipSolution





It’s about 0.75, because that’s the (approximate) height of the Kaplan-Meier curve at 2.5 years since diagnosis.





85.3.2 Problem 2
Why doesn’t the Kaplan-Meier curve above reach zero?






TipSolution





In order for the Kaplan-Meier curve to reach zero, there must be some \(k\) where \(\hat{P}(T > t_k | T \ge t_k) = 0\). For this to happen, \(\hat{P}(T = t_k|T \ge t_k)\) must be 1, meaning \(D_k = N_k\). In other words, there must be a time when everyone who is still at risk dies. The fact that the Kaplan-Meier curve above doesn’t reach zero means that at the time of the last death, not everybody at risk died.

title: 86  Hazard Rate
text: 86.1 Learning Objectives

title: 86  Hazard Rate
text:
Define, use, and interpret discrete hazard.
Define, use, and interpret hazard rate.

title: 86  Hazard Rate
text:
86.2 Lesson
The hazard rate is a very important concept in survival analysis, but it’s also very difficult to define and interpret. So, we’re going to start with something easier, which I will call the discrete hazard or discrete time hazard.

86.2.1 Discrete Hazard
If \(T\) is the time to an event, and time is measured in discrete units, then the discrete hazard is \(P(T  = t| T \ge t)\). In words, the discrete hazard at time \(t\) is the probability that the event occurs at time \(t\), given that it has not occurred before time \(t\).
What do I mean by “discrete time”? I mean that time is measured in units that don’t allow fractions. For example, imagine time is measured in days, where you can’t have any partial days. Or, imagine time is measured in the number of trials, like the number of times you turn on a light before the bulb dies.
Note that the discrete hazard is a probability, but it’s a conditional probability. In general, \(P(T  = t| T \ge t) \ne P(T = t)\). To illustrate this, suppose \(T\) is time from birth to death, measured in whole years. \(P(T = 100)\) is probably pretty low; very few people survive to age 100. In contrast, \(P(T = 100|T \ge 100)\) is probably relatively high. Among all 100-year-olds, a relatively high percentage die before turning 101.


86.2.2 Hazard Rate
Now suppose time is measured as a continuous variable, so it can take any positive decimal value. For any value \(t\), \(P(T = t) = 0\). So, \(P(T  = t| T \ge t) = 0\), which is not very useful to us. So, we have to use limits.
Consider the quantity \[
\frac{P\left(t \le T < t + \delta \middle| T \ge t\right)}{\delta} \text{.}
\] When \(\delta = 1\), we essentially have our discrete time hazard: \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{P\left(t \le T < t + \delta \middle| T \ge t\right)}{\delta} &= \frac{P\left(t \le T < t + 1 \middle| T \ge t\right)}{1} \\
&= P\left(t \le T < t + 1 \middle| T \ge t\right) \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\]
To get a hazard rate, we’re going to make \(\delta\) smaller and smaller. \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{P\left(t \le T < t + 1 \middle| T \ge t\right)}{1} &= P\left(t \le T < t + 1 \middle| T \ge t\right) \\
\frac{P\left(t \le T < t + \frac{1}{2} \middle| T \ge t\right)}{\frac{1}{2}} &= 2P\left(t \le T < t + \frac{1}{2} \middle| T \ge t\right) \\
\frac{P\left(t \le T < t + \frac{1}{3} \middle| T \ge t\right)}{\frac{1}{3}} &= 3P\left(t \le T < t + \frac{1}{3} \middle| T \ge t\right) \\
\frac{P\left(t \le T < t + \frac{1}{4} \middle| T \ge t\right)}{\frac{1}{4}} &= 4P\left(t \le T < t + \frac{1}{4} \middle| T \ge t\right) \\
\frac{P\left(t \le T < t + \frac{1}{5} \middle| T \ge t\right)}{\frac{1}{5}} &= 5P\left(t \le T < t + \frac{1}{5} \middle| T \ge t\right) \\
\end{align*}
\]
As \(\delta\) gets smaller, \(P\left(t \le T < t + \delta \middle| T \ge t\right)\) gets smaller, too, but \(\frac{1}{\delta}\) gets bigger. So, by dividing by \(\delta\), we’re balancing out the decrease in \(P\left(t \le T < t + \delta \middle| T \ge t\right)\).
We define the hazard rate to be \[
h(t) = \lim_{\delta\downarrow 0} \frac{P\left(t \le T < t + \delta \middle| T \ge t\right)}{\delta} \text{.}
\] This is also \[
\begin{align*}
h(t) &= \lim_{\delta\downarrow 0} \frac{P\left(t \le T < t + \delta \middle| T \ge t\right)}{\delta} \\
&= \lim_{\delta\downarrow 0} \frac{P\left(t \le T < t + \delta , T \ge t\right)}{\delta P\left( T \ge t\right)} \\
&= \lim_{\delta\downarrow 0} \frac{P\left(t \le T < t + \delta \right)}{\delta P\left( T \ge t\right)} \\
&= \frac{1}{P\left( T \ge t\right)} \lim_{\delta\downarrow 0} \frac{P\left(t \le T < t + \delta \right)}{\delta } \\
&= \frac{1}{P\left( T \ge t\right)} f(t) \\
&= \frac{f(t)}{P\left( T \ge t\right)}  \\
&= \frac{f(t)}{P\left( T > t\right)} \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\] The numerator is the probability density function or PDF. The denominator is the survival function.
The hazard rate is, unfortunately, very difficult to interpret. It’s a conditional probability per unit time. It’s like a PDF in that we arrive at it via a limit, but it’s unlike a PDF in that we don’t get a probability if we integrate it. Some people interpret the hazard rate as “instantaneous risk”, which is pretty close to correct. The hazard rate is the risk (probability) that the event happens right now, given it hasn’t happened before now, scaled by time.

title: 86  Hazard Rate
text:
86.3 Problems

86.3.1 Problem 1

86.3.1.1 Part (a)
Is it possible for \(h(t) = 5\)? Why or why not?






TipSolution





Yes, this is possible. Since \(h(t)\) is not a probability, we can have \(h(t) > 1\). If \(f(t) = 5 \exp(-5t)\), then \(h(t) = 5\).





86.3.1.2 Part (b)
Is it possible for \(h(t) = -5\)? Why or why not?






TipSolution





No, we can’t have a negative hazard rate. In the definition, all the terms are non-negative, so we can’t end up with a negative value.





86.3.1.3 Part (c)
Is it possible for \(P(T = t|T \ge t) = 5\)? Why or why not?






TipSolution





No. This is a probability, so it must be between 0 and 1.

For generic \(w\), the discrete time hazard is \[
\begin{align*}
h(w) &= P(W_i = w|W_i \ge w) \\
&= \frac{P(W_i = w,W_i \ge w)}{P(W_i \ge w)} \\
&= \frac{P(W_i = w)}{P(W_i \ge w)} \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] These are the hazards for specific values: \[
\begin{align*}
h(2) &= \frac{P(W_i = 2)}{P(W_i \ge 2)} \\
&= \frac{0.00364}{1} \\
&= 0.00364 \\
h(3) &= \frac{P(W_i = 3)}{P(W_i \ge 3)} \\
&= \frac{0.00364}{1 - 0.00364} \\
&= \frac{\frac{1}{275}}{1-\frac{1}{275}} \\
&= \frac{1}{275-1} \\
&= 0.00365 \\
h(4) &= \frac{P(W_i = 4)}{P(W_i \ge 4)} \\
&= \frac{1}{1+1+1+10+2+258} \\
&= \frac{1}{273} \\
&= 0.00366 \\
h(5) &= \frac{P(W_i = 5)}{P(W_i \ge 5)} \\
&= 0 \\
h(6) &= \frac{P(W_i = 6)}{P(W_i \ge 6)} \\
&= \frac{1}{272} \\

\]





86.3.2.2 Part (b)
Compare and contrast the example above with this example:

Suppose you are studying a new face wash for treating acne. You give the face wash to \(n\) people and ask them to use it every day. Let \(X_i\) be the number of days until the \(i\)th person’s acne disappears. (This count includes the last day, when the acne is gone.) You decide that \(X_1,\dotsc,X_n\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\text{geometric}(p)\), where \(p\) is the probability that the acne disappears on a given day.


A random variable follows a geometric distribution if it represents the number of trials until the first success; there are only two outcomes (success and failure) on each trial; the trials are independent; and the probability of success is the same for each trial. (The parameter \(p\) is the probability of success on each trial.)







TipSolution





The Hot Ones example is sort of the opposite of the face wash example. In Hot Ones, \(P(W_i = w)\) is constant for five of the possible values of \(w\). The hazard, in contrast, is increasing. In the face wash example, \(P(X_i = x)\) is decreasing and the discrete time hazard is constant.





86.3.2.3 Part (c)
Which is greater, \(P(W_i = w)\) or \(h(w)\)? Is this true in general?






TipSolution





In this example and in general, \(h(w) \ge P(W_i = w)\). This is because \[
h(w) = \frac{P(W_i = w)}{P(W_i \ge w)}
\] and \(P(W_i \ge w) \le 1\). Dividing by something smaller than 1 results in something bigger than what you started with.

title: 87  Assumptions of the Cox Proportional Hazards Model
text:
87.1 Learning Objective
Explain the assumptions of the Cox proportional hazards model.
crumbs: 87  Assumptions of the Cox Proportional Hazards Model

title: 87  Assumptions of the Cox Proportional Hazards Model
text:
87.2 Lesson
The Cox proportional hazards model has the following assumptions, where \(h_i(t)\) is the hazard rate for the \(i\)th observation and \(h_0(t)\) is the baseline hazard rate:

\(\log h_i(t) = \log h_0(t) + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\)
The observations are iid.
Censoring is independent of time to event.

Note that there’s no \(\beta_0\). With the Cox proportional hazards model (which I will abbreviate to the Cox model or Cox regression), we don’t estimate an intercept. This means we don’t estimate the baseline hazard rate. At no point do we say what \(h_0(t)\) is.
We can write the first assumption above with exponents instead of logs: \[
h_i(t) = h_0(t) \exp\left(\beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\right) \text{.}
\]
crumbs: 87  Assumptions of the Cox Proportional Hazards Model

title: 87  Assumptions of the Cox Proportional Hazards Model
text:
87.3 Problems

87.3.1 Problem 1
Compare and contrast these assumptions with those of a generalized linear model.






TipSolution





Similarities:

We have a linear function of the covariates, i.e., \(\beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip}\).
We’re modeling the log of the hazard, which is similar to modeling the log of the rate or mean in Poisson regression.
We assume the observations are independent.

Differences:

There’s no \(\beta_0\).
We don’t assume a distribution for the time to the event. This implies there’s no assumed mean-variance relationship.
Here, we have to make an additional assumption about censoring.
crumbs: 87  Assumptions of the Cox Proportional Hazards Model

title: 88  Interpretation
text:
88.1 Learning Objective
Interpret the coefficients in a Cox proportional hazards model.

title: 88  Interpretation
text:
88.2 Lesson
How do we interpret the coefficients in the Cox model? Consider the first assumption: \[
\log h_i(t) = \log h_0(t) + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \text{.}
\] If we exponentiate both sides, we get this: \[
h_i(t) = h_0(t) \exp\left( \beta_1 X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \right) \text{.}
\] So, we can get \(\exp(\beta_1)\) as follows: \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{h_0(t) \exp\left( \beta_1 (x+1) + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \right)}{h_0(t) \exp\left( \beta_1 x + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \right)} &= \frac{\exp\left( \beta_1 (x+1) + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \right)}{\exp\left( \beta_1 x + \cdots + \beta_p X_{ip} \right)} \\
&= \frac{\exp\left( \beta_1 (x+1)  \right)}{\exp\left( \beta_1 x  \right)} \\
&= \frac{\exp\left( \beta_1 x + \beta_1  \right)}{\exp\left( \beta_1 x  \right)} \\
&= \exp\left(\beta_1\right) \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
So, \(\exp\left(\beta_1\right)\) is the hazard ratio at time \(t\) comparing two populations that are identical except for a difference of one unit on the first explanatory variable. Phrased another way, the hazard rate at time \(t\) for a population with \(X_1 = x+1\) is \(\exp(\beta_1)\) times the hazard rate at time \(t\) for a population with \(X_1 = x\), holding all else equal. Phrased yet another way, the hazard rate at time \(t\) for a population with \(X_1 = x+1\) is \(\left(\exp(\beta_1) - 1\right)\times 100\%\) greater than the hazard rate at time \(t\) for a population with \(X_1 = x\), holding all else equal.
Note that I kept saying “hazard rate at time \(t\)”. We can’t compare the hazard rate in one group at time \(t\) to the hazard rate in another group at time \(s\).

88.2.1 Example
Let’s look at data from a trial comparing two adjuvant therapy regimens for colon cancer (Moertel et al., 1995). These are the variables:

time: Time until death in days. Unfortunately, I don’t know the time origin.
status: 1 is death, 0 is censoring.
rx: This is the treatment variable, and it has three levels: Obs for observation; Lev for Levamisole, and Lev+5FU for Levamisole plus 5-FU.
sex: 1 for male, 0 for female.
age: This is in years, but I don’t know when it was measured. Maybe at the time origin?

The results of a Cox regression is below.

                               event = status) ~ rx + sex + age,
                data = d_colon)
summary(mod_01)

Eyes in risk group 9 have a 35% lower hazard rate at time \(t\) than eyes in risk group 6, holding age at diagnosis and treatment status constant.

title: 89  Proportional Hazards Assumption
text:
89.1 Learning Objectives
Explain what “proportional hazards” means.

title: 89  Proportional Hazards Assumption
text:
89.2 Lesson
With the Cox proportional hazards model, we assume that if you fix \(t\), one hazard rate is a constant multiple of the other. In other words, the hazard rates are always proportional to each other.
Suppose we have two groups, group 1 and group 2. Let \(h_1(t)\) and \(h_2(t)\) be the hazard rates of groups 1 and 2, respectively, at time \(t\). The proportional hazards assumption is that \(h_2(t) = c h_1(t)\), where \(c\) is a positive constant.
I’d like to look at what this means for the survival curve, but in order to do so, I have to introduce a new function. The “cumulative hazard” in group 1 is \[
\Lambda_1(t) = \int_0^t h_1(s)\,ds \text{.}
\] You don’t need to memorize this; it’s just an interim step between the hazard and the survival function. What you need to know is that \[
\Lambda_1(t) = -\log S_1(t) \text{,}
\] where \(S_1(t) = P(T_1 > t)\). If you don’t believe me, you can check out the proof in the callout below.






CautionCaution: Math





First, note that \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{d}{ds} \log S(s) &= \frac{1}{S(s)} \frac{d}{ds} S(s) & \text{chain rule} \\
&= \frac{1}{S(s)} \frac{d}{ds} \left(1 - F(s)\right) & \text{definition of cumulative distribution function} \\
&= \frac{1}{S(s)} \left(-f(s)\right)  & \text{definition of probability distribution function} \\
&= - \frac{f(s)}{S(s)} \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] Next, \[
\begin{align*}
\Lambda(t) &= \int_0^t h(s)\,ds \\
&= \int_0^t \frac{f(s)}{S(s)} \,ds \\
&= \int_0^t \left(-\frac{d}{ds} \log S(s)\right) \,ds \\
&= - \int_0^t \frac{d}{ds} \log S(s) \,ds \\
&= - \log S(t) \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]



Now we can connect the hazards to the survival functions. Proportional hazards means \[
\begin{align*}
h_2(t) &= ch_1(t) \\
\int_0^t h_2(s)\,ds &= \int_0^t ch_1(s) \,ds \\
\int_0^t h_2(s)\,ds &= c \int_0^t h_1(s) \,ds \\
\Lambda_2(t) &= c\Lambda_1(t) \\
-\log S_2(t) &= -c\log S_1(t) \\
-\log S_2(t) &= -\log S_1(t)^c \\
S_2(t) &= S_1(t)^c \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\] So, at any time \(t\), we can get the survival probability for group 2 by raising the survival probability for group 1 to the power \(c\).
To see visual representations of proportional hazards, I recommend checking out Fall 2025 Quiz 13 and Fall 2025 Quiz 14

title: 89  Proportional Hazards Assumption
text:
89.3 Problems

89.3.1 Problem 1
True or false: Proportional hazards is equivalent to proportional survival.






TipSolution





False. Proportional hazards is equivalent to \(S_2(t) = S_1(t)^c\), not \(S_2(t) = c S_1(t)\).

title: 90  Checking the Proportional Hazards Assumption
text:
90.2 Lesson
Proportional hazards is a strong assumption. So, we really should check it before interpreting the results of a Cox regression model. How do we check this assumption? I’m going to present two methods.

90.2.1 Complementary Log-Log Plot
Recall that proportional hazards means \(h_2(t) = ch_1(t)\), where \(h_2(t)\) denotes the hazard rate at time \(t\) for group 2, \(h_1(t)\) denotes the hazard rate at time \(t\) for group 1, and \(c\) is a positive constant. Proportional hazards implies \[
\begin{align*}
h_2(t) &= ch_1(t) \\
\int_0^t h_2(s)\,ds &= \int_0^t ch_1(s) \,ds \\
\int_0^t h_2(s)\,ds &= c \int_0^t h_1(s) \,ds \\
\Lambda_2(t) &= c\Lambda_1(t) \\
-\log S_2(t) &= -c\log S_1(t) \\
\log(-\log S_2(t)) &= \log(-c\log S_1(t)) \\
\log(-\log S_2(t)) &= \log c + \log(-\log S_1(t)) \text{.} \\
\end{align*}
\] How is this helpful to us? Well, we know how to estimate \(S_2(t)\) and \(S_1(t)\): we can create Kaplan-Meier curves. If we plot \(\log(-\log \hat{S}_2(t))\) and \(\log(-\log \hat{S}_1(t))\), and the two curves are parallel, that’s evidence for proportional hazards.
Let’s look at an example. Let’s return to the data from the trial comparing two adjuvant therapy regimens for colon cancer (Moertel et al., 1995). These are the variables:

time: Time until death in days. Unfortunately, I don’t know the time origin.
status: 1 is death, 0 is censoring.
rx: This is the treatment variable, and it has three levels: Obs for observation; Lev for Levamisole, and Lev+5FU for Levamisole plus 5-FU.
sex: 1 for male, 0 for female.
age: This is in years, but I don’t know when it was measured. Maybe at the time origin?

We can look at a complementary log-log plot to check for proportional hazards by treatment.

# Complementary log-log plot
ggsurvplot(fit = survfit(Surv(time = time,
                              event = status) ~ rx,
                         data = d_colon),
           fun = "cloglog")








These lines are clearly not parallel. They intersect multiple times.
What if we stratify by sex?

# Complementary log-log plot
ggsurvplot(fit = survfit(Surv(time = time,
                              event = status) ~ sex,
                         data = d_colon),
           fun = "cloglog")








These are also not parallel.
So far, we don’t have evidence for proportional hazards in our data. However it’s worth noting that the complementary log-log plot requires splitting the data set into groups. If we tried to make such a plot for a model with treatment, sex, and age as explanatory variables, it would include a separate curve for each unique combination of treatment, sex and age. That’s not really feasible for a model with many variables, or a model with even a few continuous variables.


90.2.2 Schoenfeld Residuals
Schoenfeld residuals are another way to assess the proportional hazards assumption for a given model. Fortunately, they can be used even when there are many covariates in the model, and/or continuous covariates. I’m not going to get into how Schoenfeld residuals are computed, but I’ll explain how to intepret the associated hypothesis tests and plots.
If you use the function cox.zph from the package survival, it will perform a few hypothesis tests: one for each explanatory variable in the model, and another global test. The null hypothesis for a specific covariate is that the proportional hazards assumption holds for that covariate. The null hypothesis for the global test is that the proportional hazards assumption holds for the model as a whole.

# Cox regression
mod_01 <- coxph(formula = Surv(time = time,
                               event = status) ~ rx + sex + age,
                data = d_colon)

# Schoenfeld residual test
mod_01_ph_test <- cox.zph(mod_01)
mod_01_ph_test

       chisq df    p
rx     1.498  2 0.47
sex    0.932  1 0.33
age    0.391  1 0.53
GLOBAL 2.778  4 0.60


We can see above that the p-values for every test are higher than any reasonable cutoff. This means that we fail to reject the hypotheses that the proportional hazards assumption holds for treatment, sex, age, and the model as a whole. This means we can interpret our coefficients.
Note that this contradicts what we saw in the complementary log-log plots. I would trust the Schoenfeld residuals test more than the complementary log-log plots for this example because we weren’t able to make a single complementary log-log plot that accounted for every covariate in the model.
What if we rejected the null for some covariates but not others, or for the global test but not the covariate-specific tests? I would recommend looking at the Schoenfeld residual plots to get a better sense of what’s going on. Actually, I would look at the Schoenfeld residual plots no matter what the tests say.

# Plots
plot(mod_01_ph_test)





















ggcoxzph(mod_01_ph_test)








In the code above, I’ve used both base R plotting and the function ggcoxzph from the package survminer. You only need to do one or the other.
In each plot, time is on the horizontal axis and Beta(t) for a specific covariate is on the vertical axis. These plots are trying to display graphically how the estimated coefficient changes over time. The proportional hazards assumption means that the coefficient doesn’t change over time. So, if the curve is flat, that’s evidence for the proportional hazards assumption being correct. In all the plots above, the curve is flat, which is consistent with the results from the Schoenfeld residuals test.
If you find, through either the test or the plots, that the proportional hazards assumption doesn’t hold, you may have to use other methods and/or change your model.
