title: 91  Hypothesis Testing
text:
91.1 Learning Objective
Interpret the results of a hypothesis test in the context of the Cox proportional hazards model.

title: 91  Hypothesis Testing
text:
91.2 Lesson
As always, the null hypothesis for a specific covariate in Cox regression is that the coefficient equals zero, i.e., \(\beta_j = 0\). Since \(\exp(\beta_j)\) represents a hazard ratio, and \(\exp(0) = 1\), the null hypothesis is that the hazard ratio is 1, i.e., the hazards are equal. The alternative hypothesis is that the hazards are not equal.
Let’s look at an example. Let’s return again to the data from the trial comparing two adjuvant therapy regimens for colon cancer (Moertel et al., 1995). These are the variables:

time: Time until death in days. Unfortunately, I don’t know the time origin.
status: 1 is death, 0 is censoring.
rx: This is the treatment variable, and it has three levels: Obs for observation; Lev for Levamisole, and Lev+5FU for Levamisole plus 5-FU.
sex: 1 for male, 0 for female.
age: This is in years, but I don’t know when it was measured. Maybe at the time origin?


# Cox regression
mod_01 <- coxph(formula = Surv(time = time,
                               event = status) ~ rx + sex + age,
                data = d_colon)
summary(mod_01)

91.3 Problems

91.3.1 Problem 1
To quote the help page for this data set, “The 197 patients in this dataset were a 50% random sample of the patients with ‘high-risk’ diabetic retinopathy as defined by the Diabetic Retinopathy Study (DRS). title: 92  Interactions
text:
92.2 Lesson
Since you’ve learned how to interpret interaction terms in linear, logistic, and Poisson regression, I’m sure you can do it with Cox regression. Let’s dive directly into an example.
These are the variables for the colon cancer example:

time: Time until death in days. Unfortunately, I don’t know the time origin.
status: 1 is death, 0 is censoring.
rx: This is the treatment variable, and it has three levels: Obs for observation; Lev for Levamisole, and Lev+5FU for Levamisole plus 5-FU.
sex: 1 for male, 0 for female.
age_50: This is in years minus 50, but I don’t know when it was measured. Maybe at the time origin?

The results of a Cox regression is below.

How do we interpret these coefficients?

\begin{align*}
\hat{h}_i(t) &= \hat{h}_0(t) \exp\left( -0.9667 (1) - 0.9403 (1)\times (0)\right) \\
&= \hat{h}_0(t) \exp\left( -0.9667 \right) \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
The estimated hazard at time \(t\) for an eye treated with argon is \[
\begin{align*}
\hat{h}_i(t) &= \hat{h}_0(t) \exp\left( -0.9667 (1) - 0.9403 (1)\times (1)\right) \\
&= \hat{h}_0(t) \exp\left( -0.9667 - 0.9403 \right) \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
This leads to the following interpretations:

Eyes treated with xenon have a 62% lower hazard rate than untreated eyes.
Eyes treated with argon have an 85% lower hazard rate than untreated eyes, since \(0.3803 \times 0.3905 = 0.1485072\).






92.3.1.3 Part (c)
Which model is better, the one with laserargon or the one without? Or, is there a third model that would surpass both? Justify your answer.






TipSolution





The model with laserargon allows for untreated eyes assigned to argon to differ from untreated eyes assigned to xenon. I don’t think there’s a good reason to believe these two groups of eyes would differ, since both are untreated. In the model, we see that the p-value for laserargon is high, meaning the difference is not statistically significant. This is an argument for leaving out that variable.
I would argue, though, that the best thing to do would be to include both eyes for each person. That way, each person could serve as their own control. Including both eyes would violate the independence assumption, though, so to do that we would need methods that aren’t covered in this class.

93.2 Lesson
Cox regression models are fit with “partial” likelihood, which allows us to use likelihood-based methods to compare them. This includes the AIC, BIC, and likelihood ratio test.
For example, let’s compare these two interaction models using the diabetic retinopathy data.


[1] 657.9377


[1] 656.8841


[1] 664.6401


[1] 661.3523


Analysis of Deviance Table
 Cox model: response is  Surv(time = time, event = status)
 Model 1: ~ trt * laser
 Model 2: ~ trt + trt:laser
   loglik  Chisq Df Pr(>|Chi|)
1 -325.97                     
2 -326.44 0.9463  1     0.3307


The simpler model has a lower AIC and lower BIC, and the likelihood ratio test is not significant, indicating that the simpler model is better.
Since the Cox proportional hazards model doesn’t estimate a baseline hazard, we can’t use it to generate predicted values. This means we can’t use a training-test set split or cross-validation to compare the performance of Cox models. However, there is another way to kinda-sorta get at prediction accuracy. If we look at the output for the two models above, we see something called “Concordance”.

Wald test            = 19.51  on 2 df,   p=6e-05
Score (logrank) test = 24.06  on 2 df,   p=6e-06


Concordance is a value between 0 and 1. It’s interpreted as a probability. The concordance for model 1 is 0.656, meaning that in 65.6% of randomly-selected pairs of observations, the observation with the higher hazard has the shorter survival time.
You might be thinking, “How do you estimate concordance in the presence of censoring?” Good question. In the presence of censoring, it’s not necessarily possible to determine which of two observations had the shorter survival time. This has led to a fair number of publications on the correct way to estimate concordance. We’re not going to get into the specifics; it’s more important to me that you know how to interpret the result.
It’s also worth noting that the concordance estimates above are for the data set that was used to estimate the model, so they’re inflated. Again, accounting for this can be complicated, so I don’t want to get into details.

title: 93  Comparing the Performance of Different Cox Models
text:
93.3 Problems

93.3.1 Problem 1
Can you use the likelihood ratio test to compare any two Cox models? Justify your answer.






TipSolution





No. The models still need to be nested, just like for any other likelihood ratio test.





93.3.2 Problem 2
What measure of performance did we cover in logistic regression that’s an analog of concordance?






TipSolution





The AUC, also known as the “probability of superiority” or “common language effect size”. The AUC is the probability that a randomly-selected observation with an outcome of 1 will have a higher fitted value than a randomly-selected observation with an outcome of 0.

text:
96.1.1 Part (a)
Subset: Observations taken when the person was awake
Explanatory variable: Respiratory rate
Outcome variable: Heart rate

# Load ggplot
library(ggplot2)

# Subset data
awake <- sleep[sleep$state == "AWAKE", ]

# Run model
mod_01 <- lm(formula = heart_rate ~ respiratory_rate,
             data = awake)

# Check assumptions
ggplot(mapping = aes(x = awake$respiratory_rate,
                     y = mod_01$residuals)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0,
             colour = "red") +
  xlab("Respiratory Rate") +
  ylab("Residual") +
  ggtitle("Awake")







boxplot(x = mod_01$residuals,
        ylab = "Residuals",
        main = "Awake")







hist(x = mod_01$residuals,
     xlab = "Residual Value",
     main = "Awake")







qqnorm(mod_01$residuals)
qqline(mod_01$residuals)







# Interpret coefficients
summary(mod_01)


Call:
lm(formula = heart_rate ~ respiratory_rate, data = awake)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-28.853  -5.408  -0.093   5.351  36.351 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)      55.723132   0.145660  382.56   <2e-16 ***
respiratory_rate  0.620370   0.009035   68.67   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 8.008 on 93750 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.04788,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.04787 
F-statistic:  4715 on 1 and 93750 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Assumptions

It appears to me that Assumption 1 is met for these data. The horizontal line in the residual scatterplot goes essentially through the center of the points.
Assumption 2 is not met. We have multiple observations for each individual; these observations are more similar to each other than to observations for other individuals. Thus, the data are correlated, i.e., not independent.
There does appear to be an equal vertical spread of the residuals, no matter the value of the respiratory rate.
The residuals are approximately normally distributed.

Interpretation
Both of the following interpretations only apply to people who are awake, since that’s the subset of the data we used.

Among people taking zero breaths per minute, we would expect a heartrate of about 56 beats per minute.
An increase of one breath per minute is associate with an increase in heartrate of 0.6 beats per minute, on average. Alternatively, we could say that we would expect two populations of people who differ in their respiratory rate by one breath per minute to differ in their heart rate by 0.6 beats per minute, on average.

Hypothesis Testing
Since Assumption 2 is not met, the p-values are not valid, so we cannot interpret the hypothesis tests.


96.1.2 Part (b)
Subset: Observations taken when the person was in deep sleep
Explanatory variable: Snoring
Outcome variable: Respiratory rate

# Subset data
deep <- sleep[sleep$state == "DEEP", ]

# Run model
mod_02 <- lm(formula = respiratory_rate ~ snoring,
             data = deep)

# Check assumptions
mean(mod_02$residuals[deep$snoring == "True"])

[1] -2.434104e-13

mean(mod_02$residuals[deep$snoring == "False"])

[1] -3.767823e-14

        xlab = "Snoring",
        ylab = "Residual",
        main = "Deep Sleep")
abline(h = 0,
       col = "red")







boxplot(x = mod_02$residuals,
        ylab = "Residuals",
        main = "Deep Sleep")







hist(x = mod_02$residuals,
     xlab = "Residual Value",
     main = "Deep Sleep")







qqnorm(mod_02$residuals)
qqline(mod_02$residuals)







# Interpretation
summary(mod_02)


Call:
lm(formula = respiratory_rate ~ snoring, data = deep)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-6.9765 -1.9765  0.0235  1.0235 15.0235 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 14.976534   0.007536 1987.30   <2e-16 ***
snoringTrue -1.698701   0.031799  -53.42   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 2.189 on 89396 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.03093,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.03092 
F-statistic:  2854 on 1 and 89396 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Assumptions

With a single dichotomous explanatory variable, the model is ``saturated.’’ This means that we are using regression to estimate group means; the fitted value for an observation will be the mean of whatever group it’s in. Because of this, the mean of the residuals in any group will be zero. In the code above, you’ll see that the means of the residuals in the two groups is slightly off from zero; this is essentially rounding error. So, for a saturated model, we don’t really need to check Assumption 1.
For the same reason as in Problem 1, these data are not independent.
It appears that the variance of the residuals for people who are not snoring is greater than the variance of the residuals for people who are snoring. So, the third assumption is not met.
The residuals are definitely not normally distributed.

Interpretation
Both of the following interpretations only apply to people in a deep sleep, since that’s the subset of the data we used.

Among people who are not snoring, we would expect a respiratory rate of about 15 breaths per minute.
On average, we would expect people who are snoring to take about 1.7 fewer breaths per minute than people who are not snoring.

Hypothesis Testing
Since Assumptions 2 through 4 are not met, the p-values are not valid and we cannot interpret the hypothesis tests.

-24.330  -5.218  -0.867   4.350  51.875 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -58.97291    3.15197  -18.71   <2e-16 ***

Multiple R-squared:  0.3483,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.348 
F-statistic:  1246 on 1 and 2331 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Assumptions

It appears like the red reference line at zero is going straight through the center of our cloud of residuals, so Assumption 1 is met.
These participants were selected independently of each other, from the same population. So, Assumption 2 is met.
The vertical spread of the residuals appears to the same for any value of \(X\), so Assumption 3 is met.
The histogram of the residuals is bell-shaped, but it’s slightly right-skewed. So, I wouldn’t say that Assumption 4 is met.

Interpretation
I could not find a statement in the paper about the units for height and weight. I hypothesized that height was in centimeters and weight was in kilograms. I used the formula for BMI (kg/m\(^2\)) to check my hypothesis.

We would expect someone who is zero meters tall to weigh about -59 kilograms. This makes no sense.
Each additional centimeter of height is associated with about 0.7 additional kilograms of weight, on average.

Hypothesis Testing
Since the first three assumptions are met and we have a large sample size, the p-values are valid.

Since the first p-value is smaller than 0.05, we can conclude that the intercept is not equal to zero. This is not something we really care about.
Since the second p-value is smaller than 0.05, we can conclude that the slope is not equal to zero. This means that there is a linear relationship between height and weight. This is not surprising; we would expect larger people to weigh more.

-31.691  -7.806  -0.973   6.463  57.233 

Coefficients:

(Intercept) 64.899625   1.632632  39.752  < 2e-16 ***
chol         0.050861   0.008693   5.851  5.7e-09 ***

Multiple R-squared:  0.01677,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.01628

Assumptions

It appears like the red reference line at zero is going straight through the center of our cloud of residuals, so Assumption 1 is met. There are a few high residuals at lower cholesterol levels, but not many.
These participants were selected independently of each other, from the same population. So, Assumption 2 is met.
The vertical spread of the residuals appears to the same for any value of \(X\), so Assumption 3 is met. You might argue that the variance of the residuals for high cholesterol is smaller than the variance of the residuals for low cholesterol, but there are also far more observations that have low cholesterol. So, it could be that we’re seeing greater variance where there are more points simply because with more points, you’re more likely to see extreme points.
The histogram of the residuals is bell-shaped, but it’s slightly right-skewed. So, I wouldn’t say that Assumption 4 is met.

These interpretations are only for people with total cholesterol of at least 150.

We would expect someone with zero total cholesterol to have a diastolic blood pressure of about 65. This doesn’t really make sense, since no one has zero total cholesterol.
We would expect an increase of about 0.05 mm Hg in diastolic blood pressure for each increase of 1 mg/dL of total cholesterol.

Since the first three assumptions are met and we have a large sample size, the p-values are valid.

Since the first p-value is smaller than 0.05, we can conclude that the intercept is not equal to zero. This is not something we really care about.
Since the second p-value is smaller than 0.05, we can conclude that the slope is not equal to zero. This means that there is a linear relationship between cholesterol and diastolic blood pressure.

text:
98.1.1 Part (a)
Create a scatter plot of the residuals as a function of the fitted values. Include a horizontal line at zero.

plot(x = mod_02$fitted.values,
     y = mod_02$residuals,
     xlab = "Fitted Values",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     col = alpha(colour = "black",
                 alpha = 0.3))
abline(h = 0,
       col = "red")








What do you conclude?
It appears that for each fitted value, the residuals average out to zero. This is actually guaranteed to be the case, because we have a “saturated” model.
It also appears that there is relatively constant vertical spread of the residuals throughout the plot, which means the assumption of constant variance is met.
Note that there are only four possible fitted values. This is because there are two binary explanatory variables, yielding four possible combinations of values, i.e., \((0,0)\), \((0,1)\), \((1,0)\), and \((1,1)\).
Below, I’ve plotted a boxplot of the residuals for each possible combination of the explanatory variables. I haven’t changed the labeling of the axes so that you can see what R does by default. This plot also supports our assumptions of linearity and equal variance.

boxplot(formula = mod_02$residuals ~ mod_02$model$statins * mod_02$model$exercise)










98.1.2 Part (b)
Plot a boxplot, histogram, and q-q plot of the residuals.

boxplot(x = mod_02$residuals,
        ylab = "Residuals")







hist(x = mod_02$residuals,
     xlab = "Residuals",
     main = "")







qqnorm(mod_02$residuals)
qqline(mod_02$residuals)








What do you conclude?
Based on the histogram, the residuals are approximately bell-shaped. The boxplot reveals that the residuals are right-skewed, and the q-q plot seems to show that the residuals deviate from normal in their right tail. Still, the sample size is large, and my understanding is that the observations are independent (and identically distributed), so I’m not super concerned about this last assumption being met. Even if it isn’t, we can still interpret the p-values.


98.1.3 Part (c)
Interpret the intercept in real-world terms.
This is the expected LDL cholesterol for someone who is not on statins and who does not exercise.


98.1.4 Part (d)
Interpret the estimate for statinsyes in real-world terms. Interpret the results of the hypothesis test associated with this coefficient as well.
This is the expected difference in LDL cholesterol between someone who does use statins and someone who doesn’t, where neither of these people exercise. The fact that it’s negative means that we would expect someone who uses statins to have lower LDL cholesterol than someone who doesn’t (again, assuming neither of these people exercise).
How did I arrive at that interpretation? Define:

\(L_i\) is the LDL cholesterol for the \(i\)th individual.
\(S_i = 1\) if the \(i\)th person uses statins and \(S_i = 0\) otherwise.
\(E_i = 1\) if the \(i\)th person exercises and \(E_i = 0\) otherwise.

Our model is \[
L_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 S_i + \beta_2 E_i + \beta_3 S_i E_i + \epsilon_i \text{.}
\] We’re trying to interpret \(\beta_1\), which is \[
\begin{align*}
&E\left(L_i\middle|S_i = 1,E_i = 0\right) - E\left(L_i\middle|S_i = 0,E_i = 0\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (1) + \beta_2 (0) + \beta_3 (1) (0) - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 (0) + \beta_3 (0) (0)\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1  - \left(\beta_0 \right) \\
&= \beta_1 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
The p-value for this coefficient is less than 0.05, so we reject the null hypothesis and conclude it’s not zero. (I didn’t tell you what alpha level to use, but 0.05 is a reasonable one.) Thus, we can conclude that there is a statistically significant difference in LDL cholesterol between people who use statins and people who don’t, assuming all of these people don’t exercise.


98.1.5 Part (e)
Interpret the estimate for exerciseyes in real-world terms. Interpret the results of the hypothesis test associated with this coefficient as well.
This is the expected difference in LDL cholesterol between someone who does exercises and someone who doesn’t, where neither of these people use statins. The fact that it’s negative means that we would expect someone who exercises to have lower LDL cholesterol than someone who doesn’t (again, assuming neither of these people use statins).
We’re trying to interpret \(\beta_2\), which is \[
\begin{align*}
&E\left(L_i\middle|S_i = 0,E_i = 1\right) - E\left(L_i\middle|S_i = 0,E_i = 0\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 (1) + \beta_3 (0) (1) - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 (0) + \beta_3 (0) (0)\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_2  - \left(\beta_0 \right) \\
&= \beta_2 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
The p-value for this coefficient is less than 0.05, so we reject the null hypothesis and conclude it’s not zero. Thus, we can conclude that there is a statistically significant difference in LDL cholesterol between people who exercise and people who don’t, assuming all of these people don’t use statins.


98.1.6 Part (f)
Interpret the estimate for statinsyes:exerciseyes in real-world terms. Interpret the results of the hypothesis test associated with this coefficient as well.
This is the expected difference in the expected change in LDL cholesterol associated with using statins between people who exercise and people who don’t. Because it has the opposite sign of statinsyes, we would expect the effect of statins among people who exercise to be closer to zero than the effect of statins among people who don’t exercise.
We’re trying to interpret \(\beta_3\), which is \[
\begin{align*}
&E\left(L_i\middle|S_i = 1,E_i = 1\right) - E\left(L_i\middle|S_i = 0,E_i = 1\right) - \left(E\left(L_i\middle|S_i = 1,E_i = 0\right) - E\left(L_i\middle|S_i = 0,E_i = 0\right)\right) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (1) + \beta_2 (1) + \beta_3 (1) (1) - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 (1) + \beta_3 (0) (1)\right) - \beta_1 \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1  + \beta_2  + \beta_3  - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_2 \right) - \beta_1 \\
&= \beta_3 \text{.}
\end{align*}
\]
The p-value is high, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis, i.e., that this coefficient is zero. This tells us that the effect of statins is the same regardless of exercise status.


98.1.7 Part (g)
Fit a new model (I’ll call this Model 3) that’s the same as Model 2 but does not have the interaction term.

             data = d)
summary(mod_03)

exerciseyes   -3.620      1.445  -2.505   0.0123 *

# Load packages
library(readxl)

This problem uses data from “Association between particulate air pollution exposure during pregnancy and postpartum maternal psychological functioning” (Sheffield et al., 2018). This is a direct link to the data. Download the data and put the file in the same folder as this Quarto document.

# Load data
a <- read_xls("pone.0195267.s001.xls")

New names:
• `` -> `...1`

# Remove the first column that R added for some unknown reason
a$...1 <- NULL

The purpose of this problem is to demonstrate model selection when the goal is prediction. We will try to predict pmw1, which is the “particulate matter (PM2.5) weekly average from” week 1 of gestation. (I’m quoting the Data Dictionary in sheet 2 of the Excel file.) We’ll allow ourselves to use any variable in the data set from mat_age through lookfwd612. In other words, we’re excluding from consideration random_id and all the pmw variables. Just to make that more clear, I’m going to remove anything that’s not our outcome or an eligible explanatory variable.

a$randomid <- NULL
exclude <- paste0("pmw",
                  2:40)
a <- a[ ,!(colnames(a) %in% exclude)]


99.0.1 Part (a)
If our goal is prediction, we should evaluate our model based on how well it predicts new data. So, we should randomly split our data into a training set and a test set. We can fit our models on the training set and test them on the test set.
Randomly select 80% of the data set and store it as a training set. Store the remaining 20% as a test set.


99.0.2 Part (b)
Use the training set to regress the outcome on only those variables that you think would be predictive. Note that “predictive” is not the same as “causal”. Many of the explanatory variables were measured after the outcome, so they could not have caused the outcome. However, they still might be predictive.
I’ll call this model the “judicious” model.


99.0.3 Part (c)
Use the training set to regress the outcome on all candidate variables. I’ll call this the “full” model.


99.0.4 Part (d)
For this part of the problem, I’d like you to use backward selection. If you try to do this with the full model, R will protest once it removes a couple variables and realizes that it can include more rows for smaller models. This is because some of the rows are missing data, so they can’t be included in the full model, but can be included in any model that doesn’t use the variables for which they’re missing values.
So, regress the outcome on all possible explanatory variables in the training set after removing all rows with missing data. Then, run backward selection. I’ll call this the “backward” model.
You might want to use trace = 0 to prevent R from printing out all the intermediate models in the backward selection process.


99.0.5 Part (e)
Order the three models (full, judicious, and backward) from best to worst using the adjusted \(R^2\).
Do the same using the AIC.


99.0.6 Part (f)
Use predict to get predictions of the outcome for the test set. Then, find the root mean squared error for each model in the test set. Rank the models from best to worst using the RMSE.

This is because some of the rows are missing data, so they can’t be included in the full model, but can be included in any model that doesn’t use the variables for which they’re missing values.
So, regress the outcome on all possible explanatory variables in the training set after removing all rows with missing data. Then, run backward selection. I’ll call this the “backward” model.
You might want to use trace = 0 to prevent R from printing out all the intermediate models in the backward selection process.

mod_back <- step(object = lm(formula = pmw1 ~ .,
                             data = a_train[complete.cases(a_train), ]),
                 direction = "backward",
                 trace = 0)



100.0.5 Part (e)
Order the three models (full, judicious, and backward) from best to worst using the adjusted \(R^2\).

# Adjusted R^2
summary(mod_jud)$adj.r.squared

[1] 0.09837558

summary(mod_full)$adj.r.squared

[1] 0.09530892

summary(mod_back)$adj.r.squared

[1] 0.124071


The best model is the backward model, the worst model is the full model, and the judicious model is in the middle.
Do the same using the AIC.

# AIC
AIC(mod_jud)

[1] 1845.599

AIC(mod_full)

[1] 1068.019

AIC(mod_back)

[1] 1042.862


This was a trick! We can’t compare these models using the AIC because they were fit on different data sets. We didn’t use the same rows in the data set for each because some rows were missing data.


100.0.6 Part (f)
Use predict to get predictions of the outcome for the test set. Then, find the root mean squared error for each model in the test set. Rank the models from best to worst using the RMSE.

# Get predictions for test data
pred_full <- predict(object = mod_full,
                     newdata = a_test)
pred_jud <- predict(object = mod_jud,
                    newdata = a_test)
pred_back <- predict(object = mod_back,
                     newdata = a_test)

# Get error
sqrt(mean(x = (a_test$pmw1 - pred_jud)^2,
          na.rm = TRUE))

[1] 3.298781

sqrt(mean(x = (a_test$pmw1 - pred_full)^2,
          na.rm = TRUE))

[1] 3.479368

sqrt(mean(x = (a_test$pmw1 - pred_back)^2,
          na.rm = TRUE))

[1] 3.415111


The best model is the backward model, the worst model is the judicious model, and the full model is somewhere in between. Actually, the full model is pretty close to the backward model.
Perhaps we’ve identified the utility of backward selection. When you have lots of candidate explanatory variables to choose from, and all you care about is prediction, backward selection might be a fast way to eliminate variables. Still, I’m not sure how it compares to other variable selection methods like LASSO, which is beyond the scope of this class.

101.1.1 Part (a)
In the chunk below, I’ve generated data according to the assumptions of linear regression.

n <- 1e3
x <- rnorm(n)
beta_0 <- 0
beta_1 <- -2
sigma <- 1
epsilon <- rnorm(n = n,
                 sd = sigma)
y <- beta_0 + beta_1 * x + epsilon

Use lm to regress y on x. Then, create a scatterplot of the residuals as a function of x. Add a horizontal line at zero.


101.1.2 Part (b)
In the chunk below, I’ve generated new data. I’ve kept everything the same except for \(Var(Y_i|X_i) = \sigma^2\). I’ve greatly increased the variance of the random error.

epsilon_new <- rnorm(n = n,
                     sd = 10 * sigma)
y_new <- beta_0 + beta_1 * x + epsilon_new

Use lm to regress y_new on x. Then, create a scatterplot of the residuals as a function of x. Add a horizontal line at zero.


101.1.3 Part (c)
What is the \(R^2\) for the models in Part (b) and Part (c)?
For the remaining parts of the problem, we will try to see an analog of this phenomenon with a binary outcome.


101.1.4 Part (d)
In the chunk below, I’ve generated a binary outcome according to the assumptions of logistic regression. I have changed the values of any parameters or of the explanatory variable.

y_binary <- rbinom(n = n,
                   size = 1,
                   prob = plogis(beta_0 + beta_1 * x))

Regress y_binary on x using logistic regression. Then, create a calibration plot for the model.


101.1.5 Part (e)
In the chunk below, I’ve attenuated \(\beta_1\) toward zero.

y_binary_new <- rbinom(n = n,
                       size = 1,
                       prob = plogis(beta_0 + beta_1 / 100 * x))

Why did I do this? Now, the expected values of the observations are closer to 0.5.

range(plogis(beta_0 + beta_1 * x))

[1] 0.001538344 0.999946656

range(plogis(beta_0 + beta_1 / 100 * x))

[1] 0.4838169 0.5245769


This means that x is not very predictive. Even when you know x, whether you observe a 0 or a 1 is basically a coin toss.
Regress y_binary_new on x using logistic regression. Then, create a calibration plot for the model.


101.1.6 Part (f)
Plot ROC curves and obtain areas under the curves for the models in Part (d) and Part (e).

text:
102.1.1 Part (a)
In the chunk below, I’ve generated data according to the assumptions of linear regression.

n <- 1e3
x <- rnorm(n)
beta_0 <- 0
beta_1 <- -2
sigma <- 1
epsilon <- rnorm(n = n,
                 sd = sigma)
y <- beta_0 + beta_1 * x + epsilon

Use lm to regress y on x. Then, create a scatterplot of the residuals as a function of x. Add a horizontal line at zero.

# Regression
mod_1a <- lm(y ~ x)

# Plot
plot(x = x,
     y = mod_1a$residuals,
     ylab = "Residuals")
abline(h = 0,
       col = "red")










102.1.2 Part (b)
In the chunk below, I’ve generated new data. I’ve kept everything the same except for \(Var(Y_i|X_i) = \sigma^2\). I’ve greatly increased the variance of the random error.

epsilon_new <- rnorm(n = n,
                     sd = 10 * sigma)
y_new <- beta_0 + beta_1 * x + epsilon_new

Use lm to regress y_new on x. Then, create a scatterplot of the residuals as a function of x. Add a horizontal line at zero.

# Regression
mod_1b <- lm(y_new ~ x)

# Plot
plot(x = x,
     y = mod_1b$residuals,
     ylab = "Residuals")
abline(h = 0,
       col = "red")








Note the difference in the scale of the residuals between the two plots. Although both data sets meet all of our assumptions, the second one has way more error.


102.1.3 Part (c)
What is the \(R^2\) for the models in Part (b) and Part (c)?

summary(mod_1a)$r.squared

[1] 0.8079067

summary(mod_1b)$r.squared

[1] 0.06576859


For the remaining parts of the problem, we will try to see an analog of this phenomenon with a binary outcome.


102.1.4 Part (d)
In the chunk below, I’ve generated a binary outcome according to the assumptions of logistic regression. I have changed the values of any parameters or of the explanatory variable.

y_binary <- rbinom(n = n,
                   size = 1,
                   prob = plogis(beta_0 + beta_1 * x))

Regress y_binary on x using logistic regression. Then, create a calibration plot for the model.

# Regression
mod_1d <- glm(formula = y_binary ~ x,
              family = binomial)

# Calibration plot
cal_plot_breaks(.data = data.frame(truth = as.factor(mod_1d$model$y_binary),
                                   estimate = mod_1d$fitted.values),
                truth = truth,
                estimate = estimate,
                event_level = "second")










102.1.5 Part (e)
In the chunk below, I’ve attenuated \(\beta_1\) toward zero.

y_binary_new <- rbinom(n = n,
                       size = 1,
                       prob = plogis(beta_0 + beta_1 / 100 * x))

Why did I do this? Now, the expected values of the observations are closer to 0.5.

range(plogis(beta_0 + beta_1 * x))

[1] 0.001538344 0.999946656

range(plogis(beta_0 + beta_1 / 100 * x))

[1] 0.4838169 0.5245769


This means that x is not very predictive. Even when you know x, whether you observe a 0 or a 1 is basically a coin toss.
Regress y_binary_new on x using logistic regression. Then, create a calibration plot for the model.

# Regression
mod_1e <- glm(formula = y_binary_new ~ x,
              family = binomial)

# Calibration plot
cal_plot_breaks(.data = data.frame(truth = as.factor(mod_1e$model$y_binary_new),
                                   estimate = mod_1e$fitted.values),
                truth = truth,
                estimate = estimate,
                event_level = "second")







# Distribution of fitted values
hist(mod_1e$fitted.values)







# Calibration plot (more bins, zoom in)
cal_plot_breaks(.data = data.frame(truth = as.factor(mod_1e$model$y_binary_new),
                                   estimate = mod_1e$fitted.values),
                truth = truth,
                estimate = estimate,
                event_level = "second",
                num_breaks = 100) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.42,0.57))








I don’t love the way these plots look. As great as cal_plot_breaks is, it has some limitations. In the chunk below I’ve created some alternative calibration plots.

# Part (d)
ggplot(mapping = aes(x = mod_1d$fitted.values,
                     y = y_binary)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1,
              intercept = 0,
              linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Part (d)",
       x = "Fitted Values",
       y = "Outcome")

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'gam' and formula = 'y ~ s(x, bs = "cs")'








# Part (e)
ggplot(mapping = aes(x = mod_1e$fitted.values,
                     y = y_binary_new)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1,
              intercept = 0,
              linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Part (e)",
       x = "Fitted Values",
       y = "Outcome")

`geom_smooth()` using method = 'gam' and formula = 'y ~ s(x, bs = "cs")'









The blue line is a smoother. You can think of it like a moving average. The dashed line has the same meaning as in the original calibration plots. If the blue line falls on the dashed line, it means that the fitted values (our estimated probabilities) are approximately equal to the true probabilities.
Since both data sets meet our assumptions, the blue line in both plots is approximately on the dashed line.


102.1.6 Part (f)
Plot ROC curves and obtain areas under the curves for the models in Part (d) and Part (e).

# Part (d)
plot.roc(x = y_binary,
         predictor = mod_1d$fitted.values)

Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1


Setting direction: controls < cases








auc(response = y_binary,
    predictor = mod_1d$fitted.values)

Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
Setting direction: controls < cases


Area under the curve: 0.8565

# Part (e)
plot.roc(x = y_binary_new,
         predictor = mod_1e$fitted.values)

Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
Setting direction: controls < cases








auc(response = y_binary_new,
    predictor = mod_1e$fitted.values)

Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
Setting direction: controls < cases


Area under the curve: 0.5242

title: 103  Poisson Regression (Solutions)
text:
103.1.1 Part (a)
Create the following variables:

n: This will be the sample size. Make this at least 100.
beta_0: This will be the intercept. You can make this any real number.
beta_1: This will be the slope. You can make this any real number other than zero.



103.1.2 Part (b)
Generate n iid standard normal random variables. Store them as x.


103.1.3 Part (c)
For this problem, we will assume the following:

\(\log \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i\)
The observations are iid.
\(Y_i |X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_i)\)

To make our lives easier, we’re not going to worry about offsets right now. We’re going to assume that \(t_1 = t_2 = \cdots = t_{n-1} = t_n = 1\).
Create a vector mu that contains \(\mu_1,\mu_2,\dotsc,\mu_n\). Then, use summary(mu) to get some descriptive statistics on the means. Create a histogram of \(\mu_1,\mu_2,\dotsc,\mu_n\) as well.


103.1.4 Part (d)
Generate \(Y_1,\dotsc,Y_n\) according to the assumptions above.


103.1.5 Part (e)
Perform Poisson regression and quasi-Poisson regression with \(Y_i\) as the outcome and \(X_i\) as the single explanatory variable.
Is there evidence of overdispersion?


103.1.6 Part (f)
Using the Poisson regression model, make the following plots:

A calibration-style plot with fitted values on the horizontal axis, observed values on the vertical axis, and a reference line with intercept 0 and slope 1.

Modify beta_0 and/or beta_1 in Part (a) so that \(\mu_1,\dotsc,\mu_n\) are all at least 100. (You can check Part (c).) Then re-run all your code. What do the plots in Part (f) look like?

103.2 Problem 2
For this problem, you will analyze the data set from Obesity Is Independently Associated with Spinal Anesthesia Outcomes: A Prospective Observational Study. You’ll have to download the data set and put it in your working directory. The authors of this paper performed logistic regression with “successful anesthesia” as the outcome. Use summary to print the results to screen.

title: 103  Poisson Regression (Solutions)
text:
103.3 Problem 3
Suppose you visit \(n\) emergency rooms to observe how busy they are. Define the following:

\(t_i\) is the number of hours you spend observing the \(i\)th hospital.
\(Y_i\) is the number of patients you see enter the emergency room at the \(i\)th hospital.
\(T_i\) is the temperature outside in degrees Fahrenheit.
\(W_i = 1\) if you observe on a work day (Monday through Friday) and \(W_i = 0\) if you observe on a weekend (Saturday or Sunday).

You assume the following:

\(\log E(Y_i|T_i,W_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T_i + \beta_2 W_i + \beta_3 T_i W_i + \log t_i\).
The observations are iid.
\(Y_i|T_i,W_i\sim\text{Poisson}(\mu_i)\).


103.3.1 Part (a)
Interpret \(\exp(\beta_0)\) in real-world terms.


103.3.2 Part (b)
Interpret \(\exp(\beta_1)\) in real-world terms.


103.3.3 Part (c)
Interpret \(\exp(\beta_2)\) in real-world terms.


103.3.4 Part (d)
Interpret \(\exp(\beta_1 + \beta_3)\) in real-world terms.


103.3.5 Part (e)
Interpret \(\exp(\beta_2 + \beta_3)\) in real-world terms.

# Calibration-style plot
plot(x = mod_01$fitted.values,
     y = y,
     xlab = "Fitted Values",
     ylab = "Observed Values")
abline(a = 0,
       b = 1,
       col = "red")







# Deviance residuals
resid_dev <- residuals(object = mod_01,
                       type = "deviance")
boxplot(x = resid_dev,
        ylab = "Deviance Residuals")







hist(x = resid_dev,
     xlab = "Deviance Residuals",
     main = "")







qqnorm(resid_dev)
qqline(resid_dev)







plot(x = mod_01$fitted.values,
     y = resid_dev,
     xlab = "Fitted Values",
     ylab = "Deviance Residuals")
abline(h = 0,
       col = "red")







# Response residuals
resid_response <- residuals(object = mod_01,
                            type = "response")
plot(x = mod_01$fitted.values,
     y = resid_response,
     xlab = "Fitted Values",
     ylab = "Response Residuals")
abline(h = 0,
       col = "red")







# Response residuals
resid_pearson <- residuals(object = mod_01,
                           type = "pearson")
plot(x = mod_01$fitted.values,
     y = resid_pearson,
     xlab = "Fitted Values",
     ylab = "Pearson Residuals")
abline(h = 0,
       col = "red")










104.1.7 Part (g)
Modify beta_0 and/or beta_1 in Part (a) so that \(\mu_1,\dotsc,\mu_n\) are all at least 100. (You can check Part (c).) Then re-run all your code. What do the plots in Part (f) look like?
Then, modify beta_0 and/or beta_1 in Part (a) so that \(\mu_1,\dotsc,\mu_n\) are all below 2. (You can check Part (c).) Then re-run all your code. What do the plots in Part (f) look like?
When the means are large, the plots in Part (f) look how we want them to. The points in the calibration-style plot fall along the reference line; the deviance residuals are normally distributed; and in the scatterplots, the reference line goes straight through the center of the cloud of points.
When the means are small, the plots are weird. All of the scatterplots have striations or banding, which is a result of the restricted range of the outcome. Consider the response residuals: If \(Y_i\) has to be a counting number then plotting \(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\) as a function of \(\hat{Y}_i\) will result in a bunch of lines that intersect the vertical axis at \(Y_i\) and have a slope of \(-1\).
Keep in mind that no matter what \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are, we’re not violating any of the assumptions of Poisson regression. This is why assumption-checking is so hard for this analysis; even when the assumptions are met, we get weird plots.

title: 104  Poisson Regression (Solutions)
text:
104.2 Problem 2
For this problem, you will analyze the data set from Obesity Is Independently Associated with Spinal Anesthesia Outcomes: A Prospective Observational Study. You’ll have to download the data set and put it in your working directory. The authors of this paper performed logistic regression with “successful anesthesia” as the outcome. We will be examining the variable HospitalStay instead. Although there’s no data dictionary, we’re going to assume this variable represents the duration of the hospital stay in days.

# Load data
d <- read_xls("pone.0124264.s001.xls")


104.2.1 Part (a)
Knowing what you know about Poisson regression, does it make sense to use Poisson regression for this outcome? Why or why not?
I don’t think it makes sense to use Poisson regression for this outcome. Although the outcome is a count, it’s not a count of the number of events, where the events are occurring at a constant rate.


104.2.2 Part (b)
Use Poisson regression to regress HospitalStay on at least two explanatory variables of your own choosing.
Do not supply an offset. There’s not really a \(t_i\) here, so we’re sort of assuming \(t_i = 1\) for everyone. This means that we’re modeling the mean of the distribution, and not really a rate.
Use summary to print the results to screen.

# What are the ages in the data set?
summary(d$Age)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   49.0    65.0    72.0    70.3    76.0    85.0 

# Create shifted age variable
d$Age_70 <- d$Age - 70

# Poisson regression
mod_03 <- glm(formula = HospitalStay ~ Age_70 + SuccessAnesthesia,
              data = d,
              family = poisson)
summary(mod_03)

No, there appears to be underdispersion. The variance is about half of the mean.


104.2.4 Part (d)
Interpret the intercept and at least one non-intercept coefficient in real-world terms.

exp(mod_03$coefficients)

      (Intercept)            Age_70 SuccessAnesthesia 
        7.0551623         0.9988225         0.8883495 



We would expect a patient who is 70 years old and had unsuccessful anesthesia to have a hospital stay of 7 days.
With each additional year of age, the expected hospital stay decreases by \((1 - 0.9988225)\times 100 = 0.12\) percent, holding anesthesia success status constant.
Successful anesthesia is associated with a \((1 - 0.8883495) \times 100 = 11.2\) percent decrease in expected hospital stay, holding age constant.



104.2.5 Part (e)
Use hist and summary on the outcome variable, HospitalStay. What do you notice?

hist(x = d$HospitalStay,

summary(d$HospitalStay)

The minimum hospital stay is 4 days. This doesn’t match the support of the Poisson, which includes 0, 1, 2, and 3. It appears that this procedure always requires a hospital stay of at least four days. It’s almost like the first four days are non-random, and only the excess beyond those four days is random.


104.2.6 Part (f)
Repeat Parts (b) and (c), but change the outcome to a transformation of HospitalStay that makes sense based on what you saw in Part (e). Use the same explanatory variables.

title: 104  Poisson Regression (Solutions)
text:
104.3 Problem 3
Suppose you visit \(n\) emergency rooms to observe how busy they are. Define the following:

\(t_i\) is the number of hours you spend observing the \(i\)th hospital.
\(Y_i\) is the number of patients you see enter the emergency room at the \(i\)th hospital.
\(T_i\) is the temperature outside in degrees Fahrenheit.
\(W_i = 1\) if you observe on a work day (Monday through Friday) and \(W_i = 0\) if you observe on a weekend (Saturday or Sunday).

You assume the following:

\(\log E(Y_i|T_i,W_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T_i + \beta_2 W_i + \beta_3 T_i W_i + \log t_i\).
The observations are iid.
\(Y_i|T_i,W_i\sim\text{Poisson}(\mu_i)\).


104.3.1 Part (a)
Interpret \(\exp(\beta_0)\) in real-world terms.
The expected number of new patients per hour when it’s zero degrees Fahrenheit outside and a weekend.


104.3.2 Part (b)
Interpret \(\exp(\beta_1)\) in real-world terms.
Each one-degree Fahrenheit increase in temperature is associated with a \((\exp(\beta_1) - 1)\times 100\)% increase in the number of new patients per hour, assuming it’s a weekend.


104.3.3 Part (c)
Interpret \(\exp(\beta_2)\) in real-world terms.
If it’s zero degrees Fahrenheit outside, the rate of new patients per hour on work days is \(\exp(\beta_2)\) times the rate of new patients per hour on the weekend.


104.3.4 Part (d)
Interpret \(\exp(\beta_1 + \beta_3)\) in real-world terms.
Each one-degree Fahrenheit increase in temperature is associated with a \((\exp(\beta_1 + \beta_3) - 1)\times 100\)% increase in the number of new patients per hour, assuming it’s a workday.


104.3.5 Part (e)
Interpret \(\exp(\beta_2 + \beta_3)\) in real-world terms.
If it’s one degree Fahrenheit outside, the rate of new patients per hour on work days is \(\exp(\beta_2 + \beta_3)\) times the rate of new patients per hour on the weekend.

title: 105  Introduction
text:
This appendix contains past quizzes from when I’ve taught the course. I administer one quiz per week, for a total of fourteen quizzes per semester. The quizzes are paired, such that I use the highest score from quizzes 1 and 2, quizzes 3 and 4, quizzes 5 and 6, and so forth. This allows students to miss a quiz without me having to schedule a make-up. It also allows students a second opportunity to demonstrate mastery of the material if they made mistakes the first time. The material on the quizzes is cumulative throughout the semester, so the last two quizzes are effectively comprehensive final exams, except they’re worth the same as all the other quizzes, and if you don’t like your score on the first one, you can take the second one.
In general, the quizzes say this on the first page:

This quiz lasts 40 minutes.
No calculators are allowed.
You are not allowed to use notes, your computer, or any textbook.
There is no additional paper. Please use this cover sheet if you need more room.
Please ensure that your writing is legible. We cannot award credit for responses that we can’t read.

I often re-use questions from previous quizzes within the same semester if a lot of students got them wrong.

title: 106  Fall 2025 Quiz 1
text:
106.1 Problem 1
Please identify each of the following statements as true or false. Each problem is worth one point.

title: 106  Fall 2025 Quiz 1
text:
106.1.1 Part (a)
We usually consider parameters to be random.






TipSolution





False.





106.1.2 Part (b)
We usually consider parameters to be unknown.






TipSolution





True.

A statistic is a function of the population.






TipSolution





False.

TipSolution





True.

TipSolution





True.

If you know the expected value of \(X\), you should be able to compute the probability that \(X\) is in any given range.






TipSolution





False.

The expected value is a measure of the spread of a distribution.






TipSolution





False.





106.1.8 Part (h)
The support of a random variable must be between 0 and 1.






TipSolution





False.





106.1.9 Part (i)
A statistic can have a distribution.






TipSolution





True.

“Statistic” is another word for “parameter.”

False.

title: 106  Fall 2025 Quiz 1
text:
106.2 Problem 2
(1 point) Which of the distributions in Figure 106.1 could describe the time in months from diagnosis to death from a fatal form of cancer? Select all that apply.

A
B
C
None of the above







TipSolution





B and C

title: 106  Fall 2025 Quiz 1
text:
106.3 Problem 3
(1 point) In one to three sentences, justify your answer to Problem 2.






TipSolution





The time to an event must be non-negative. The support of distribution A includes negative values, so it cannot be the distribution of the time to death. The supports of distributions B and C are both non-negative, so each could be the distribution of time to death.
Some students pointed out that diagnosis could be made via autopsy. If a student said this in their justification and selected A, B, and C, I gave them the points for both questions.

title: 106  Fall 2025 Quiz 1
text:
106.4 Problem 4
(1 point) Which of the distributions in Figure 106.1 is most likely to yield observations greater than 2?

A
B
C
It’s impossible to tell from the information provided.







TipSolution





C

title: 106  Fall 2025 Quiz 1
text:
106.5 Problem 5
(1 point) In one to three sentences, justify your answer to Problem 4.






TipSolution





The height of distribution C is higher than the other distributions for all values greater than 2. Thus, the area under the curve to the right of 2 will be greatest for Distribution C. Since area under the curve corresponds to probability, Distribution C is most likely to yield observations greater than 2.
Some students described Distributions B and C as left-skewed, which is incorrect. Both of these distributions are right-skewed. The direction (left or right) refers to where the tail is, not where the hump is.

title: 106  Fall 2025 Quiz 1
text:
106.6 Problem 6
(1 point) Identify the correct ordering of the expected values of the distributions in Figure 106.1, from smallest to largest.

A, B, C
A, C, B
B, A, C
B, C, A
C, A, B
C, B, A







TipSolution





A, B, C
Distribution A is symmetric around zero, so its expected value is zero (assuming the expected value exists). Distributions B and C both have positive supports, so they must have positive expected values. Because Distribution B has most of its mass close to zero and Distribution C has most of its mass greater than zero, the expected value of Distribution B should be less than the expected value of Distribution C.

text:

A
B
C
None of the above







TipSolution





D
Nobody has a height less than zero and no one is more than four meters tall.

107.1.1 Part (a)

TipSolution





The expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point) cholesterol (1 point) for a Bostonian whose commute is zero minutes long (1 point). No points lost if you don’t mention that we’re talking about Bostonians specifically.





107.1.2 Part (b)
(6 points) Assuming the necessary assumptions are met, what does the value 6.998 represent in real-world terms? In other words, intepret the slope for this study.

The expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point) change (or increase; 1 point) in cholesterol (1 point) associated with a one-minute (1 point) increase (or change; 1 point) in commute duration (1 point). No points lost if you used a causal interpretation; that’s not our focus right now.
Alternatively, the expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point) difference (1 point) in total cholesterol (1 point) between two populations of Bostonians that differ (1 point) by one minute (1 point) in the duration of their daily commute (1 point).





107.1.3 Part (c)

No (1 point). The p-value associated with commute is \(0.167 > 0.05\) (1 point), so we fail to reject the null hypothesis that the slope is zero.

title: 108  Fall 2025 Quiz 3
text:
108.1 Problem 1
Suppose I recruit a sample of \(n\) teachers to study the effect of hydration and sleep on voice quality. Define the following variables:
Suppose I fit the following model: \[
H_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 S_i + \beta_2 W_i + \epsilon_i \text{.}

title: 108  Fall 2025 Quiz 3
text:
\(H_i\) is the harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR) of the \(i\)th participant’s voice. This is a measure of voice quality and is measured in decibels.
\(S_i = 1\) if participant \(i\) slept well the night before they were assessed and \(S_i = 0\) if they slept poorly.
\(W_i\) is the number of liters of water the \(i\)th participant drank in the previous 24 hours.



108.1.1 Part (a)
(4 points) What does \(\beta_0\) mean in real-world terms?






TipSolution





The expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point) HNR (1 point) for a teacher who slept poorly the night before (1 point) and drank no water (1 point) in the past 24 hours.





108.1.2 Part (b)
What does \(\beta_1\) mean in real-world terms?






TipSolution





The expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point) difference (1 point) in HNR (1 point) between those who slept well (1 point) and those who slept poorly (1 point), holding water consumption constant (or “all else constant”; 1 point).





108.1.3 Part (c)
What does \(\beta_2\) mean in real-world terms?

title: 109  Fall 2025 Quiz 4
text:
\(H_i\) is the harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR) of the \(i\)th participant’s voice. This is a measure of voice quality and is measured in decibels.
\(S_i = 1\) if participant \(i\) slept well the night before they were assessed and \(S_i = 0\) if they slept poorly.

109.1.1 Part (a)

109.1.2 Part (b)
(7 points) Compute \(E(H_i|S_i = 1,W_i = w) - E(H_i|S_i = 0,W_i = w)\) and interpret its meaning in real-world terms.






TipSolution





\[
\begin{align*}
    &E(H_i|S_i = 1,W_i = w) - E(H_i|S_i = 0,W_i = w) \\

    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1  + \beta_2 w + \beta_3  w - \left(\beta_0  + \beta_2 w \right) \\
    &= \beta_1 + \beta_3 w \text{ (1 point)}
\end{align*}
\]

    &= \beta_0  + \beta_2 w + \beta_2   - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_2 w  \right) \\
    &= \beta_2 \text{ (1 point)}
\end{align*}

\end{align*}
\]

Model 2: \(E(Y_i|A_i,B_i,C_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 A_i + \beta_2 B_i + \beta_3 C_i\); and
Model 3: \(E(Y_i|A_i,B_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 A_i + \beta_2 B_i\).



113.1.1 Part (a)
(4 points) Suppose \(D_3\) is missing in the data set, i.e., the third participant is missing a value for the fourth explanatory variable. There is no other missing data in the data set. Which of the following metrics could you use to compare Model 1 and Model 2? Select all that apply.

\(R^2\)
\(R_\text{adj}^2\)
Likelihood
AIC







TipSolution





i and ii
Since these two models are fit on different observations, you can’t use likelihood-based methods to compare them. Model 2 is fit on all \(n\) observations and Model 1 is fit on \(n - 1\) observations, i.e., all the observations except the third.
This doesn’t matter for \(R^2\) because it’s a ratio. The contribution of the third observation is removed from both the numerator and denominator of the \(R^2\) for Model 1. This also doesn’t matter for \(R^2_\text{adj}\) for similar reasons.
For a more thorough explanation: the key here is that Model 1 and Model 2 were fit using different datasets (Model 1 using \(n - 1\) participants, Model 2 using all \(n\) participants). Therefore, the likelihood of Model 2 is based on the distribution of the all of the observations, while the likelihood of Model 1 is based on the distribution of a subset of those observations. As a result, the two models aren’t properly comparable using likelihood-based metrics, since those essentially rely on checking which model has a higher likelihood \(\mathcal{L}\) based on the same distribution of observations.





113.1.2 Part (b)
(4 points) Suppose \(D_3\) is missing in the data set, i.e., the third participant is missing a value for the fourth explanatory variable. There is no other missing data in the data set. Which of the following metrics could you use to compare Model 2 and Model 3? Select all that apply.

\(R^2\)
\(R_\text{adj}^2\)
Likelihood
AIC







TipSolution





i, ii, iii, and iv
Since Models 2 and 3 don’t use the fourth explanatory variable, it doesn’t matter if one of the observations is missing the fourth explanatory variable. Both Models 2 and 3 can be fit on all \(n\) observations.





113.1.3 Part (c)
(4 points) Suppose \(A_3\) is missing in the data set, i.e., the third participant is missing a value for the first explanatory variable. There is no other missing data in the data set. Which of the following metrics could you use to compare Model 2 and Model 3? Select all that apply.

\(R^2\)
\(R_\text{adj}^2\)
Likelihood
AIC







TipSolution





i, ii, iii, and iv
Since both Models 2 and 3 use the first explanatory variable, the third observation couldn’t be used to fit either of them. So, Models 2 and 3 will be fit on the same \(n - 1\) observations.





113.1.4 Part (d)
(4 points) Suppose you use a likelihood ratio test to compare Model 1 to Model 3. You obtain a p-value of 0.00001. What is a reasonable conclusion from this result? Select all that apply.

Model 3 is at least as good as Model 1.
Model 3 fits the data better than Model 1.
Model 2 is at least as good as Model 3.
Model 1 fits the data better than Model 3.







TipSolution





iv
The null hypothesis is that the smaller model is the true model. With such a low p-value, we would reject this hypothesis and conclude that the larger model, Model 1, fits the data better than the smaller model, Model 3.

116.1 Problem 1

title: 116  Fall 2025 Quiz 11
text:
116.1.1 Part (a)
The hazard ratio at time \(t\) comparing postmenopausal to premenopausal patients, among patients who have no positive lymph nodes.






TipSolution





1.082660
\[
\begin{align*}
    \frac{\lambda_j(t)}{\lambda_i(t)} &= \frac{\lambda_0(t) \exp\left(0.079421 \texttt{meno}_j + 0.060853 \texttt{nodes}_j - 0.003607 \texttt{meno}_j\times\texttt{nodes}_j\right)}{\lambda_0(t) \exp\left(0.079421 \texttt{meno}_i + 0.060853 \texttt{nodes}_i - 0.003607 \texttt{meno}_i\times\texttt{nodes}_i\right)} \\
    &= \frac{ \exp\left(0.079421 (1) + 0.060853 (0) - 0.003607 (1)\times(0)\right)}{ \exp\left(0.079421 (0) + 0.060853 (0) - 0.003607 (0)\times(0)\right)} \\
    &= \exp\left(0.079421 \right) \\
    &= 1.082660
\end{align*}
\] You might have thought to yourself, “These patients have ‘node-positive’ breast cancer, and the minimum number of positive lymph nodes is 1. How can we estimate a hazard ratio among patients who have no positive lymph nodes?” The interpretation of the coefficient is the same, even though there aren’t any observed patients with no positive lymph nodes. We are extrapolating beyond our observed data, which is never a good idea. But, that’s how you interpret this coefficient.





116.1.2 Part (b)
The hazard rate at time \(t\) for a postmenopausal patient with one positive lymph node.






TipSolution





Impossible.
Cox regression returns hazard ratios, not hazard rates.
A couple people wrote \(h_0(t) \exp(0.079421 + 0.060853 - 0.003607)\) in response to this question. If you would admit this as a correct answer, you should admit any function of \(t\). If a student wrote, for example, \(h_0(t) \exp(5)\), they could argue that \[
h_0(t) = g_0(t) \exp(0.079421 + 0.060853 - 0.003607 - 5) \text{,}
\] so that \[
\begin{align*}
    h_0(t) \exp(5) &=  g_0(t) \exp(0.079421 + 0.060853 - 0.003607 - 5) \exp(5) \\
    &=  g_0(t) \exp(0.079421 + 0.060853 - 0.003607) \text{.}
\end{align*}
\] The point here is that Cox regression does not estimate hazard rates.





116.1.3 Part (c)
The hazard ratio at time \(t\) comparing patients with one positive lymph node to patients with zero positive lymph nodes, among patients who are premenopausal.






TipSolution





1.062743
\[
\begin{align*}
    \frac{\lambda_j(t)}{\lambda_i(t)} &= \frac{\lambda_0(t) \exp\left(0.079421 \texttt{meno}_j + 0.060853 \texttt{nodes}_j - 0.003607 \texttt{meno}_j\times\texttt{nodes}_j\right)}{\lambda_0(t) \exp\left(0.079421 \texttt{meno}_i + 0.060853 \texttt{nodes}_i - 0.003607 \texttt{meno}_i\times\texttt{nodes}_i\right)} \\
    &= \frac{ \exp\left(0.079421 (0) + 0.060853 (1) - 0.003607 (0)\times(1)\right)}{ \exp\left(0.079421 (0) + 0.060853 (0) - 0.003607 (0)\times(0)\right)} \\
    &= \exp\left(0.060853 \right) \\
    &= 1.062743
\end{align*}
\]

The hazard ratio comparing postmenopausal patients at one year to premenopausal patients at two years, among patients who have no positive lymph nodes.






TipSolution





Impossible.
Cox regression gives hazard ratios for a specific time \(t\). So, we could compare these groups at one year or we can compare them at two years; we can’t compare one at one year to the other at two years.





116.1.5 Part (e)
The hazard ratio at time \(t\) comparing postmenopausal to premenopausal patients, among patients who have fifty positive lymph nodes.






TipSolution





\(\exp\left(0.079421   - 0.003607 (50)\right)\)
\[
\begin{align*}
    \frac{\lambda_j(t)}{\lambda_i(t)} &= \frac{\lambda_0(t) \exp\left(0.079421 \texttt{meno}_j + 0.060853 \texttt{nodes}_j - 0.003607 \texttt{meno}_j\times\texttt{nodes}_j\right)}{\lambda_0(t) \exp\left(0.079421 \texttt{meno}_i + 0.060853 \texttt{nodes}_i - 0.003607 \texttt{meno}_i\times\texttt{nodes}_i\right)} \\
    &= \frac{\exp\left(0.079421 (1) + 0.060853 (50) - 0.003607 (1)\times(50)\right)}{\exp\left(0.079421 (0) + 0.060853 (50) - 0.003607 (0)\times(50)\right)} \\
    &= \exp\left(0.079421   - 0.003607 (50)\right) \\
\end{align*}
\]





116.1.6 Part (f)

TipSolution





Impossible.
If we wanted to estimate this, we would’ve had to create a new categorical variable containing membership in these groups.





116.1.7 Part (g)

TipSolution





0.592
This is the interpretation of the p-value.





116.1.8 Part (h)

387
The output tells us that the sample size was 686 and there were 299 events, so \(686-299=387\) patients were censored.





116.1.9 Part (i)
The median survival among premenopausal patients with one positive lymph node.






TipSolution

If we had the hazard function, \(h(t)\), we could find this value. Since we only have hazard ratios, we can’t compute survival probabilities.





116.1.10 Part (j)

TipSolution





Impossible.
In frequentist statistics, parameters are fixed, not random, so we don’t compute probabilities like this.

title: 116  Fall 2025 Quiz 11
text:
116.2 Problem 2
(2 points) Please provide a reasonable method to check the proportional hazards assumption in this analysis and what results from that method would indicate that the assumption is met.






TipSolution





You could conduct a Schoenfeld residual test. High p-values would indicate that the assumption is met, and low p-values would indicate that the assumption is not met. Another way of saying this is that a non-significant result on the Schoenfeld residual test would indicate that the assumption is met and a non-significant result on the test would indicate that the assumption is not met. It’s not enough to just say ``check p-values’’. You need to say what results from that method would indicate that the assumption is met.
A complementary log-log-plot would not be reasonable for this analysis because there are so many levels of the nodes variable. However, you can still get a point for saying that parallel lines on the plot would indicate that the assumption is met.
Looking at Kaplan-Meier curves would not be reasonable for this analysis since nodes is effectively a continuous variable. Even if there were no continuous variables, though, you couldn’t check the PH assumptions using a Kaplan-Meier curve. The PH assumption implies that \(S_1(t) = S_2(t)^c\). How would you check this visually?

title: 116  Fall 2025 Quiz 11
text:
116.3 Problem 3
(2 points) Do you think there is effect modification? Justify your answer.






TipSolution





No, because the p-value for the interaction term is very high.
You may have thought that, even if the p-value is high, there might be clinically meaningful effect modification. Let’s consider an extreme case. Consider part (e): “The hazard ratio at time \(t\) comparing postmenopausal to premenopausal patients, among patients who have fifty positive lymph nodes.” This is \(\exp\left(0.079421   - 0.003607 (50)\right) = 0.9039972\). The hazard ratio at time \(t\) comparing postmenopausal to premenopausal patients, among patients who have zero positive lymph nodes, is \(\exp\left(0.079421 \right) = 1.08266\). That’s just not a huge difference in the effect of menopause for two wildly different numbers of positive nodes.

The proportional odds model, which assumes that for each \(m\in\{0,1,2,\dotsc,M-1\}\), \[
\log \left(\frac{P\left(Y_i \le m \middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}{P\left(Y_i > m \middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}\right) = \beta_{0m} + \beta_{1} X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_{p} X_{ip} \text{.}
\]
The adjacent categories model, which assumes that for each \(m\in\{1,2,\dotsc,M\}\), \[
\log \left(\frac{P\left(Y_i = m\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}{P\left(Y_i = m - 1\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}\right) = \beta_{0m} + \beta_{1m} X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_{pm} X_{ip} \text{.}
\]
The restricted adjacent categories model, which assumes that for each \(m\in\{1,2,\dotsc,M\}\), \[
\log \left(\frac{P\left(Y_i = m\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}{P\left(Y_i = m - 1\middle|X_{i1},\dotsc,X_{ip}\right)}\right) = \beta_{0m} + \beta_{1} X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_{p} X_{ip} \text{.}
\]

title: 118  Fall 2025 Quiz 13
text:
118.2 Problem 2
For each of the following examples, identify the best analysis method from the options provided. Each is worth one point.

118.2.1 Part (a)
You want to know whether using mechanical lifts decreases the incidence of musculoskeletal injuries among nurses in hospitals. You randomly assign some hospitals to receive mechanical lifts; those that don’t receive the lifts serve as controls. You measure a variety of variables for each hospital, including the number of nurses employed, how many hours they work, how many patients are treated, what they are treated for, etc. Your primary outcome measure is the number of new musculoskeletal injuries in the six months following installation of the lifts.

Cox regression
Logistic regression
Multinomial regression (baseline category logit model)
Poisson regression







TipSolution





iv
The outcome is a count, so Poisson regression is the best bet.





118.2.2 Part (b)
You want to know the impact of journaling on mental health. You recruit undergraduates at your university and randomly assign them to one of three categories: no journaling; journaling about what happened to them each week; or journaling about what they’re grateful for each week. At the beginning and end of the study, you have participants fill out the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), a 21-item pencil-and-paper questionnaire that results in a score between 0 and 63, with higher values representing worse depression. You also measure other variables, including gender, age, time spent socializing, and other coping mechanisms.

Multinomial regression (baseline category logit model)
Linear regression
Logistic regression
Cox regression







TipSolution





ii
The outcome is not strictly continuous, but it’s nearly continuous. Also, it’s definitely not categorical, binary, or a time to event.





118.2.3 Part (c)
You are testing the efficacy of a variety of smoking cessation methods. You recruit a large sample of people who are trying to quit smoking. You measure several variables, including sex, age, age at first cigarette, etc. You ask each participant when they last smoked, and your outcome is the time until their next cigarette.

Logistic regression
Multinomial regression (proportional odds model)
Cox regression
Multinomial regression (adjacent categories model)







TipSolution





iii
The outcome is time to an event, so Cox is the best option among those provided.

title: 119  Fall 2025 Quiz 14
text:
119.2 Problem 2
Please identify each of the following statements as true or false. Each problem is worth one point.

119.2.1 Part (a)
Cox regression estimates hazard rates.






TipSolution





False.
Cox regression estimates hazard ratios.





119.2.2 Part (b)
The raw estimates of coefficients in logistic regression represent odds ratios, and therefore cannot be negative.






TipSolution





False.
The raw estimate of the intercept is a log odds and the raw estimate of a slope is a log odds ratio. Both of these can be negative.





119.2.3 Part (c)
I’ve developed a new blood test for a previously difficult-to-identify cancer. The test has high sensitivity. This means that if someone has the cancer, they have a high probability of testing positive.






TipSolution





True.





119.2.4 Part (d)
I’ve developed a new blood test for a previously difficult-to-identify cancer. The test has high specificity. This means that if someone tests negative, they have a low probability of having the cancer.






TipSolution





False.
High specificity means that if someone does not have the cancer, they have a high probability of testing negative.





119.2.5 Part (e)
We can only compute \(R^2\) for normally-distributed data.






TipSolution





False.





119.2.6 Part (f)
Suppose you have a normally-distributed vulnerability index (\(V_i\)) that you hypothesize has a different mean depending on race (\(R_i\)). It doesn’t make sense to write the linear model equation as \(E(V_i|R_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 R_i\) because \(R_i\) is a categorical variable, not a numeric variable.






TipSolution





True.
We would have to turn race into dummy variables in order to write down a linear model that makes sense.
